As the ashen remains of the milk tooth and paper fell to the carpet, she felt marginally stronger, if a little dizzy and uncomfortable, her shirt chafing against her crawling skin.

 

            Washing her hands in the basin, Lena poured herself some water from the pitcher on the nightstand and listened to the muffled shouts outside. Nursing the tin cup, she drifted towards the yellowed windowpane and cracked open the window as she craned her head outside.  Visible in the middle of the main thoroughfare was the Sheriff and Mayor, six feet separating them as they yelled back and forth beneath the searing sun. Alex had doffed her hat and held its creased crown in hand as she pointed accusingly.

 

            “She can’t stay here, Kelly. We’ve got that businessman who bought the mine coming tomorrow! What’s he going to think about a necromancer taking up residence in the same hotel as him, huh?”

 

            “ Oh, you’re just superstitious, darlin’. Besides, I was thinking that maybe she’d be able to help with the mine anyways, maybe bring some of them back for us. Some loved ones, like your Kara’s husband.”

 

            With a scathing sound of contempt, Alex pointed at her with a finger. “He was a good for nothing scoundrel; I wouldn’t let some witch use black magic to bring him back! And if you’d let her go near anyone … you’re a damn fool, Kelly Olsen.”

 

            Alex forcefully tossed her hat into the dust at her feet and turned around, stalking off. Lena heard a quiet chuckle behind her and whirled around, hand straying towards her gun before her eyebrows rose in surprise.

 

            “Enjoying the show?”

 

            “Your sister, I presume?” Lena said with a wry smile.

 

            Sighing heavily, Kara stepped into the small room and shook her head with exasperated amusement. “She’s always been a little … hotheaded. It’s not a week gone by in this hole of a town without her causing a public spectacle. She don’t mean nothing by it, I assure you.”

 

            “No,” Lena slowly replied, “she means plenty. No need to downplay it for my benefit, ma’am. I’m used to this. At the very least, they gave me that bed you were saying they wouldn’t so …”

 

            Shifting uneasily on the threshold of the door, Kara cleared her throat, twisting the brim of her own hat in her hands. Nodding at Lena’s stomach, she raised her eyebrows, a mild look of concern in her eyes.

 

            “How’s your wound looking?”

 

            Tugging up her shirt, Lena looked down at the unmarred alabaster skin and touched her fingers to it. “Like brand new.”

 

            Looking up, she watched as Kara’s sun tanned skin paled, her uneasiness written in the tense lines of her body as her blue eyes widened with fear.

 

            “I don’t bite,” Lena said with a rakish smile.

 

            Kara let out a strained laugh despite herself, lips twisting ruefully. “Look, Miss, I ain’t got no quarrel with you … we just ain’t about the likes of that funny business 'round here. I mean no offence.”

 

            “Why’re you here then?” Lena curtly asked.

 

            “I had to come into town and caught the end of what happened off Nia; thought I’d come up here and see how you was doing.”

 

            “Well, I appreciate your concern and all, but you don’t need to fret about a stranger. Especially not one so vile as a creature like me.”

 

            “I don’t think you’re vile at all, I just- we’re honest, god-fearing people around here and … death and murder and sacrilege … it don’t go over too well.”

 

            “I am a murderer, yes,” Lena said as she roughly tucked her shirt back in, eyes shining bright with smouldering anger. “But very rarely of the truly living. I imagine your sister has killed more people than I have, being Sheriff and all.”

 

            “Oh, I- well-“

 

            With a quiet derisive snort, Lena gestured to the door, “if you’ll excuse me, ma’am.”

 

            She walked forward towards Kara, who instinctively backed up until she’d stepped over the threshold of the room. Grabbing the splintering edges of the door, Lena slammed it shut in her face, locked it and then kicked off her boots.

 

            With a rough sigh, she shut the window and drew the gauzy curtain against the bright sunlight and then collapsed on the bed. The mattress was lumpy and the sheets itchy, the lingering smell of sweat embedded in it as Lena tried to get comfortable. The room was close and hot with the window closed and she was restless as she tried to get comfortable. Noon was upon her when she finally drifted off to sleep, her fingers curled around the grip of her pistol as she breathed slowly, cheeks flushed.

 

            A loud banging roused Lena hours later and she jerked awake, finger pulling back the hammer as she looked around with wide eyes. The door shuddered with another knock and she raked a hand through her dusty hair, sweat beading her forehead and dampening her clothes as she hunched forward, groggy with sleep.

 

            “Miss? Are you eating supper? We got fresh chicken and biscuits.”

 

            It was the young girl again, Nia, and Lena sighed as she braced her hands on her knees and climbed to her feet. Unlocking the door, Lena fixed her with a blank stare, watching as she recoiled slightly but stood her ground, eyes straying down to the Colt in Lena’s hand.

 

            “J’onn’s wife makes a damn mean apple pie as well.”

 

            “I’ll take it in my room.”

 

            “Oh, um, alright then, Miss, I’ll bring it up as quick as it please you.”

 

            Nodding, Lena shut the door and rubbed at her tired eyes. Setting her pistol down on the rumpled bedsheets, Lena drank a cup of sulphurous water and then stripped off her shirt. It was torn and bloody from being shot through and through but she doubted anyone around would be willing to sell her a new one, which left her to don her spare and try her best to wring out days of blood, sweat and dust in the washbasin.

 

            Feeling a little more refreshed, she lit the oil lamp, the kerosene catching quickly and casting a yellow glow over the sparse furnishings. Parting the curtains, Lena opened the windows to the evening air and breathed in the smell of dust and lingering heat, even as the surrounding plains cooled. The sun was starting to set, a faint purplish tint to the sky as the whole world dimmed and Lena closed her eyes as she braced herself against the rotting windowsill.

 

            A knock on her door stirred her and she moved to open it, finding Nia standing there with a laden tray. Stepping into the room, she placed it on the bed and nodded curtly at Lena before making herself scarce.

 

            Sinking onto the lumpy mattress, Lena sighed and dug into the food. It was the best thing she had eaten in months, better even than Kara’s stew, and she sipped a cup of beer in between mouthfuls of green beans and corn, grateful for the sweetness of fresh vegetables. She left the slice of pie for last, eating it slowly as the sugar melted on her tongue and the tartness of the apples made her eyes close as she savoured it.

 

            Once she was finished, feeling so full that she could barely move, Lena set the empty tray outside her door and then locked up, settling back down on the bed with her pistol held tightly beneath her pillow. Night fell slowly outside, the sky deepening as shadows lengthened and the room cooled with the breeze gusting in. Lena slept soundly, so exhausted that the raucous sound of music, laughter and shouting below didn’t disturb her at all.

 

            Rising with the dawn, Lena roused herself and splashed water on her face before donning her coat and buckling on her belt. Heeled boots on, Lena grabbed her hat and wiped off a layer of dust and unlocked the door, pocketing the little key after locking it behind her.

 

            It was early enough that a few groggy fur trappers and soldiers were snoring at tables, not turned out yet, and her heels thudded on the stairs as she made her way down. A woman was behind the bar, shining up glasses in the dim light of the oil chandeliers suspended throughout the hotel’s saloon. She slowed at the sight of Lena, her dark eyes watchful and openly scrutinising and Lena gave her a curt nod as she made for the open doors.

 

            The sky was a pale pink, the town lazy and full of its ever-present dust as it billowed in the morning breeze. On the deck of the long boardwalk, Lena breathed in the stench of silver rising from the chimneys, the caustic lyes from a nearby tannery and the congealed blood from a slaughterhouse. It was the same as any other town in the nowhere west, manure trampled and piled near troughs of water and a woman sweeping the dirt outside a law firm.

 

            Eyeing the doors of a grey-bricked building that named itself the local bank, Lena donned her hat and quickly strode across the street. Roads drifted off from the main thoroughfare, wood and brick houses of varying wealth and appearance mingling with the meeting hall and billiards hall, brothels and more saloons and gambling dens, the telegraph office, sheriff’s office and jail, the fresh wood-shaving smell of the carpenters. Laundry flapped in the quiet air and Lena watched as an old woman knitted from a rocking chair in the shade of her verandah.

 

            The bank was still as she pushed open the door and stepped into the cool interior. The floor was wood, much like most of the town, polished and scarred and matching the deep richness of the wall panelling. Clearing her throat, Lena hedged further inside.

 

            “Morning.”

 

            She listened to the sound of rustling paper and a chair scraping against the floor before a wooden door was opening behind the counter. A small man with dark hair falling to his starched white collar stepped out, his skin brown and a small pair of spectacles on his nose. At the sight of her, a troubled look clouded his face and he adjusted his navy cravat.

 

            “Good day, Miss. Can I assist you?”

 

            “I’ve got a note here to withdraw some money,” Lena said, holding out a folded piece of paper.

 

            Hesitating, his mouth flattened to a grim line and he sighed, holding his hand out and gesturing her forward. Feeling the tension inside her dissipate slightly at his easy cooperation, she crossed the room and handed it to him. He hummed as he eyed the note and the details.

 

            Waiting patiently, Lena eyed the room with its wide windows and smell of paper and the ammonium of ink, the quiet removal from the sunny plains and demands of the job. What it would’ve been like to put her mind to books and numbers instead of calling in debts with the dead and wounded.

 

            “This all seems to be in order, ma’am. I’ll be right back in a tick, don’t you go nowhere.”

 

            Nodding at him, Lena eyed him as he grabbed a pair of keys and unlocked an iron door before locking it behind himself. Waiting ten minutes for him to come back from the secured vault, Lena paced the room, eyeing the framed paintings and photographs, some detailing the town’s creation.

 

            She wrapped things up quickly once he was back, pocketing her coins in her purse and thanking him once he’d finished making a record in the thick ledger. Stepping out into the blustery warmth of the morning, Lena made her way through the town, looking for another general store that would serve her. Passing by the firehouse and butchers, the bakers with the heady smell of freshly baking bread and pens of livestock as chickens pecked at sparsely grassed earth and grain.

 

            Past the saddlers and blacksmith, she made a right and passed a few houses and a flour mill and found a store nestled beside a schoolhouse where children were already flocking to. Mounting the steps to the front door, Lena ducked inside.

 

            A stern-faced woman manned the counter and although Lena could see the hatred for her in her face, the flash of coins was enough for the woman to comply. Albeit, not in a friendly manner, dumping beans and coffee and oats on the counter with a firm message that Lena wasn’t welcome there.

 

            After being shorted her change, Lena bit back a curse and pocketed the rest before taking her wares and storming out. Arms laden, she wandered back through the town, cutting down another street as she passed behind more stores opening up for the day. Folks milled about, smoking and chatting in the shade as horses stood hitched outside houses, business being discussed or goods traded. Lena hurried along, not wanting to put to the test whether the hateful stares sent her way would progress to anything more.

 

            Rounding a corner, she made a right at the intersection and found herself back on the main street, just beside the telegraph office. Kicking up dust as she walked, Lena slowed as a carriage drawn by six bay stallions careened down the street, hooves thundering and whip cracking as they hauled their load. Standing on the porch of the hotel was the Mayor, Sheriff and hotelier, and Kara Danvers standing back in the shade with Nia and M’gann.

 

            As Lena slowed, her eyes shaded by the brim on her hat, the carriage came to a stop outside the hotel, gouging furrows in the mud, a haze of dust shrouding it as the horses snorted and stomped. The door opened as Kelly walked down the steps. They all watched as a dark-haired woman stepped out, layers of lace and wool gathered in her hand as she smiled up at the hotel. Her hair was curled and a hat was pinned on top, the cinched corset of her dress and the sharpness of her jawline giving her a distinctly wealthy bearing as her heeled boots ground into the mud. The white lace of the undershirt was a stark contrast to her light brown skin and everyone was silent for a moment as her blue eyes creased at the corners, taking everything in.

 

            “Well, isn’t this a welcome greeting? Now, which one of you would be the Mayor?”

 

            “Kelly Olsen, ma’am,” Kelly said, holding out a hand as she descended another step. “And who might you be?”

 

            “Andrea Rojas. You were expecting my father, I believe; he recently bought your mine.”

 

            Surprise and understanding crossed Kelly’s face as Andrea shook her hand. “Your father is Mister Rojas?”

 

            “He was, ma’am. But by unfortunate circumstances, he won’t be arriving anytime soon, I’m afraid.”

 

            “And what … unfortunate circumstance would that be?”

 

            “He was murdered by some vicious outlaws; as the sole inheritor of Obsidian North and all its investments, I thought I’d come to see about this mine myself.”

 

            A man ducked out of the carriage a moment later, dressed in a long wool coat with a bowler hat. He had tight black curls beneath his hat and a trim beard, giving them a perfectly white smile as he nodded his head.

 

            “This is Mister Russell Rogers, from the British School of Mines. He’s here as my mining engineer.”

 

            “How do you do?” Russell greeted them, touching the brim of his hat.

 

            Sharing uneasy glances with Alex and J’onn, Kelly cleared her throat and smiled. “We’re honoured, Miss Rojas, Mister Rogers. This here is our Sheriff, Alex Danvers, and our hotelier Mister J’onn J’onzz. Shall we go inside?”

 

            Lena took the moment of introduction as her window to slip inside unnoticed, casting wary glances at the mining heiress’ security as they loitered on horses behind the wagon. Making for the steps, she was about to slip past J’onn when she drew the attention of Andrea Rojas, caught on the colour of her duster and the book hanging from her leaden belt.

 

            “Witch Doctor,” Andrea called out, bringing everyone to silence.

 

            Clearing her throat, Alex glanced sideways at Lena, venomous and tense. “She’s just passing through, ma’am. She’ll be on her way shortly; we don’t keep no resident necromancers here, I assure you that.”

 

            “I know you,” Andrea said, ignoring Alex as she stepped towards Lena with a look of recognition in her eyes and open interest on her face. “You’re the one that saved my daddy’s life four years ago. Aren’t you?”

 

            Hesitating, Lena looked at her properly, a frown puckering her brow as she pressed her lips together. Raking through her mind to where she’d been four years ago, Lena tried to place the young woman. They were about the same age, but she met many people on her travels.

 

            “Bernardo Rojas. In California.”

 

            It clicked in Lena’s head and she blinked in surprise. Back then, Andrea had barely been an adult, the spoilt daughter of the mining tycoon, one of the wealthiest Latin families in the country as her father reaped the benefits of the gold rush out west. She remembered her then, her face tear-stained as she begged, dressed in white, pretty and demanding.

 

            “I remember, ma’am,” Lena murmured, ducking her head in a nod. “I’m sorry to hear of his passing.”

 

            Touching the brim of her hat, Lena carried on up the steps and into the dim hotel. Taking the steps up to the mezzanine, she let herself into her room and quickly packed everything away. Making plans to leave tomorrow, Lena felt hunger gnaw at her stomach and left again to find some food. Elsewhere, at one of the dingier saloons, where the roof was sagging and the walls were bare, where they were as eager for her money as her blood. 

 

            Making sure her gun was loaded and her knife visible on the table, she holed herself up in such a place as she ate her way through fried eggs and grits and drank warm beer from the local brewery. No one troubled her and she played a few rounds of cards with a group of merchants and trappers before taking her winnings and leaving.

 

            Making her way back to the hotel, ignoring the looks of the locals as the Sheriff, Mayor and hotel staff all stood around the bar in muttered conversation, Lena made her way back upstairs and shed her layers. Fishing her book out of the bottom of her bedroll, she sprawled on the bed with the windows open and flipped through it, savouring the chance to rest up and relax before she found herself back on the road again.

 

            The morning bled into the afternoon and then onwards into the evening as Lena steadily read through her book. She was thinking of asking for dinner in her room when a knock disturbed her. Rolling off the bed and climbing to her feet, Lena kept her place in the book with a finger as she opened the door. M’gann stood outside, twisting a cloth in her hands as she fixed Lena with a piercing stare.

 

            “Ma’am, you’ve been asked to join Miss Rojas for dinner tonight. A private parlour has been made up for y’all to enjoy.”

 

            “Who’s all?”

 

            “Just the Sheriff and the Mayor and the other mining folk.”

 

            “I’ll kindly pass,” Lena curtly replied.

 

            As she made to shut the door, M’gann stopped her with a hand. “If you don’t mind me saying, you could probably use some friends 'round here, Miss. It ain’t gonna hurt no one to have a hot meal before you move on now, is it?”

 

            Begrudgingly, Lena nodded and was given a wan smile. “Make your way down once you’ve made yourself up; the other folk are already having a few drinks in the parlour.”

 

            Nodding, Lena shut the door then and briskly washed her face and hands before braiding her hair back neatly. Foregoing her jacket, she donned a waistcoat and a clean neckerchief, leaving her belt with the pistol and grimoire in her room out of courtesy for the hospitality rules of dining with company.

 

            Making her way downstairs slowly, Lena was apprehensive as she wound through the tables, until J’onn noticed her and jerked his chin towards double doors that were shut. M’gann set down two dishes at a table and met her at the doors before opening them for her.

 

            A table was set with a white tablecloth, a fire crackling in the grate and the warm glow of oil lamps making the place feel intimate as the dark crept in behind curtained windows. The walls were papered in pink and the room wasn’t quite as shabby as the rest of the hotel. Lena supposed it was one of the nicest rooms in the town, a place for the honoured and wealthy guests.

 

            Conversation stopped as she stepped into the doorway, feeling bare as all eyes trained on her. She wished for her wide-brimmed hat and the heavy weight of her coat, the feel of her pistol in hand and blood on her fingertips. Instead, her power eluded her for the moment and she felt vulnerable.

 

            “Here, Miss,” M’gann said, gesturing Lena towards an empty seat set for her before clicking her fingers at Nia, who carried a decanter of whiskey over and poured some into a crystal glass.

 

            Settling herself into her seat at the head of the table, Lena looked sullen as she shook out her napkin and set it gracefully in her lap, looking up to meet Andrea’s gaze. To her left was Kara and Lena looked sideways at her before taking in the rest of the party. Alex, Kelly, the lithe banker, Russell Rogers and a tanned man with a smug air about him as he smoked a cigarette and nursed a glass.

 

            “Ma’am,” Lena murmured to Andrea.

 

            “What did you say your name was again?”

 

            “I didn’t.”

 

            The table was quiet as they waited for Lena’s forthcoming answer, but it never came. She was ramrod straight in her seat, reaching out stiffly for her glass and taking a small sip as she levelled her cool gaze at Andrea. She could see Kara’s mild surprise beside her but the rancher was mercifully silent, perhaps aware of the scrutiny she’d bring on herself for admitting to being acquainted with Lena.

 

            “Well … alright then. I’m sure you’re acquainted with most of the fine folk in Midvale-“

 

            “I’m afraid not,” Lena murmured. “I’m not here on business, ma’am. Just passing through, as the good Sheriff said.”

 

            Pausing again, Andrea looked irritated as she raised her glass and took a sip, taking the measure of Lena over the crystal.

 

            “You’re not here to help with the mining situation?”

 

            “I’m not all that familiar with what happened, to be frank.”

 

            “Mine collapsed a couple of months ago. Took most of the men in this town with it. Those that didn’t get crushed went up in flames when all the coal dust in that shaft lit on fire by one of the oil lamps.”

 

            Lena barely glanced at the man who spoke and Kelly cleared her throat. “That’s Mister William Dey, chief editor of The Midvale Review. Prints to the local towns too. This here’s Querl Dox, banker and finance manager.”

 

            “Ma’am,” William and Querl nodded in turn, returned silently by Lena.

 

            Dinner started being served then, starting with a chicken soup with fresh biscuits. Lena was silent as she spooned it into her mouth and sipped the whiskey in between, letting the conversation wash over her as it lingered on talk of the mine.

 

            From what she could gather, Obsidian North had bought sole ownership with the intention of making a pretty profit from reopening it, with enough men to work it once it’d been cleared out from the accident. The Mayor and other residents were looking for a cut of those profits by staking their own fortune in it. Silently letting the talk of business go on, Lena started on the second course placed before her, the thick ham and collard greens and potatoes vanishing all too fast on her plate.

 

            Once she was finished, waiting for everyone to catch up as they smoked and talked and drank in between mouthfuls, she caught Andrea’s attention again.

 

            “Where did you grow up, Doctor?”

 

            “Back East. At my family’s ancestral home just north of New York.”

 

            “Old money,” Andrea guessed.

 

            Inclining her head, Lena shifted uncomfortably. “My ancestor was one of the first Witch Doctors in the colonies. It’s been a family trade ever since.”

 

            “Fascinating,” Andrea murmured. “And is it true they teach you how to summon demons at those schools?”

 

            Stiffening, Lena’s mouth twitched. “No, ma’am. Those are just ghost stories.”

 

            “Hm.”

 

            The attention turned from her after that and Lena was left to eat the pie brought out after in peace. It was mulberry and gooseberry and sweet with sugar and Lena ate hers with another glass of whiskey to wash the pastry down. She was offered a cigarette by Russell on her right, smoking in companionable silence with the Englishman as the talk of business and Midvale’s longevity as a prosperous town took hold of everyone.

 

            In the warmth of the fire, with a haze of cigarette smoke and the cloying smell of fat from the food and oil in the lamps, Lena grew restless. She’d never been good with company, least of all dining with them, and wished she was out in the raucous saloon, gambling away her stipend and drinking moonshine as she swindled soldiers. Still, the food was good and the whiskey better than she would’ve ordered for herself, and it wasn’t long before Andrea wanted to retire, giving her her escape.

 

            “And when will you be off, Doctor?” Alex asked as Lena rose from her chair.

 

            “I’ll be off with the sunrise, Sheriff.”

 

            “Where’re you headed?”

 

            “North, for the present, but it’s a wandering path. I go where I’m needed.”

 

            “Is there much need for your kind?” Alex challenged with a haughty tilt of her chin.

 

            With a rueful smile, Lena jerked her head to Andrea. “Those who’ve lost someone might tell you there is. I pray you never need to find out just how valuable my craft is yourself. Good evening.”

 

            Ducking her head, Lena slowly walked from the room and plodded wearily upstairs. Kicking off her boots and untying the neckerchief, she drank some water and climbed into bed, finding herself eager to leave Midvale, come morning.

 

            She woke with the early streaks of sunlight, the sky a middling blue as the trees and shrubs of the plains gave the view from her window a smudged look. As promised, she rose early, carrying her packs downstairs as M’gann was starting to kick out late-night revellers. Lena slid money onto the counter to pay for her two nights, murmuring her thanks as she asked for Hecate to be brought around.

 

            The woman bid her to sit down for breakfast and Lena obliged on account of it being her last good meal for a while. Eating bacon and a thick porridge with strong coffee, she was soon outside, buckling her tack and saddlebags and medicinal supplies onto the back of her horse and swinging up into the saddle.

 

            Well rested, Hecate tossed her head and stamped at the muddy ground in anticipation of being able to stretch her legs after two days in a stable. Tugging her hat down low over her face and turning up the collar of her coat, Lena set her heels to her horse’s flank and was soon trotting down the road. Before making her way out of the shallow valley Midvale was nestled in, the warren of mines rising before her as the cliffs reached up, Lena caught sight of a trio of women standing on the shaded porch of the Sheriff’s office.

 

            As she looked at them, Alex and Kelly turned and made their way inside, but Kara lingered on the porch, a hand shading her eyes as she gripped a rifle by its muzzle with the other hand. Lena met her stare with her own, confused, and frowned slightly as Kara raised her hand in farewell. Urging Hecate onwards, Lena rode out of town with Kara’s stare burning into her back and raised her hand towards her throat, swallowing as she rubbed the healed skin of her gunshot wound.

3. Chapter 3

            Travelling east, Lena scarcely stopped out of fear of being caught unawares by another Necromancer, dozing in the saddle as she swayed with Hecate’s steps, reversing the sun’s path and navigating by the stars once night arrived. Her neck prickled with the feeling that something was wrong , that unsettling sensation that she was being hunted unshakable, even though all of her attempts at divining any foreboding events through drops of her blood failed to reveal anything to her.

 

            Pale and thin, dark circles ringing her eyes and dust dried in tracks on her skin, Lena narrowed her eyes against the harsh sunlight and pulled the wide brim of her hat down lower as she hunched her shoulders and moved on. The only time she stopped was to give Hecate a break, watering the horse and letting her forage through the grass and weeds at riverbanks, crunching rotting apples and rolling in the dust as flies made her irate. Lena would doze in the shade after summoning something to protect her, letting her blood soak the ground and ward the earth while the skeleton of an unfortunate fur trapper or prospector, or even a black bear or mountain lion, lurching about in a daze, made to stand guard for her. Her grimoire remained at her side with half a dozen half-completed spells on hand, requiring the last stroke of a symbol and the infusion of her magic to defend her.

 

            But she saw no one. Work eluded her too, although that was mostly due to her own aversion to towns in case the Necromancer who’d shot her happened to be staying at a hotel or asking questions about her passing. The only job that Lena had taken on was purely by accident, a farmer and his young son out hunting and encountered in the hazy dust of midday as she trotted past their ramshackle camp. She could see the fear in their eyes, but the man had been bitten by a western massasauga rattlesnake, the venom leaving his leg inflamed and in dire need of attention.

 

            Despite the fear and spark of hatred in his brown eyes, he knew as well as Lena did that if it was anyone else who had come to his aid, his leg would have needed amputation. He didn’t want her help, but her help was a blessing or the worst kind, even as he made the sign of the cross as she skimmed her fingertips across the blade in her sleeve and drew strange symbols on a blank piece of paper. Exposing his bloated leg with the deep gouges of fangs, Lena crumpled the paper in hand and drew on the magic of a milk tooth before drawing the venom out, black blood trickling down his reddened skin and dripping onto the sandy ground beneath him. Every tendon in his body went taut beneath his tanned skin and she could hear his young son quietly sobbing, but slowly the wound was reversed and Lena left him resting with a healing tincture of wild herbs and took the trapped rabbit and a sack of crab apples as payment.

 

            The rabbit was lean but fresher than the salted stuff Lena had with her, and the crab apples with sour and spongy but they made a welcome change from her usual fare as she went on her way, the plains spread out around her as the sky slowly deepened to violet. There was a storm that night, stinging rain and arcs of lightning keeping her company as Hecate dutifully plodded onwards, miserable as the darkness encroached on them and coyotes and foxes skulked through the deluge, illuminated with every flash of lightning. 

 

            The thunder seemed to shake the skies but it let up before dawn, leaving Lena damp and shivering until the sun rose and warmed her. That day was mercifully cool and lacked the usual clouds of dust and gritty sand and it was almost pleasant as she saw the distant rising of Pike’s Peak Country. She had no specific town in mind, only distance, and a week’s ride east gave her some breathing room.

 

            It was on the dawn of the eighth day after leaving Midvale that Lena rode into a mining town called Georgetown, at the Front Range of the Rocky Mountains up in Clear Creek country. She’d followed the tributaries to the stream that wound its way through a gorge, cliff walls of granite and limestone and shale rising around her, crowded trees nesting eagles that soared overhead while the hills she came out to were covered in yellowing grass and washed in bright sunlight.

 

            Georgetown was on the rise at that time, chasing after the Pike’s Peak gold rush that had brought prospectors to the place, and staying for the silver found in the mines nearby, brothels and saloons and gambling dens sprouting up to accommodate the new arrivals. The mines were up in the foothills of the mountains and cliffs that she’d stepped into the shadow of, smaller towns with workers and good, honest people keeping their own company the two miles by railcar it took to get up there, on switchback tracks that spanned the gorge and then some. Georgetown was a busier place than those small towns, nestled in the valley as the centre of commerce and entertainment for miles around, but even Lena’s arrival didn’t go unnoticed by the foot traffic and idle bystanders.

 

            Soldiers in uniform from a nearby garrison loitered about, smoking and rolling dice on the shaded awning of the main street through town. Suspicious eyes were drawn to Lena as she picked her way down the dusty street, past the Masonic temple and firehouse, past a variety of stores from the butchers to the bakery, dress shop and cobblers and post office, until she found the best hotel in town. That was a luxury she could afford herself after a week of discomfort in the saddle.

 

            Hitching Hecate to the post outside, Lena didn’t have to worry about anyone stealing her things - it was generally seen as bad luck to cross paths with a Necromancer and most folks were too wary to steal from them and find out what the consequences would be - and she patted the horse’s muzzle before walking up the steps and ducking into the cool shade.

 

            It was a little shabby in a well-worn way, but its former grandeur still lingered in the signs of lace and oil paintings and faded wallpaper. The shrewd eyes of the owner fixated on her and his mouth twisted into a bitter grimace.

 

            “You gonna take my head off if I turn you out?”

 

            “No, sir,” Lena said, taking off her hat and holding the brim in her hands.

 

            She looked pitifully small and exhausted, covered in dirt and reeking of sweat. Her green eyes were wide and earnest and perhaps that was convincing enough for the man because he sighed and beckoned her forward.

 

            “You got a horse?”

 

            “Yes, sir. She’s hitched outside.”

 

            “You’ll stay no longer than one night.”

 

            “Yes, sir.”

 

            He paused and looked at her again with renewed suspicion. “You’re mighty politer than the last one of your lot that came this way, that’s for sure.”

 

            Pausing, unease coiling at the base of her spine, Lena cocked her head to the side and licked her dry lip, clearing her throat as she spoke softly. “There’s … another Witch Doctor in town?”

 

            “Was,” the man bluntly replied, fishing out a key and setting it roughly on the countertop. “Rode out this morning. Threatened to shoot me if I didn’t let him stay the night.”

 

            “He?” Lena echoed with a shred of relief, her knotted shoulders slumping.

 

            “That’s right. Nasty as they come. Came through here with half a dozen bandits and a few skeletons; nearly started a mob in the streets but folks were too scared to do much but watch him coming.”

 

            Now Lena’s fear came anew, the hairs on her arms standing on end as her heart thundered in her chest with sickening nausea curling in her stomach. Her knuckles whitened as she clenched her hands into fists and she could barely make herself ask as her eyes shone bright with hatred and anger.

 

            “Did he leave a name?”

 

            “He sure did; made sure everyone knew it. One by the name of a Mister Lex Luthor. Put the fear of God in everyone.”

 

            Paling, Lena swallowed thickly and reached out with a trembling hand to push the keys back across the counter.

 

            “You know this man?”

 

            Expression darkening as her lips flattened into a grim line, Lena dipped her chin and put her hat back on her dark braided hair.

 

            “I know him.”

 

            “He’s got the devil in him, that one.”

 

            Nodding, Lena rubbed at her neck, restless and scared as she paced a few steps. Turning back around, she clenched her teeth as she looked at the old man in his worn suit, hesitating before giving him a piercing stare.

 

            “Do you know where he went?”

 

            “Last I heard he was up to Silver Plume with his posse.”

 

            Fishing a coin out of her purse with a shaking hand, Lena slapped it down on the counter for payment of information and then stalked out without another word. Her leather coat flapped around her thighs in her rush, boots tramping loudly on the wooden boards of the decking, and despite her exhaustion, she was up in the saddle in one smooth motion, flicking the reins and urging Hecate on.

 

            Part of her wanted to bolt from the town as fast as possible, take the gorge back the way she’d come and take her chances in the north, further away from gunslingers and outlaws and the drudgery of dust and sand and wide plains of open, sun-saturated earth. She would lose herself easily, slipping through mountains of pines as sheets of rain soaked her to her core and the mining towns dwindled as rugged nature monopolised the wide swathe of the north.

 

            A larger part of her burned for vengeance, which wasn’t an admirable quality in a Witch Doctor, bound by an ancient Hippocratic Oath predating the colonisation of the New World that they would enact their duties to heal and to revive those who paid for their services. But her brother wasn’t just anyone and Lena had long held to her fear and desire for revenge since parting ways with him. She had her own reasons for seeking out the west that largely was to do with Lex and only a small part to do with the territorial Witch Doctors staking out their territory, and while she’d thought he’d stick to the East Coast and let his madness spread there, for him to have come so far west made her itch to find him and foil his plans.

 

            Making up her mind, Lena took the circuitous path back around Georgetown and picked her way up the steady incline of the pass, making for Silver Plume in the odd chance that her brother was still there. She didn’t plan on stalking him through the wild, but she could sit tight and observe well enough, waiting for her chance to strike, biding her time as she had for years now.

 

            Recently, she’d been branded a Rogue, and while she didn’t know what she’d done to deserve it, the bounty on her head meant that there was little else to do but stay away from anyone who knew her, but Lena couldn’t resist the temptation. She was filled with the nagging suspicion that it was his fault too, these dangerous waters she’d landed herself in, and Lena fell deep in thought as she urged her horse through the valley, following the rusting slats of the railroad.

 

            Stewing in her confused thoughts as she passed bushes and trees and ponds of stagnant water, her passing startling birds and rabbits and squirrels into motion, she felt the close sensation in the air of something amiss. Her ears were ringing faintly and Lena’s skin prickled. There, faintly on the wind was the tang of gunpowder and a haze of grey lingered in the air before her, the acrid smell of dynamite threading around her.

 

            Urging Hecate onwards, Lena pulled the hammer back on her gun and bent down low over the horse’s neck as they created a ridge. It dipped down to a wide stretch of land wedged between two sides of the valley before spreading out into nothing but grasslands covering the dips and bumps of the wild terrain. Just below her, the railroad, which cut across a section of the flat ground and then made a turn up through the next pass to Silver Plume, visible in the lower slopes beneath the mineshaft burrowing into the mountainside, was occupied by a steam locomotive, come to a stop in the middle of its trip. The reason was evident, the front few carriages derailed and furrowed in the torn-up ground as black coal smoke rose from its chimney. 

 

            Narrowing her eyes, Lena could make out a dozen or so figures, most of them in varying states of death and decay with a few live outlaws along for the ride. All of them were on horses of similar states of life and at the front in all black, still sitting on that tall black horse, was Lex. Lena couldn’t even make out his face, but she would’ve known him anywhere, that burning hatred ignited in her stomach as she clutched her reins tighter.

 

            “Bastard.”

 

            Quieter now, she urged Hecate onwards, her soft hoof steps muffled by dry sand that sent plumes of dust up around her in a haze that helped obscure her approach. Gunshots fired off as a few of the passengers and the expressman got too mouthy and started fighting back, and Lena could see a couple of skeletons on the roof of the train, clearly the instigators of the derailment at her brother’s command.

 

            In the ruckus, she managed to slip around to the other side of the train, listening to her brother’s maniacal tirade, punctuated with gunshots as he performed his executions. If she’d had the time, she would’ve stayed to revive them all, regardless of if her supplies dwindled down to nothing with no chance of stopping at a Waypoint to restock. But she didn’t have the time. As Hecate sidled along the back of the train, her steps slow and quiet, Lena barely had time to take care of the burly man inside, grabbing a young woman by the throat and slamming her against the windows as she scrabbled at his large hand. But she did take care of him, slipping in through the open window with her bowie knife in hand, plunging it into the man’s shoulder.

 

            He whirled around as she pulled the knife free, groping at his shoulder as blood sprayed from the wound, quickly soaking into the brown of his jacket. Eyes widening as his face went slack, he looked at her with surprise and confusion, staggering back.

 

            “Lena?”

 

            She was just as surprised to see Otis Graves there too, knowing him through her brother’s close acquaintance with him as his sister. Floundering for a moment, mouth opening and closing at the prospect of another Necromancer to fight with, she quickly slammed the butt of her knife into his nose, breaking what had already been thrice broken and badly set with a sickening crunching sound and a spatter of blood on her face, before he slumped to the floor of the train car.

 

            The young woman was bone white and trembling with fear as she cupped her bruised throat but Lena spared her no more than a glance as she eased herself silently back through the window onto Hecate’s back. Putting a finger to her lips in a gesture for the woman to be silent, Lena tugged her neckerchief back up over the lower half of her face and continued further along the train. Fear made her skin prickle and her heart pound, the knowledge that there were at least a couple of Necromancers in her brother’s gang with him setting the odds against her. But Lena had always been one to gamble. 

 

            Even when Lex’s roar drowned out all other sounds, her name sounding like a curse from his mouth, having seen her through the carriage windows, she still hedged her bets with her having one up on him. He didn’t know her anymore, and a few years out west had hardened the little sister he’d mistreated, on top of all the lessons he’d left her with.

 

            “Lena!”

 

            The train cars had separated in the explosion a few carriages down from the front and she rode out into the gap, harsh sunlight beating down on her as she fixed her eyes on her brother. The years hadn’t done him kindly, weathered lines creasing his face, his dark eyes gleaming beneath the brim of his hat, and a dark beard covering his cheeks and chin. His lips twitched into a smile and Lena stared blankly at him.

 

            “Why are you doing this?”

 

            “Ride out, Lex. You’re too far from home.”

 

            “What’s got you so mad at me, little sister?”

 

            Lips curling with a snarl, Lena lowered her neckerchief and spit into the dirt, giving her brother such a venomous look that it was enough to make a few of the outlaws clinging to his pack of undead shy back from the showdown. They knew well enough from the colour of her coat that she was as dangerous as the man they were tagging along with for slim pickings of pilfered gold and silver. In the midst of them, she caught sight of Mercy Graves, her dark hair fluttering in the wind and a wicked spark in her eyes, dressed in black, having shed the uniform of their order. Dragging her attention back to her brother, Lena’s lip curled with contempt.

 

            “Damn it, I taught you everything you know, Lena.”

 

            “Ride on out or I take your fucking head off.”

 

            He gave her a sharp smile, his horse shifting beneath him as he looked at her with flat brown eyes beneath the brim of his hat. 

 

            “This isn’t my death, little sister.”

 

            Licking her dry lips, Lena’s eyes darted around and she tightened her grip on her revolver. Her hand inside her glove was clammy but her grip was sure and the bullet she squeezed off struck the rotting corpse between the eyes, lifting the reanimated man from his saddle to crumple to the dry earth. With a sharp whistle, Lena lit a tooth and called to the dead horse’s bones, urging it towards her as loose banknotes fluttered from the bulging saddle bags, caught in the wind.

 

            Before Lex could fire off a shot at her, she was galloping away with the packhorse, kicking up clouds of dust in her wake as her brother was left to scramble his wits and take chase. She didn’t glance back over her shoulder, too afraid that she’d find him near enough to reach out and grab her, she just bent low over Hecate’s neck and urged her onwards as the undead horse easily kept pace, rotting flesh peeling back to expose yellowed bone, now kept well preserved and unfailing, so long as she kept her brother’s spell going.

 

            Behind her came the hollering calls of Lex and a few of his lackeys that took chase with her, scattered amidst the posse of skeletons on horseback. Lena knew they were her biggest threat, their stamina as enduring as the packhorse’s, and while she’d made the conscious decision to find a new horse instead of reanimating Osiris, preferring the company of at least one alive being even if it was a horse at that, she desperately wished that she hadn’t been so unwilling to weigh the advantages of having a horse that would never tire. Usually, a live horse was well enough to outrun anyone chasing her out of a particularly unwelcome town, but the same couldn’t be said for horses who would run until their bones fell apart.

 

            Holstering her gun, she grabbed the lead rope of the packhorse and tied it to Hecate’s saddle, already outpacing the chasing mob of outlaws. But as she glanced over her shoulder, unable to stop herself any longer, she watched as the earth erupted in patches, skeletons clawing their way free as the Necromancers summoned them forth. Cursing, Lena fumbled for her own bag of teeth, scooping out a handful and yanking her bowie knife out, tearing a glove off with her teeth and clumsily gouging a cut into the flesh at the base of her thumb. Her glove was lost, to be trampled into the dirt, and a rivulet of blood ran into her cupped palm, welling up over the teeth and staining them as the magic sang in Lena’s veins.

 

            Igniting it with a sharp intake of breath, she felt into the earth with roots of magic, kindling a shadow of life into what bones she could find, the tendrils of her power snaking out ahead of her. She could taste blood at the back of her throat and her vision dimmed around the edges, her body flagging with exhaustion that hadn’t dogged her for years.

 

            But still, she felt the things she resurrected beneath her, clawing their way to the surface with a determination that only the dead could manage, rock and earth giving way to clawing bones that hadn’t seen the light of day in centuries or more. One particularly shocking discovery she unveiled burst from the ground in a shower of gritty pebbles and sand, monstrously big and hunched over with small arms and a long tail. Lena barely had time to process what she was seeing as it heaved itself out of the ground, clumps of black earth clinging to its bones, wet from the depths it had been buried, and not a shred of hair or hide on it. 

 

            Suppressing a shiver as the creature drew itself to its full height, a staggering six metres tall once on its hind legs, Lena felt the curdling darkness of her power and felt a moment of reason as she acknowledged the terror the common folk felt at what she could do. Behind her, aided with a few skeletons of long dead colonisers foolish enough to brave the west and two corpses of buffalo, one still relatively well-preserved, the ancient creature lashed out with its tail in a sweeping blow that caught two skeletal riders and horses, before it snapped out with teeth longer than Lena’s hand, narrowly missing one of the outlaws.

 

            Lex’s band was momentarily scattered, his control slipping as he ducked past a charging buffalo corpse, and Lena took advantage of his lapse to get a few more feet ahead. Still, it was a tiring chase, hours past steep cliffs and through miles and miles of rocky shrubland that snagged at her booted feet while the harsh sunlight made her throat dry, the coppery taste lingering on her tongue while the blood that had seeped from her eyes and nose dried in flaky tracks.

 

            She had no idea where she was going, only that it was north and then west again, hoping that her brother would be as lost as she was and unable to spring any nasty surprises on her. But as Lena urged Hecate into a sprint across the floor of a wide basin, nearing the back of it, she could see nothing but sheer cliffs rising before her.

 

            Breathlessly cursing as dread coiled in her stomach, Hecate flagging beneath her after being run too hard, Lena saw slim options before her. Closing her eyes for a brief moment, sand and tiny stones stinging her cheeks as the dry, fine grit worked its way down her throat with an inhale, she cobbled together a flimsy plan.

 

            Untying the lead rope, she eased her feet out of the stirrups and grabbed the saddle of the packhorse, keeping it alongside Hecate, who was foaming with sweat and losing what little ground Lena had bought them miles back. Her pursuers were close enough to shoot now and Lena instinctively ducked as a shot was fired off, a spray of dirt gouting into the air as it went wide.

 

            With an effort, she heaved herself over the gap between the horses and fell hard onto the pack horse's saddle, the fetid smell of rotting flesh making her gorge rise and the sour taste of bile coat her tongue. Leaning across the gap, she slapped Hecate’s rump and sent her horse careening off to the right, away from the narrowing entrance to the cul de sac of the gully.

 

            Picking up speed with the tireless horse, its gait a little uneven because of a broken hoof, Lena waited until she neared the spot where the wide basin converged to a narrow entrance with a sheer, dead-end rise of rocks speckled with shrubs and narrow paths foreign to Lena and more likely unsafe. Drawing in a deep breath, Lena slipped her gun from her holster and pressed it to the base of the horse’s neck.

 

            With an ear-splitting shot, she brought her mount down while still in the saddle, twisting her body so that when the dead horse found its final rest, she was already half out of the saddle. The gritty sand was hot to touch, felt through the knees of her cotton trousers, and Lena hunkered down behind the horse’s dwindling bulk as flies settled on the open ribs and the smell of its flesh made her sick.

 

            Closing one eye, she watched the horde approach, shadows careening out of a dust cloud, and marked the first skeleton. She took its head off with a perfectly aimed shot, shooting, again and again, thinning out her attackers. In the time it took for her to spit out a mouthful of blood and dirt, she’d taken out seven of them, leaving still too many for her to handle alone.

 

            One of the outlaws came right at her as she was thumbing new bone bullets into the chambers with practised speed. Lena just managed to spin the cylinder and click it back into place before she lunged sideways and raised the gun. The man in the saddle fired his shot too early and narrowly missed, the bullet striking the ground beside Lena’s head as she fired her gun.

 

            The bullet took him in the face, flesh and bone tearing apart, concaving his nose with a spray of blood as he tumbled from his saddle and thumped limply to the ground. Scrambling back to her kneeling position, huddled over her saddlebags of pilfered money, Lena watched as Lena came next, new skeletons clawing their way free.

 

            Her throat was parched and sweat streaked down her skin, and she knew that too much blood magic could prove fatal for her - and she wasn’t exactly confident Lex would bring her back - but she still scooped out a few teeth and gouged a fingernail into the wound she’d already opened on her thumb. Tearing a page from her spell book at random, she dropped her gun beside her and dabbed a trembling finger into the thick blood and finished off the last line of the spell.

 

            Crumpling the paper and clenching a bloody fistful of teeth, Lena tossed them out before her and pulled on the magic before releasing it. It went out in a wave, tearing skeletons apart from each joint, pulling half-decomposed corpses to shreds as ligaments and tendons and skin stretched and came away, bodies scattering into a dozen pieces as the charade of puppetry ended. Some of them still twitched with the vestiges of Lex’s power scrambling to reassemble them, but he was too slow as Lena scooped up her gun, finger finding the trigger, and shot him in the arm.

 

            It wasn’t a killing blow, but it tore through skin and muscle and shattered bone, a curdling scream of pain falling from his lips. He bared his teeth in a snarl but Lena watched him sway in the saddle, his arm hanging limply and Mercy Graves riding up beside him, shouldering him upright before he could fall from horseback.

 

            Lena knew she had won this fight, her brother needing time to retreat and have his arm stitched back together with the aid of his fellow Necromancers, but she knew this wasn’t the last of it. He wouldn’t forgive her for making a fool out of him, stealing the fortune from out under his nose and leaving him helpless for at least a few hours. Still, she was tense as she watched the ragged band retreat, leaving half of their number behind, most of them twice dead now, at least, with only a few humans. One of them was a Necromancer too, that medallion around the woman’s neck leaving Lena with a sour taste in her mouth as she rolled her over with the toe of her boot. She was unfamiliar but another of their Order gone was a blow.

 

            Snatching the medallion from the corpse’s neck, she tucked it into a pocket and made her way over to the packhorse. With as much blood as she could spare, feeling faint and her face white as bone, Lena used a tooth to bring it back to its shadow of life. A little bit more than Lex had, its eyes turning white with a milky film as it was brought back as a wight. Lena always found them easier to handle when she didn’t have to handle their every movement, preferring to be their master rather than a puppeteer holding the strings.

 

            The horse was heedless to anything that had occurred and to her presence, climbing to its feet and standing still beneath the sun as maggots crawled through its ribs. With some reluctance, Lena hauled herself onto its back and nudged it onwards, heading out in the direction she’d sent Hecate.

 

            It took her an hour to find her horse, laying beside a shallow watering hole, in the shadow of a rocky outcropping. Lena’s heart lurched with relief and she swung off the dead horse, staggering from the jarring impact of her feet hitting the packed earth, and stumbled over to her.

 

            “Hecate,” Lena whispered, dropping to her knees beside the horse, her fingers running over her mane and muzzle as she reassured herself of her good health.

 

            Still, as a precaution, Lena dug out a tonic from her small chest and forced it down the horse’s throat, Hecate snorting and tossing her head as she objected to the bitter taste. Fishing out the dwindling supply of crabapples and some oats, Lena set them out for her and turned to look at the packhorse.

 

            It wandered freely like it was sleepwalking, the vacant look in its milky eyes unnatural, and she moved over to it, unbuckling the saddlebags before she sighed regretfully and shot it again for a final time. Lugging her loot over to Hecate she transferred the bulging saddlebags into the foot of her bedroll and then took stock of herself.

 

            She was fine - for the most part. The cut on her hand stung and she was lightheaded from blood loss, tired from her arduous travel and spent magic, and couldn’t taste anything except the dankness of earth and coppery blood. Fishing a tonic for blood replenishing from her crate, made with copper water, lemon and sesame seeds with a dash of her own blood, Lena drained it and then drank deeply from her canteen.

 

            After wolfing down some food, her eyes already heavy-lidded and the effort to raise the dried meat to her lips getting harder with each bite, it was all she could do to flop down into the shade before she passed out.

 

 

            Lena had been gone for a little over two weeks now, yet Kara couldn’t stop thinking about her. Not when she mucked out the horses, dug the new well until she was covered head to toe in runny mud, plucked the chickens or rode into town for drinks with Alex in the saloon of the hotel. It was almost impossible to keep her mind off her longer than a few minutes and Kara had turned quiet and contemplative of late, observed with confusion by her family and friends.

 

            That night, she was back in town again, eating dinner with Alex and Kelly and J’onn as they discussed the proposals put forth by Andrea Rojas about the mine. Cutting into her chicken and wild vegetables, Kara was comfortable near the wide fireplace as other rowdy patrons played cards and sang bawdy songs to the sound of a fiddle player and the banker, Querl Dox, who had come in for business but stayed to entertain on the old upright piano.

 

            It was a quiet night, as ordinary as any others, save for the presence of Andrea and her retinue of advisors and personal gunslingers for hire. She stayed mostly to herself, Midvale an unwelcoming sort to outsiders even though they were cordial and respectful, and Kelly thought they’d etch out a plan for reopening soon. As mayor, she was trying to get the heiress to offer up a bigger cut of the mine to the residents than Andrea wanted to, but without the business of it, and without more men to do the hard work, it wouldn’t matter how much each party was getting; Midvale would die out to nothing but starving dwellers too stubborn to leave for greener pastures. 

 

            As it was, a few families had up and left since the mining accident, looking for other towns with better prospects. It was mostly men with other trades, the elderly men retired after the war, and women that lingered there now, and, truthfully, Kara was worried about who she’d sell her horses to once she’d broken them in. She had a potential deal struck with the indigenous Ute people that lived a few hours south in La Plata, but the town needed horses too, and Kara couldn’t afford to sell her stock at a loss out of loyalty and friendship.

 

            Taking a sip of J’onn’s best moonshine, she leaned back in her chair and stared thoughtfully into the fire. She was half-listening to the conversation as she nursed her drink when the batwing doors swung inwards to let in a broad-shouldered man. Kara glanced over and blinked in surprise, straightening up as a smile spread across her face.

 

            “James!”

 

            He walked over to their table, his Marshal’s badge on his belt glinting in the amber light, and he pulled a chair out after kissing the top of his sister’s head.

 

            “You didn’t tell me you was coming back here,” Kelly scolded him.

 

            “I weren’t supposed to be,” he wearily sighed, running a hand over his face and the couple of days of growth that prickled his jaw. “I was down in Texas when I heard the news. Another mine robbery out near Pike’s Peak.”

 

            M’gann let out a low whistle as she brought whiskey over to James and set it down in front of him before taking a seat. “Weren’t you out in Texas for another one of those?”

 

            Nodding, he sipped at his drink, dark eyes grave as he looked around. Kara took in the weary signs of long travel and wondered about what had him riding so hard for home unannounced. He worked for the courts, tracking down outlaws all over the west and some nearer to the east and south too, and was rarely home for long these days.

 

            “Fourth in as many months. It gets worse - reports say it ain’t the usual kind of thieves and outlaws. It’s them Necromancers.”

 

            “Necromancers?” Kelly echoed, shifting with unease. “They normally don’t cause that much trouble. We had one come through here a couple of weeks back. I thought she might be helpful with the mine and all but … well, she left soon after.”

 

            “One passed through town?”

 

            “‘Bout two weeks ago now,” J’onn rumbled.

 

            Shrugging, James’ mouth thinned and he sipped at his drink. “Could be a coincidence.”

 

            “This is where again?” Alex asked.

 

            “Up in Georgetown. They say he hit the silver mine up in Silver Plume. Payroll comes into town on this little narrow gauge; only two miles from Georgetown to Silver Plume. Derailed the train with some dynamite and took the payroll and anything worthy from the passengers.”

 

            Kara felt her knotted insides unclench slightly at he , seeming to relax as she listened to the unfolding story. James took off his hat and leant forward, running a hand over the bald pate of his head and taking a swig of whiskey before carrying on. His dark eyes were troubled and suspicious and Kara listened with rapt attention, an anxious look of disbelief on her face.

 

            “Now her,” James continued in his slow, meandering way, scratching at the growth of stubble on her jaw. “No one knows when she showed up; might be she was there the whole time, or maybe she crept up on him later. Hard to say. I only got the one witness and she weren’t very reliable. But she said the man called her Lena and he was afraid of her.”

 

            A jolt ran through Kara and her knee jerked up to hit the underside of the table as her heartbeat quickened. Mouth opening and closing, she glanced sharply at Alex before leaning forward.

 

            “Did you say Lena?”

 

            “You know her?”

 

            “The woman that came through here … she said that was her name. Didn’t seem like the kind that wanted trouble though; she was badly hurt. Running from something, I reckon,” Kara murmured as she rubbed at her furrowed brow. “She was all alone; I wonder what she was doing, keeping that sort of company.”

 

            “You mean her own kind,” Alex seethed.

 

            Sighing, James shook his head. “They had words; I don’t know which but they would’ve been unkind. She rode off with his packhorse of notes, he followed after her, and the miners from Georgetown rode up. Town sent word they had a couple of Luthor’s boys so I put a posse together and headed up that way but they took care of it themselves ‘fore I got there. Seems like someone turned around though; I don’t know which but the whole mob was dead when I reached there. Silver Plume is nought but a ghost town of ashes now. The folks at Georgetown don’t know what it was that went down, but each and every one of them’s dead. Saw it with my own damn eyes.”

 

            “It’s a real shame,” M’gann sighed, shaking her head as she braced her hands on her hips.

 

            “A real damn shame,” Alex murmured in agreement. “Bless the Lord for sparing us that horror. See, I knew that Witch Doctor was no good. Didn’t I tell y’all? And to think we let her stay in here.”

 

            “Mines have been hit up all over the place out east; it’s only a matter of time ‘fore they come out this way. You might want to send out some scouts to keep an eye on things, Sheriff.”

 

            Nodding thoughtfully, Alex chewed on tobacco as she ran her fingers over the handle of her holstered pistol. Frowning, Kara stepped forward, arms folded over her chest.

 

            “But … we’re shut down. Why would either of them come here?”

 

            “Well, Lex Luthor don’t know all that, and when he finds out who all’s mostly living here … and you say his sister rode through not two weeks past? Maybe she was scouting out the place. Could be either of them is the thief.”

 

            “She near died on my doorstep, James,” Kara snorted. “And I nearly put a bullet through her throat to boot before she collapsed in the mud; she weren’t a threat to no one, I’m telling you.”

 

            He shrugged dismissively and knocked back his drink. “All I’m saying is all you ladies here ain’t exactly going to be a discouragement to anyone looking to rob the place now, is it?”

 

            “This is all the discouragement I need,” Alex cockily replied as she patted her gun. “‘Sides, we all know how to shoot here. Ain’t no one getting past us without getting riddled with bullets.”

 

            “You best hope you’re right,” James darkly warned them.

 

            The conversation drifted to other topics but Kara was too preoccupied with what she had heard to contribute. Finishing off her drink in silence, she excused herself afterwards, donning her coat and hat and leaving a few coins on the scarred table. Alex walked her out, watching as Kara unhitched her bay stallion, Comet, from the post.

 

            “You should consider moving into town.”

 

            Kara glanced up and smiled wryly, “you ain’t worried about me are you?”

 

            “I mean it, Kara. It ain’t safe anymore. Not with the sorts of people out here.”

 

            “Lena ain’t going to hurt no one, Alex,” Kara exasperatedly sighed.

 

            Rankling, Alex thundered down the steps with a look of fear in her eyes. “She ain’t your friend . You don’t even know her.”

 

            “That’s beside the point,” Kara flushed, “I’ve got my horses to break. I got the ranch. I can’t just up and leave it now, can I?”

 

            “I don’t like you out there all by yourself.”

 

            “I’ll be fine, Alex,” Kara placatingly replied, reaching out to jostle her sister’s shoulder. “I got a gun, don’t I? And a Sheriff for a sister.”

           

            “You keep an eye out for anything funny, alright? If anything happens to you, I’ll have to hire that Witch Doctor to bring you back to life just so I can kill you myself.”

 

            Snorting at her sister’s joke, Kara gave her a crooked smile and pulled herself up onto the horse’s back. Touching the brim of her hat in parting, she clicked her tongue to urge Comet onwards, gently putting her heels to flank, and rode out of town and into the night.

 

            It was a peaceful ride, her skirt rippling in the wind and the darkness pierced by the river of stars. She couldn’t see far in front of her, but Kara had grown up on the ranch, had been riding back and forth to town for half of her life, and was sure of herself as she navigated the dark road, taking the turning up the long path to her dark house.

 

            But something was amiss as she arrived at home, the darkness quite so complete as it should have been and Kara slowed.

 

            Light seeped out between the cracks of the barn, just enough to ward off the darkness as Kara came up the long, dusty path to the low house. She reined in Comet in the middle of the open courtyard and dismounted silently, creeping towards her house to fetch a rifle. It wasn’t often she had to deal with intruders, but it wasn’t the first time and she steeled her nerves to do what had to be done.

 

            The door quietly creaked open and she plucked a rifle from just inside the door, already loaded as a precaution, and stole back down the deck and steps as she slid the bolt home with the whisper of metal. In the pen, horses whickered softly and the gentle sigh of the breeze helped muffle her slow, grinding footsteps across the hard-packed earth.

 

            The darkness was like velvet wrapped around her ranch, pinpricks of stars offering no light in the moonless night, and Kara’s hands turned slick on the wood of the rifle as she sidled up along the barn doors, inching closer. Drawing in a deep breath, the aroma of hay and wood and horse all commonplace as it assaulted her senses, she reached out with a foot and nudged one side of the wide barn door open. It let out a quiet groan and she clenched her teeth as she hefted the rifle and slipped into the dim light.

 

            “I know you’re in here,” she called out, her voice level and full of bravado. “Come out. Come out right now, and I won’t turn you in to the Sheriff.”

 

            There was the sound of movement in the back corner, around one of the wooden stall walls, and Kara narrowed her eyes as she inched towards it.

 

            “Who’s back there?” she demanded. “I have a gun.”

 

            A hoarse laugh sounded behind her and she whirled around to find a figure in creamy leathers, barely able to stand on their feet. They still managed to level their revolver at her though and Kara’s stomach clenched.

 

            “So do I,” Lena gravelly replied, giving her a bloody smile.

 

            “Damn you, Lena, I nearly took your head off,” Kara scolded her, cheeks flooding with red as she slid the boot back and lowered her rifle. 

 

            “Wouldn’t be the first time.”

 

            Her gallows humour didn’t go over too well with Kara, who watched her sag with exhaustion. Dashing forward as Lena sank down to the dirt floor, letting her gun clatter beside her as she removed her hat with a trembling hand, Kara sank to her haunches a few feet away.

 

            “What in God’s name are you doing in my barn?”

 

            “I didn’t have anywhere else to go.”

 

            “What happened?”

 

            Eyes shuttering, Lena smiled thinly and Kara took in the gaunt hollows of her face with concern. She looked like she hadn’t slept in days, purple bruises smudged beneath her eyes and caked on layers of dust and grime, etched into the lines of her face as she let out a dry, rattling cough.

 

            “Nothing you need to fret about.”

 

            “This about your brother?”

 

            Raising her chin in a defiant manner, Lena narrowed her eyes, licking her cracked and scabbed lips as she watched Kara.

 

            “How do you know about my brother?”

 

            “I reckon that’s the least of your concerns right now. Come on; let’s get you inside. I could do without the questions about a dead body on my land.”

 

            “Your sister is the Sheriff.”

 

            “All the more reason to pretend like you was never here,” Kara darkly muttered as she hauled Lena to her feet and slung her thin arm over her shoulder.

 

            Not having much room to protest, Lena let her hat gently thump to the floor, alongside her gun, as Kara hauled her out of the barn and into the night. Neither of them spoke and she could feel Kara’s bristling tension as she towed them across the empty space, a haze of fog creeping in as the breeze swirled it around them.

 

            Up the steps, she was led inside and released in the darkness to stand on her own two feet, the scratching of dog paws on the floorboards falling on her ears as Kara fussed over the scruffy staghound. The hissing scrape of flint whispered in the dark, Kara softly muttering as sparks briefly illuminated her hands before she managed to light a lamp. Lifting it, she bathed Lena’s face in the warm glow seeping from the orb and gestured to the table.

 

            “Sit.”

 

            Lena obeyed, a sense of deja vu washing over her as she sank heavily onto one of the wooden chairs, watching as Kara knelt before the fireplace and set about lighting a fire. Soon enough, its orange glow banished the darkness and filled the cold night with its warmth as it curled about them deliciously.

 

            Kara set a heavy kettle on to boil before disappearing into the night, while Lena rested, a feeling of tenuous safety wrapping around her. She closed her eyes, feeling the grit between her lids, and let her body sag, finally giving out on her. Lena almost thought she’d never be able to move again, would have happily died in that chair before the warm fire with the dog quietly panting at her feet. It felt homely.

 

            A few minutes later, Kara came back inside and bolted the door shut behind her, the smell of leather and oil and horse clinging to her as she brushed behind Lena’s chair and made for the stove. Shedding her coat and hat, Kara washed her hands in clean water and dried them off before serving up some strongly steeped tea.

 

            “Here. Drink.”

 

            “Thank you?”

 

            “You eaten?”

 

            “No.”

 

            Her boots thumped heavily with each step as she moved around the place, the sprawling dog watching her with dark, liquid eyes. She set thick-cut slices of that morning’s bread down before her, a wedge of butter and a block of cheese to go with it, before taking a seat perpendicular to Lena. Hunched over her own tea, looking brawny as her shirtsleeves strained against her arms, muscled from years of working the ranch, Kara studied her with shockingly naïve blue eyes.

 

            “You alright there?”

 

            “Perfectly well, thank you,” Lena curtly replied, taking a sip of tea.

 

            “Eat up, now,” Kara urged her, nudging the butter closer. “And then you can tell me the truth.”

 

            Giving her a rakish smile, Lena lifted the small knife and cut a thin piece of cheese off the block. “I can assure you, ma’am, I haven’t lied to you.”

 

            “You ain’t been honest neither. You know, we get news in town. Folks been talking; your name’s been cropping up. I have half a mind to turn you out into the night.”

 

            Slowly chewing her bite of cheese, Lena lowered her arm and gave Kara a wary look. “What have they been saying?”

 

            “That you slaughtered a town of people up in Silver Plume. Made off with the payroll that you stole from your brother.”

 

            “I never went to Silver Plume,” Lena hedged.

 

            “But you stole the money.”

 

            “I stole it from someone who had already stolen it.”

 

            Raising her eyebrows, Kara narrowed her eyes slightly. “What did you do with it all?”

 

            Giving her a crooked smile, Lena shrugged nonchalantly. “I took care of it.”

 

            Exhaling roughly, Kara pressed her mouth into a flat line before taking a sip of tea. She set the cup down a little harder than necessary and fixed Lena with a hard stare. It didn’t exactly inspire fear in Lena but she knew better than to misjudge her; Kara was taller, stronger and within reach of her gun. All Lena had going for her was half-baked spells and teeth that wouldn’t be much help unless Kara had dead bodies buried beneath them.

 

            “You’re in trouble, you know. People are looking for you.”

 

            Rolling the black tea on her tongue, rinsing the taste of dust and blood from her mouth, Lena exhaled sharply through her nose with amusement. Arching an eyebrow she traced a dirty fingertip around the rim of the cup as her lips twisted with wry humour.

 

            “I was being hunted before I came here the first time.”

 

            “That’s why you were shot?”

 

            Dipping her head in reluctant affirmation, Lena hunched her shoulders as her eyes darted around the house. “A … misunderstanding.”

 

            “You seem to have a lot of those. It’s bad for your health, you know. Someone might want you dead enough to kill you. ‘Specially that brother of yours, if rumours don’t lie.”

 

            “I’ve died before,” Lena bitterly replied, a flash of dark anger in her eyes as she looked away, fingers straying to rub at the middle of her forehead.

 

            Kara seemed to wilt in her chair, her mouth opening and closing as she was caught speechless. “I- you’ve … died before? You were … brought back?”

 

            “It’s irrelevant,” Lena muttered, quickly picking up the butter knife and smearing a lump over a slice of bread.

 

            “That don’t sound irrelevant to me, Doc. You ain’t supposed to die and come back. It ain’t natural.”

 

            “Natural is relative to perspective. A doctor might bring back a drowned man by thumping him on the chest and bringing up all that water. No one wants to lynch them.”

           

            “They don’t bring back those that was dead for a lot longer. They don’t bring back skeletons and the like.”

 

            Snorting, Lena crammed her slice of bread into her mouth. Chewing quickly, she roughly shoved back from the table, chair legs scraping on the wooden floorboards and Krypto skittering away from her.

 

            “Well, I’m sorry for being a Necromancer. As if it’s my fault,” Lena snapped. “I’ll be gone tomorrow.”

 

            “Lena-“

 

            Unbolting the door, Lena strode out into the night, the wind catching the door and blowing it open, the shuddering bang of it bouncing off the wall splitting the quiet. She was unsteady on her feet, tired and wilting more with each passing step as she walked across the empty yard and stepped into the close air of the barn.

 

            Hecate was stabled at the back, free of her saddle and packs, brushed free of the dried mud and dust and settled in with oats and water and some pilfered hay. She seemed content, properly resting for the first time in two weeks, and Lena settled down on the mound of hay in the corner, using her coat for a pillow and dragging her blanket over herself.
