            The tea made her sleepy and her body was bone-tired, but her mind wouldn’t rest. Looking up at the rafters, listening to mice squeak beneath her and the wind whistle through the cracks, she sighed and shifted restlessly, stuck on thoughts of Kara. 

 

            An hour slipped by with no luck, sleep still evading her, and she was starting to consider making herself a tonic when the sound of the barn door dragging open quietly creaked through the barn. The soft glow of a lantern cast a warm halo on the ground and illuminated Kara’s wary form, Krypto at her heels as he loped inside, sniffing around.

 

            “I don’t mean to cause offence,” Kara sighed, drifting closer as a gust of wind ruffled her blonde curls, sweeping in behind her. “It ain’t easy to accept though; we ain’t used to all that ‘round here. Gives me the chills just thinking about it.”

 

            Pushing herself up to a sitting position, hay clinging to the back of her shirt and the soft air of tiredness blurring the edges of Lena’s sharpness, the Witch Doctor reached up and thumbed the medallion hanging from her neck.

 

            “You think it more gruesome than it is, but it’s all just superstition. I can’t blame you, of course not, but can you imagine how it feels to hear the stories? People think I’m a murderer, that I kill people and bring them back to serve me.”

 

            “Don’t you?”

 

            Lena snorted and clenched her jaw. “It’s rude to assume every Necromancer murders people for a skeleton army, you know. Aside from the fact that there are more than enough people dying every day without me wasting valuable time making more corpses, I am a physician. First and foremost. You have no idea how much we can learn from the dead. It could advance medical treatment decades. I’ve saved a hell of a lot more lives than I’ve taken.”

 

            “It’s wrong to use the dead. They can’t consent.”

 

            A smile briefly flashed across Lena’s face as she narrowed her eyes with amusement, head cocking to the side. “That’s what offends your principles? Would you prefer I have living people die for me than dead people live for me? Interesting. The dead are long gone, they feel no pain. You should concern yourself more with the living, ma’am.”

 

            “I’d prefer neither, if I’m being honest, Doc. And I know all about the dead being gone. I ain’t afraid of that; it’s them coming back that I don’t like.”

 

            “The day will come when this town will be nothing but melancholy dust,” Lena murmured, her shoulders slumping with exhaustion as she rubbed at tired eyes. “The dead will fill so many graves, and you and I will be long gone by then. But there will always be another Necromancer searching for bones; I can’t give you the comforting knowledge that your body will rest, but your soul will.”

 

            Hesitating, Kara warily eyed her, inching closer as she clenched her hand around the pewter thing held in her hand. Lena couldn’t see what it was but she saw the confusion in Kara’s eyes, the flicker of hope.

 

            “You believe in all of that?”

 

            “I don’t know. We have to go somewhere, don’t we? I've died but I don’t know if I believe we go to some higher place, home to some God, and I don’t care if it’s blasphemous to say it, but … we have to go somewhere. We can’t just vanish; at the very least we’re in the wind and the sea and the trees. I think that would be enough for me.”

 

            Biting her lip, Kara took a bold step forward, sinking down to sit a few feet away from Lena. She set the lantern down beside her and fiddled with the other thing in her hands - a flask, Lena realised.

 

            “You said you’ve died before. What was it like?”

 

            Lena turned her head away, closing her eyes as she swallowed thickly. She could smell the blood on her skin, the sweat and dirt and hay, but mostly the blood. It’s coppery tang, the thickness of it, how it smeared over the paper and how quickly it escaped a body, all so familiar to her from her work and from the times she’d died. More times than she liked to think.

 

            In her memory, she could feel the pain as sharply as if it was yesterday, the way the bullet drove into the soft parts of her, the blackness of the times she didn’t see it coming, swift and sure. Those she brought back never remembered how it happened, but they all came back screaming; Lena remembered though. She remembered every time.

 

            Drawing in a shuddering breath, she swallowed thickly. “It’s like … nothing. You wake up cold all over and it hurts but you’re alive and … you don’t remember it. How it happened or where you were. It’s like being asleep and waking up the next morning. Death isn’t so scary.”

 

            “How do you do it?”

 

            A wry smile curled Lena’s lips. “It’s considered bad luck to ask.”

 

            Nodding, Kara hesitated and then held out the flask without a word. It was whiskey, burning and honeyed and warm in Lena’s belly. Kara watched her drink, and Lena tossed the flask back to her after a couple of swigs, catching it before she spoke.

 

            “Look, I got about forty horses outside that needs breaking. Seems to me like you need somewhere to lie low so this brother of yours don’t catch up to you. You seem to know horses; that mare of yours is damn well trained or I don’t know what the hell I’m talking about. Now, I don’t have much to offer, but … you could stay here, in the barn. I’ve got enough to feed you and … I won’t tell no one if you stay hidden.”

 

            “Why?”

 

            “I need the help.”

 

            “What about your sister?”

 

            Kara smiled faintly, shrugging as she climbed to her feet, dusting off her skirt. “What she don’t know won’t hurt her, Doc.”

 

            “But you don’t like my kind.”

 

            “You don’t seem so stone-cold to me.”

 

            She picked up her lantern and turned to leave, whistling for Krypto, who scarpered after her, and stepped out of the barn. Closing the door behind her, Kara inhaled deeply and exhaled softly, uncapping the flask as she walked towards the beckoning glow of the house.  Stepping inside, she took a sip of the whiskey, slowly, like it wasn’t the flavour she was savouring, all the while thinking about those sad green eyes.

4. Chapter 4

            The good thing about living in the middle of nowhere, a few miles out of town, was that nobody disturbed them. Alex, on occasion, came out of her way to check up on her sister, but Kara was usually in town a couple of times a week for something , conducting most of her business there in the saloon as she caught up with her friends over beer and moonshine and M’gann’s food.

 

            As a result, Lena was mostly given free rein of Kara’s ranch, skulking around unnecessary given the secluded nature of the cluster of buildings. She rose each morning, feeding Hecate and letting her out to roam freely before she let herself into the paddock to walk amongst her new charges. They were skittish and wild, snorting at the tang of blood and death that always clung to her. Even if it wasn’t a perceptible scent, her profession was tangible, the strange magic she’d trained and learnt always singing in her veins.

 

            Despite what most people thought of her, animals were quick to overcome their prejudice. These horses were no less quick to at least quieten their discomfort, her scent becoming familiar and the slivers of crabapples she gave them winning them to her favour. She’d had to train her own horses on more than one occasion and was patient with them, the docile ones soothed by her presence first, and then the wilder ones.

 

            Still, they weren’t broken in, and it was time-consuming, not including the other farm work she pitched in with. She’d been there a week, silent for the most part, undisturbed and alone unless Kara was about - which she usually was - and they’d found an almost comfortable rhythm. Lena helped peel potatoes at night for dinner, quick and quiet while Kara kept the conversation going, and one day she found herself head-to-toe in mud from helping Kara dig the well.

 

            The night was her favourite part though. Working beneath the sun was harsh, and she’d always been fond of the cool darkness that soothed her warm body. Unused to so much physical labour, Lena would be exhausted, but that didn’t stop her from sitting outside to look at the stars if the weather permitted, or stretching out on a pile of hay with Hecate close by. Most nights Kara would join her, creeping into the dimly lit barn once she’d finished her chores - sometimes with Krypto and sometimes without - the walls slowly retreating until she was able to overcome her wariness and let her natural curiosity pepper Lena with a dozen questions of her craft.

 

            Amused, Lena would answer them as well as she could, trying not to frighten Kara off any more than she already was. At the very least, she was grateful for the company, and when Kara would leave, taking the flask of whiskey or the empty tin cups with the dregs of tea, Lena felt a twinge of loneliness in her chest. It would’ve been nice to sit and talk in that in-between space where time seemed to stretch on infinitely with no demands of their time.

 

            “It’s peaceful here,” Lena murmured one night, leaning against a bale of hay while Kara perched on an overturned crate a few feet away. 

 

            The sugar and manure, apple and peat smell of the horses after they had been rubbed down for the night surrounded them, the leathering smell of polishing saddles and mending tack clinging to Lena’s clothes. She no longer smelled so much of blood and death, although it was still there, that coppery undercurrent, like old pennies as the magic fizzled in her veins. There was something to be said for hard work, labouring away beneath the sun as her clothes drenched with sweat and the horses learnt to trust her, and Lena only used her blood magic to heal her cracked ribs from the hard kick of a spirited stallion, to fix the broken leg that normally would’ve meant a bullet in the horse’s brain to end its suffering.

 

            “One could be stuck with a worse lot,” Kara agreed, her eyes wandering around the eaves of the barn. “Better, too. Like that prissy heiress in town.”

 

            Lena let out a quick laugh, drinking her moonshine and humming. “She’s got no one left, you know. I met her a few years back and she begged me to save her father, and now look where she is: stuck here with the rest of us, trying to make money off a collapsed mine. I don’t envy her that.”

 

            “You were like her,” Kara said, jerking her chin towards Lena as her eyes narrowed.

 

            Tilting her head to the side, Lena’s mouth turned down at the corners and she gestured vaguely. “She is … what I could’ve been, in another life. If my family didn’t practice this craft. Then, yes, I imagine she and I would’ve been much the same. But here I am, reviving the dead and sticking to the open road.”

 

            “It must be a rough life; don’t you want somewhere comfortable to wind down? A family? Kids?”

 

            “Now, what would I do with a kid?” Lena asked, a crooked smile on her face. “That seems more like your lot, ma’am.”

 

            “Maybe one day it was, but my husband passed and I got too much to worry about to consider a child. Or another man telling me what’s what and how it is.”

 

            Eyebrows rising a fraction, Lena gave her an appraising look. “You don’t mean to marry again?”

 

            “I never intended it the first time,” Kara sighed, “only that it happened and I was as close to happy as I thought I’d ever get. Sometimes .. you settle for what you got, and not what you ain’t, and that’s it. Only, my husband had to go and die on me, and now I’m spent going over my mistake of ever settling for a small town and a ranch, but I don’t know any better.”

 

            “Blaming the dead for our mistakes never accomplishes much.”

 

            “Perhaps. But it’s easier than blaming yourself, ain’t it?”

 

            And Lena knew all too well the guilt that came with the blame that saddled her, those that had been reckless and died and rotted too far past what she could make whole and hale again. Those clients were never happy, cursing her out for the useless magic they cursed her for having in the first place. It was easier to blame the deceased for their failings than to acknowledge the failings in her own magic, the limitations that she knew were in place, but those who condemned her thought were limitless. 

 

            It didn’t fix anything to blame the dead, but it helped bury that hopelessness long enough to set a broken leg or treat a bout of measles and bring back a newborn who’d passed from typhoid or scarlet fever. They would go on to lead healthy lives, long lives - or maybe they passed a month after Lena had healed them - and that was enough to dispel the despair for a while. It never made digging the graves of the truly gone any easier, covering them with a burial shroud and leaving with apologies to the bereaved.

 

            But she was free from that task for a while longer, a merciful reprieve spent with the company of those who didn’t judge, and Kara, who judged a little less now. A week passed by quickly, a comfortable routine settling in, and Lena knew that she could easily get lost in this delusion of normalcy. How long it could continue was inevitably not for long.

 

            Just shy of two weeks with her new boarder, Kara left the barn late one night, a gentle warmth in her chest as she whistled softly and made for the house. They’d talked for a long while, sharing stories and harmless information, somewhat comfortable, if it could be called that, and over the whickering of the horses, they hadn’t heard the arrival of anyone else.

 

            Boots heavy on the steps, Kara’s shoulders slumped with contented exhaustion and she reached for the door, oblivious to the lurking guest outside.

 

            “She stinks of death, that one. And if she stays here long enough, she’ll make us stink of it too.”

 

            Kara startled at the low voice, her head whipping sideways to catch sight of a cherry red tip of a cigarette. It dimmed as Alex pulled it from her lips and exhaled a plume of grey into the darkness and Kara shifted uneasily, a scowl darkening her pretty features.

 

            “What’re you doing skulking ‘round in the dark?”

 

            “How long she been here?”

 

            “Who?” Kara blithely feigned ignorance.

 

            Sighing, Alex stubbed out the rest of her cigarette and tucked a thumb through her gun belt as she stepped closer to her sister. Faint moonlight illuminated the grave look on her face as her boots scuffed the wooden decking.

 

            “Look, I know you mean well - you always have - but she can’t stay here, Kara.”

 

            “But-“

 

            “She ain’t like us,” Alex softly cut her off, clapping a hand on Kara’s shoulder as she gave her an earnest look. “Now, I’m leaving for a while, and she best be gone when I’m back.”

 

            Surprise softened Kara’s irate expression, her eyebrows rising and lips parting. “Where’re you going?”

 

            “I’m looking into what James said happened. Something ain’t adding up right to me; something bigger than a simple rail car robbery, I bet. I won’t be longer than a few weeks.”

 

            “She ain’t guilty like you think.”

 

            “I don’t think it either,” Alex said, sucking on her teeth for a second as she deliberated. “It’s just best not to bring that kind of trouble here. We got the mine to think about, and like I said … she stinks of death. Listen to your big sister, alright?”

 

            Exhaling as her shoulders slumped, Kara pressed her lips into a flat line and nodded in concession. “You take care of yourself out there; don’t be reckless.”

 

            Quietly laughing, Alex embraced her and Kara kissed her cheek as she returned the hug. “Kelly’s in town if you need her.”

 

            “Don’t you worry about me,” Kara murmured, squeezing Alex’s shoulders for a second, “I’m alright out here by myself.”

 

            Alex didn’t respond to that and a moment later she was thudding down the steps and making for the dark shadow of a horse that Kara had missed when exiting the barn. Swinging up into the saddle with the practised ease of a lawman who spent hours on horseback chasing down local petty criminals, Alex whistled a chirping goodbye and put her heels to the flanks of the stallion.

 

            A haze of dust blurred the night and the sound of galloping hooves was soon out of earshot, leaving Kara lingering outside in the night. She shivered as a cool wind grasped at her hair and clothes, cicadas humming and the speckled expanse of stars overhead, and she watched as the barn doors cracked open an inch, expelling orange light.

 

            She took in the silhouette of Lena’s form and considered telling her what had transpired, but hesitated and made for the front door of her house instead. Stepping inside, she bolted the door shut behind her and leant back against it, Krypto raising his head from his paws where he stretched before the smouldering coals of a fire.

 

            Making herself some bitter tea, Kara drank it before the fire as she scratched behind her dog’s ears and stared into the low-burning flames before banking the fire and turning off the lamps. Kicking off her muck-stained boots she fell into bed in her undershirt and felt Krypto’s heavy weight at her feet, the smell of horse and hay clinging to her from her evening spent talking in the barn to the most unlikeliest of companions.

 

            Kara’s mind was heavy with thoughts of what to do as she tried to sleep. She had every right to kick Lena out of her barn and off her land, Witch Doctor or not, but she did need the help and the pitiful look in Lena’s eyes always made her resolve to strengthen to let her stay. She didn’t know what made the Necromancer so afraid, only that she would do what she could to hide her, no matter Alex’s warnings.

 

            The next morning, Lena was already up when Kara rose with the dawn. The day still clung to a purplish tint of night, the grass and hills smudged as the sun rose, and Lena walked amidst the horses as they snorted and baulked and then quietened with gentle pats on their noses.

 

            Brewing coffee, Kara carried two tin cups outside and leaned against the wooden fence of the paddock. She watched as Lena smoothly mounted, riding bareback on a spirited mare as she let her tire herself out before reining her in in front of Kara. Reaching down, she took the extending cup, her fingers and cheeks pink from the early-morning cold.

 

            “Who was here last night?” Lena asked, her breath hanging before her.

 

            “My sister. Don’t worry, she’s going away for a while. Came to say goodbye,” Kara dourly told her, ruffling her unkempt hair.

 

            “It’s not me who looks worried,” Lena murmured.

 

            Waving a hand as she chuckled weakly, Kara sipped her coffee. “Don’t fret none. I ain’t worried about her; she can look after herself better than most.”

 

            “Where’s she going?”

 

            Chewing on her lip, Kara shrugged and narrowed her eyes out at the plains, avoiding Lena’s eyes. “She’s following up a trail. Nothing you need mind yourself with.”

 

            “Yes, ma’am,” Lena murmured, touching the brim of her wide hat and draining her coffee.

 

            She set the tin cup down on the post of the fence and dug her heels into the flank of the restless horse. Kara watched her for a long moment, her eyes a stormy blue and watchful as a hawk, taking in the way Lena’s braid whipped behind her, the form of her sitting straight, moving with the motions of the spirited horse. It reared a few times, trampling the packed earth, but Lena clung to its mane without a flicker of concern.

 

            Knocking on the post as she pressed her lips into a flat line, Kara quelled her concerns with the shake of her head and picked up the empty cups. In the kitchen, she made them a thick porridge for breakfast and that was that, the companionable silence becoming all too familiar to them as Lena took up space in Kara’s kitchen, as if she’d been there all along. And Kara didn’t tell her what Alex had said or tell her she needed to go; she told her about a fence that needed fixing on the border of her property and how she needed to go into town for supplies.

 

            Life continued on much as it had been, two weeks stretching into the third as Alex went away and the two of them were left alone, miles out of town as they tended to the ranch. Dust storms and rainstorms blew past, a mare gave birth to a healthy foal, and Lena made progress with the horses. But they were complacent, thinking that there were no other eyes around, no one besotted with Kara enough to venture out to the ranch, until it brought trouble knocking a few days later.

 

            Knuckles rapped on the doorframe and Kara turned and wiped her hands on a cloth, stepping up the lip to the main decking of the house as she ducked through the door. Her hair was unkempt and curling out of its braid, an apprehensive yet sunny smile on her face as she hushed a barking Krypto.

 

            “Deputy Sheriff,” Kara said with mild surprise, wiping a hand on her skirt. “What brings you out this way? Has Alex been telling you to keep an eye on me?”

 

            With a grave sigh, Vasquez removed her hat and ducked inside, her eyes darting around the place. “I wish it were that pleasant, ma’am, but someone said you might be harbouring someone you ain’t allowed to be.”

 

            “Me?” Kara echoed, her eyebrows rising as her smile wilted a fraction. “I don’t know nothing about that.”

 

            “Is that so? I got reports of that Witch Doctor sniffing around again, and in your sister’s absence … well, that leaves me to do what’s needing done.”

 

            “Has she done something wrong?” Kara mildly asked, placing the cloth on the table and catching a flicker of movement behind Vasquez as Lena skulked on the porch out front, silent and out of sight as she eavesdropped. 

 

            Mouth thinning, Vasquez tucked one hand into the waistband of her pants and shook her head. “I’m sure you heard what went on out East, what with where Alex has gone and all. If she did what they’re saying she done … she ain’t the kind of criminal you want shacking up here with you, Miss Danvers. So if you know anything-“

 

            Lena’s footsteps thudded on the planks as she made herself known, Vasquez turning as her hand twitched towards her holstered gun. At the sight of Lena, in her worn clothes, Necromancer coat left in the barn, hatless and unarmed, she could’ve been any young woman working a ranch. But she had that medallion around her neck and that tangible air of danger that made Vasquez straighten up, raising her chin as she sized the slender Necromancer up.

 

            “Ma’am,” Vasquez said, “I ain’t looking for trouble, so if you’ll come quietly …”

 

            “Yes, ma’am,” Lena murmured, ducking her head.

 

            Anger knifed through Kara in an uncharacteristic flare, white-hot and making her cheeks turn splotchy as she watched Vasquez take a pair of manacles from her belt.

 

            “Now hold on a damn minute-“

 

            “The law‘s the law, Kara,” Vasquez sighed. “I gotta take her ‘til she’s cleared. ‘Fore anyone else gets hurt.”

 

            Scoffing, Kara’s face pinched with worry as she stewed in quiet anger, arms folded over her chest as she watched the manacles clap around Lena’s thin wrists. And as much as she wished to deny it, panic seized her as she watched Lena duck her head and stroll outside into the morning’s sunshine.

 

            “You’re making a mistake,” Kara heatedly replied, stepping out onto her porch and folding her arms over her chest. “You can’t just lock her up.”

 

            “I can; I’m the Deputy Sheriff, it’s quite literally my job, ma’am,” Vasquez wearily replied.

 

            She nodded her head toward her grazing horse and Lena made for it without complaint. That only infuriated Kara more, the way Lena so easily welcomed everyone else’s orders, allowing them to lock her up or turn her out or hurl curses and worse at her.

 

            “You’re just gonna let her take you?”

 

            “Not much I can do about it, is there?” Lena asked, gesturing with her shackled hands as she squinted at Kara, the sun in her eyes as she stood beside the horse.

 

            Making a scathing sound of contempt, Kara shook her head and dusted her hands, but lingered outside as she watched Vasquez boost Lena onto the horse’s back, hauling herself into the saddle before her and touching the brim of her hat before she set off down the long path to the main road into Midvale.

 

            Scowling, Kara shook her head and moved off the porch to draw water from the well to fill the troughs. She worked beneath the hot sun, the back of her neck protected by the kerchief tied around it, her palms rough as she hauled buckets and mucked out manure and used Comet to help drag a fallen tree back towards the house, getting to work splitting its bleached limbs into logs with an axe. 

 

            Her muscles were aching from a hard day’s work by the time the sun started to set, the sky streaked orange and violet as she washed herself clean and thought angrily of Lena. All of her belongings were still in the barn, from her horse to her gun and grimoire, and Kara chewed wild mint in the damp room of earthen floors and crumbling bricks as she pickled beets amidst the bundles of herbs and food.

 

            It was almost completely dark before her frustration made her restless enough to do something about it. The sky was a deep blue, the first stars appearing like specks of silver, and Kara found herself donning her coat, hat and snatching up her rifle from inside the house. Saddling Comet in the barn, she hauled herself into the saddle and ordered Krypto to stay before flicking the reins.

 

            Night descended as she rode the few miles into town, a chill seeping into it as the warmth of the day faded. It was a familiar route and Kara stewed in her simmering anger as Comet kept a steady pace, moving with the horse’s lurching gate as she gripped her rifle in the other hand.

 

            The town was alive with muffled laughter and music, an off-key piano being played in a dingy saloon, women spilling out of gambling halls and brothers, drunk and raucous and freed of their husbands. Soldiers loitered about, playing cards outside guard huts, old men smoking on the main boardwalk while the sound of a keening fiddle spilt out of the hotel. She caught sight of Nia leaning over the wooden railing as she called out to Querl Dox, leaving the bank after a long day, and tugging at his collar with nerves at the girl who was sweet on him.

 

            At the sight of Kara, Nia called out a greeting and asked if she needed to get J’onn to stable her horse for the night. Kara typically only came into town so late with the intention of staying with Alex for the evening, but she had other plans this time and declined the offer, barely a thin smile for her friend as she swung down into the mud. 

 

            The heels of her boots sank into the churned earth as she rounded Comet and hitched him to a post, touching the brim of her hat in silent greeting as M’gann stepped outside to fetch Nia. Her friends eyed the rifle in her grasp with doubt, and Kara turned her back on them as she made for the Sheriff’s office, oblivious to their frantic whispers before they disappeared into the saloon.

 

            Kara’s footsteps were loud on the planks as she strode up the steps and opened the door to the Sheriff’s office, announcing her arrival as she filled the doorway with her tall stature. It was quiet inside, dimly lit by a couple of lamps, and her eyes landed on the deputy, who was lounging with the remains of supper amidst wooden filing cabinets and policing equipment.

 

            “Why, Miss Danvers, why am I not surprised,” Vasquez sighed with exasperation, taking her boots off the desk and setting down the paper book she was reading. 

 

            Kara’s eyes strayed to Lena, locked in one of two spacious cells, the iron bars keeping her trapped inside. She was sitting on a low cot, looking content, if a little bored.

 

            “Open up the cell.”

 

            With a quiet laugh, Vasquez straightened up in her seat, boots striking the floor as she gave Kara an apologetic smile.

 

            “Oh, no, I ain’t allowed to do that. You can leave any baked goods you might’ve brung with me, though. Can’t even let you stay for a visit, I’m afraid.”

 

            Mouth thinning as she kept her rifle pointed at the ground, Kara made a low sound of displeasure at the back of her throat. “I didn’t bake anything. I want to take her home with me.”

 

            “She ain’t going nowhere ‘til the Sheriff-“

 

            As Vasquez pushed herself to her feet, Kara levelled the rifle at her, calm and unbothered as she gestured slightly. “Take off your gun belt.”

 

            “Ma’am, please.”

 

            Biting back a weary sigh, Kara pulled back the bolt and slammed a bullet into place, watching as the deputy cautiously raised her hands.

 

            “Now, hold on-“

 

            “Take it off.”

 

            “Alright,” Vasquez slowly said, reaching for the buckle of the belt.

 

            She undid one, setting the pistol and cartridge belt down on the desk, and then unbuckling the other to set it down beside it.

 

            “Good, now open up the cell.”

 

            At Vasquez’s hesitation, Kara swallowed thickly and raised the barrel of her rifle again, adjusting her sweaty palms on the polished wood.

 

            “Do it. Or you’re gonna be awful damn sick from a bullet in your chest.”

 

            Lena was silent in her cell, but Kara could see the shifting unease in her, masking the mild surprise of Kara’s recklessness as she bargained for her freedom. Sighing, the deputy scuffed her booted feet along the worn, dusty floors and jangled the keys as she fitted the correct one into the lock. It scraped as it turned and she looped an arm through the bars as she leaned against it and arched an eyebrow at Kara.

 

            “Now, Doc, why don’t you come on out of there, and Vasquez … you go on in,” Kara ordered, her voice hitching with uncertainty as she realised the magnitude of the trouble she would be in.

 

            “Ma’am,” Lena warily hesitated, glancing to the deputy and back to Kara as she lingered on the edge of her rumbled cot.

 

            “Do it,” Kara said, gesturing with the rifle.

 

            Climbing to her feet, Lena ambled out of the cell and stepped aside, looking at Vasquez, who was giving Kara a venomous look. Recognising defeat, the deputy pushed past into the cell and Lena held her hand out for the keys. At Kara’s nod, the Necromancer shut the barred cell door and paused.

 

            “Oh, uh, Deputy, you’re going to have to show me which key. I don’t know.”

 

            Lowering her rifle, Kara waited impatiently, brimming with agitation as she watched the murmured conversation between the other two women as they locked the door up. 

 

            Turning, Kara stalked out of the jail, her feet thundering on the steps before she trampled through churned mud, making for where she’d hitched Comet. Lena followed behind, almost unwillingly as she glanced about uneasily.

 

            “Kara Danvers, what in the world do you think you’re doing?” a voice called out, chiding her.

 

            Grasping her rifle, Kara scowled as she rounded on the mayor striding towards her with her hands on her hips, summoned by her friends to stop her from her rash actions. Nudging the brim of her hat up a tad, Kara made a low sound of annoyance at the back of her throat and jerked a finger to the horse as she brushed past Lena, the escapee dipping her head and quietly hitching the horse.

 

            “It ain’t fair, Kelly. You know it ain’t. You can’t keep a woman locked up when she’s committed no crimes.”

 

            “Now, how do you know that?” her sister-in-law asked with faint amusement, a glimmer in her dark eyes as her lips quirked wryly.

 

            “I just know it,” Kara frustratedly replied. “And I won’t allow her to rot in a jail cell ‘til Alex returns. And- and if you don’t like that … well, ma’am, you’re gonna have to lock me up with her.”

 

            “And who’d look after them poor horses if you was gone too?”

 

            Mouth opening and closing, Kara’s scowl deepened as she flushed with embarrassment. “Well, it ain’t likely going to do them any good if I got no one to help me break them anyways, so … I’m taking her home with me. She ain’t running nowhere and you know where I live.”

 

            She phrased it like a statement but she lingered with a worried look on her face as she held her ground with the mayor. Kara loved Kelly like family, but even she knew that it would only extend so far, and if the mayor had Lena locked back up, short of starting a shootout, Kara wouldn’t be able to do a thing about it, save join her in the cell like she’d threatened. Blowing the air out of her cheeks, Kelly shook her head, mouth a grim line as she stared Kara down.

 

            “You Danvers women are the bane of my existence, you know that? Go on now, off with you.”

 

            “But-“

 

            Vasquez came lurching outside, bristling with anger, which was only mildly tempered by J’onn, his big hand clamping down on her shoulder and bringing her to a stop a few feet behind Kelly. Kara gave her a sheepish smile of apology, her shoulders rounding as if you curl in on herself.

 

            “I ain’t protecting you when the Sheriff’s back in town,” Kelly warned her with a pointed finger. “Oh, aye, I knew she was there, Kara Danvers, so don’t be thinking you’re as smart as all that. Alex told me ‘fore she left and said Miss Lena here was leaving, so you can sort that out yourself when your sister gets back and finds her shacking up with you.”

 

            Cheeks reddening, Kara scuffed a toe through the dirt as she hung her head. “It ain’t like that, Kelly.”

 

            “It ain’t my business neither way, not if it keeps the peace in this town. Locking up the Deputy, may the Lord have mercy, girl, has that Witch Doctor made you lose your damned mind already? What kind of lawless land do you think this is?”

 

            “I didn’t want to hurt Vasquez, and I figured someone would find her, come morning.”

 

            “Go on now,” Kelly shooed her, clicking her tongue in annoyance and waving a hand dismissively. “Better her out of town than in it. Don’t let her back here; I tried to convince everyone the good her services could do for us, but they won’t take to it and I’d hate to have blood in the streets. Keep your own eyes open too, mind you; might be that folks might pay you a visit in the middle of the night. The kind you won’t like.”

 

            The blossoming look of joy was quickly quelled with Kelly’s warning, sobering Kara up, and she nodded quickly as she swallowed thickly.

 

            “Thank you,” she hoarsely murmured.

 

            Turning, she made for Comet and swung up into the saddle, holding him still as Lena mounted behind her. She was a solid warmth at Kara’s back, pressed up behind her, their thighs flush while she gripped the back of the saddle. Clicking her tongue, Kara urged Comet onwards and led them out of the town centre to a smattering of watchful eyes, nosey and suspicious.

 

            Riding double on the way back to the ranch, they went slow to not tire out the horse, and Lena felt the slight chill in her cotton shirtsleeves as she huddled behind Kara, who seemed to radiate warmth like a furnace. The Witch Doctor couldn’t help but worry as they left the town behind, the few miles slipping away as she dwelled in her troubled thoughts. 

 

            Eventually, Kara brought them up the long dirt track to the ranch, still lit by the faint glow of the fire, and Krypto barked a warning at their approach before Kara silenced him. Swiftly dismounting, Lena held the bridle and patted Comet’s nose as Kara dismounted and led him to the barn to remove his tack and brush him down.

 

            Lena reached out and snagged her arm before she could lead the horse more than a few steps, and ignored the barb of pain as Kara flinched from her touch and winced slightly with guilt. She couldn’t blame her, of course, because for all she’d helped Lena, it was still deeply ingrained in her to not trust a Witch Doctor.

 

            “Hey,” Lena softly pressed on, her face a mask of concern, “you shouldn’t have done that. I don’t want to cause you any trouble.”

 

            “You ain’t causing any,” Kara murmured, her eyes fixated on the barn. “But I weren’t going to let you rot there ‘til they decided what to do with you.”

 

            “The Sheriff … she went to look into what happened in Silver Plume?”

 

            Doffing her hat, Kara rubbed at her forehead. “Folks just want to know the truth. If it’s just you … well, they’ll do what they have to, but if there’s more than that … we need to know if any danger’s heading out here.”

 

            “It will,” Lena firmly replied, a bitter taste in her mouth as she looked down. “If word gets out that I’m here, it will. I’m not lying … and he’ll come for me.”

 

            Giving her a sympathetic look, Kara sighed softly. “What did you do to make him so mad?”

 

            “Aside from stealing his money?” Lena asked with a wry smile as she glanced up. “Not a whit. The only offence I’ve caused my dear brother is not joining his righteous cause of chaos and war.”

 

            “Now, what war would that be?”

 

            “It’s nothing you need concern yourself with, ma’am. But I should leave you now. I’ll be on my way, come first light.”

 

            Snorting, Kara gave her a grim look of amusement. “You won’t be doing anything of the kind, I’m afraid. Alex wouldn’t have sought justice if you’d moved on unseen, but … well, what with the whole town knowing now … they ain’t going to let it rest if you run off.”

 

            “I can’t stay,” Lena protested.

 

            Cocking her head to the side, Kara’s eyes creased at the corners as she smiled slightly. “What’s stopping you? If you’re as innocent as you say-“

 

            Scoffing, Lena’s lips curled with contempt and she ground her teeth. “You don’t even like my kind, so why’re you fighting so hard for me?”

 

            “Maybe I just like the company,” Kara murmured after a long moment.

 

            Lena’s mouth opened and closed as she watched Kara urge Comet on to the barn, and after a moment she blew the air out of her cheeks and followed after her. 

 

            In companionable silence, they settled Comet down in a stall adjoining Hecate’s, Lena brushing his flank down as Kara raked fresh hay and scooped out oats before the rancher dusted her hands and made for the door. Hesitating, she glanced over her shoulder at Lena.

 

            “You must be starving. I can’t imagine the slop they serve at the jail would’ve filled you up.”

 

            Lena softly laughed and shrugged. “I’ve certainly had worse.”

 

            Lips twitching, Kara shrugged in return. “Well, my cooking can’t be worse, if you’d like a bite before bed.”

 

            Hesitating, Lena ducked her head in acceptance and followed after Kara. They crossed the trampled ground to the low house, and Kara unlocked the door before ushering them and Krypto inside. Adding a log to the fire, she set her hat down and the rifle against the wall, before hanging her coat up and rinsing her hands in the basin.

 

            “Take a seat. It won’t be much tonight; I don’t have it in me for cooking right about now. How’d you like some moonshine though? Might take the edge off the night.”

 

            Lena didn’t reply but Kara poured her a healthy dose from a clay jug all the same, burning and unrefined as it went down, but warming and strong all the same. Quiet and watchful, Lena sipped the moonshine and scratched Krypto between his ears as he sat beside her seat, and quietly thanked Kara when a plate of cold chicken, leftover unleavened bread and blanched greens were set down before her.

 

            As ravenous as she was, unwilling to touch the food in the jail in case it had been laced with toxins, Lena forced herself to eat slowly. Kara didn’t say much to start with as she picked chicken off the bones and fed the scraps to Krypto, who crunched them at her feet, but she wiped her greasy fingers on a cloth and turned to Lena after a moment as she cleared her throat.

 

            “So, you’ll stay?”

 

            “Until your sister returns,” Lena ceded, taking a sip of her drink.

 

            “And when she clears you?”

 

            Slowly chewing a bite of bread, Lena shifted and swallowed. “It might not do for me to linger long, ma’am. I’ll do what I can for the horses until then though, but … he’s after me, and I’d be risking your good hospitality to endanger you.”

 

            “I’ve got a gun.”

 

            “He’s got blood magic.”

 

            “And so do you.”

 

            “It’s not all-powerful.”

 

            “You could bring any of us back though, right? Maybe Kelly was right and it would be good to have you around-“

 

            Sighing heavily, Lena rubbed her forehead with a knuckle and closed her eyes. “It wouldn’t. I have a job to do, I have a duty I enlisted for. No one here could afford my services outside of my own charitable prices, and once my supplies run out … well, I’d need to go somewhere to restock them, and they’ve got a bounty on my head.”

 

            “Surely if they knew it was your brother committing these acts-“

 

            “It wouldn’t matter,” Lena forlornly interrupted, “he’s turning them, one by one, to his ideology. It’s been slowly happening and it’s spread out west now, and they’ll believe what he says is true.”

 

            “And what ideology is that now?”

 

            Suppressing another sigh, Lena grimaced and set her fork down, leaning back in the chair as she turned the small knife in her hand. Her eyes were dark and her cheeks hollowed out by the shadows and dim light of the fire, a ghostly creature that Kara could believe would gut her and steal her bones, if not for the melancholy defeat on her face.

 

            “My brother believes … he thinks that the war could’ve been tipped in the favour of the Confederacy if they’d enlisted the help of Necromancers. There were a few, of course, on both sides, but the Witch Doctors were mostly there for healing and resurrecting. They never used the dead as puppets - it goes against our oaths and tenets - but my brother thinks that … we should use what is supplied to us. His practice is rogue, illegal, and it isn’t sanctioned by any of the Witch Doctors.”

 

            With a quiet snort of laughter, Lena’s cheek dimpled with a crooked smile as she pierced the tip of her finger with the knife and watched a bead of blood well up. Magic fizzled in the drop and she reached into the pouch at her waist for a milk tooth, drawing it out and turning it in her nimble grasp, the creamy-white smeared red.

 

            Crunching it between her fingertips as she burned the spark of magic inside it, Lena reached down into the earth, feeling for the array of bones, scattered or half-formed, and found the skeleton of a snake beneath the house, where it had died years before. Working it up, she climbed to her feet and opened the door to the slithering skeleton, stopping to let it wend itself around her wrist and finger.

 

            Turning, she took in the guarded look on Kara’s face and held her hand out. The snake was barely a foot long, a baby, its bones held together by magic as it wound around Lena’s arm.

 

            “It’s not the same as a full resurrection. There’s no soul to it. My brother wants to create an army of the undead to seize control of the Southern states and instate himself as the governing power. And he’s slaughtering and robbing mining towns to fund it. There’s nothing quite so convincing as human greed. He’ll buy as many Necromancers to his cause as he can, giving them that which has been denied them for far too long; power and respect.”

 

            “How do we stop him?”

 

            Eyes snapping up to Kara’s, Lena smiled faintly. “I wish I knew. All I know is that … once he’s done what he wants to, there’s going to be a lot of bodies to bury.”

 

            “You won’t be able to save them?”

 

            “Once the soul is too far gone … nothing can bring them back. There’s a window of opportunity, and stages to resurrecting them - merely a puppet, or perhaps a mindless zombie, and then true life with free-will - and if they’re not brought back completely, the best thing for them is a bone bullet and a grave to rest in.”

 

            Lena let the snake slither back outside and burrow back underground before she snapped the thread of magic and let the bones separate, still once more. Locking the door, she reclaimed her seat and leaned back, watching Kara as she sipped from her cup.

 

            “The miners …”

 

            Shaking her head, Lena set her cup down. “They would’ve been rotting a long time. To bring back someone like that … it would be a curse. It’s why my profession works primarily as healers, to stave off death before it arrives, and to use our ability only as a last resort once the inevitable comes.”

 

            “How many times can you bring someone back?”

 

            Lena idly rubbed at her forehead as her expression clouded. “When we resurrect someone … we make the body anew. If one dies of heart failure, the heart is healthy once more, or a broken bone that pierced a lung is no longer broken. All wounds and ailments are gone. One could live indefinitely that way, indeed most Necromancers do in some capacity before exhaustion catches up to them. We still age.”

 

            Blinking in surprise, Kara’s eyebrows rose slightly at the facet of information. “You never die?”

 

            “We’re never really dead or alive,” Lena cynically retorted. “We just exist.”

 

            “And you … is that- you’ll live forever?”

 

            Lena hummed, deliberating as she cocked her head to the side, looking at the swept floorboards as the wind whistled through the cracks. A log popped and her lips pressed into a flat line, some unreadable darkness crossing her face as she murmured a reply.

 

            “No, I don’t think so.”

 

            “Why not? Don’t everyone want to be immortal?”

 

            “I’m not always … attached to being alive,” Lena haltingly replied. “Maybe I’ve just spent too much time on the other side, but … being brought back is always more painful than existing elsewhere.”

 

            Her sober demeanour changed as she raised her eyes and gave Kara an impish smile, draining her cup and leaning her elbows on the table as she laced her fingers together.

 

            “And what about you, Miss Danvers? Would you say yes to the chance for unlimited lives? To live recklessly and know there were very few consequences?”

 

            Kara let out a quiet scoff of laughter and shook her head as a smile curled her lips. “Well, now, ma’am, that’s entirely dependent on whether it was a life worth coming back to.”

 

            “They rarely are worth it,” Lena wearily sighed, nodding her thanks as Kara refilled her cup. “But maybe mine is just an empty cup with nothing worth filling it; I might feel different if I had a home, had people to love and who loved me. All I have is a horse and my craft, and that isn’t worth much in these parts.”

 

            Hesitating, Kara cocked her head to the side and opened her mouth, silent for a moment before she voiced her question. “Is it- is it true that you can … see the future?”

 

            Lena let out a bark of laughter and rolled her cup between her palms as she eyed her hair shrewdly. Jerking her chin towards her, Lena gave her a wry smile.

 

            “Why? Do you want me to tell you your destiny?”

 

            “No,” Kara murmured, ducking her head as she picked at the smoothed edge of the worn table, aiming for nonchalance. “Curiosity is all.”

 

            “You should be careful, Miss Danvers,” Lena whispered as she leaned forward. “Those God-fearing Christian’s might think you’re making a deal with the Devil if you start getting too curious about my craft.”

 

            Freezing, Kara peered at her, the fire illuminating the spark of fear in her eyes as she chewed on her bottom lip, hesitating. 

 

            “You don’t- I mean … the Devil- is that where your magic comes from? Don’t you ever … worry ‘bout what God thinks?”

 

            A regretful look passed Lena’s face and her mouth turned down at the corners as she hunched her shoulders. “I’ll let you in on a little secret, ma’am; there are no Gods, and the only devils I’ve ever encountered were made of flesh and blood, same as you and I.”

 

            Easing back, Lena picked up her knife and lifted it, the slightly blunted tip limned orange by the fire. She held her other hand out, upturned as it rested expectantly on the tabletop.

 

            “So if you’d really like to know what awaits you, by all means, I’d be happy to tell you. All I require is your blood.”

 

            Kara blanched, looking horrified as she cradled her hands to her chest. She brusquely pushed her chair back, legs screeching against the wooden floor as she fluidly rose to her feet, snatching dishes from the table and setting them in the sink. Lena could see the tension in her shoulders and a prickle of guilt welled up inside her; she’d pushed Kara’s tenuous trust too far for one night, eliciting a flicker of fear from her.

 

            Draining her drink, Lena set the cup down and climbed to her feet. “I’ll be retiring now. Thank you, ma’am. For the jail and the food.”

 

            Kara slowed her movements and turned her head slightly to the side, not looking at Lena but acknowledging her presence. “Night, then, Doc.”

 

            “Goodnight, Miss Danvers.”

 

            She parted with a quick pat to Krypto’s head before stepping outside, listening to the quick footsteps across the creaking floorboards to slam the bolt into place. Wearily sighing, Lena kicked up a clod of dust and dirt as she meandered towards the barn, warm from the whiskey and annoyed at herself. It was no use scaring away the only person outside of her craft who’d shown her any sort of welcome, but Lena wouldn’t pretend to be someone she wasn’t just to appease a kind stranger. She was cynical and wary and unused to socialising with someone for longer than it took to heal or resupply.

 

            Shutting herself into the barn for the night, she checked on Hecate and then bedded down, burrowing into the hay where she could hear mice squeaking, and covering herself with her blanket as the darkness blotted everything out. Despite her frustration, sleep was quick to come, too many years on the open road leading her to sleep under the worst conditions without hesitation, but Lena woke early feeling hollow and sullen.

 

            Kara was as polite and warm as ever though, setting out tea and porridge for breakfast before they got to work. It was familiar now, and Lena didn’t think about how Alex would be back soon, to toss her out or lock her up to be hanged for a crime she hadn’t committed - she had killed, but only in self-defence, and things like that were brushed aside in the west - but it still hung over the two of them like a pall. 

 

            One night, Lena woke to the sound of hooves approaching, multiple horses that set Krypto off barking in the house. She fetched her pistol from beside her, crouching in the dark as her other hand already scrambled through the pages of her grimoire, ready to tear a half-baked spell free. 

 

            The sound of something breaking was punctuated by a warning shot a minute later, the sound of hooves quickly retreating before Lena could even yank the barn door open. She looked small and unthreatening in the gloom, pale and pinched with panic as she adjusted her grip on the pistol, a spell crumpled in her other hand as she readied herself to call on the magic making her skin prickle.

 

            But against the night, she could see the tall shadow of Kara on the porch, moonlight illuminating the haze of smoke from the barrel of her rifle while Krypto raced down the path to the main road. Swallowing thickly, her heart hammering in her chest, Lena crossed halfway to the house, meeting Kara in the middle, both of them in their undershirts and socks.

 

            “Are you alright?” Lena asked.

 

            “They smashed a window. No harm done,” Kara said, a tremor in her voice - from fear or anger, Lena couldn’t discern. Her eyes strayed down to Lena’s gun and her expression clouded. “What were you going to do?”

 

            “Frighten them a little, that’s all,” Lena murmured.

 

            The crumpled spell would’ve summoned fire, enough to scorch the earth and create a wall to block the way to Kara’s house. The gun would’ve been for what came next, if they didn’t heed the warning, and a bone bullet wouldn’t bring them back if her aim was true enough.

 

            “Go back to bed,” Kara gently urged her. “Ain’t no one going to harm you under my roof.”

 

            “Ma’am.”

 

            Lena ruffled her long hair, the ghost of sleep but a memory to her as adrenaline coursed through her body. She knew she wouldn’t close her eyes for the rest of the night now, but looking at Kara’s sleepy face, blinking owlishly as she hid a yawn, she knew the rancher needed her rest but was stubborn enough to refuse in order to keep watch.

 

            Reaching out, Lena gently touched the sliver of skin at Kara’s wrist, a jolt running through her as she let her power affect the chemicals in Kara’s body. It was a small bit of magic, nothing more than the flip of a switch that made exhaustion wash over Kara, her eyes struggling to stay open. She wouldn’t have known it was Lena’s doing.

 

            “Get some rest.”

 

            Lena walked back toward the barn but lingered in the dark mouth of the doorway until she was sure Kara was safely back into bed. Only then did she settle down on the overturned crate and read by candlelight as the late hours of the night gave way to early morning.

 

            Up before the sunrise, she had planks sawn to the right length by the time Kara had cooked them breakfast. Then Lena lingered back in the grey pre-dawn light as she watched the other woman nail them over the jagged hole through the warped window of her house. It twisted Lena’s stomach with unease, knowing she risked both of their lives, but she couldn’t leave now, not when Kara could be in trouble for harbouring her and breaking her free from the jail.

 

            The days after that slipped by without any further disturbances, both of them falling back into that uneasy peace. They ate lunch on the front porch steps one day, shaded as they shared a jug of cold tea sweetened with sugar. One sunset, Kara took Lena out to an outcropping of rocks along a dwindling river, where the sloping land gave way to foothills. They shot rabbits and enjoyed supper in the long grasses, and just past sunset, the sky shifted rapidly from shades of burnt orange into a deep violet blue. The women sat in awed silence, as the plains shimmered a thousand indescribable shades of crimson in the wavering mirage of heat that dimmed with the encroaching night.

 

            Alex was due back any day now, as Lena bordered on nearly a month spent at the ranch. She spent hours each day with the horses, glad for her years in the saddle, or else she would’ve hardly been able to walk. As it was, she was a mess of scrapes and bruises from falls off the backs of reading horses, angry bites and quick kicks leaving her purple and blue.

 

            At night, once the work was done, Kara would sometimes sneak into the doorway of the barn, watching as Lena lifted her shirt or rolled her pants up to heal the injuries. Lena always knew she was there, that spark of life in her periphery always part of her awareness, but she’d pay her no attention, hoping that displays of her healing would ease Kara’s skittish discomfort at her magic. 

 

            Lena would grind herbs up, sometimes into a paste, sometimes a tincture, and swallow the mixture or apply it as a poultice, and for the worst ones, with broken bones that send throbbing pangs of pain shooting through her body, she’d cut her fingertips and pluck teeth from her cherished supply, blood and bone mingling with the aroma of herbs as she leached blood from beneath the surface of the skin, fading bruises or knitting the bone back together. She never fully healed herself, not wanting to spend too much of her power in case she was in danger, and so she’d splint her bitten fingers or wrap her trampled foot tightly in bandages and get on with it. Just like Lena always had.

 

            She was in the barn one midday, sweating and pale, her left arm a mess of blood and muscle as the yellowish bone poked through the skin from a nasty fall. Lena had to admit that her relative immunity to death left her reckless, her years around horses leaving her fearless, which induced more injuries than was wise. This time, the bone had shattered and knifed through her arm, blood quickly soaking through her shirt as she’d turned a nasty shade of grey, her arm hanging limply at her side.

 

            Kara hadn’t been in sight, so Lena had stumbled to the barn, biting back an agonising groan as her vision furred at the edges as the sour taste of bile rose at the back of her throat. With a trembling hand, she peeled back her shirtsleeve and opened her healing chest, scrambling for willow bark for pain and amaranth leaves to help clot the blood. 

 

            She chewed them quickly through clenched teeth and burned through a large molar as her vision blurred and pain knifed through her arm. The bone pulling itself back together was nauseating, her skin crawling from the sensation as she clung to her magic and consciousness. New bone fibres grew and reached for each other, latching onto both halves and Lena was too absorbed in her healing to hear the galloping sound of hooves arriving.

 

            The clamour of voices tore her from her work a minute later as Kara stepped into the barn, someone else behind her, a question half-formed on her tongue before she trailed off at the sight of Lena’s arm.

 

            “What in God’s name- is that bone?”

 

            “It’s nothing,” Lena rasped, swaying slightly in her seat as she staunched the bleeding. “You should leave. It’s not for the faint of stomach.”

 

            “I’ve seen plenty worse, but that ain’t natural,” Kara shakily replied, twisting her hat in her hands as she stared at Lena’s exposed bone, looking pesky at the sight of it.

 

            Lena squeezed her eyes shut and then opened them, taking a swig of whiskey and blinking back the pain to focus on the sight of Kelly. She looked ruffled and stricken, mostly on account of Lena’s broken arm, but harried in a way that spoke of distressing matters. Out of politeness, Lena ducked her head slightly.

 

            “Madam Mayor.”

 

            “One of your kind’s come through town asking questions,” Kelly said, cutting the niceties short. “Questions about you. It won’t be long until someone tells her they seen you, and where you’re staying, but it don’t seem like good business to be had between you.”

 

            “What did she look like?” Lena cautiously asked.

 

            Shrugging, Kelly wiped her sleeve across her brow. “Brown hair. Same coat as you. She had a- a rotting dog with her. Sacrilegious, I’m telling you.”

 

            As Lena stiffened, Kara cocked her head to the side. “Do you know her?”

 

            Lurching to her feet, tying her handkerchief around the gaping wound, Lena made a scathing sound of contempt at the back of her throat. Donning her coat and hat, she buckled on her gun belt, grimoire holstered and teeth purse tied to it, and gave Kara a bitter smile.

 

            “Aye. I know her. She’s the one who shot me when I collapsed on your doorstep.”

 

            “What does she want with you?”

 

            “There’s a bounty on my head,” Lena reminded her, shouldering past her, looking faint and unsteady as Kelly instinctively moved away from her, leaving a clear path out through the door. “I intend to keep my head attached.”

 

            A panicked sound of surprise slipped from Kara’s mouth as she followed her outside, snagging the sleeve of Lena’s coat. “You can’t be going nowhere in that condition. Your arm is near split in two .”

 

            Snorting, Lena wiped the ash from the tooth on her thigh and made for Kelly’s horse. Gritting her teeth as she cradled her left arm to her side, Lena got a foot in the stirrup despite Kara’s resistance and swung up onto its back.

 

            “A broken arm is the least of my worries, ma’am,” Lena said as the horse stepped, anxious at the new rider.

 

            She spurred the horse into motion then, leaving the spluttering rancher and the mayor behind in the dust before they scrambled to saddle a horse and pursue her. The lurching gait of the horse jarred her arm with each step, an agonising pain that she endured, burning another tooth as she clung to the saddle with her knees, trying to repair what damage she could. She’d lost a fair amount of blood though and the motion of the horse made her too nauseous to concentrate, the edges of her vision darkening.

 

            Eventually, she made it to the town though, still in the saddle but stumbling as if she was drunk as she made it to the main thoroughfare and dismounted. The sight of that cream dusted with red piping made her vision turn red, a flush in her pale cheeks as she stormed forward.

 

            “Witch Doctor,” Lena shouted to catch the woman’s attention.

 

            She turned with a mild look of surprise on her face, which slackened as she watched Lena fist a tooth and the earth before her churn. Her motions mirrored Lena’s and the residents of Midvale skittered away from the ensuing duel, yet close enough to fearfully watch from the awnings of shopfronts. That rotting hound snarled at Lena, its ruined vocal cords letting out a broken bark as a skeleton clawed its way free from the earth.

 

            Lena was quicker than the other woman, having gotten the jump on her, and she controlled it with clawed hands, her fury driving her through her pain. The skeleton was blocked by one summoned by the other woman, smaller and not well-chosen from the dead beneath their feet. It could’ve been a child, if not an adult on the shorter side, and was no match for Lena’s bigger boned one she’d pulled forth.

 

            Her own skeleton lashed out with a big fist, knocking the jaw from the smaller one, before the dog leapt into the fray, tearing the ulna from the forearm and pushing Lena’s chosen fighter off balance. That was how they fought their duels, with chosen representatives, battling it out until guns were drawn, if warranted. And Lena did warrant it, watching as the hound tore the femur and left her skeleton off-kilter with one leg, the child’s remains now without a skull but still moving about in a manner that terrified the townsfolk.

 

            She heard a thundering horse behind her, knew the moment Kara arrived, but it all faded, distant and tinny as soldiers shouted, shouldering rifles as they spilt out of a watch hut, while the Deputy barked orders that went unheeded. And as the skeletons fell apart, the teeth they held burnt away and blood traced from eyes and noses, Lena reached for her gun first.

 

            Pulling it from the holster, she spun it around her finger and fired off a shot before the other Necromancer had a chance to fully draw her own. It was a merciful shot though, taking her in the stomach, a mirror to Lena’s own injury, and she stumbled backwards, falling into the dust.

 

            Gun smoking, Lena stalked forward, looking ghastly and dangerous, adjusting the grip on the bone handle of the pistol as she bristled with anger. Kicking the gun from her acquaintance's hand, she pressed her foot to the woman’s stomach, eliciting a gasp of pain as she pointed her pistol at her face.

 

            Hands up, the woman’s face spasmed with fear, and Lena had the sense that she’d never been killed before. She still clung to that fear, and it was both amusing and pitiful.

 

            “Please,” the woman rasped, bloodless lips stammering. “Please, don’t.”

 

            “Why shouldn’t I?” Lena snapped. “You shot me.”

 

            “The bounty-“

 

            A quiet snarl curled Lena’s lip. “Who set the bounty?”

 

            The woman licked her lips but didn’t reply until Lena put pressure on the gunshot wound and she cried out. Face screwing up in agony, the tendons in her neck taut, the woman grasped Lena’s boot to try and alleviate the pressure.

 

            “Okay, okay. I’ll tell you. It was- it was Selena.”

 

            Face crumpling, Lena stared down at her with bewilderment. “That old hag from the waypoint?”

 

            “Mhm. That’s her,” the woman quickly agreed. “She said you was to blame for a massacre. A wrongful breach of our tenets. I-I was just- just following orders.”

 

            Bending over, Lena gave her a contemptuous look. “Your orders were lies.”

 

            “How was I supposed to know that now, hm?”

 

            “Alright, alright, you best put that gun away now, Doc,” a new voice said.

 

            Looking up, Lena blinked in surprise at the sight of Alex standing there, travel-worn and wary as she pointed a gun at Lena. There was caution in her brown eyes, as if waiting for Lena to strike like a wild animal, but Lena would never have harmed her, and after a tense moment, she holstered her pistol and raised her hands as she stepped off the woman’s stomach.

 

            Alex lowered her own and holstered it as she moved behind Lena, grabbing her by the collar of her coat as she muttered quietly.

 

            “How did I know I was going to come back here to find you not gone. Raising the dead in the streets though? You’re mighty foolish, Miss Luthor; some might think you have one of them death wishes yourself. And ain’t no one ‘round here going to be able to bring you back.”

 

            “My apologies, Sheriff. And welcome back; I hope your trip was … enlightening.”

 

            Alex scoffed as she propelled Lena towards the jail by the back of her coat, pulling her to a stop a moment later to jerk her chin at the other Necromancer.

 

            “Take that one to the doctor for sewing up.”

 

            “May as well let her bleed out,” a soldier with a scarred face said, spitting in the dust at the woman’s feet as Kara warily helped haul her up. “Ain’t worth saving someone like that. Better one less rat and we all sleep safer, I says.”

 

            “Well, I’m the Sheriff here, Lockwood, and I says she’s getting stitched up, you hear me?”

 

            There were grumbles through the crowd of onlookers, but Alex wasn’t so soft that they didn’t heed her orders. And Lena wasn’t likely to get off easy this time as she was guided up the steps, sagging from blood loss and the pain that adrenaline couldn’t quite mask. It was almost a relief when Alex opened a cell door and gave her a gentle push inside and Lena collapsed on the grimy cot with a heavy sigh as the key turned in the lock.

 

            Peeling off her coat, Lena looked down at the blood-soaked handkerchief wrapped around her arm and slumped back against the wall, looking pale and clammy. And as the edges of her vision dimmed and unconsciousness crept in, dulling the pain, Lena settled in for another night in jail - this time without a foolish blonde to rescue her.

5. Chapter 5

            “She alright in there?”

 

            Lena peeled her eyes open at the sound of Kara’s concerned voice, hauling herself into a sitting position as she gritted her teeth against the pain in her arm. Her brow was beaded with sweat and her face ashen, but she still gave Kara a wry smile as she brooded in the confines of the cell.

 

            “Ma’am.”

 

            “Caught her with them teeth,” Alex said, shuddering as she gave Lena a sceptical look. “Don’t know what she was planning on doing with them.”

 

            “I have a fever, Sheriff,” Lena wearily called over to her, a sharp smile on her face as her eyelids shuttered and she sagged against the wall. “You’re more than welcome to come and see for yourself. I don’t bite - much.”

 

            Alex made a sound of irritation as she tucked her thumbs into her gun belt and shook her head, eyes trained on her sister. Kara’s face was pinched with worry as she eyed Lena’s slumped posture and ghastly pallor, anxiously biting her lip as she held a cloth-wrapped bundle in her hands.

 

            “You know, she did hurt her arm,” Kara insisted. “Might be that it’s paining her, somewhat.”

 

            “She ain’t made a fuss.”

 

            “She ain’t likely,” Kara scoffed, mouth turning upwards with amusement. “She don’t like talking much, or asking for help.”

 

            With a contemptuous scoff, Alex gave her sister a disgruntled look. “You seem to know her mighty well, considering she was s’posed to be gone ‘fore I came back.”

 

            Shifting guiltily, Kara shrugged as she gave her a sheepish smile. “Well … was she guilty?”

 

            Lips twisting ruefully, Alex folded her arms over her chest and glanced over at Lena. “Was her brother, they says. They chased her for miles and I found the bodies where she shot them dead. She might be innocent, but she’s dangerous. Took one bullet each for her to take them down; you know how hard it is to shoot like that?”

 

            “I have an idea,” Kara warily agreed. “What d’you mean to do with her now, then? You can’t lock her up until her death.”

 

            Sighing, Alex raked a hand through her hair and dropped down onto her seat behind the desk. Leaning back, she was silent for a moment before reaching out to pull Lena’s gun from its holster, eyeing the bone handle and raising it to look down the length of the barrel. After a second, Alex holstered it again and looked up at her sister, expectant and as naïve as always.

 

            “She’s disturbing the peace-“

 

            “That woman shot her. I reckon that was warranted.”

 

            “So she says. Might be that woman is the victim here, so I’ll have to wait until they finish stitching her up. Either way, she’ll be spending the night here, and more likely a few days after that.”

 

            “You’re wrong,” Kara quietly objected.

 

            Giving her a grim look, Alex shook her head. “I ain’t wrong, Kara; I’m the Sheriff, I make the law here. And it’s keeping you safe, whether you like it or not. Now, go on, I got things to catch up on. I’ll see you later for supper.”

 

            “I ain’t staying,” Kara snarkily replied, “and I’ll be seeing the Doctor before I leave.”

 

            “What you need to see her for, then?”

 

            “She’s sick, Alex. I don’t care what she is, I ain’t going to let her suffer for it. Not when she’s helped me so much.”

 

            Clicking her tongue with irritation, Alex rolled her eyes and leaned forward. Snagging the leather pouch off the table, she tossed it to Kara, who nimbly caught it.

 

            “Fine. Let her fix herself with her sinner’s magic and be done with it. Let no one say I’m cruel.”

 

            “No, but you ain’t likely to be a saint, sister,” Kara snorted, holding a hand out for the keys.

 

            Alex dangled them out for Kara, who snatched them from her and stalked over to the cell. The key scraped in the lock and Lena arched an eyebrow as she stepped inside. The smell of tobacco drifted through the bars as Alex lit a cigarette, her hand resting on her gun, ready to draw it if Lena made a move, but the necromancer could see that her heart wasn’t really in it, as if she knew Lena wouldn’t harm her sister.

 

            “Roll your sleeve up, now,” Kara gently ordered her, easing the cell door shut but not locking it.

 

            Lena sat up and gave her a wary look. “Miss, you shouldn’t worry yourself about me. I’m doing just fine in here.”

 

            “That ain’t what I said. Now, do as I say.”

 

            A crooked smile hitched up one side of Lena’s mouth and she made quick work of rolling her bloody sleeve up with deft fingers. Unwrapped the soaked handkerchief, she watched as Kara blanched slightly and sank down to the floorboards. The bone was half-mended and the wound still gaping, muscle rent and weeping.

 

            “Well,” Kara said after a moment, swallowing the taste of bile in her mouth. “It’s a damn good thing you ain’t a horse or I’d have to put you out of your misery. Don’t it hurt?”

 

            Choking on a laugh, Lena gave her a ghost of a smile as she took in the wide-eyed look of innocence and compassion. “It’s not so bad.”

 

            Hesitantly reaching out, Kara pressed the back of her hand to Lena’s perspiring brow and frowned, her expression turning grave.

 

            “You’re burning a fever.”

 

            “Nothing I can’t fix with a tooth and a sharp knife,” Lena murmured, reaching up to gently, but firmly pull Kara’s hand away.

 

            “Here,” Kara said, holding the bag aloft.

 

            “Just one will do.”

 

            She fished one out and pressed it into Lena’s bloody fingers before turning toward the bars. “Alex, fetch me a knife, would you?”

 

            “You planning on slitting her throat?” Alex snorted.

 

            “Don’t be so crude,” Kara snapped.

 

            Pushing herself to her feet, Alex rolled her eyes as she pulled Lena’s knife from its sheath and walked over to the bars. She exhaled a haze of grey and slapped the blade against the bars, eliciting a dull clanging sound that made Lena’s head ache.

 

            “Just a joke,” Alex assured her, a guarded look of worry in her own eyes as she appraised Lena. “Now that you says it, she don’t look too good.”

 

            Kara climbed to her feet and yanked the knife from her hand. “Neither would you if you snapped your arm in half ‘til the insides were out.”

 

            Humming in agreement, Alex leaned against the bars as she smoked and watched with fascinated horror as Lena took the knife from Kara and took a steady breath, cutting into the meat of her hand, into the soft mound of flesh just above her thumb. Thin red blood ran in stripes, circling around to drip to the ground and both women watched the Necromancer as she burned the tooth to ashes.

 

            Eyes closed, face still streaked with dried, flaky blood, Lena could’ve passed for a corpse as she lay slumped against the wall, her chest shallowly rising and falling as she breathed through the pain. It was by no means the worst injury she’d ever had, but pain was pain. A side effect of her job was that she was more susceptible to feeling it too, as closely tied to death as it was, and it was a keen ache that only mildly retreated as the flesh of her arm started wriggling back together.

 

            Much to the fascination of her audience, only the faint white mark where her skin had been split remained by the time Lena dusted ash off her fingertips. The echo of pain was still there, and she’d have to be cautious with her mended bones, the break not as strong as one left to naturally calcify, something almost artificial as her body tried to fix and strengthen it in its own time.

 

            “Well, I’ll be damned,” Alex muttered after a moment. “It ain’t natural, not in the slightest, but … it’s really something to watch with your own eyes, I won’t lie.”

 

            “Why, thank you, Sheriff,” Lena lightly replied, giving her a roguish smile before she winked at Kara, who stared at her with quiet awe.

 

            Flexing her fingers and rotating her arm, Lena straightened up and cleared her throat, tasting blood and dust as she swallowed.

 

            “I don’t mean to bother, but could I get some water, Sheriff?”

 

            Grunting noncommittally, Alex turned away and Kara grabbed Lena’s wrist, pulling the knife from her grasp. Setting it in her lap, Kara pulled her own spotless handkerchief out with a flourish and tied it around the cut at the base of Lena’s thumb, pulling it tight and knotting it.

 

            “Are you angry with me?” Lena softly asked, tilting her chin up slightly as she looked down at Kara with confusion.

 

            “What gives you that impression?”

 

            “I’m a perceptive person, ma’am," Lena said with a thin grin. "You seem awfully upset with me.”

 

            “I can’t imagine why going out on a limb for someone like you, only for you to shoot someone in the streets and wind up back in prison would cause offence.”

 

            With a soft laugh, almost maddening in its nonchalance, Lena rubbed at a sore spot above her eyebrow. “Well, now, I’m sorry, ma’am. Don’t be planning any hold-ups to break me out of here this time. I don’t think the Sheriff would appreciate that.”

 

            Quietly scoffing, Kara shook her head as she looked down at her lap, the pouch of teeth and the knife resting on her skirts. “Don’t you fret about that, ma’am. I won’t be interfering again.”

 

            Lena’s face softened and she smiled faintly as she looked at Kara. There was a tender look of gratitude in her green eyes and she shifted up on the cot, reaching out to gently touch Kara’s shoulder.

 

            “I don’t take your help lightly, only that I don’t want to be a bother to you. I thank you all the same.”

 

            “If you don’t mean to be a bother, then stop getting yourself into trouble,” Kara snapped.

 

            Lena scowled as her cheeks flushed and leaned back. “Now, I didn’t ask for you to bail me out. Quite the opposite, ma’am. You should go on back to your ranch and forget we ever met, now.”

 

            “And what about your horse?”

 

            “Well … that depends entirely on what happens to me next.”

 

            “She ain’t going to kill you,” Kara scoffed. “And I wouldn’t allow it if she tried.”

 

            Arching an eyebrow, Lena smiled faintly. “You’re mighty confident that you’d be able to stop our Sheriff here from doing something she set her mind to.”

 

            “And so I am,” Kara murmured, pushing herself to her feet. “But seeing as you was saying you don’t need my help … I’ll pray for your good fortune instead, Doc.”

 

            “That’s generous of you, ma’am.”
