            With a scathing sound of irritation, Kara whirled around, skirts flaring out, and yanked open the cell door. She left it wide open as she strode past Alex, and Lena didn’t so much as stir at the chanced escaping.

 

            “Supper tonight,” Alex called after her sister, who dumped everything on the desk. “You hear me?”

 

            The door slammed shut and Alex shook her head, giving Lena a wary look. “What you say to her, now?”

 

            “Only that it’s best if she stayed away.”

 

            “Now that is something I agree with,” Alex said as she turned the key in the cell door, locking Lena back in, and held a canteen through the bars.

 

            Hesitating for a moment, Lena pushed herself to her feet and moved over to Alex, taking the canteen and murmuring her thanks as she turned back to the bed. After draining half of it, she felt marginally better, the pain no longer a keen fire in her arm, and she stretched out on the cot, folding her arms beneath her head as she closed her eyes and tried to get some rest.

 

            It was hot inside though, a sweltering day that brought irritating flies and made the jail suffocatingly hot. Alex came and went, her footsteps pounding on the floors as she moved about, occasionally whistling to herself as she opened drawers and spoke to her Deputy.

 

            She didn’t acknowledge Lena, and Lena was content to doze as her body rested until the day grew cooler, the air inside not quite so close and the shadows starting to lengthen. Feeling stiff, Lena took to pacing as Alex watched her from the corner of her eyes, and eventually, she cleared her throat and stood up.

 

            “She brought you food,” Alex said, picking up the wrapped bundle. “If you’re hungry.”

 

            Turning, Lena nodded and moved toward the bars, reaching a hand between them for Alex to hand it to her. Giving her a perturbed look, Alex’s mouth curled slightly.

 

            “You might consider cleaning up. You’re a right sight with that muck all over you.”

 

            “If you’d be so kind as to fetch the water,” Lena agreed.

 

            Humming, Alex retreated to her desk, perching on the edge as she fished out a cigarette and lit it from a candle. “I’ll ask Vasquez to get some from the pump. You’ll have to sit tight ‘til then.”

 

            “Yes, ma’am.”

 

            “You smoke?” Alex asked after a moment, exhaling a grey plume.

 

            “Not often.”

 

            “Bet you could use one now. Go on then, I won’t tell if you don’t.”

 

            Lena watched as she pushed off and rolled another cigarette, lighting it for her and moving over to the bars. Alex handed it through and Lena retreated over to the cot, the rolled tobacco between her lips as she sank onto the bed and unwrapped the bundle. Alex leaned against the bars, smoking as she watched Lena spread out the cheese and bread and cold cuts of beef.

 

            “You’re a quiet one, ain’t you?”

 

            “I’m used to being alone,” Lena murmured, giving her a crooked smile as she lowered the cigarette and exhaled.

 

            “Mhm.”

 

            She watched her for a minute longer, dark eyes curious yet wary, before pushing off the bars at the sound of Vasquez stepping inside. Donning her hat, Alex clapped her Deputy on the shoulder and shifted an oil lantern just out of reach of the bars before telling Vasquez to fetch Lena some water and a cloth and ducking out into the night.  Lena ate her food in silence and thanked the Deputy for the water jug nudged through the bars, using it to scrub her face clean as best as she could, before working the dirt and blood from beneath her fingernails. She washed out the cut on her palm too before retying Kara’s handkerchief around it again.

 

            It was a quiet evening, the bawdy laughter and strains of music drifting in, and it was as close to that life as Lena would ever get so she settled in to enjoy it. Drifting in and out of consciousness, oddly comforted by the watchful eyes of the distrustful Deputy to ensure no harm came to her, Lena bided her time as she wondered what plan the Sheriff had in store for her.

 

            She awoke fully at a later hour, sitting up at the sound of voices and footsteps before the door creaked open. Vasquez removed her feet from the desk and sighed heavily as a trio made its way inside.

 

            “Here you are, Deputy. One heretic, all stitched up as best can be,” said the soldier from earlier, sneering as he pushed the woman forward.

 

            The woman stumbled forward, shackled and pale, and sagged to her knees. There was a spark of anger in her eyes and a stubborn set to her jaw as she pushed herself to her feet.

 

            “Aw, hell, ” Vasquez muttered, climbing to her feet and unhooking the ring of keys from her belt.

 

            “You enjoy, now,” Lockwood said with a sharp grin, him and the other soldier chuckling as they soldiered their way back out into the night in their rumpled uniforms.

 

            Lena eyed him derisively as she sat in the shadows of her cell, watched as the Deputy unlocked the door of the adjoining cell and unlocked the woman’s manacles. Ushering her inside, she locked the cell door and her eyes slid over to Lena, a flicker of fear in them.

 

            “Now, you both best be playing nice, alright? I ain’t wanting no more trouble here.”

 

            “Yes, ma’am,” Lena wearily replied, touching two fingers to her brow as a wry smile curved her lips.

 

            The other woman didn’t deign to reply, slumping onto her cot with a groan and stretching out with a listless sigh. The tension was thick in the air, and Lena studied her in irate silence as the three women sat in close proximity to each other without a word spoken.

 

            The hour grew late and Vasquez fell asleep at the desk, feet up as she slouched in the chair, and Lena could barely see through the shadows but felt the other woman’s wakefulness.

 

            “What’s your name?” she softly called out.

 

            “Sam.”

 

            “Where are you from?”

 

            “Cuba. My father moved us up to Tennessee when I was young. And you?”

 

            Lena hesitated slightly. “Back East. Why’d you shoot me?”

 

            “I already told you, Selena-“

 

            “But why did she tell you to?”

 

            “Your blood,” Sam replied, “she said she divined your blood and you was there and you had to be stopped.”

 

            Scoffing, Lena shifted on her cot and glanced sideways through the bars. “I was there afterwards . Just long enough to see the wreckage. But I didn’t kill a soul - at least not one that was truly alive.”

 

            “I was just following orders, sister.”

 

            “How many has she sent after me?”

 

            “Three, as far as I know. Selena taught the three of us the craft. She ain’t likely to tell anyone else what she saw though; she wants a promotion to a waypoint back East and wants to be the one to hand you over. I don’t know if the one who told her has told anyone else.”

 

            “What’s in it for you?”

 

            “Money.”

 

            Lena let out a quiet chuckle, “such a silly thing to motivate people, and yet, so effective. What was the price given for my head?”

 

            “Well, it’s more money than I’d likely see in my whole life,” Sam said with wry amusement. “And I got a little girl that needs taking care of. Selena said he’d pay-“

 

            “He?”

 

            “The Necromancer who set the bounty. He told her you was dangerous and that he’d pay her handsomely. He said he’d be in control of the Order soon enough and would make her as high as she’d like. Real charming, he was.”

 

            “You met him?”

 

            “I read it, from Selena’s blood.”

 

            “What did he look like?” Lena anxiously asked.

 

            Her skin prickled as she climbed to her feet, sinking down to a crouch as she gripped the iron bars and stared at Sam’s shadowed form beyond. White-knuckled and tense with anger and a flicker of fear, Lena felt the hairs on the back of her neck stand on end, her breathing loud to her own ears in the cramped space.

 

            “Well, he was bald. Had a dark beard and dark eyes. Wasn’t a very intimidating man by his stature, but there was a powerful aura about him. Couldn’t miss it, even through a reading.”

 

            “A name,” Lena tensely pressed, a lump in her throat. “Give me his name.”

 

            Sam shifted up and moved to sink down before Lena, gripping the bars just about her hands as they stared at each other.

 

            “I think you’s already knowing his name, ain’t you?”

 

            Lena slowly forced her fingers to uncurl and pushed herself to her feet. Turning, she paused as Sam spoke, quiet and curious.

 

            “What did he do to frighten you so much?”

 

            “It’s what he’s about to do,” Lena murmured. “But he killed all those people - not me.”

 

            “Oh.”

 

            A floorboard creaked loudly as she turned, boots scuffing the floor, and Vasquez stirred as Lena started to speak.

 

            “Hey! You best get away from each other right now. Ain’t no talking in here. Go on now, ‘fore I have to give you a beating.”

 

            “Deputy,” Lena conceded, ducking her head in a polite nod before she sank back down onto her cot.

 

            Stretching out, she used her coat as a blanket and turned on her side, staring at the wall as she waited for sleep to come and take her. When it came, it was restless and uncomfortable, the thin mattress lumpy and the sound of drunken revelry from late-night drinkers and gamblers periodically woke her up. It was almost a relief when morning came with the Sheriff’s arrival.

 

            Kicking the metal bars, Alex woke them with the dawn, a grim look on her face as she looked at Lena through the slats. “Wakey, wakey.”

 

            “Morning, Sheriff,” Lena cordially greeted her, pushing herself up onto her elbows.

 

            “Breakfast is served,” Alex exasperatedly replied, crouching to slide a bowl of slop beneath the cell door.

 

            “Thank you kindly.”

 

            “And you,” Alex brusquely said to Sam, sliding a bowl beneath her door too. “Be quick.”

 

            Lena climbed to her feet and stretched out her stiff muscles before retrieving her bowl. A wooden spoon was in the thin mixture of oats and she gingerly lifted it before spooning mouthfuls down without tasting it. It wasn’t the worst thing she’d ever eaten, not by a mile, but it made her wistful for Kara to bring her something. As it was, she didn’t think she was likely to see the rancher any time soon.

 

            “Lord, I seen better fare on the road than this slop,” Sam muttered.

 

            Lena begrudgingly smiled around a mouthful and then set her empty bowl back down before the slot beneath the door and sat back down. It was a cooler day but the smell of blood still clung to her and made for a pungent odour after a day’s wear, rotting and coppery, filling her nostrils as she sat with her eyes closed and her head tipped back against the wall.

 

            It was a slow day, a drunken woman brought in to sit in Sam’s cell with her until she’d sobered up some, Vasquez going to sort out a spat over a stolen chicken, and the suffocating silence as each slight scuff or creak inside the jail was magnified.  They had their lunch of hard bread and a cup of tepid water each before Sam cleared her throat, leaning against the bars with a pallid look on her face. She cradled her stitched up side and Lena felt a pinch of guilt at the thought of how much pain the Witch Doctor must be in.

 

            “Hey, Sheriff. How long you planning on keeping me in here?”

 

            “As long as I feel like it,” Alex curtly replied from her desk, where she was reading from a small book, languidly at ease with one foot skimming back and forth across the floor and the other on the chair.

 

            “I ain’t done nothing wrong. She was the one who shot me.”

 

            Lena shot Sam a filthy look and scoffed quietly. Alex didn’t even look up from the page. “Is it true you shot her first?”

 

            “Orders are orders. I’m sure you, of all people, can respect that.”

 

            “Oh, I respect it alright,” Alex said with a wry smile, “but I don’t got to like it when you cause a ruckus in my town.”

 

            With a sound of contempt, Sam struck the bar and retreated back to her cot while Lena chuckled quietly to herself, a smile stretching across her face.

 

            “You don’t have to enjoy it so much,” Sam snapped.

 

            “Oh, but revenge is sweet.”

 

            “You already shot me - ain’t that enough revenge?”

 

            “That depends.”

 

            “On what?”

 

            “You planning on shooting me again when you have the chance?”

 

            She opened one eye and let her head loll to the side to peer at Sam. Silent for a moment, the other woman deliberated before replying.

 

            “I guess we’ll find out, won’t we?”

 

            Lena ruefully smiled and returned to her thoughts, passing the time by thinking about where to go next. West would perhaps be safest, or maybe even north, to the colder regions that suited her better, but there was too much unfinished to be left alone and she knew she’d stay in the state while she kept an eye on her brother.

 

            As the afternoon wore on, the door opened once more, disturbing her from her thoughts, and she straightened up as her face softened, watching as Kara strode inside. Lena waited for her to glance her way, her stomach twisting uneasily, but after a short conversation with Alex, in which she didn’t so much as acknowledge that there was anyone else in the room, Kara left as quickly as she had come, leaving Lena with the disgruntled thought that she’d come in on a trifling matter just to purposely ignore her.

 

            “Who’s she?” Sam quietly asked once the door had shut.

 

            “The Sheriff’s sister.”

 

            “What’d you do to piss her off?”

 

            Lena scoffed and scowled, drawing her feet up onto the cot and bracing her arms on top. “Nothing.”

 

            “She didn’t so much as look your way. You soft down on her? Shoot, you sittin’ her? ”

 

            “Don’t be a coot,” Lena snapped, flushing.

 

            “My apologies. Just don’t go expecting her to fall for a sawbone like you. They don’t like the kind with blood on their hands too much; I know it well and clear.”

 

            “I don’t even know her,” Lena defensively replied, shifting uncomfortably.

 

            “Mhm.”

 

            Her irritation at the Witch Doctor only seemed to grow, and she had the itching urge to put another bullet in her and let her suffer until she got her hands on some teeth to fix it. Lunging to her feet, Lena moved towards the bars and gripped them tightly as she pressed her face between them.

 

            “Hey! Sheriff. Why don’t you go on and let her out of here; I’ll take full responsibility for shooting her.”

 

            “I don’t remember you being the Sheriff, Doc. How ‘bout you let me do my job?”

 

            “If she stays in here, I might just kill her,” Lena hissed through clenched teeth.

 

            Sighing, Alex climbed to her feet and walked over to them, standing in line with the bars separating the two prisoners as she planted her hands on her hips. Glancing at both of them, she arched an eyebrow.

 

            “What’s gotten into you both?”

 

            “She tried to kill me,” Lena exclaimed, her eyes widening with indignation.

 

            “And you returned the favour,” Sam shot back. “It’s bad blood but it’s the done thing. No point getting yourself all worked up over it - or is it that blonde-“

 

            “Shut it,” Lena snapped. “Or the next bullet will be a little higher.”

 

            “Alright, alright,” Alex sighed. “You,” she said, curling a finger at Sam before reaching for her keys, “are going to get on your horse and go far away from here, alright?”

 

            A thin smile curled Sam’s lips as she ducked her head. Alex glowered at the expression, fitting the key into the lock. “Don’t look so smug; if you set foot back in my town, I’ll be the one to blow your fucking head off, you hear me?”

 

            “Loud and clear, Sheriff.”

 

            Alex nodded and yanked the cell door open, waiting until Sam stepped out to prod her out of the jail. Lena sucked on her teeth, quietly seething as she climbed to her feet and paced, waiting for Alex’s return. It was twenty minutes later, after seeing the Necromancer onto her horse and north, past the boundary of Midvale, satisfied that she wasn’t returning, before she stepped back into the jail, whistling.

 

            “Why did you do that?” Lena ground out, her brow creased with confusion as her eyes flickered with annoyance.

 

            “I got my reasons, and you don’t need to know them,” Alex said, almost tauntingly as she grinned.

 

            “And what about me?” Lena asked as she stubbornly jerked her chin forward.

 

            Sighing, Alex dropped down onto her chair and picked up a flask, taking a swig before clearing her throat. It was getting dark outside, dusk encroaching and hunger gnawing at Lena’s stomach as she bristled with annoyance in her cell.

 

            “I haven’t made my mind up yet,” Alex said after a moment. “Drop of hooch?”

 

            Lips pressed into a flat line, Lena glowered at her but still thrust her arm through the bars. Alex chuckled and pushed herself up, pouring a measure of whiskey into a cup as if she couldn’t bear the thought of Lena drinking from her flask.  Sipping her drink quietly, Lena settled down for the night, her meagre supper of a watery broth left to grow a cold, oily scum on top of it. Alex topped her cup up once more in silence and it burned its way down Lena’s throat in a pleasant manner, leaving her warm and sleepy.

 

            She awoke to a shaft of pale sunlight falling across her face from where she sat slumped against the wall. Alex was there again, quiet and watchful as ever, and Lena caught her sneaking furtive glances throughout the day as if trying to gauge her person.  The day passed by slowly and Kara stopped by twice, blatantly ignoring Lena as she spoke with her sister, who seemed exasperatedly impatient with her presence. Lena knew that Kara was far too busy with her ranch to be frequenting the town, let alone the jail, so often in a few days, and she watched with quiet amusement until Kara left again and boredom crept back in.

 

            The following day she awoke to the sound of rain, a rare storm blowing through with a deluge turning the streets to muck and driving the townsfolk indoors to dance halls, gambling dens and saloons if they had nothing better to do. A fresh air swept into the jail, clean and smelling of mud and prairie grass and plants. Lena was even quieter than usual and it was nearing upon noon when Alex interrupted her brooding by climbing to her feet with a heavy sigh.

 

            “Go on then,” she loudly spoke, reaching for her keys and unlocking the cell door.

 

            Lena looked up, surprise flashing across her face, and slowly unwound her legs. She gave Alex a questioning look and the Sheriff smiled at her, jerking her head towards the front door.

 

            “Off with you.”

 

            “You’re letting me go?”

 

            “I don’t like you, Doc, but I don’t think you’re a danger to anyone here.” There was a rueful edge to Alex’s words as she pressed on, “and I looked into it and what you said was true, so I ain’t got no reason to rightly keep you here seeing as you ain’t killed no one who didn’t deserve it or was already dead.”

 

            “What about Sam?”

 

            Rolling her eyes, Alex shook her head, “if I had to imprison everyone ‘round here who shot someone … well, we’d be a jail town.”

 

            Lena hesitated and Alex exhaled roughly. “Go on now, ‘fore I change my mind.”

 

            Climbing to her feet, she pulled on her coat, dusting off the dirt, and followed Alex out of the cell, her legs aching from three days of sitting. Handing over her gun belt, knife, grimoire and leather purse of teeth, Alex watched with trepidation as if she didn’t trust her own judgement, but ultimately let Lena walk out the front door and into the onslaught of rain without stopping her.

 

            Lena paused on the boardwalk for a second, staring at the blurred figures standing under the eaves of the verandah through the sheets of lashing rain as she breathed in the dampness of it. Wishing for her hat at least, Lena squared her shoulders and descended the steps, stepping into soft mud that sucked at her boots.  Setting off toward Kara’s ranch to claim her horse and meagre belongings, Lena buried her hands in her pockets and ducked her head as rain drummed onto her leather coat and plastered her hair to her face. 

 

            She’d never truly taken into account the distance to Kara ranch before, the miles seeming paltry when travelled on horseback, but in the heavy rain, as thunder rumbled overhead in a deep cry sky, rain sliding beneath the collar of her coat and a chill burrowing into her, it felt like an eternity. Her socks were wet and her boots chafed, producing painful blisters, and her clothes hung heavily off her, saturated with water. By the time Lena reached the dirt track, flooded with large puddles of water in the pitted path, Lena was exhausted and relieved.

 

            Kara saw her coming through the sheets of rain, salting a slab of pork at the table to preserve it while a loaf of bread baked in the oven, giving the place a heavenly smell. Through the small window, she saw the blurred image of the Witch Doctor making for the barn and wiped her brow on her sleeve as she frowned.  Wiping off salt with a cloth, Kara tore off her apron and was outside in a second, splashing through puddles as cold rain saturated her. She’d settled in for a long day of chores on account of the rain, darning socks and fixing the uneven leg of a chair while salting some fresh meat cuts she’d bought in town only the day before for an excuse to have been there, but she couldn’t help but plunge through the downpour at the first sight of Lena. She hadn’t known she was getting out today and her heart lurched in her chest.

 

            “Hey!” Kara called out, somewhat crossly.

            

            She watched as Lena’s head jerked up to look at her, her hand on the barn door before she turned to face the rancher. Kara crossed the open space with long strides, her hands knotting in her skirts, and her face darkened with stubborn irritation as she bore down on Lena.

 

            “Don’t say you’re going again,” Kara fiercely ordered. “Don’t you dare say it again.”

 

            A smile hitched up one side of Lena’s mouth as her eyes dressed faintly at the corners. “We both know I’m nothing but a nuisance to you, so why would you want me to stay anyway?”

 

            Opening and closing her mouth as she stopped a few feet away from her, rain lashing down on the two of them as it puddled at their feet, Kara couldn’t form a reason. She twisted her skirts between her hands, teeth clenched as she warred with herself, before lunging forward with her hands coming up.

 

            They found Lena’s face, cradling her cheeks with surprising gentleness despite the hard calluses from years of labour, and Lena stood still as Kara loomed over her, breathing heavily for a moment, her breath hot on Lena’s lips. There was a wild spark in her blue eyes, determined and a little apprehensive before she crushed her lips against Lena’s, firm and unyielding.  The force of the kiss pushed Lena backwards, into the unlatched door, which gave way beneath her weight and swung wide open. Slipping on a patch of rain-softened mud, Lena went backwards, reaching out to grab a fistful of Kara’s damp shirt as she dragged her down with her.

 

            Hitting the packed earth hard enough to inevitably leave bruises, Lena was left gasping for air for a moment, the wind knocked from her lungs. Arms spread out, staring up at Kara, who was pink-cheeked and beautiful with her damp hair curling from the rain and a surprised look on her face as her lips parted and she lay on top of her, Lena couldn’t even form a sentence.

 

            “I think you’re pretty,” Kara said after a moment.

 

            She said it as if that was an answer to Lena’s posed question, pushing herself up to her knees, still straddling Lena’s waist, while she wiped mud and hay off her hands. Then she climbed the rest of the way to her feet and left without another word, while Lena was left propped up on her elbows on the barn floor.  With a perplexed look on her face, Lena touched two fingers to her lips, staring out into the rain long after Kara had disappeared into the house. Eventually, she climbed to her feet and dragged the door shut though, the dismal day already lengthening the shadows as the sun started to sink.

 

            Soaking wet and covered in grime and blood so caked on that even the rain couldn’t wash it away, Lena huddled in the dark barn, a single oil lamp offering a halo of orange light as she shivered beneath a blanket. Rain was never a comfortable experience on the road, and after a long walk, bruised and blistered, Lena was in for a miserable night. There was only so much that necromancy could fix.  Fortunately for her, a knock sounded an hour later before the barn door creaked open. Kara was a shadow in the doorway, the sky outside only a little lighter than she was.

 

            “You’ll catch your death in them clothes,” Kara hesitantly said. “I heated some water from the well in the tub. A hot bath will do you some good.”

 

            Warmth spread through Lena’s chest at the gesture and she was quick to scramble to her feet, trembling as her clothes clung to her. She’d already shed her leather duster, hanging it from a stable post to dry off, and her shirt clung to her as her tangled mess of hair dripped. She must have been a sorry sight for Kara to have gone through the effort of drawing water in a storm for a bath.

 

            They crossed the yard quickly, the mud sucking at their boots and the horses' vague lumps in their pen as they soldiered through it too. Krypto was restlessly pacing the porch, nails scratching at the wood as he panted, his fur damp from a wary foray into the rain before he’d retreated to the house. He nosed at Lena as she passed by him, fingers brushing along his back, and she slipped into the warmth of the house with a sigh of relief.  Her cheeks felt freezing in the wall of heat that hit her, her toes numb in her boots and her clothes itching, and as Kara directed her down the raised platform of the main house and into the adjoining brick mudroom with its hanging herbs and food stores, Lena almost smiled at the sight of the tub occupying the middle of the cramped space.

 

            She murmured her thanks and kicked off her boots with haste before fiddling with the fastenings of her clothes. Stepping into the tub and feeling the searing heat of the boiling water was almost enough to make Lena cry, and despite the cramped size of it, she managed to submerge herself in it, hot water seeping into every cold and aching part of her as steam wafted up from the surface.  Kara hesitantly stepped in a few minutes later, a pile of folded clothes in her hands which she set down on a chair, a safe distance from any splashing. Lena thanked her again as she huddled in the water, not yet mustering the energy to scrub the dirt from her body.  She watched as Kara sank down onto the top step in the doorway of the main house, staring at Lena’s shadowed face as lit candles and the glow from the fire inside partially illuminated her.

 

            “I’m sorry,” Kara said after a moment. “I know I judge you harshly … truthfully, I’m frightened, ma’am. I ain’t used to all this and there’s a part of me that thinks … no good is going to come from you being here. But I ain’t used to being alone, and there’s something in you that’s worth trusting.”

 

            “Do you think I’m terrible?” Lena asked with a thin smile, trailing her fingers through the water as her eyes shone with amusement, trying to mask her hope. “It’s okay if you do; I’ve been terrible at many different moments in my life.”

 

            “I don’t think you’re terrible at all,” Kara softly replied, not knowing how much it made Lena’s heart ache to hear her say it. “I think … maybe you was made to do some bad things, but that ain’t the same as being bad.”

 

            Lena swallowed thickly, slowly inclining her head as she looked at the bathwater, flakes of blood and gritty dirt swirling atop it. A ripple of pained confusion crossed her features, darkening them for a second before she looked up. The steam and rain had left the blood and dirt streaky, her pallid skin almost ghostly in the dimness as she looked at Kara, hollow-cheeked and dark-eyed, looking like someone who could be capable of gruesome acts.

 

            “Kara,” Lena murmured, an odd note of strain in her voice that was made intimate by the use of her first name. “Why’d you kiss me?”

 

            “I already told you,” Kara quietly replied, ducking her head as her cheeks reddened in the gloom, gently rocking herself as nerves crept in. “I think you’re mighty pretty, and I been trying not to do that for a while now and got tired of it. Is- is that alright?”

 

            Lena pressed her lips into a flat line as she hid a smile, not quite looking at Kara as she nodded slightly. “It’s alright.”

 

            Nodding, Kara pushed herself to her feet. “I’ll let you get washed up.”

 

            She vanished back into the house, the clanging of pots sounding the preparation of dinner as she hummed, while in the adjoining brick room, Lena scrubbed herself clean, relishing the steaming water and brick of soap. Cleaning days worth of dirt from beneath her fingernails and working the suds into the lank strands of her hair, Lena emerged from the bath pink-skinned and feeling better than she had in days. Warmed through to her core, she dressed in Kara’s clean clothes, the overalls sturdy and knitted sweater warm, if a little too big for her shorter stature.

 

            “Here. Tea to warm you.”

 

            “Thank you,” Lena murmured, her fingers brushing Kara’s as she reached out to take the cup.

 

            She pulled them back quickly and looked away, the warmth of the tin cup seeping into her hands as she cradled it close.

 

            “You look more human, that’s for sure,” Kara commented as she picked up a knife and started slicing a loaf of bread.

 

            Lena nodded distractedly and Kara smiled to herself as she watched her from the corner of her eye. “Go on and sit by the fire and keep warm.”

 

            “Do you need some help?” Lena asked, breaking herself out of her brooding thoughts.

 

            “No, no,” Kara assured her. “Go on now. Sit.”

 

            They ate quietly, Lena wolfing down her chicken and greens and bread with what little manners ingrained into her she was able to hold onto in her hunger. Kara watching her from the corner of her eyes as she picked at her own meal, Krypto sitting at her side, shuffling impatiently for scraps.  Once she was finished, Lena insisted on scrubbing the pots in the sink while Kara sat before the fire, hunched forward as she warmed her hands while the storm rumbled on around them. Wiping suds from her hands, Lena softly cleared her throat, catching Kara’s attention.

 

            “Thank you. For everything.”

 

            Kara rose to her feet, a mournful look on her face as she dusted off her hands and squared her shoulders with tension.

 

            “Are you leaving or staying?”

 

            Hesitating, Lena shrugged uneasily. “I don’t know that there’s much here for me.”

 

            “There could be,” Kara insisted. “I know we says a lot about folk like you, but … truthfully, there ain’t a person in town who wouldn’t take your powers over death if it came to it. And James seems to think it’ll come to it soon, with your brother out there.”

 

            Lena stiffened, her teeth clenching as she pressed her lips together. “Lex … he’s a fickle creature. He can seem courteous, charming, even, but he’s mercurial. I pray that he never finds his way to you.”

 

            The breath was expelled from Kara’s lungs as she took a desperate step forward, closing the distance and reaching for Lena’s hands. She clutched them tightly, a plea in her eyes.  “You could protect us.”

 

            Shaking her head, Lena tried to pull her hands back but couldn’t escape Kara’s grasp. “Not from him. Not all of you.”

 

            “You’d be better than what we got,” Kara said with a sad, uneven smile. “Old men and boys and women who ain’t never held a gun before. My sister says you’re a dead shot.”

 

            Lena let out a quiet scoff of laughter and smiled crookedly, “she’s finally right about something.”

 

            “She won’t ask you,” Kara murmured, “because she’s stubborn, same as me, but … I don’t want to die, Lena. Not in that way. And you can feel it comin’, can’t you?”

 

            Rolling her shoulders, Lena glanced aside, Kara’s tough hands cupping her own, warm and solid and real. She couldn’t imagine them stiff and grey and cold with death. Didn’t want to.  “You’d be safer without me. Chances are … he’d blow right past here if you told him where I’d headed.”

 

            “I wouldn’t do that,” Kara softly replied.

 

            She gripped Kara’s hand tightly in return, a grave look in her green eyes. “You must. There’s a war coming, and it’s everyone for themselves. For the kindness you’ve shown me this past month … you send me to the wolves to save yourself. I won’t begrudge you that. In fact, I encourage it.”

 

            “Stay.”

 

            “It would mean chaos like you’ve never seen if he were to find me here. It’s likely he’ll come even without knowing, if only for the mine.”

 

            “Well, I choose chaos with the chance of coming back rather than a coward’s way out.”

 

            Lena chuckled softly and reached up to tweak Kara’s chin in an affectionate manner. “You’d hate being resurrected, ma’am. You and I both know it.”

 

            “I’d hate to die alone even more. Everyone here’s got someone but me.”

 

            “If I stayed … I couldn’t guarantee I’d stay alive to bring you back.”

 

            “All the same, I wouldn’t die alone,” Kara said with more bravery than she felt, her smile wavering slightly.

 

            Finally relinquishing her hold on her, Lena stepped back, a regretful look of guilt passing her face as she sighed heavily. “I never should have come here. But … as it is, I’ll do what I can to keep you safe.”

 

            There was a firm determination to her words and she watched as a flicker of surprise rippled across Kara’s face, blue eyes softening with gratitude as her shoulders dropped. Lena’s stomach knotted with the uneasy sensation that she would inevitably regret that decision, the threat of war and death on the horizon leaving her fearful of what she might bring down on the town. Still, Kara has asked, and for some reason she couldn’t quite place, Lena agreed to stay in one place for the first time since she’d left New York City.

 

            “Thank you,” Kara whispered, a sheen in her eyes as she cradled her hands to her chest.

 

            “I’ll say goodnight then, ma’am.”

 

            Lena ducked out into the rain before she could reply, yanking the door closed and hurrying across the yard. It was still early yet and the sound of the rain pounding on the roof, as well as the dozen leaks that let it in, kept Lena from sleeping just yet. She hadn’t seen Hecate in days but found her fed and watered and brushed down, thinking about how Kara must have made the time in her busy day to do it for her. Still, the horse was affectionate at Lena’s appearance, nosing her and tossing her head while Lena rubbed along her cheek and muzzle, the motions soothing as she allowed her mind to drift.

 

            After a while, she bedded down for the night, dragging her bedroll into Hecate’s stall and sleeping beside her for huddled warmth as the cold seeped through the cracks. Lena slept well for a change, too worn out to wake from nightmares, and she rose after dawn, well-rested and stiff from laying down for too long.

 

            She emerged from the barn to the sight of Kara on horseback, hat low over her face and shirtsleeves rolled up to expose tanned forearms. It was a clear day, the sky blue and the sun shining now that the storm had blown past, and Lena shaded her eyes as she walked over to her. Grabbing the bridle, she steadied Comet for Kara to dismount, patting his nose as she smiled faintly.

 

            “Mornin’,” Kara greeted her, boots sinking into soft mud as she landed beside Lena.  She doffed her hat and smiled widely, eyes crinkling at the corners. “You look like you slept well,” Kara noted, gesturing to Lena’s eyes. “No more circles under your eyes.”

 

            “Mm, well, a jail isn’t the best place for a rest.”

 

            “You’re telling me,” Kara chuckled, taking the reins up and leading Comet to the barn.

 

            “You’ve spent a night in the jail?”

 

            “Oh, many. Too much whiskey and not a lot to do ‘round here leads even the best of us to a night in jail. The Sheriff being your sister or no.”

 

            Lena snorted, running a hand through her dark hair as she yawned widely. “And are you a habitual drunkard?”

 

            Kara gave her a surprised look of amusement and nudged her in her ribs. “When the occasion arises, Doc.”

 

            “What work do you have in mind today?”

 

            “Well, on account of the storm, I had to go and check the fences. A few posts been blown down a few miles west of here that needs mending before the horses can be let out. A rockslide out in the foothills too from all the mud; I’ll need to clear that out before it comes crashing the rest of the way down and takes out the herd I got out there.”

 

            “They’re alright after the storm?”

 

            Waving a hand, Kara smiled, “they’re wild creatures; they do fine on their own. Got a few nearly ready to be broken in, come next spring, I think.”

 

            Scratching at the back of her neck, Lena’s lips twisted wryly. “Well, I’m not much use for the physical labour, but, if you’re willing, I can make it easier for us both.”

 

            Wariness crept into Kara’s features as she came to a stop, giving Lena a sceptical look. “You mean … with what you can do?”

 

            “I know you don’t like it, but they’ll lighten the load and have it done in a few hours.”

 

            Kara reluctantly agreed, and it wasn’t long before Lena had Hecate saddled and was eating breakfast in the saddle with her hat tugged down low over her eyes and the sun warming the back of her leather coat.

 

            They picked their way out to the shadows of foothills, through plains of long grasses as the arid dust and sand gave way to greener pastures, perennial flowers dotted here and there as hunting birds circled overhead, looking for rabbits and other small creatures. It took them nearly an hour of riding to make it to the rockslide, halfway up a sloping incline that gave way to higher peaks, the mountain in the near distance looming tall behind them.

 

            Swinging down from her saddle, Lena fetched her belongings from her saddlebags and set Hecate to grazing while Kara did the same with Comet. Looking up at the jumble of boulders and rocks, perilous to any creature that disturbed them, Lena sucked on her teeth for a moment as she thought.

 

            “Let me see what I can resurrect and then we’ll see what we’re working with,” she told Kara, unsheathing her knife as she spoke.

 

            Looking pale with apprehension, Kara hung back and watched with wide eyes as Lena shook a few teeth into her palm and then cut into her flesh. Blood beaded up and pooled around the teeth, staining them red as she sheathed her knife again.

 

            “That ain’t sanitary, you know,” Kara muttered.

 

            Lena cracked a smile as she curled her fingers around the mess in her hand and braced herself against the sandy earth. She could feel the sparks of life from a million insects crawling around them, and deeper, the ones hidden in soft clay and black soil, reaching down and down and out around her for the telltale spark of bones that called to her power. 

 

            Her mouth flooded with the coppery tang of magic and she felt the answering call of bones, some nothing more than decomposing remains of prairie dogs and snakes, and others the fragments of disassembled humans, but she found five in the near vicinity that would do. One could think about her magic was that there was always plenty of dead around to answer; it would have unnerved normal folk to know that at any point, she could have summoned a dozen skeletons to do her bidding, without putting a dent in the bodies below her feet at varying depths.

 

            Climbing to her feet, Lena burned through the teeth as the earth churned and fingers clawed at the earth. Two climbed free first, both of them moderately decomposed, more recently than the others would be, with their skin shrunken to a leathery covering, one still dressed in rotting clothes, while the other had clumps of hair.

 

            Kara made a retching sound, murmuring her apologies as she turned away from the atrocity of unburying the dead. Lena paid her little attention, trying not to take it personally as she focused on coaxing the other three free. They were all skeletons, flesh disintegrating to nothing, leaving bones from yellow to brown, and one was missing a few ribs and an arm.  Controlling them, Lena sent the five bodies up the slope, their bony fingers grasping at grass and roots as their bones rattled. They didn’t speak or breathe or do anything she didn’t tell them to, and Kara found herself watching with repulsed fascination.

 

            It wore Lena out as she held her control over them, burning through teeth and plucking out new ones as she reopened the cut and bathed them in fresh blood. The sun was hot and her throat dry with dust as she worked, but she didn’t let up, the skeletons shifting rocks between them, triggering another rockslide. They broke bones and lacked the muscle for anything requiring too much strength, and when a boulder found it's way free and turned a skeleton to crushed fragments, Lena saw Kara wince at the thought of it being them, before she summoned another to replace it.

 

            An hour passed by and blood ran from Lena’s eyes and nose, the taste in her mouth as she kept on, watching the slow progress. Kara seemed satisfied with the work and almost grew bored , using the time to forage for edible herbs in the clusters of bushes and plants growing in the rich soil.

 

            When Lena was finally done, she let ashes fall from her hand after making the skeletons crawl back into their graves, and collapsed to the ground in a heavy heap. Her breathing was shallow and her heart beating rapidly and she closed her eyes to the dizzying sensation of depleting her magic too much.

 

            “Here,” Kara murmured, suddenly before her and reaching for her cut hand. 

 

            She uncurled Lena’s fingers and poured cool water onto her palm, gently working ash and blood from the skin and cleaning out the shallow cut. Unknotting her blue neckerchief, Kara tied it around her palm, an annoyingly familiar act of late, and pushed the canteen into Lena’s hand.

 

            Draining it, she felt slightly better and spat out pinkish saliva as she rinsed the blood from her mouth. Kara made her eat, cuts of cold turkey and wild berry jam slathered on bread plied on her until she had more life back in her. Her hands were still cold and tingling and Lena wiped at her eyes and nose with a damp handkerchief, wiping away the blood.

 

            “It costs you,” Kara noted, displeased.

 

            “Everything has a price,” Lena retorted, hauling herself to her feet. “The physical toll is less than it would’ve been to shift them ourselves.”

 

            “Still, I don’t like it.”

 

            “I sure just saved you a couple of hours though,” Lena cockily replied before letting out a sharp whistle to call Hecate.

 

            The horse trotted over and Lena heaved herself up, patting Hecate’s neck. She smelled of fresh grass and sunshine and Lena enjoyed the two of them stretching their legs in the wild together. It had been too long since they’d ridden that well.

 

            “How about a wager, Miss Danvers.”

 

            “What kind?” Kara dubiously asked.

 

            Giving her a goading smile, Lena arched an eyebrow and pulled her hat down snugly. “A race back to the ranch.”

 

            “And what’s the prize?”

 

            Thinking about it for a moment, Lena shrugged. “We’ll leave it as something to be asked for at a later time.”

 

            “Alright then,” Kara slowly chewed out. “Ain’t no cheating now, you hear?”

 

            “I’m a well-bred lady, ma’am. It wouldn’t be in the name of sportsmanship or honour if I did.”

 

            “It don’t matter; I’ve been riding horses for years.”

 

            “Ah, well, Miss, so have I.”

 

            With that, Lena spurred Hecate into motion, the horse surging forward as Lena ducked low over her back, leaving Kara to scramble after her. Comet was a few hands taller and stockier, but Hecate was the faster horse, and both of them grinned at the challenge, a mere few feet between them the entire way back.

 

            They were careful not to tire the horses out, but Lena let Hecate have her heard, content for the horse to set her own breakneck speed as she kicked up clouds of dust in her wake. Although she led by a tiny amount, Lena deferred to Kara’s directions and quicker than they’d gotten out to the rocks, the ranch appeared before them.

 

            A savage smile curled Lena’s lips as she put on a last burst of speed, whispering encouragement in her horse’s ear as Hecate snorted and barrelled toward the yard. Lena pulled her up to a gentle stop, laughter bubbling up in her chest and falling from her lips as she trotted Hecate around in a small circle to watch as Kara thundered behind her and brought Comet up short.

 

            “Damn you,” Kara breathlessly replied, slapping her thigh as she laughed, her eyes creasing. She shook her head and led Comet to sidle up beside Hecate. “I almost had you. I did.”

 

            “It was a pleasure,” Lena said with a crooked smile, touching the brim of her hat.

 

            They were still laughing when the sound of hooves trotted up the road to the ranch, and they both turned to watch as a man in a black suit and a bowler hat came upon a chestnut horse.

 

            “Mister Rogers,” Kara said with wary surprise. “What a surprise. I weren’t thinking I’d ever find you all the way out here; are you lost?”

 

            “Miss Danvers, Witch Doctor,” the Englishman greeted them both, lifting his hat off his dark curls as he gave them a charming smile. “I come on business, although a lovely excuse it is to see more of Midvale. Miss Rojas and your Madam Mayor are in the midst of brokering a deal for the mine and your presence has been requested.”

 

            Russell’s eyes slid over to Lena as he finished speaking and Kara shot her a bewildered look. “What do they want with her?”

 

            A smile curled his lips as he looked at Kara, shrugging slightly as his horse shifted beneath him. “I can’t rightly say, ma’am, I’m just the messenger. Although, I may add, your presence has been requested at your earliest convenience, but it seemed they wished for you to make haste.”

 

            Lena looked to Kara and arched an eyebrow in silent question, wariness flickering in her eyes at what they could want with her. The last thing Lena could imagine was them wanting to involve her in the town’s business, especially when it seemed a dozen people were trying to oust her from their streets as quickly as possible.

 

            “I’ll accompany you,” Kara reassuringly offered.

 

            “Then, may I escort you now?” Russell offered, courteous as he gestured back the way he’d come.

 

            As weak as she felt, a hollowness inside her, leaving her a little shaky and exhausted, Lena conceded with a weary nod, pressing her feet to Hecate’s flank.

 

            “Lead on.”

6. Chapter 6

Notes for the Chapter:

soz about the shit ending but at least we're free now!!

            The trio rode into town, still damp and muddy from the rain the day before, and dismounted outside the hotel, hitching their horses to the post outside and climbing up the creaking steps. Lena pushed through the batwing doors last, peering through the gloomy interior as a few far candles offered minimal light and a few early drinkers quietly knocked back beer and moonshine and kept to themselves.

 

            Russell led them through to the parlour off the main saloon, where they’d had dinner that one night, and Lena removed her hat and slowed at the sight of the assembled group. Alex and Kelly, Brainy and J’onn and the heiress, Andrea Rojas. They were all bent over the table, bare of any food or the usual trappings of a dinner table, and Lena hovered apprehensively, suspicion flashing in her green eyes.

 

            “Doc,” Alex cordially greeted her with a nod, gesturing her in. “Come on in, we- Kara , now why did you come all the way into town? Ain’t you got work to do on the ranch?”

 

            Pushing past Lena, Kara jerked her chin up, “you callin’ a meeting without me?”

 

            “You ain’t gonna want to hear this,” Alex heavily sighed.

 

            “What’s going on?”

 

            Lena stepped further into the room and Russell shut the double doors to the parlour, closing them all inside. The place smelled of beer and ashes and the suffocating heat pressing in from outside while too many bodies packed in close made it worse. The cloyingly sweet smell of Andrea’s perfume made Lena’s nose wrinkle faintly as she moved over to the table and looked down at the maps spread out over it, yellowed and curling at the corners where they weren’t weighed down.

 

            “The mine?” Lena asked, looking up and meeting Kelly’s eyes.

 

            “We’re working out the details for the deal. Miss Rojas here bought it, but we want a cut of it - seeing as it’s our town - but none of that really matters much if we ain’t got a working mine.”

 

            “You’re going to dig it out?” Kara quietly asked.

 

            Alex nodded, a grim set to her mouth. Then she hesitated, her lips twitching slightly as her gaze drifted to Lena’s face, piercing and steady as Lena looked at her as the skin-crawling feeling of being watched caught her attention.

 

            “Well … hopefully, not us.”

 

            Blinking, Lena’s mouth opened but she didn’t speak, a perplexed look crumpling her brow as she withdrew slightly. Clearing her throat as she twisted the hem of her hat through her hands, she swallowed.

 

            “You mean for me to do it?”

 

            “Look, Doc, you know you ain’t well-liked ‘round here. Ain’t no way to say it politely, so I’ll say it plainly. My sister … well, she’s got a soft heart, and then some, and she says she likes you so you can stay. And you been honest with me, which I ‘ppreciate greatly. But that ain’t going to stop folks from hatin’ you now, is it?”

 

            Arching an eyebrow, a faint smile curled Lena’s lips as Alex shrugged nonchalantly, her frankness almost refreshing, in a way. It usually came by way of insults and curses chasing her out of towns, of guns in shaking hands and more than one fired at her, and while she knew she wasn’t welcome in Midvale, it was still better than most places out west. And, truthfully, if Lena had wanted to stay somewhere where she would’ve been respected, she would’ve stayed east, in the big cities rife with death and fortunes and a dozen necromancers for every wealthy patron willing to pay.

 

            “The way I see it,” Alex continued, “we got a mine full of the dead and not a townsperson who’ll go near them. Not for love or money. Now, you on the other hand … well, you don’t know a damn soul who died in there, and you’re mighty familiar with the dead now, ain’t you, Doc? Seems like you might have some use to us , and if you help us out a bit … well, maybe folks won’t think so harshly of you, will they?”

 

            “You’re asking her to dig out the dead bodies?”

 

            Humming in agreement, Andrea nodded. “Your Madam Mayor seems to think that the residents here won’t take too kindly to the mine being reopened unless all the deceased are removed and given the proper burials they deserve. And it’s been months since it collapsed, and no volunteers are forthcoming to excavate the tunnels. Perhaps your Witch Doctor could provide useful, Miss Danvers.”

 

            “She ain’t my Witch Doctor,” Kara scoffed, folding her arms over her chest. “And she ain’t likely to start digging out dead bodies for us; she ain’t a gravedigger.”

 

            Clearing her throat, Lena shifted slightly and gave her the barest hint of a wry smile. “Actually, it is part of my profession that we perform certain death rites if requested. I can assure you, this wouldn’t be the first grave I’d ever dug.”

 

            “We’d pay, of course,” Kelly murmured, “most of them are loved ones to the people left here in town; their souls laid to rest would ease some of the grief, I’m sure.”

 

            Lena glanced sideways at Kara at the mention of loved ones, taking in the pinched and pale look on her face as a muscle twitched in her jaw. She imagined Alex hadn’t wanted her to be there to listen to them make arrangements to dig out her dead husband. Clearing her throat, Lena nodded tersely.

 

            “I’m sure it would, ma’am. I wouldn’t begrudge the dead the chance to rest respectfully, but I ask that you all leave the decisions for this work up to me; my methods may not be to your liking, but I can assure you, I have trained for years in my profession. I know the best way to put the dead to rest as quickly as possible.”

 

            With a strained laugh, Brainy smiled faintly. “So long as they don’t come back to life, I’m sure there will be no objections.”

 

            The silence was tense and heavy for a moment and Lena shifted uncomfortably. “Well … I couldn’t bring them back to life , but …”

 

            “You want to reanimate them?” Kara disbelievingly replied.

 

            Turning to her, Lena gave her a beseeching look to not cause a scene. “You of all people have seen how quickly work can get done with tireless hands.”

 

            “What?” Alex spluttered.

 

            “It would only be to speed up the process,” Lena assured them all, face flushed slightly pink as she tried to earn their cooperation. “Else, it could take months of labouring to find them all at rest in their own graves. A Necromancer, I may be, but a labourer , I am not . Not even mentioning the fact that I have given Miss Danvers my word that I would help her break her horses to be sold in exchange for food and board. I’m only one woman, to be doing so much work.”

 

            None of them spoke and Lena looked at each face in turn, expectant as she clasped her hat before her. “I will do as you ask and see your dead buried, but it’ll be on my own terms. Do we have an agreement or not?”

 

            Alex and Kelly glanced sideways at each other before Alex nodded ever so slightly. Clearing her throat, Kelly nodded more agreeably and met Lena’s eyes. “It looks like we do, Doc.”

 

            “The payment will come from the bank of Midvale,” Andrea firmly said. “As the dead belong to you, it seems … unfair to put the cost of hiring the Witch Doctor on my ledgers, does it not?”

 

            “Do we have a deal otherwise?” Alex warily asked.

 

            “Indeed, Sheriff. I think the terms will be agreeable. Forty-sixty, as discussed.”

 

            “And we can afford that, Mister Dox?” Kelly anxiously asked Brainy, who rifled through the sheath of papers before him, lips moving soundlessly as he muttered to himself, before wringing his hands nervously before himself and concurring.

 

            Lena lingered back on the fringes of the room, a few feet away from Kara, as they watched the banker set out the legal paperwork and both parties signed their names with flourishes and shook hands to seal the deal. She couldn’t rightfully say why, only that Lena didn’t much like the idea of excavating the mine; it seemed like they would be tempting Lex into coming down to visit them, even though it would be a while yet before it was up and running enough to turn a profit. Keeping her words of caution to herself, Lena was the first out of the hotel, standing in the bright sunshine as she leaned against the wooden post and scowled out at the main street of the town, watching people mill about, working or socialising and otherwise.

 

            “They’re all having a celebratory drink if you was looking to join them.”

 

            Glancing sideways, Lena straightened up and gave M’gann a polite nod. “I don’t expect I’ll be much welcome inside, ma’am. Even by you, as much as your hospitality extends. A room at your esteemed establishment seems to have pushed the boundaries, as it is.”

 

            Her lips twisted into a mocking smile as she spoke and M’gann let out a snort of laughter, the rag in her hand snapping as she shook it out and then flung it over a shoulder. “You’re politer than most of my guests, I’ll give you that, Doc. Blood and death and all.”

 

            “I’m not in the habit of looking for trouble,” Lena grumpily murmured.

 

            “I’ll bet it finds you all the same. Least you could do is enjoy a drink while you can. Go on now.”

 

            She jerked her chin towards the batwing doors and Lena hesitated, watching as M’gann moved over to the pile of damp bedsheets she was shaking out and hanging up to dry in the sunshine. After a moment, Lena ducked back inside and wound her way past tables to order a beer, setting down a coin on the bar and sliding it towards J’onn. Glancing sideways, she took in the sight of Kara at the opposite end of the bar and set another coin down, jerking her head towards her. A faint smile made his expression soften as he stopped polishing a glass and swept the two coins up, putting a mug of beer down before her and pouring another for Kara.

 

            When J’onn refused her coin and jerked his head towards Lena, she turned to look and Lena quickly snatched up her mug and turned her back on her. Her cheeks warmed slightly and she retreated to the far corner, shadowed, as far from the front windows as it was, and busied herself with glancing at framed black and white photos and articles documenting the development of the town and notable events.

 

            “Thank you.”

 

            Blinking, she looked up at Kara’s appearance beside her and nodded, a low hum at the back of her throat all the acknowledgement she gave her as her eyes nervously roamed about the saloon. Leaning against the wall beside her, Kara cocked her head to the side and smiled slightly.

 

            “You look like you’re thinking mighty hard there, miss.”

 

            Lips twitching with a ghost of a smile, Lena raised her mug to her lips and took a sip, sour beer washing away the dust of the road as she surveyed the room with a wary sweep of her piercing eyes. Soldiers and old men smoked and played cards - those that weren’t serious gamblers enough to visit the dens - while a few women laughed in a corner, free from the burden of husbands and children.

 

            “I’m not too sure about this deal.”

 

            “It ain’t fair for them to ask you to dig ‘em all out for us,” Kara murmured, nudging her gently as she gave her a concerned look of sorrow.

 

            Lena’s smile was knife-sharp and thin, her eyes sliding to Kara’s pretty, tanned face with her wide blue eyes, naïve and full of understanding as she stood in her dusty rancher’s clothes. Dust rimed her forehead in a dark line where the brim of her hat had protected her hairline and Lena had the oddest urge to take out her handkerchief and wipe it away, dusting off the dirt that hid the freckles scattered across her nose and smearing a drop of blood across her cracked lips to heal them anew. 

 

            Clearing her throat, she balled her hand into a fist and looked away, taking another sip of beer as she stamped down her thoughts. “It’s not the job that I’m not sure about. Only … if the mine reopens, a word’s going to spread sooner or later, especially once money starts pouring out and gold and silver find their way into pockets. It puts one hell of a target on a town.”

 

            “You thinking about that brother of yours again? Don’t you go worrying about him now, he don’t got a clue you’re here and ain’t nothin’ to be getting all worked up over when that mine’s blocked in well enough to keep you busy for a month trying to dig them all out. It’ll be ages before any workers get back down in them shafts - and that’s if we can even find any, seeing as most of them are still in there.”

 

            “Be that as it may,” Lena murmured, “if you go knocking on enough doors asking to see the devil, eventually he may answer.”

 

            “Is he all that bad?” Kara curiously asked.

 

            Lena rubbed at her forehead, a spasm of imperceptible pain crossing her face as she shifted uneasily and then fixed Kara with a hard stare. “Worse.”

 

            Kara’s face delicately crumpled with a bewildered look of disbelief, not quite sure what to make of Lena’s cryptically vague comments about her brother. Lena just didn’t have the capacity to put it into words, his maniacal thinking, his relentless obsession when he had an idea in his mind, the pure genius of his practises. She’d witnessed it firsthand, the experimentation of things that they had never been taught while learning their craft, things that she thought even her old teachers in the damp and decaying graveyards of New York City would have blanched at, sacrilegious and twisted as they were. She suppressed a shudder and drained her beer.

 

            “I’ll be seeing you,” she said, setting her empty mug down on the nearest table and tapping her hat back down on her head, touching the rim before she stalked out of the saloon.

 

            She didn’t make her way back to the ranch. Instead, Lena took off out of town on Hecate, who had been watered and rested while discussions and drinks were had, keeping up a steady trot to not wear out her horse as she looped around Midvale. The wide arc took her miles out, nothing but dust and pale dried grass and small prairie animals scampering about at small watering holes and through the endless stretch of shrubbery. Lena skirted the foothills north of the town, their shade cool and more fertile as birches and aspens sprung up with abundance, birds calling and a stream trickling, making a westward loop down through the stretch of plains before passing through Kara’s land, a herd of horses grazing and the more southerly foothills they’d been at this morning.

 

            It was a few hours of riding, and Lena was alert the whole time, her magic spider-webbing out around her in a wide net, cast out for signs of trouble, signs of the undead or approaching bodies pumping with tangible blood to signify approaching strangers. She sensed nothing save old bones and small creatures, bagging a couple of hares and a wild turkey as she made through a mountain pass, looped around the bottom of it and headed for an easterly path through small gaming trails. Mountain goats bleated and sent loose rocks scattering as they bounded away from her approach, and at her advantageous height amidst the outcroppings and fresh greenness of trees, she could see for miles to the north and west, with nothing prickling her senses. 

 

            Descending through the mountain to the east of Midvale, she came out near the old mine, that haunted feeling of death she was all-too-familiar with near a site where many unrestful spirits lie but didn’t linger long. All she caught was sandy stone and trees and sunlight bleaching the colour from everything before retreating further down the path, knowing what lay ahead of her and leaving it until she started excavating the old mine shaft. Reassured that they were safe, for the time being, at least, Lena urged Hecate for home with the squeeze of her knees and was left with a heavy mind as she headed south, back to the ranch.

 

            Kara was home when she arrived back, an extra layer of dust coating her and the beginnings of a sunburn across the bridge of her nose and high cheeks. Settling Hecate down in the cool shade of the barn, refilling the oats and checking she had enough water, Lena walked to the water barrel outside, coat and hat shed, and scooped warm water over the back of her neck and her face. Rivulets cut through the grime and she looked up to find Kara watching her from the porch of the low house, carving an apple up with a knife as she leaned against the wooden railing.

 

            Lena hesitantly raised a hand in greeting and then washed her hands off, flinging droplets of water to the dry ground, the sand greedily drinking it up. Ducking back into the barn, she changed into a clean shirt and pants and left the dirty clothes to be rubbed clean when she had the chance before sinking down onto the dry floor of the barn and rifling through her medicinal chest of tinctures and herbs. Her energy was spent from hours of working, the faint tinge of pink to her skin washing away the last remnants of her exertion, and she knocked back a tincture to restore herself before using a milk tooth and the prick of her finger to heal the stinging sunburn and take the aches from her muscles.

 

            Making a soothing poultice from ground oats, water and some aloe vera gel she’d picked up further south and stored in a vial, Lena stretched out on the hay with it spread over her dry skin. She napped lightly, the day weighing down heavily on her, and before she could stop herself, she slipped into a deep sleep, oblivious to the mice burrowing into the pile of hay or the day passing into night as the light faded and a hushed quietness blanketed the land.

 

            Lena came to hours later to the cracking sound of gunshot splitting the silence. It startled her so much that she bolted upright, heart hammering in her chest, and found her eyes stinging as she let out a hacking cough, more shouts sounding outside. Holding an arm up to cover her face as she squeezed her eyes shut, Lena coughed and gasped as she struggled to suck down a lungful of searing air, her shirt plastered to her skin with sweat as she scrambled to the cool dirt floor of the barn, on hands and knees.

 

            Hunched over, Lena let out a hacking cough and tried to look through the haze of smoke, her chest aching and her fingers slick with sweat. She didn’t know where the fire had come from, only that it was consuming the barn and she’d slept through it. Fortunately, the smoke was still relatively high and closer to the ground, she was able to clear her mind and get her bearings.

 

            A frantic whinny forced her into motion, lurching to her feet with a damp sleeve pressed over her mouth and nose as she made for the stall. Hecate’s eyes were rolling, exposing slivers of white as she snorted and tossed her head, panicking as smoke settled over her in a haze. Yanking the door open, Lena slapped her rump and sent her galloping out.

 

            Before she could make it to the barn door, it was torn open to reveal a pale and terrified Kara, holding a rifle and smelling of gunpowder. She’d been the source of the gunshot that had woken Lena and stumbled back with surprise as Hecate bolted past her into the cool darkness of night.

 

            “The barn-“ Lena started.

 

            “People from the town,” Kara said, a tremor in her voice from barely controlled rage. “They snuck up; I didn’t see the fire was set until Krypto started barking. I don’t know what they think they’re playing at.”

 

            With a scoff of laughter and a wry smile, Lena let out a rough cough, her eyes dry and stinging as she looked at Kara. “I think you know well enough, ma’am; they mean to kill me.”

 

            “They wouldn’t,” Kara firmly objected.

 

            “You and I both know well enough they would.”

 

            “We can argue ‘bout that later, Doc. You need to get away from this barn before the roof collapses. It’s about to come down any minute now, I reckon.”

 

            Wheezing slightly, the heat at her back a dangerous reminder as the roar of the fire grew, devouring wood and hay quickly as beams cracked and blackened and threatened to crumble around them, Lena nodded.

 

            “I need to get my things.”

 

            Staring at her with disbelief, Kara grabbed her arm. “You ain’t serious.”

 

            Gently pulling her arm free, Lena fixed her with a grave look. “My gun, my teeth and those bullets are worth more than my own life. Without them, I’m no use to anyone.”

 

            “But-“

 

            “I’ll be quick,” Lena whispered, a faint smile softening her face.

 

            Kara was left standing outside with her rifle in hand, watching as thick smoke streamed from the blazing barn, an orange beacon against the backdrop of night.

 

            Inside, Lena doubled over as she stumbled blindly through the barn. The fire had caught quickly, the timber old and dried out after the last storm, and smoke gathered thickly inside, sucking all the air from it. As she lurched ahead, a heavy beam gave way as a portion of the tall wall collapsed inwards, and it was only by sheer luck that the heavy beam missed her. Thinner planks that had snapped in half, blackened and hot to the touch struck her shoulders and sent her sprawling, forced to drag herself forward on her elbows.

 

            She felt like she was suffocating as she crawled forward, stubborn determination leaving her unwilling to leave the tools of her trade inside to be melted to nothing. Lena knew that it was foolish, but without them, she was more vulnerable than she cared to admit, and it would’ve been better to die in the fire than be left a sitting duck for Lex to come and torture for amusement.

 

            The pile of hay she’d been sleeping on was ablaze from falling embers and mice scurried out through cracks, and nearby was a pile of her belongings. The chest was too heavy to try and take with her, and while difficult to replace most of the herbs and tonics and salves, it wouldn’t be impossible - the doctor in town would probably be able to sell her most. Opting to leave it, Lena grabbed her belt with its holstered gun, grimoire, teeth and bullets and snatched it up. Her leather coat and her old hat were pooled beside it in a heap and it was out of fondness for them that she grabbed them in her arms too before staggering blindly to the door.

 

            As thick as the smoke was, she blundered straight through it, relying on her memory to guide her as she squeezed her eyes shut and held her breath. All in all, she was only in there for a few minutes, but it felt like an eternity before she emerged, spilling out into the cool night, streaked with soot and sweat as she flung her armful of meagre belongings to the ground and let the rest burn inside.

 

            Dropping hard to her knees, Lena braced herself against her thighs and coughed until she thought she was about to bring up a lung. Her skin felt tight and her breaths were shallow and wheezing, each one a ragged effort that made her feel like she was suffocating. She’d inhaled too much smoke, could taste it at the back of her throat and feel it in her eyes as she retched and coughed until she was spent.

 

            It was Kara who heaved her to her feet, pulling her arm around her shoulders and dragging her towards the house. She dropped Lena onto a chair unceremoniously before rushing off and returning with a pitcher of water a moment later. Forcing mouthfuls down her throat, until Lena was coughing and spluttering, wet drops splashing over the scarred table and the warped floorboards, Kara poured the pitcher with shaking hands.

 

            Once Lena couldn’t stomach another mouthful, her chest rising and falling quickly as she sat slumped in her seat, sweaty and sooty and dazed, Kara dumped the rest of the water over her face. Stiffening at the shock of it, Lena let out a squawk of complaint and blinked water out of her bloodshot eyes, eyelashes clinging together as her dark hair plastered to her head,

 

            “You need to heal yourself,” Kara ordered her, an edge of panic in her voice. “Your back- your throat- all that smoke.”

 

            Nodding, Lena hunched forward, squeezing her eyes shut and shaking her head. She felt faint, her chest constricting painfully, not enough air making it to her lungs, and when Kara hauled her back upright, Lena blinked at her slowly.

 

            “Heal yourself,” Kara barked.

 

            Sagging in her seat, head lolling as she blinked sluggishly, Lena’s hearing turned tinny, so distant that she was unaware of her surroundings. Exhaustion and smoke made her tired, the lack of oxygen making her vision blacken at the edges as she clung to consciousness. She didn’t hear the sounds of hooves thundering up the long road to the house, the heavy thud of footsteps on the porch, and the loud voices that barged inside were muffled to her.

 

            The stinging slap to her cheek snapped her back to reality for a minute, clarity washing over her as if she’d been plunged into a freezing river, mid-winter. Pain blossomed on her cheek as it reddened angrily, and she stiffened in the seat, sitting up straighter as she threatened to lunge. Firm hands clamped down on her shoulders and she stared with sharp green eyes, taking in the mildly concerned look of the Sheriff.

 

            “Wake up, damn you.”

 

            Lena made a vague humming sound of acknowledgement and blinked lazily at her, raising a limp hand to rub at her cheek. Alex caught it and stabbed the tip of her knife into Lena’s hand, eliciting a hiss as it cut deep enough for blood to quickly well up and drip down her wrist in stripes of vivid red.

 

            A tooth was pushed into her hand, a yellowed molar, nearly an inch long, and she stared down as her fingers were curled around it, allowing the blood to wet it. As she struggled to breathe, she clung to the edge of pain to keep herself awake and let the familiarity of years of practice take over. She burned through the tooth quickly, her magic eating away at it as she delved into the shallow pool that hadn’t been expended that day. As drained as she was, she consumed the rest of it recklessly, feeling the ache in her chest lessen, the pain in her back as burnt and blistered skin sloughed off and knitted together into perfect alabaster. 

 

            Sweating and breathing heavily - deep, full breaths - she rubbed the tiny pile of ash off on the thigh of her pants and looked at Kara. Her eyes were bright and almost feverish, although not from the fire, but her foolish exertion that left her desperate to sink down into sleep, and she blinked slowly, her eyes falling to the red-soaked sleeve of Kara’s shirt.

 

            Reaching out with a hand, Lena’s fingertips barely brushed the trail left behind by a skimming bullet before it thumped heavily back down, her knuckles painfully catching the edge of the sturdy table as a listless sigh escaped her.

 

            “You’re hurt.”

 

            Her eyelids shuttered then as her eyes rolled up into her head and her body went slack. Unconsciousness claimed her fully this time, and not even a hard slap from Alex would have been able to bring her out of it.

 

            Lena slept all through the next day and into the following morning, waking to predawn darkness in a bed. It was thin and lumpy but softer than anything she’d slept on in months, at least, and she woke with the sluggish confusion of not knowing where she was. It had been years since she’d come to, unaware of her physical presence, not since she’d been shot dead and dragged onwards, revived somewhere new and left to scramble herself back together,  miles from her last memory.

 

            Sitting up, her body protested, heavy and aching and stiff from lying still for too long. Dressed in nothing but her shirt, Lena breathed in the smell of smoke that saturated her entire being, singed hair and the linen and her ashy skin. Drawing in a lungful of air, deep and cool and fresh, she coughed and pressed a hand to her throat. It had been healed but was still scratchy and dry. The sound of it brought forth rustling motion from the kitchen and she looked up at the sound of the heavy tread of boots stopping in the doorway.

 

            Silhouetted against the open mouth of the doorway was Kara. Lena couldn’t see her but it was undeniably her, the silence of her presence radiating anxiety and concern and that odd tenderness that she harboured for Lena that the latter hadn’t been able to parse. Her skirts rustled as she stepped in.

 

            “You’re awake.”

 

            “The barn?”

 

            “All but gone entirely. It’ll need rebuilding.”

 

            Lena sighed softly with defeat and raked a hand through her hair. The mattress jostled as Kara took a seat at the foot of the narrow bed, reaching over to a unit to strike the flinch on an oil lamp. A tongue of flame flickered to life and cast a wan orange glow over the room and Lena took in her grim expression and the lump of a bandage beneath the sleeve of her shirt.

 

            “Your horse is alright-“

 

            “Your arm-“

 

            They both spoke at the same time and then fell silent, staring at each other as they waited for the other to speak. Lena leaned forward, reaching out with a shaking hand to cup her arm, gently so she didn’t agitate the wound, and then looked up at Kara.

 

            Scant inches separated them and she watched as Kara’s lips parted, her eyes darting down to them and then away. Gently rubbing her thumb over the bandage, a bittersweet feeling twisted in Lena’s stomach.

 

            “You tried to frighten them off.”

 

            “They’d already lit it before I heard them. They came quietly; wouldn’t have heard them all the way in here. I thought for sure they’d run the second I started shouting - didn’t think anyone in town would shoot me , at least, but … guess I was wrong. They got off a few shots. Took out one of the windows too. It only scraped me, though.”
