            Lena turned her head and took in the sight of her pouch, growing perilously lighter with each week spent lingering in Midvale. She took a tooth out and hesitated before reaching out to grab the cuff of Kara’s shirt. Her other hand glided down the sleeve and quickly unfastened the button. As she slowly rolled it up with deft fingers, Kara sat still, her heart fluttering quickly, nervously, and Lena paused and looked up at her as she exposed the bandage.

 

            When Kara didn’t speak, Lena carefully removed the bandage to reveal the gunshot wound. It wasn’t deep, but it was wide and had bled a lot, still raw and pink and seeping as she peeled back the last layer. It probably would’ve been less painful had it gone straight through and needed stitches, Lena thought, rather than the constant burning sting on it, but it didn’t matter now.

 

            She couldn’t see her knife in the nearby vicinity but there was a jagged splinter on one of the wall planks, which Lena used to prick her fingertip. It made her hiss, having to gouge it deep enough to draw blood, and she saw Kara wince and move to stop her. Lena was already turning back to her though, running the blood over the tooth before she closed her eyes and caught the thread of power, using it to grow fresh skin over the angry slash through Kara’s tanned skin.

 

            “It … itches,” Kara murmured, rolling her shoulders uncomfortably.

 

            “It’ll pass.”

 

            “Thank you.”

 

            Giving her a pained look of amusement, Lena shook her head as she slowly rolled Kara’s sleeve back down, head ducked as she fiddled with the button.

 

            “You shouldn’t be grateful. It wouldn’t have happened if it wasn’t for my being here.”

 

            “It weren’t your fault.”

 

            Lena let out a quiet scoff of laughter and her head jerked up as Kara’s warm hand covered hers. Her eyes were dark in the dim light but no less insistent and Lena swallowed thickly as guilt nagged at her.

 

            “You don’t have to lie to comfort me, Miss. It won’t help.”

 

            “It ain’t a lie; I should be apologising to you for what they did. I didn’t think-”

 

            “It’s alright,” Lena softly assured her, a crooked smile curving her lips as her shoulders slumped. She let out a sad laugh and shrugged helplessly, looking small and oddly vulnerable as she seemed to shrink in on herself. “It’s not the first time, and it surely won’t be the last.”

 

            Kara’s brow creased with bewilderment as she laid a hand on Lena’s knee over the blankets. “I know I’ve been harsh, but … what could fill them with such hatred? I don’t like it but … I’d never hurt you, Lena. Not like that.”

 

            The sound of her name brought a lump to Lena’s throat, and her eyebrows drew together in a confused frown as she picked at the pilled blankets, trying to stifle the heaviness that rose in her chest. Drawing in a shallow, shuddering breath, she sighed softly.

 

            “I know. But you’re not everyone, and some people … sometimes they pretend you’re a bad person so they don’t have to feel guilty about what they do to you. If- if they thought that perhaps I wasn’t such a bad person, they’d have no one to blame for their fear about death. The truth is, people don’t want to die, but they don’t think it’s natural to come back, either. But I’ll let you in on a little secret.”

 

            “Oh?”

 

            “One day, we all fall into a sleep that lasts forever, no matter how many times we’re brought back in between. Eventually, we all go to the same place, and it’s not so scary.”

 

            Kara let out a quiet huff of laughter, her lips twitching wryly as she cocked her head to the side. “Well, I thought you was going to that place a little early, Doc. You gave me a real fright there.”

 

            “Well, now, I’m sorry, ma’am,” Lena murmured, biting back a smile. She hesitated for a moment, deliberating before letting out a short, scratchy laugh. “Some might say it’s a little overdue , though.”

 

            “Not me. And I’ll thank you kindly to take more care next time. If it weren’t for Alex, I don’t think you would be awake right now.”

 

            Humming faintly, Lena touched her fingertips to her cheek and smiled sardonically. “Mm, your sister has a good slap, I’ll give her that. Remind me not to brawl with her.”

 

            “You will be doing no such thing,” Kara said, climbing to her feet and sighing heavily. “You need to rest, while I have to go and see about a pregnant mare.”

 

            Clicking her tongue, Lena pulled the blankets back and waved a hand dismissively, “don’t you go worrying about me now, I’m alright. I’ve got work that needs to be done.”

 

            Kara set a heavy hand on her shoulder and stopped her, giving her a stern look as blue light filtered in through the window. “You need to stay in that bed, ma’am. I ain’t no sawbone like you, but if there’s one thing I do know, it’s that you don’t flog a tired horse.”

 

            “And what’s that supposed to mean?” Lena snorted, arching an eyebrow.

 

            “It means that you used that power of yours too much yesterday, and I reckon that needs more than a day of rest to recover from. ‘Specially after you went and got yourself nearly burnt to death.”

 

            “It was just a little smoke.”

 

            “A lot of smoke, you stubborn witch.”

 

            Letting out a snort of laughter, Lena leaned back against the thin pillow and pulled the blankets back up. “I think I should be offended, but you’re technically half right. Go on then, off with you.”

 

            “Food’s in the kitchen. Make sure you eat it ‘fore Krypto does. He’s a sly one, that old dog. I’ll be back around noon, I s’pose, so … try not to get shot or burnt or … fall down a well.”

 

            “You know, the last person to shoot me was you. You do remember that, don’t you?”

 

            “Well, don’t go sneaking up on me again,” Kara murmured, genuine warmth in her voice that caught Lena off-guard.

 

            Her smile faltered and she made a vague sound of acknowledgement before pulling the blankets up to her chin and turning on her side. Kara lingered a second longer before her boots scuffed the floorboards and she ducked out past the fireplace and shut the door behind her. Lena was left in her bed, with the sheets that smelled like her, as her mind reeled at the surprising nugget of information that had made itself known to her; Kara liked her. 

 

            It wasn’t so surprising, given that she’d liked Lena well enough to house her in the barn and let her work for her supper, that she’d kissed her and defended her when she deemed fit. The surprising part was that, despite her hardest efforts, her wariest reservations and suspicious distrust, Lena liked her too. The thought burrowed itself deep into her mind, echoing and reverberating until it consumed her every thought, unable to be drowned out by burying her head beneath the pillow and trying to think of something else.

 

            Eventually, she yanked the covers back and climbed to her feet, determined to work and take her mind off the uneasy thoughts. Getting attached to someone wouldn’t bode well for her and was unfamiliar territory that she wasn’t sure it was safe to wade into. Instead, she raided Kara’s closet and found a worn skirt that was just a little too long but fine once she donned her boots, already longing for her clothes that had been reduced to ash.

 

            Eating cold sausages and biscuits from the covered pan, Lena scratched Krypto behind his ears and fed him the scraps before stepping out into the dawn. Firstly, she made a visit to Hecate, smoothing the horse’s muzzle and checking her for any injuries from the fire. She seemed perfectly healthy and, satisfied, Lena made for the charred husk of the barn. What remained was blackened and twisted.

 

            Kicking through the cinders and scorched planks, looking for anything salvageable, Lena soon gave up and resolved to shift the splintered beams and pile of blackened wood off into a pile for Kara to deal with later. She wasn’t sure what plans she had to rebuild it, but Lena would do her best to help and made quick work of tearing apart the remains of the stalls and walls with an axe until her palms were blistered from swinging it.

 

            She was wiping sweat from her brow when the sound of hooves caught her attention. A part of her hoped it was Kara, but it was too early for her to return and it was coming from the road. Squinting against the sunlight, Lena watched as Alex rode up on the ranch and easily swung down from the saddle, hoisting a sack down with her. She spotted Lena immediately.

 

            “Howdy, Doc,” Alex leisurely greeted her as she strode across the yard, a burlap sack clinking as she sucked on a lit cigarette, her face shaded by her Sheriff’s hat. “You’re looking a right sight better than last time we spoke.”

 

            “All thanks to you, if I recall correctly,” Lena wryly replied, setting the axe against the remains of the doorway’s posts. “That’s a real nice slap you’ve got there.”

 

            Nodding, Alex smiled around the cigarette and kicked a twisted lump that Lena thought had been her cup. Eyeing her for a moment, Alex hummed to herself and then spoke.

 

            “You seen my sister anywhere ‘round here?”

 

            “She said she was going to check on a pregnant mare,” Lena slowly informed her, a wary look crossing her face as she dusted off her dirty hands and nudged her hat up, leaving black streaks of soot behind.

 

            “Well, then, maybe I’ll sit around here and wait for her. Where’s that pretty gun of yours? It melt in that fire?”

 

            Frowning, Lena chewed on the inside of her lip for a moment as she paused, before reluctantly replying. “In the house. No use wearing it for breaking horses and yard work.”

 

            With a quiet laugh, Alex dipped her chin in agreement. “Don’t fret none; mine’ll do you just fine.”

 

            “Pardon me?”

 

            “Come on, now. I got bottles and tin cans,” Alex said, rustling the burlap sack and shouldering past Lena, back out into the yard and away from the ranch. “I ain’t seen you shoot yet.”

 

            Doffing her hat, Lena bent the edges as she squinted against harsh sunlight, her face crumpling as she gave Alex a rueful look and hurried after her, scuffing a foot through the ashes until it turned to dusty earth, the dried grass whispering at the touch of her hurried footsteps.

            

            “I’ve got work to finish, Sheriff. I’m afraid I have to decline.”

 

            “I wasn’t asking.”

 

            Biting back a frustrated sigh, Lena set her mouth into a grim line and donned her hat again, tapping it down low over her brow as the wind snatched at the ends of her ponytail and she stalked after the Sheriff. A prickle of fear rippled across her arms and the nape of her neck, mouth dry and tasting of dust, ever-present and ever blowing out in these parts, and now mingled with acrid ash, and she wasn’t entirely sure if she was going to end up as a dead body buried out on Kara’s ranch or not. She found Alex wildly unpredictable, despite her steadfast justice.

 

            They didn’t go too far from the ranch, the house still low and long behind them, but they were at the opposite end to the pen of horses grazing beneath the sun, near the bleached stump of a long-dead tree. Lena hung back as she watched Alex line up a few bottles and cans, the tins slightly twisted and the bottles shining green and brown as light filtered through them.

 

            Removing one of her revolvers, Alex spun it around a finger and gave her a grin, slowly moving back towards her and holding it out by the grip. Eyeing her with outright suspicion, Lena took the gun from her, the grip warm in her hand, the weight different to her own revolver, and cleared her dry throat as she looked down at it.

 

            “Why?”

 

            Shrugging languidly, Alex plucked her cigarette from her lips and dropped it to the ground, crushing it underfoot and exhaling a plume of grey as she spoke. “Guess I’m just curious now, ain’t I? I saw the bodies, you know. Ain’t seen anyone shoot like that before; won’t rightly believe it ‘til I see it now, either.”

 

            “I could shoot you,” Lena pointed out.

 

            Letting out a bark of laughter, Alex clapped her on the shoulder good-naturedly before her hand had her gun drawn, spinning around her finger in a display of showmanship before she pointed the barrel at Lena’s head. Her laughter died off but a smile still played on her lips, brown eyes warm.

 

            “Go ahead. Do it then. Let’s see who can shoot first.”

 

            “I didn’t say I wanted to.”

 

            With a softer chuckle, Alex lowered the gun and her smile widened a fraction. “I know . Else I wouldn’t be putting a gun in your hand in the first place, now, would I?”

 

            Lips twitching, Lena spun the gun around a finger like Alex had and cast her eyes towards the row of bottles and cans. Eyes narrowing, she let out a quiet huff of laughter. “How far away?”

 

            “What’s your best shot?”

 

            Shrugging, Lena deliberated for a moment, “I don’t know, fifty yards?”

 

            “Fifty yards it is.”

 

            Alex’s voice was full of amusement and Lena gave her a long look before she retreated backwards, the heels of her boots gouging into the soft dirt as dry prairie grass rustled and crunched beneath her feet. She backed up far enough, until the bottles and cans were small targets, and popped open the cylinder, eyeing the simple bullets. Content, she spun the cylinder and clicked it back into place and eased back the trigger with a calloused thumb.

 

            Raising the gun, Lena narrowed her eyes to focus, aware of Alex standing out of the line of fire and closer to the stump than Lena was. She hadn’t moved and watched on with patient anticipation, curiosity lending her features a kinder edge to them as she watched Lena closely.

 

            The gun fired with a bang and the smell of gunpowder shrouding Lena, the recoil jerking her slightly and a tin can flying backwards from the punch of a bullet through its metal. Alex let out a low whistle, audible across the distance between them and crossed over to the stump in long strides to inspect the hole torn through the can.

 

            “Well, I’ll be damned. You are a dead shot.”

 

            “Yes, ma’am,” Lena quietly called back.

 

            “How’d you get so good?”

 

            Shrugging uncomfortably, Lena put the safety back on and slowly meandered towards Alex. “Just part of the job. It isn’t always healing and bringing people back. Sometimes, people who haven’t been trained fuck it up so badly that there are reanimated corpses just … wandering about. Sometimes, the likes of my brother are wandering around, wreaking chaos for the sake of it. It leaves a lot to clean up, and when bullets are in short supply … well, you want to make sure you don’t miss,”

 

            “Fair enough.”

 

            They fell into an awkward silence for a long moment and Alex rubbed the back of her neck as she kicked the toe of her boot through the dust. “Listen … I’m real sorry about what happened. I’m looking into it - fair is fair - but, well, for what it’s worth …”

 

            Nodding as she masked her surprise, Lena softly cleared her throat, “well, don’t be too genuine, Sheriff. The good people of this town might mistake it for you actually liking me, and then the world would truly be ending.”

 

            Snorting, Alex gave her a droll look before she sobered up. “You know, Doc, I think you’re right. Maybe I am growing fonder of you, and that can only mean more trouble.”

 

            Without another word, she strode off to Lena’s mark with a pistol in hand and fired off a few shots at the bottles and cans while Lena watched on. Gunpowder scented the air and the clanging of cans and shattering of glass cut through the peaceful day. They took it in turns until they were out of things to shoot at, and Lena returned Alex’s gun to her and watched her holster it before walking over to the stump. Picking up twisted tin cans, riddled with bullets, they cleaned up their mess as well as they could and walked back to the distant house in silence.

 

            Alex let herself inside, scratching the dog behind his ears before she washed off her hands and raided the kitchen. Pouring out moonshine into tin cups for them, a little early in the day for Lena but taken all the same, they sat at opposite ends of the wide porch steps, staring out at the remains of the barn as they sipped the distilled liquor and ate dried strips of beef and hard cheese, throwing scraps to the chickens to peck at.

 

            “My sister,” Alex said after a long stretch of silence, leaning back on her elbows as sunshine slanted across her outstretched legs. She picked at her teeth and then glanced sideways at Lena. “You down soft on her?”

 

            “She’s, ah, been … generous,” Lena hedged, squirming uncomfortably.

 

            “Generous. That’s what they’re callin’ it these days, is it?”

 

            Snorting, Lena’s lips curled derisively as a muscle ticked in her jaw and she looked out across the plains, the nearby foothills a smudged blue in the distance. “You’re as much a coot as that hag that tried to kill me.”

 

            “Oh,” Alex snorted, “ that’s what got you all riled up now, was it? What she say to you, huh?”

 

            “No, it couldn’t have possibly had anything to do with the bullet she embedded in my side, now, Sheriff, could it?” Lena evasively replied, nettled by her amusement.

 

            Holding her hands up defensively as she grinned, Alex lazily shrugged. “Fine by me, Doc. I don’t much like the idea of you sittin’ my kid sister any more than I liked the idea of her and that wasted scoundrel she found herself hitched to the first time. Hell, maybe I like you more; you’re better to look at, ain’t that the truth.”

 

            Letting out a bark of laughter, Lena’s eyebrows rose and fell quickly. “A glowing commendation from you .”

 

            “She’s sweet on you,” Alex continued, her voice softening. “I don’t like that. I don’t like that she ain’t as scared of you as she should be.”

 

            “And what about you?” Lena lightly asked, her smile goading and her tone almost mocking. “Are you scared of me, Sheriff?”

 

            “No. I seen you knocked to your knees a few times now; you don’t frighten me much at all.”

 

            “Well, don’t lull yourself into a false sense of security. If I don’t frighten you, it’s because I have no cause to.”

 

            Patting the wooden planks, Lena climbed to her feet and dusted off her hands before feeding the last of the dried beef to Krypto and stalking off across the yard. The moonshine had left her pale cheeks flushed and her shirt was soon clinging to her sweaty back as she worked beneath the sun, shifting more wood as Alex refilled her cup from the clay jug and watched her. Her stare was unnerving to Lena, making her skin prickle at the sensation, and she had to stop herself from looking over at her. She knew the stares were scrutinising warnings and Lena had every intention of heeding them, if only because she knew she’d be risking more than Alex’s wrath to allow herself to feel anything for Kara. It didn’t stifle the feelings or that voice at the back of her head though.

 

            Kara came back soon and Lena was broodingly silent, offering no banter to the scoldings she received for being up and working. The crestfallen look on Kara’s face made her heart twinge with guilt though as she coldly rebuffed her, hunching her shoulders as her muscles ached and the sun burned the back of her neck. She listened to their muffled conversation on the porch, felt their stares and the whispered remarks, before Alex eventually left, touching the brim of her hat as she passed by the remains of the barn and swung up into the saddle.

 

            “You should take a break now,” Kara called out across the yard, cupping her hands around her mouth.

 

            Lena’s movements slowed and she nodded reluctantly. Washing off as much as the soot and ash as she could, which didn’t help much, she dragged her feet on the way back to the house and lingered on the shaded porch as she listened to Kara bustle about inside. When she caught sight of the Necromancer lingering outside, Kara stepped into the doorway, gripping either side of it and eyeing her skirt that Lena had borrowed. Her blue eyes softened and a smile slightly curled the corners of her mouth.

 

            “You alright?”

 

            Glancing over her shoulder, Lena’s lips twitched but didn’t quite smile. She hummed and then sighed heavily as she leaned on the railing, a thoughtful look on her face as she brooded. “I think … I should take my leave now,” Lena cautiously spoke, slow and uncertain.

 

            “What?”

 

            “I-”

 

            “No,” Kara spluttered, stepping out of the house and storming over to Lena. She roughly grabbed one of her arms and forced her to look at her, which Lena did with great reluctance, chewing on the inside of her lip as she tried to look everywhere but at Kara’s face. 

 

            “You said,” Kara started before trailing off. Letting out an impatient huff, she tried again. “You said you weren’t going to go again.”

 

            Brow creasing with a troubled look, Lena’s mouth turned down at the corners and she covered Kara’s hand with her own for a brief moment, before prying her fingers off her arm. Shaking her head slowly, guilt and regret crept into Lena’s eyes. 

 

            “I didn’t say that, Kara.”

 

            “You-”

 

            “I said I’d do what I could to keep you safe,” Lena gently interrupted. “But … well, it’s rotten work when the only reason you’re not safe is because I’m here. So, for everyone’s sake, I should just go.”

 

            Letting out a hollow laugh, Lena gestured at the charcoal husk of the barn, “I mean, where am I going to sleep anyway?”

 

            “With me,” Kara firmly murmured, reaching out for Lena’s hand. “Stop trying to leave all the time.”

 

            Blinking in surprise, Lena let out a quick laugh as her face crumpled with confusion. Holding Kara’s hand in hers, dry and calloused and warm , she felt her stomach twist uncomfortably. It was unfamiliar, unnerving , and even her dalliances with her kind on her travels had never left her feeling so disoriented at what it was she was even feeling. All she knew was weeks of living in Kara’s barn, sharing meals under the same roof and making sniping remarks in her defence had left her fond of the rancher.

 

            “Why do you want me to stay?”

 

            “Because … I already told you,” Kara frustratedly replied. “I don’t- I don’t want to be alone.”

 

            Softly sighing, Lena reached up and hesitated before laying her palm against Kara’s cheek. She gave her a pained smile, regret welling up inside her. “You don’t even know what real loneliness looks like.”

 

            Flinching back, hurt blossomed on Kara’s face as she pressed her lips into a flat line. She turned quickly, unwilling to let Lena watch as she regathered her composure, but there was a tremor in her voice as she spoke quietly.

 

            “And the mine?”

 

            Hesitating, Lena cleared her throat, awkwardness making her roll her shoulders as she shifted uncomfortably. “I’m sure there are soldiers willing to do the work.”

 

            “This town will run dry ‘fore they finish dragging their feet through that. ‘Sides, most of them are afraid of those tunnels now. Folks say they’re haunted, and the like.”

 

            “They’re just silly stories,” Lena whispered, “you’d find better in a penny dreadful.”

 

            “Well … I won’t beg,” Kara said, her voice oddly cold as she kept her back to Lena. “I ain’t got it in me to do it again, so … go on then. Best get off my land, Witchdoctor. Best get far away from here.”

 

            Lena clenched her teeth and was silent for a moment before she ground out a reply. “Don’t worry, I will. Any trouble heading this way will surely follow; I’ll keep my promise to keep you safe.”

 

            With a scathing laugh, Kara folded her arms over her chest, “some promise.”

 

            “Well …”

 

            “You know, Doc, one day, your past is gonna catch you, whether you keep running or stop and wait for it. You say I don’t know real loneliness, but you don’t know real companionship and that’s worse. Least you could’ve had that while you waited.”

 

            A spasm of wounded hurt flickered across Lena’s face as Kara’s words knifed through her. She hesitated for a moment and then ducked into the house, finding her dirty clothes from that morning and changing into her pants before she donned her ash-streaked coat and buckled on her belt. Anger simmered inside her and she snatched up her meagre belongings without giving any thought to it, her gun and grimoire and pouch of teeth familiar weights as they hung from the belt, her fingers running reassuringly over the bullets and the knife strapped to her thigh.

 

            Shaking out her hat, she stepped back out onto the porch and shoved it down over her windswept and sweaty hair and strode past Kara, back stiff and straight before her feet thundered down the steps. Slowing once she hit the dried earth, she glanced down and to the side, but not up at Kara, who hadn’t moved.

 

            “I thank you for your hospitality. With any luck, this will be the last time we meet; take comfort in that - it means you’re safe.”

 

            Kara offered no reply save for a scoff of contempt and Lena walked onwards, over to where Hecate had been penned along with the unbroken wild horses. A pinch of guilt reared its head again at the fact that Lena hadn’t fulfilled her end of the bargain, try as she might, but she was too far in now for her stubborn pride to meekly crawl back to the house and ask if she could stay. Cheeks flushed and eyes bright with hurt and irritation, Lena opened the fence and whistled for her horse to come.

 

            Some of the others answered her call too and she had to fend them off as Hecate pushed through their packed bodies. It was with a pang of longing that Lena realised she would miss them, the press of their damp muzzles and the hard stomp of their hooves when they got into contrary moods. 

 

            Most of all, she’d miss the woman that had vanished from the porch, the slam of the front door cutting through the quietness of the day, and it was with a bitter taste in her mouth that she hauled herself up onto Hecate’s bare back, her already sour mood fouling even further as she resigned herself to the prospect of an uncomfortable ride into town, chafing against the horse’s hide.

 

            Knotting her fingers in Hecate’s mane, Lena urged her onwards into a trot, and try as she might, she couldn’t stop herself from glancing backwards over her shoulder to catch one last glimpse of Kara. Disappointment sat heavily in her stomach when she didn’t come back out to watch her leave, and Lena swallowed thickly as she turned back around and clicked her tongue, settling into a gallop as she left as quickly as possible.

 

            She arrived in Midvale saddle-sore and steaming with frustration, her stare dark enough to kill as she met the eyes of wary townsfolk and ignored the curt nod from Alex and the fleeting smile from Kelly. It wasn’t until she hitched Hecate up outside the general store that Lena’s anger blanched into foolish panic as she looked at the bare back of her horse and realised that the leather purse where she kept her money had been safely tucked into the foot of her bedroll, which, in turn, had been left inside the barn.

 

            Pinching the bridge of her nose as she closed her eyes, Lena breathed slowly for a moment, trying to stifle the emotions that threatened to overwhelm her, before she quietly snarled and aimed a hard kick at the wooden post. Toe throbbing, she bit back a curse and rubbed at her brow, shoulders hunched and tense, and ran through her options.

 

            It was startlingly clear to her, even amidst her annoyance and rankling pride, that she couldn’t go riding out of town with nothing to her name but a gun, a book and some teeth. She wouldn’t last a day in the heat without a canteen of water, and wouldn’t get far without a saddle and full tack for Hecate. Covering her mouth with her hand, she tipped her head back and quickly did the math in her head, figuring out when the next instalment of her stipend would be coming, and cursed her bad luck at the fact that she had no paperwork for it. 

 

            There was one other option, of course, a large treasure trove of cash and coins from the train robbery that she’d taken from her brother and hid well enough, but it was unreachable to her now, and Lena clenched her hands into fists as she leaned her forehead against Hecate. She wanted to cry at her misfortune, at the sheer dumb luck of being stranded in the town she wanted to leave as soon as possible, embarrassment and shame on her heels.

 

            A firm hand on her shoulder startled her, and Lena’s hand shot down to her gun but was quickly ensnared by wiry fingers, stopping her before she could draw it. With a snort of laughter, Alex pulled her around and stared at her.

 

            “Something botherin’ you, Doc?”

7. Chapter 7

            “Something botherin’ you, Doc?”

 

            “It’s nothing for the likes of you to concern yourself with,” Lena curtly replied.

 

            “Lover’s quarrel?”

 

            Lena let out a scoff as she tangled her fingers in Hecate’s mane, her lips twisting bitterly. “Not exactly, but I’ll no longer be boarding with your sister. You should be pleased.”

 

            Pausing a moment as her mouth opened and closed, Alex rocked on her heels slightly as a light breeze skittered down the wide street and kicked up a light dust. Clearing her throat as she tugged the brim of her hat down snugly, Alex gave her an apprehensive look.

 

            “Where’re you staying?”

 

            “I think I’ll be on my way now, for good,” Lena firmly replied as she met her eyes.

 

            A flicker of irritation shone in Alex’s brown eyes as she frowned slightly. “The mine-“

 

            “Forgive me, but I have more pressing concerns than your mine, considering I have a mass-murdering relative sweeping through the states and wiping out entire towns. If you’ll excuse me …”

 

            “You ain’t going to get far without supplies,” Alex casually replied, removing a rolled cigarette from a battered tin case.

 

            She scraped a match along a wooden post of the covered boardwalk and lit the end of it before shaking the match and drawing in a breath. Her eyes narrowed against the harsh sunlight as she studied Lena, still and tense with Alex’s thoughts that had echoed her own, and she exhaled a plume of smoke before cocking her head to the side.

 

            “At least if you stayed a bit and helped out with the mine, you’d be able to replace all the things that were burnt. Can’t hurt, can it?”

 

            Lips twitching, Lena flexed her fingers and stalled. She knew she wouldn’t be going anywhere, but she didn’t want to agree with Alex.

 

            “I can’t go back to your sister’s.”

 

            “I didn’t say you should. J’onn will put you up; ain’t no better place in town, as you know. He’s a respectable man - he’ll make sure no one’s rough with you.”

 

            “I’m not afraid of anyone.”

 

            “So, it’s settled then.”

 

            “No.”

 

            “Don’t be a fool.”

 

            Huffing, Lena’s face stiffened as a muscle twitched in her jaw. After a moment, she swallowed and ducked her head in agreement, shoulders rising as she kicked up dust with reluctant defeat. Clapping her on the shoulder, almost hard enough to make Lena’s knees buckle, Alex turned and stalked off towards the hotel, stomping up the steps and pushing through the batwing doors. Hecate was well-trained enough that she followed after Lena’s click of her tongue and then stopped at the hitching post without needing to be hitched - not that Lena had a bridle to do that anyway. 

 

            Following Alex inside, Lena blinked at the gloominess in the near-empty saloon as the murmured conversation at the bar drifted towards her, inaudibly. Moving towards the huddled duo, Lena folded her arms over her chest and hung back slightly, before J’onn’s dark eyes landed on her and he gave her a curt nod. He didn’t look too pleased but he wasn’t unkind.

 

            “It’s settled then,” Alex said, slapping a hand on the wooden bartop and rounding on Lena. “The town’ll pay for you to stay here while you work. Full bed and board. And as much protection as you’ll get anywhere here.”

 

            Wariness threaded through Lena as she cautiously eyed the place, part of her still hedging her bets with setting off bareback without so much as a sip of water. It wasn’t that she worried that someone would kill her - sure, they’d try their worst but she had skeletons at her disposal, and the ability to make some undead to control if worst came to worst - but a midnight witch hunt was the last thing she wanted. Even if she came through unscathed, the trouble things like that brought to a town were familiar territory for her. It wouldn’t be the first or last time it happened, she imagined. 

 

            Still, it seemed a shame to cause that much strife to a town that had been moderately kinder than most - save for the burning of Kara’s barn with her inside - but Lena knew in her sinking stomach that she’d have to risk it. Perhaps putting their dead to their final rest would offer up a truce, and once the work was done and her pockets were full of coins to flee, she’d be out of town before they could light their torches and load their guns.

 

            “Look, if you’re worried about that brother of yours, J’onn knows more about what goes on in this town than anyone else. This place is the best hotel, the best saloon, it’s where every newcomer stops by before finding the seedier places, so that means news, it means gossip and warnings. I swear, if it weren’t impossible, I’d think the old man could read minds with how much he knows about other people’s business.”

 

            Alex gave Lena a wry smile as J’onn barked a quiet laugh and grinned as he shook his head. Still wary, Lena slowly let herself become convinced though, uncrossing her arms and slowly nodding as she met Alex’s eyes.

 

            “Fine.”

 

            J’onn nodded and set down his cloth before turning to the box of keys. “Put her in the best room,” Alex told him.

 

            “Miss Rojas is in that one.”

 

            “The next best then. She’s gonna be here a while; she may as well be comfortable, ain’t it?”

 

            He nodded and scrounged up a key before rounding the end of the bar and jerking his head towards the stairs. Lena glanced at Alex and hesitated, her brow puckering slightly. “I’ll be leaving as soon as possible.”

 

            “Lord, don’t we all hope so,” Alex muttered, giving her an exasperated look that forced an unwilling smile to Lena’s lips.

 

            With a quiet snort of laughter, she shook her head and trailed after J’onn. He took her upstairs and unlocked a door to a room that overlooked the main street of Midvale. It was bigger than her last room at the hotel, a little grander with its moth-eaten lounge and its small fireplace, a writing desk in one corner and even a spotted mirror above the washbasin. The bed was bigger too, with a canopy to match the faded bedsheets. Lena was indifferent to it - the austere room she’d had last time would have sufficed - but she was grateful as she thanked J’onn, taking the small key and setting it down on the small dining table.

 

            Much like the rest of the saloon and hotel, it had been a grand place upon opening, but the room’s grandeur had faded by use and by the arid heat of the searing summer months. Still, she wasn’t one to turn her nose up at a big bed and the opportunity for a proper rest. She imagined she would have been more favourable to her new living standards if not for the bitter taste of her parting words with Kara, and Lena would be lying if she said she didn’t feel a pang of longing for that pile of hay and scurrying mice and supper in the warmth of the long ranch house with that mangy dog begging for scraps at the table. It stung, just a little, and she roughly unbuckled her gun belt and shed the leather jacket before tossing her hat onto the table beside the key and making for the washbasin.

 

            Rolling her sleeves up, she washed away the remaining soot from her forearms and hands, specks of black swirling in the water, before she cupped handfuls to splash over her face, rivulets streaking through the dust. Her eyes were still dry and sore from the smoke of the fire, and she blinked as water blurred her vision, before drying off with the small towel folded beside the pitcher of water. Exhausted from the last few days, Lena walked over to the heavy drapes and dragged them across the windows to obscure the harsh sunlight before flopping down onto the bed and kicking off her boots. 

 

            Throwing an arm across her face, blotting out the lines of light that cut through the dimness of the room, Lena allowed herself to sink into unconsciousness, the mattress soft despite its somewhat lumpiness, and she was able to blot out the noise from the busy street below to dispel some of the tension and exhaustion with a few hours of rest.

 

            She woke to the muffled sound of strings and a clunky piano and rubbed the sleep from her eyes. The room was muggy and she felt the gnawing beginnings of hunger as she sat slumped on the edge of the bed. Pulling on her boots, she skipped her coat and hat and deliberated over her gun for a moment before deciding it would be foolish to walk about unarmed in the centre of town. Buckling it on, Lena snatched up the small key and stalked out of her room, music washing over her as she stepped out onto the mezzanine. Slurred and rowdy singing grew louder as she descended the steps, taking in the sight of Kara hammering away at the keys as a few half-drunken friends sang a bawdy tavern song for the amusement of the occupied saloon.

 

            Slinking off to the far corner, away from the music, Lena caught J’onn’s attention and leaned her elbows on the bar as he walked towards her. “Can I start an account?”

 

            “What can I get for you?”

 

            “Whisky, if you don’t mind,” Lena asked, “and supper as well, sir.”

 

            He smiled softly with amusement, nodding as he grabbed a clean glass and unstoppered a green bottle. Filling the cup generously, he nudged it towards her. “Supper will be out soon. You like biscuits?”

 

            “Yes, sir.”

 

            “Well, alright then. Sit tight.”

 

            His eyes sparkled with amusement that Lena didn’t quite understand, and she sipped her whisky slowly as he walked off. He refilled her cup twice more in between serving other patrons, and the music trailed off as the singing came to an end, a young boy taking over for Kara as she tousled his hair and got herself a beer, ordering at the opposite end of the bar to Lena.

 

            Neither of them acknowledged each other’s presence, but that didn’t mean they weren’t aware of the space the other one took up in the crowded saloon. Studiously ignoring her, Lena sipped her whisky while Kara watched her sideways as she moved over to the wall, breathing in the haze of tobacco as laughter and music washed over her. Taking a large gulp of cold beer, she watched people start dancing in the open space, reeling around as they drunkenly sang along, and glimpsed her sister making her way towards her from the side. Alex leaned back against the wall and exhaled loudly before her eyes landed on Lena’s lonely figure and she jerked her chin towards her.

 

            “What in the Lord’s name did you do to her?”

 

            Grumbling under her breath, Kara’s expression soured as she petulantly crossed her arms over her chest. “What makes you think I did something?”

 

            Eyebrows rising, Alex gave her a searching look as she grinned with amusement. “She was mighty keen to get out of town, with nothing more than the clothes on her back. She most of all would know that’s suicide, so I says somethin’ sent her hurrying off. And she was with you.”

 

            Mouth thinning, Kara glanced sideways at her sister and let her stubborn facade fall away, revealing the mournful look beneath it. Her blue eyes were sad and yearning, a look that made Alex want to scoff and cuff her round the ear for being stupid enough to get soft on a Necromancer, but all that welled up was pity.

 

            “She thinks it’s safer to leave; she thinks her brother will come if he finds out she’s here. That the mine has reopened.”

 

            “She ain’t wrong,” Alex hummed, taking a sip of beer. “He most likely will before long. We’re damned if we don’t open the mine and damned if we do; at least if she’s here we might have a chance of coming back.”

 

            “Back?” Kara echoed, stunned by her sister’s response.

 

            With a rueful smile, Alex shrugged, “I ain’t keen on the thought, but … I ain’t keen on dying yet either. I got plans for my girl, and they don’t involve a grave just yet.”

 

            “So … you convinced Lena to stay?”

 

            “I don’t like the way you say her name like that,” Alex slowly said with a perturbed look at Kara.

 

            Rolling her eyes, Kara sighed softly, “and what way’s that, then?”

 

            “All soft like. You’re sweet on her and I want you to be happy but there are a dozen respectable women in this town who’d be a better choice.”

 

            With a weary sigh, Kara bumped her sister’s shoulder in a gentle warning, “you don’t even know her, Alex.”

 

            “Best keep it that way,” she sternly replied, patting Kara’s arm before pushing off the wall and making over to the table where Kelly was sitting chatting to M’gann and Nia.

 

            Kara brooded for a few minutes, surreptitiously drinking in the sight of Lena’s sloped shoulders as she nursed a whisky at the shadowed end of the scarred bar, the way her muscles bunched and shifted with the motions of sipping, how her dark hair parted occasionally to reveal glimpses of her pale neck, oddly intimate. She had the strong urge to brush Lena’s hair aside and gently kiss the soft spot where her pulse would be fluttering away, but pressed her lips into a firm line and sipped her beer with stubborn resolution. A Necromancer wasn’t for the likes of her, Kara knew that, and yet, all the same, she’d never felt someone call to her so strongly before. It was with sheer willpower that she tore her gaze away and eventually moved over to the table of friends, growing as others trickled in at the thought of supper. 

 

            In her far corner, at the very end of the bar where customers could easily avoid her when ordering their drinks and socialising, Lena sipped her whisky and felt the burning gaze of being watched. She didn’t have to glance over her shoulder to know who was watching her so closely, who was giving her a sullen look of accusation from against the wall. Sipping the burning liquor, Lena shrugged off the crawling feeling and minded her own business, until a pleasant warmth had spread through her, numbing the frayed edges of her worry.

 

            Once her supper came out, she picked at the thick cuts of ham and the shelled peas swimming in butter, the luxury of well-cooked food escaping her at that moment as she brooded too. Even the freshly baked biscuits, spread with apricot preserve, weren’t enough to inspire her usual enthusiasm for something other than salted pork and beans. It was a right sight better than Kara’s cooking, but she was too irritable to properly enjoy the best meal she’d had since she’d been laid up there after being shot, and after swallowing the last burning mouthful of honeyed whisky, Lena slipped off the creaky wooden stool and nodded her thanks to J’onn.

 

            Skirting past tables, giving one crowded one a wide berth, although she found herself hyper-aware of Kara’s position amongst the group, Lena made for the stairs and hauled herself up the warped, groaning steps. Back in her room, she found herself strangely cold by the vast darkness of the room and blindly fumbled around with the dried logs and tinder left beside the fireplace, sparking a small fire that offered a cheery glow as she dragged a chair over to it and sat before its warmth.

 

            Listening to the muffled din below, she slumped in her wingback chair, the cushion worn thin and a few brass studs missing from the trim, idly rubbing her thumb over her lips as she let her thoughts be consumed by Kara. It was all straightforward in its simplicity - until she got to the kiss. Her face furrowed with confusion as her stomach twisted and she tried to parse through the discomforting feeling that made her chest ache. A few weeks in someone’s barn and a kiss shouldn’t have left her so frustrated and confused, so reluctant to move on even though fear and logic screamed at her to earn what few pennies she could from the mine work and get the hell out of town before the dead came knocking.

 

            Scoffing quietly to herself as she shook her head and smiled thinly at the fire, the pleasant warmth of cheap booze and a full stomach making her drowsy. Her body still aching and battered from the last few days, Lena started dozing in her chair, comfortable and at peace in the stillness of her room, the rest of the town blotted out behind a flimsy wooden door and a few closed, warped windows. Swimming in and out of consciousness, glimpses of the orange fire, the occasional muffled shout and a faint whistle as the wind worked its way through cracks in the window frames, Lena was a small figure curled up on the armchair as the minutes dragged on.

 

            She was drifting again when a loud banging on the door startled her awake. Heart pounding in her chest as she leapt up from the chair, Lena whipped her pistol from its holster and cocked back the hammer. The pounding continued and she wondered if it was an angry local looking for a fight, slinking towards the door with quiet footsteps as she listened. The wood shuddered in the doorframe and she swallowed, her mouth dry and thick with the taste of whisky as she breathed slowly.

 

            “I know you’re in there,” came the frustrated words of the last person she expected to be standing on the other side, a drunken laugh, scathing and slurred, hinting at Kara’s bitterness as she slapped a palm against the door.

 

            Sighing softly, Lena lowered her gun and eased the hammer back up before jerking the door open roughly and blinking in surprise as an armful of blonde curls and dusty cotton barrelled right into her. She righted Kara quickly and took a step back, shoving her gun back into the holster and pressing her lips into a hard line.

 

            “Miss Danvers-”

 

            Eyes crinkling with amusement as a hungry edge laced her smile, Kara gripped Lena’s upper arms as she caught her balance and let out a huff of laughter. So close, her breath warm as it ghosted over Lena’s cheek, her lips, a shroud of beer ensnaring her and leaving her rooted to the spot, Kara laughed, rosy-cheeked and annoyed.

 

            “Miss Danvers,” she slowly enunciated with Lena’s clipped accent before slipping back into her drawl. “As if we’re strangers. As if you haven’t worn my clothes, slept in my bed, kissed me.”

 

            She reached up and touched Lena’s cheek with featherlight fingertips as she let out a quiet laugh, eyelids fluttering. Grabbing her wrist, Lena jerked her back as a searing heat flushed through her, her throat constricting as she hoarsely replied.

 

            “You’re drunk.”

 

            “You’re still here.”  Lena made a small sound of acknowledgement at the back of her throat and Kara hummed, swaying on her feet. “You weren’t supposed to be.”

 

            “I don’t have much choice.”

 

            Kara laughed again, “I guess it was just me you weren’t wanting to be around then. Did I cause offence? The kiss- was it- was it-”

 

            Biting back a frustrated sigh, Lena dropped her wrists and roughly grabbed Kara’s face in her hands. “It’s because I want to be around you that I mustn't. And as soon as I have the means … well, I’ll be out of Midvale too. Far beyond the means to do you harm.”

 

            “Don’t go,” Kara whispered, reaching up to brush Lena’s dark hair out of her pale face, her touch gentle and intoxicating.

 

            Jerking her face away from her touch as regret welled up, Lena made an irate sound as the firelight made shadows pool in the hollows of her cheeks. Her frustration dimmed to exasperation and she was gentle as she cradled the side of Kara’s neck and held her steady by the shoulder.

 

            “You’re drunk; go home.”

 

            Stiffening at the rebuff, Kara’s cheeks reddened beyond the flush of drink and she tore herself from Lena’s grasp, ducking her head down as embarrassment washed over her. She was clumsy in her haste, fumbling for something at her waist as she bumped into a dining chair, evading Lena’s touch as she lunged forward to steady her.

 

            Eyes smarting with tears and voice thick with hurt, Kara finally managed to free her small leather purse from the pocket of her long skirt, and, with a trembling hand, tossed it at Lena, the coins clinking softly inside.

 

            “Here. Ain’t no cause to stay now, is it?”

 

            “Kara-”

 

            “Go on,” she encouragingly replied, gesturing wildly. “Now, get.”

 

            Taking a step forward, purse in her extended hand, Lena’s shoulders slumped as she watched Kara lurch from the room and smack right into her sister. Alex caught her and glanced over Kara’s shoulder, giving Lena a bewildered look. Grimacing, Lena crossed over to her and slapped the purse into Alex’s hand.

 

            “She should go home.”

 

            Dipping her chin in agreement, Alex managed to prop Kara up as she dragged her arm across her shoulders. Lena gripped the edge of the door, ready to shut it, and hesitated as Alex paused. Giving her another nod, Alex’s lips twitched ruefully. “Night, Doc.”

 

            “Sheriff.”

 

            Closing the door, Lena turned the key in the lock and sighed heavily before turning to the bed and flopping down onto the sheets. Staring up at the faded drapes of the canopy, her mind ran circles around thoughts of Kara until she fell asleep, still wearing her boots and gun and thinking about the rancher even as she dreamt.

 

            It was still dark when Lena woke, the morning lingering in that blue hour of distorted shadows and stillness, and she jerked away, still groggy, and ran a hand over her face. She’d been plagued by bad dreams - she’d been plagued by them ever since being sent into the catacombs of the old graveyard in New York City - and it was with a mind weighed down heavily with blood and the rotting decay of the dead that she dragged herself out of bed and went to clean up with the pitcher of tepid water. 

 

            The fire was nothing more than cool ashes and Lena yawned widely as she stretched her sore muscles, the blueness of the day seeping through the cracks in the curtains as she readied herself for her day. Pulling on her leather duster, she buttoned the coat against the expected chill of the blue morning and jammed her hat down on her head before sweeping out of the room and locking up after herself.

 

            Distant, rumbling snores drifted from behind closed doors of the upstairs hotel, and as Lena descended the stairs, she took in the sight of a few locals slumped at tables or sprawled out on benches, let to sleep off the drink indoors. Nia was already up and working, wiping down tables with a disgruntled look of tiredness as she looked up at Lena.

 

            “You rise early,” the young woman commented. “I ain’t got no food for breakfast yet. Boss isn’t up.”

 

            “I’m quite fine,” Lena murmured, “if you could just point me towards the stables.”

 

            Eyeing her warily, Nia tucked her cloth into the pocket of the apron tied over her skirts and cocked her head to the side. “You leavin’ again?”

 

            “No, miss. I have work that needs seeing to.”

 

            Nodding, Nia jerked her head towards the batwing doors leading out to a kitchen. Dough was left to rise for fresh bread and a window was open to let in the cool air outside as a roaring fire made the kitchen stuffy and a little hazy with smoke. Bypassing the day’s preparations, Nia led Lena over to a back door and yanked it open before walking down a few steps into the narrow alleyway. There was a low, long building made of wood situated right behind the hotel and Lena could hear the gentle whickering of horses before they even stepped inside.

 

            Hecate was in the second stall from the left, brushed down and rested with her nose in a trough of oats as she lazily swished her tail to swat away the flies. Lena moved over to her and ran a hand down the side of her neck, the ache in her chest easing with the familiar comfort of her horse. Smoothing a hand down the length of her neck, Lena gave her a firm pat and glanced over at Nia, who had her arms folded on top of the stall gate and watched her with open curiosity and no fear in her brown eyes.

 

            “Do you have a spare saddle and bridle?”

 

            “Might. J’onn won’t let it go for nothin’.”

 

            “I won’t steal it. As I said before, I’ll be returning.”

 

            With a dubious hum, eyebrows rising and falling quickly, Nia moved to the far end of the stables and started hefting heavy leather saddles. Suppressing a sigh, Lena followed after her and ensnared her wrist with her own, stopping her from lifting it.

 

            “That one is too big. And not the right design.”

 

            Rolling her eyes as Lena cracked a thin smile at her juvenile irritation, Nia took a step back and watched as Lena browsed the assortment of tack and equipment. Turning, she raised her eyebrows. “Do you have a blanket?”

 

            “You cold, Doc?” Nia teased with a mocking smile.

 

            Letting out a short huff of laughter, Lena gestured to Hecate. “For my horse.”

 

            “She sure ain’t cold.”

 

            “No miss, but she’ll be rightly sore with that saddle and no blanket. If you’d please.”

 

            Deliberating before deciding to help, Nia scrounged up a scratchy blanket and gave it to Lena, thinking it surprisingly thoughtful of one so steeped in death to care so much about a horse . Nia couldn’t imagine caring that much about anyone - well, except for an oblivious banker, if he let her. Settling the blanket over Hecate’s back, Lena eyed the selection of worn saddled and hauled an appropriate one off, hefting it over the mare’s back and ensuring it was buckled properly. Foregoing a bridle with a bit, she stroked Hecate’s nose as she got her all set up, checking each hoof for stones or painful splits, before dragging herself up into the saddle.

 

            “Thank you.”

 

            Humming as she looked up at her, arms folded and eyes narrowed, Nia hesitated. “Wait here.”

 

            Brow creasing with bewilderment, Lena held the reins limply in her lap as Hecate scuffed the ground impatiently. She let her trot to the open stable doors and watched as Nia reappeared from the hotel’s back entrance, stopping beside Lena and thrusting up a bulging cheesecloth and a leather waterskin.

 

            “Here. Boss says Sheriff says we need to be nice to you.”

 

            “That’s generous of you,” Lena murmured, ducking her head in thanks as she reached out to take the offerings, careful not to touch her. There was no fear, but Nia’s uneasiness was still clear.

 

            “Don’t go running off now, you hear? J’onn don’t like it when his things go missing.”

 

            Touching the brim of her hat, Lena put her heels to Hecate’s flank and urged the horse into motion, trotting down the narrow alleyway and out onto the main thoroughfare. It was too early for there to be many people out, but the clerk sweeping the deck before a general goods store eyed her with mistrust as she kicked up dust in her swift exit from Midvale. On the road out, staring at the pale blue sky emerging through a haze of dust, it occurred to Lena that she could leave. Sure, a bite for one meal wasn’t much, but she had a waterskin and saddle to keep her going. It was honour and duty that spurred her towards the well-beaten track to the old mine.

 

            In the months since closing, the path had given in to creeping wild grasses and weeds, rocks and dust and sand adding a gritty layer to the sloping road up through the foothills. Trees reached across and shadowed her as the sun rose, warm on the back of her neck and coat as Hecate plodded along. It was a pleasant ride, almost peaceful with the twittering of the birds and the faint sound of running water, and Lena was content to travel slowly.

 

            Eventually, she came to the dark, yawning mouth of the mine entrance though, a plateau of stone providing space for her to dismount. Crossing over to the edge, Lena peered over it, the wind buffeting her as she took in the sight of sprawling acres of wilderness and the low, tree-studded foothills she’d wound up through. And there, beneath it all, the hum of death, of bones awaiting her command, of the tragedy she was here to lay to rest. 

 

            Patting Hecate’s neck, she left her free to roam along the spacious plateau to nibble at grass and bask in the sunshine, making for the wide mouth with the rusting tracks disappearing inside. The darkness was suffocating as Lena walked through, the rotting planks beneath her feet guiding her, and she was momentarily blinded as she glanced back over her shoulder at the bright light, blinking back black spots as she turned back to the tunnel. She wasn’t too high up, the elevation of the foothills still quite low, and as she walked blindly through the tunnel, she almost felt the weight of the spearing mountain above pressing down on her. 

 

            It should have been suffocating to think of the tonnes of rock overhead, but it didn’t worry her, not even with the knowledge that some of that weight had collapsed on the local miners. Lena felt a flicker of pity for them though, imagining the men winding through this very tunnel, swinging away at the stone as they uncovered veins of gold, shoring up the tunnels with planks and carefully excavating rock and dirt. Only for it to cave in on them, beams splintering and rock crushing bones or blocking off the exit. She would have rathered to be one of the ones to succumb to the weight of the collapsing tunnels and pitied those who had survived, only to be strung along on a painfully long death of starvation and hypoxia. Although she wasn’t worried, Lena had to pause in her blind walk to draw in a deep breath, assuring herself that there was still enough air for her to breathe.

 

            She walked until she hit a wall of stone, rough beneath her fingertips as she pressed her hands to it, feeling the cool dampness as the tunnel chilled her skin. Lena couldn’t see a thing before her, as blind as if she’d been born that way, but she could see. See the web of bodies and bones and older things that had lain at rest for centuries. Things in the walls and above her head, and so many under her feet, and the new ones ahead with their bones still mostly connected making her stomach clench. The shaft they would have walked through, burrowing into the roots of the mountain, through miles and miles of stone as they slowly chipped it away, stretched on beyond that immovable wall of stone. Dynamite would do it, Lena agreed with her previous thoughts and took a while to map out the area with her creeping magic, feeling for the bodies, keeping a tally in her head to cross-reference with the numbers Kelly had given her.

 

            After surveying the damage she had to work with, Lena let out a soft sigh and trudged back down the long tunnel of the mine shaft, crunching stone and occasionally tripping over the planks of the minecart rail, until a speck of light finally appeared, growing larger and brighter. Stepping back out onto the plateau, Lena squinted against the sunshine and tugged her hat down lower. Fetching her food from the saddlebags, Lena sprawled in the dust and stubbly grass with her legs outstretched as she tore off hunks of fresh bread and broke off pieces of a hard cheese before washing it down with cool water. 

 

            Basking in the warmth of the sun for a while afterwards, watching falcons swoop overhead and the treetops sway in the breeze, she felt a sense of peace she hadn’t since stumbling upon the slaughtered town. As comfortable and rested as she felt now, holed up in a town that despised her, Lena missed the peaceful solitude of the road. Just her and Hecate on the open plains, navigating by stars and always on the move. It left her restless now, and dogged by a stubborn blonde who couldn’t see that she was trying to protect her.

 

            Mood souring as her peace was shattered by thoughts of Kara, Lena pushed herself to her feet and brushed off as much sand as she could, her scraped palms stinging slightly. Dusty and sweating beneath her layers, Lena climbed back into the saddle and took her time heading back into town. The downhill slopes of the gentle ravines and hills made for a slow, bumpy ride in the saddle and she felt the heat soak into her leather coat as she ducked beneath low-hanging branches and mused over a plan. There was too much rock and earth for mere skeletons to manage, their brittle finger bones and lack of muscle a weak contender against compacted stone, and she imagined some explosives would prove more effective to break it up before she put the dead to work. Still, she was looking at a few weeks of work, at the very least, which wasn’t a pleasant thought.

 

            It proved to be even more unpleasant as she slowed near the hotel, slipping down the side street and into the alleyway before swinging down from the saddle. Her boots crunched into the thin layer of dried mud crusting over the earth and she took the reins in hand as she led Hecate towards the stable doors, running smack bang into something solid and warm.

 

            “Oh. Excuse me, I apologise.”

 

            She swiftly backed up as the other person’s apologies fell on her ears and Lena blinked as she adjusted her skewiff hat and found herself looking at a rather grey and glum Kara. Looking worse for wear from heavy drinking, her burgundy skirt rumpled and an odour of sweat and beer clinging to her in a rather noxious cloud, the rancher seemed to pale beneath her queasy pallor at the sight of Lena. Her apologies trailed off and her knuckles whitened around the reins of her own horse, Comet, which she was leading out of the stable. Lena opened her mouth to form some cordial greeting or another apology - she wasn’t sure what - but she didn’t manage to vocalise it before Kara shouldered past her and blanked her dead.

 

            Looking after her with a mild wounded look softening her face as she frowned, Lena jerked her head around at the sound of a quiet scoff of laughter. Nia was leaning in the doorway, flour-dusted and peeling an apple with a small knife as she grinned impishly.

 

            “Oh, she’s gone right off you now, ain’t she? I ain’t never seen her give someone a cold shoulder like that before.”

 

            Scowling as her cheeks reddened, Lena stiffened and turned her back to Nia, embarrassed at letting the young girl get under her skin. The tension bled from her muscles at the sound of another voice joining them.

 

            “Nia, stop chatting. If you’ve got time to rile up my customers, you’ve got time to make sure the paying ones have drinks.”

 

            Peering back over her shoulder, Lena watched Nia roll her eyes as M’gann gently swatted her with a dish towel and then gave Lena an exasperated look of apology. “Sorry, Doc. These young girls in town … they’ve got nothing better to do.”

 

            “It’s alright. There’s been much worse said about me; don’t fret about it.”

 

            “It doesn’t bother you?”

 

            Shrugging as she fiddled with the bridle, Lena slowly started to remove it outside of the stable, chewing on the inside of her lip. “There’s more to fear from guns than a silly girl’s gossip.”

 

            “Ain’t that the truth,” M’gann sighed, leaning against the doorframe as she shook her head forlornly. “Used to be that you could walk the whole town at night with not a care that anyone would harm a hair on your head. Now, it seems like there ain’t a day without some sort of trouble. Even the good kind, like yourself.”

 

            “It’s only going to get worse from here,” Lena grimly replied.

 

            “Well, you look after yourself. Folks will tolerate you only for so long.”

 

            With a rueful twitch of her lips, Lena nodded, her eyes fixed on the buckles she was carefully undoing. “Thank you, ma’am, for your hospitality.”

 

            M’gann watched her with aloof amusement for a few minutes before returning to her business inside the worn establishment, the smell of baked apples and roasting meats and fresh bread a heavenly scent as Lena led Hecate into the stable. Returning the supplies where they’d come from, she took the liberty of helping herself to the selection of tack, scraping down Hecate’s hide, brushing dust and dirt from her bristly hair and gouging dirt out of her hooves. It was a long process, familiar and soothing as she tended to her treasured mare, and once satisfied that she was settled in, Lena made towards the open back door and knocked.

 

            M’gann poked her head around from where she was standing at the stove, working on some new concoction that made Lena’s stomach rumbled at the thought. She imagined what it must be like to be settled somewhere with her own business, creating recipes for people to enjoy while her husband tinkered with his distilling methods, both of them mastering their arts and enjoying the company of friends each night as the place filled. Lena bet that they didn’t feel so alone, didn’t feel so empty, chasing after nothing on an open road.

 

            “I believe this is yours,” Lena murmured, holding the scratchy blanket up.

 

            “For your horse? Keep it.”

 

            “Thank you.”

 

            “You hungry, Doc?”

 

            “No, thank you, ma’am. Nia gave me food to take.”

 

            Smiling fondly, M’gann picked up an egg and cracked it against the side of a mixing bowl, tossing the shells into the trash. “That girl’s a handful, I’ll tell you.”

 

            “Seems like most in this town are,” Lena said with a droll smile, bundling the blanket under her arm.

 

            “You picked a hell of a place to wind up.”

 

            “I go where the work is. Speaking of, if you’ll excuse me, ma’am, I need to speak with the Mayor.”

 

            Nodding, her attention already on the mixing bowl before her, M’gann bid her a polite farewell and Lena ducked back out of the door, steps creaking beneath her boots as she stepped into the alleyway and set off around the corner. The modest brick facade of the Mayor’s office was situated a few buildings down, and Lena stepped into the cool interior, sunlight brightening the dingy office of dark wood and order. Removing her hat, Lena softly cleared her throat.

 

            “Hello? Madam Mayor?”

 

            She heard the sound of hurried footsteps before the door behind the neat desk opened to reveal Kelly, her eyes widening a fraction at the sight of Lena and a slightly breathless edge to her words as she greeted her.

 

            “Oh. Doc. This is a surprise.”

 

            “Howdy, Doc,” Alex greeted her with a lazy smile as she appeared behind Kelly’s left shoulder, opening the door wider.

 

            “Good, I thought you might be here too. Is now a bad time?” Lena asked with a raised eyebrow.

 

            Mouth opening and closing, Kelly let slip a small sigh before stepping back as Alex opened the door wider to admit her. “By all means.”

 

            “I just returned from the mine.”

 

            Disgruntlement vanished, replaced with eager interest as Kelly sank down onto her chair behind her desk and steepled her fingers, leaning forward on the mahogany. Alex leaned against the wall behind her lover and gestured for Lena to take the rickety chair across from Kelly.

 

            “Go on then, tell us if it’s bad.”

 

            “It’s not good, but it’s possible. It will take a while to shift the earth, and then some for the bodies.”

 

            “You reckon you could do it though.”

 

            Hesitating, Lena’s mouth thinned before she replied. “With the correct supplies.”

 

            Narrowing her eyes slightly, Alex straightened up against the wall, “meaning?”

 

            “I find myself in need of dynamite. I’m sure you’re the correct person to supply me with it, Sheriff.”

 

            “Dynamite? Shoot, Doc, you trying to collapse the entire mine?” Alex startled.

 

            “Tunnel’s all blocked up, now. I can’t shift all that stone - not even with an army of the dead. I’ll let you be the one to light the fuse if you wish.”

 

            Humming dubiously, Alex returned to her slouched position as Kelly looked at Lena thoughtfully. “And what else do you require?”

 

            “A saddle. And a bridle. For my horse.”

 

            “That’s it?”

 

            “Yes, ma’am.”

 

            A faint smile curled Kelly’s lips as she leaned back, glancing over her shoulder at Alex. “Well, I think we can manage that.”

 

            “Thank you,” Lena nodded. “As soon as they’re ready, I can begin work.”

 

            Thinking for a moment, Alex nodded, “tomorrow. I’ll accompany you to the mine and we’ll blast it open. A few sticks should do the trick. I ain’t a labourer though, Doc; clearing the mine will be your own work.”

 

            Lena laughed softly, thumbs looped through her belt as she lounged in her chair, “if I thought you had any intentions of helping to open the mine, Alex, I imagine it would be clear by now, wouldn’t it?”

 

            A flicker of surprise crossed the Sheriff’s face before it turned into a grudging smile. “Maybe so, Lena.”

 

            Kelly scoffed and rolled her eyes before pushing herself to her feet. Making for the door, she held it open for Lena and looked at her with polite interest. “So … do you have a proposed timeframe?”

 

            Shrugging as she wrung the rim of her hat in her hands, Lena grimaced. “Months, I should think, ma’am.”

 

            “Even with the use of the dead.”

 

            “I’ve made no secret of the fact that my powers are draining. I can no more command the dead indefinitely than I could shift it all myself without need of rest. Don’t worry; I have every intention of being as quick as I can.”

 

            “Well, alright then. I s‘pose that’s all we can ask for.”

 

            Ducking her head in agreement before putting her hat back on, Lena’s eyes strayed towards the windows as she drifted towards the door. “Well, good day to you, Madam Mayor, Sheriff.”

 

            As she spoke, Lena’s brow pinched in a perplexed manner at the sight of Kara, still lurking about town, walking purposefully down the street. Stooping to peer outside, Lena recognised the bristling anger in her posture and wondered which poor soul had offended the stubborn ranched. She just hoped it wasn’t herself again.

 

            “I’ll, uh, I’ll take my … leave.”

 

            “Something got your interest, Doc?” Alex asked.

 

            Glancing over at her, Lena’s eyebrows rose a fraction, “your sister just passed by. She looks mighty annoyed, if I read that correctly.”

 

            Cursing, Alex stormed forward as Lena jerked the door open and stepped outside. The trio stood in the shade as they squinted at Kara’s hurrying form, and Lena could see something clutched tightly in her hand as she went on her way. 

 

            “Who do you think she’s after?” Kelly murmured.

 

            “As long as it’s not me, I’m not interested,” Lena muttered, touching the brim of her hat before stepping out into the sun.

 

            She was heading in the same direction though and slowed as she gained on Kara’s slowing figure, despite telling herself it was none of her business. Even then, she couldn’t stop the prickle of jealousy that stung her as she followed Kara’s determined line of sight and watched her march straight for the British reporter in his grey tweed suit as he smoked outside of the newsroom. Surely Lena hadn’t misread her eagerness as anger? But no, there was still that bristling tension beneath bunched shoulders, and Lena blinked at the harshness of Kara’s voice as she called out to him.

 

            “Mister Daye! Mister Daye!”

 

            “Morning, Miss Kara,” William said, tipping the brim of his hat and smiling warmly at her. His accent rankled Lena, who hovered back, fingers twitching with the urge to unholster her gun. “Good day for it, isn’t it?”

 

            “What in the good, holy hell is this?” Kara demanded, ignoring the pleasantries as she shook the newspaper in his face.

 

            “Ah, my latest run of the newspaper. Hot off the press just this morning. A delightful read, don’t you think so, Miss Kara?”

 

            Staring at him with astonishment, Kara let out a choked sound as she crumpled the papers. “You ain’t serious, are you? Do you have any idea what could happen if this gets out to the wrong hands? Writing about the mine reopening and the Doctor in town?”

 

            “The locals deserve to know what’s going on in their lovely town, and elsewhere besides,” he curtly replied, a bristling edge to his forced politeness, as if her offence at his story wounded his ego.

 

            Blanching as her mouth dropped open, Kara’s raised hand, scrunching the newspaper and staining her palm with ink, lowered as a prickle of fear ran through her. “You fool. Do you even know what you’ve done? You’ve damned us all.”

 

            Spluttering as he puffed himself up, trying to save face as Kara yelled at him in broad daylight, heads poking out of doors as nosy residents turned their ears to the raised voice. Lena grimaced from where she lingered back, glancing around sheepishly and giving Alex a pointed look, earning a careless shrug as she struck a match and lit a cigarette in response.

 

            “You mistake me,” William hurriedly assured her, shifting uneasily on his feet. “Perhaps we can discuss this further - alone. Might we have supper together tonight? You must be awfully lonely out on that ranch of yours with poor company. I’ll try my best to provide otherwise.”

 

            Flushing as she spluttered with embarrassment and indignation, Kara huffed and ducked her head, struggling to find the words. Lena bit back a smile at her blatant anger, something akin to satisfaction - although it couldn’t have been that; why would she care? - warmed her, and watched as Kara took a step back. Still, the barb at her being poor company was blunted by the secret knowledge that Kara had kissed her.

 

            “Well, sir, I ain’t got no need for company tonight, seeing as I already got some sorted for supper. Now, if you’ll excuse me, I got business elsewhere.”

 

            “Hold on,” William hurriedly stopped her, reaching out to grab her arm in a possessive manner that made Lena’s insides twist and her lip curl.

 

            Before she could even stop herself, Lena was crossing the street, scuffing up dust in her haste, and lifting the gun from its holster ever so slightly. “The lady said she’s got business elsewhere, sir,” she drawled as if she didn't have a care in the world. “And the Sheriff doesn't take kindly to people laying their hands on her kid sister - I should know.”

 

            She couldn’t stop the smugness that laced her words, that slightly arrogant curl to her thin smile as she thumbed the hammer of her Colt, fingers itching to jerk it from the holster and aim it at that shocked face. William opened and closed his mouth, a light sweat beading his brow beneath his bowler hat, and Lena was aware of Kara’s pink cheeks as she silently absorbed the aghast looks of nearby eavesdroppers who had clearly heard what Lena had said.

 

            “I- well-”

 

            “Good day, William,” Kara murmured before whirling around and grabbing Lena by her upper arm, all but dragging her away.

 

            Lena’s fingers that had been caressing the bone handle of her revolver went limp as she focused on keeping her balance, clouds of dust scuffed up from her boots as Kara towed her towards the Sheriff’s office and pushed her inside. Lena almost tripped up the steps and staggered inside, her footsteps loud on the planks as she stumbled through the door, Kara bearing down upon her with pink-cheeked annoyance.

 

            “What the hell are you doing?”

 

            “Blood and bone,” Lena hissed, scowling as she rubbed at her sore arm, “what’s gotten into you?”

 

            “You!” Kara exclaimed, gesturing to her with agonised frustration. “You’re everywhere . You’re there everywhere I turn my God damn head, Doc. You was supposed to leave and now you ain’t and you’re blabbing your mouth to the whole God damn town. ”

 

            Faint amusement mingled with gentle concern as Lena’s shoulders dropped, her head slightly cocked to the side as she listened to Kara’s tirade, her curses endearing in a way that Lena hated to be made aware of.

 

            “Apologies. I only hoped to help; forgive me if I misread your interest in him-”

 

            “My interest is none of your concern,” Kara hotly replied as her blush darkened, brushing a strand of hair out of her face as she raised her chin in a manner that might’ve been haughty on someone else, on Lena , but was petulant on her.

 

            Lena let out a quiet huff of laughter, her eyes piercing as she stared at Kara and moved towards her. Kara was still as Lena closed the distance between them, a flicker of wariness in her blue eyes as she swallowed thickly. Stopping mere inches away, Lena smiled faintly, leaning in a hairsbreadth, until she could feel Kara’s breath on her lips. It made her stomach clench and Kara’s lips parted further as Lena reached up, her fingertips ghosting along the side of Kara’s neck in a featherlight touch.
