            “Then, forgive me for overstepping, ma’am.”

 

            Her amusement was snuffed out like a flame pinched between thumb and forefinger and she gently brushed past Kara with a lingering look, the twisting discomfort at the fondness she secretly harboured for Kara making itself known as an uneasy reminder. Kara deflated, a sharp breath expelled from her lips, and Lena had to screw her hands tightly shut to stop herself from turning around and kissing her before her bravado fled. Pausing on the threshold, Lena shouldered out of the jail and almost bumped right into Alex, who was loitering outside with Kelly, smoking and waiting for their quarrel to end.

 

            “Excuse me,” Lena muttered, ducking her head.

 

            Clapping her on the back, Alex chuckled and Kelly handed her the half-smoked cigarette she nursed. Slowing, Lena plucked it from her outstretched hand and took a drag, exhaling a stream of grey as she gave Alex a sideways look.

 

            “I’ll see you tomorrow, Sheriff.”

 

            “Things would be a hell of a lot easier if you just kissed her,” Alex called after her, making Lena stiffen and blush furiously.

 

            “You should be thankful I don’t.”

 

            “I thought so too, but you’re both gonna irritate me into an early grave at this rate, Doc. And with that limey fool running his mouth with the newspaper … well, perhaps we can all cut each other some slack, and the like. I won’t hold it against you; we might all be dead, come next week. And you might be the only thing that says otherwise.”

 

            Slowing, Lena turned around, giving Alex a shrewd look as she inhaled tobacco and exhaled slowly, although thoughtfully. “Are you a religious woman, Sheriff?”

 

            “Church every Sunday, Doc, like all the good God-fearing Christians in this town. Why? You thinking of joining us this week?”

 

            With a crooked smile and a quiet laugh, Lena raised her eyebrows. “No, thank you, ma’am. A place like that would surely burn down if I stepped foot inside, don’t you think?”

 

            Kelly’s face clouded, despite Lena’s mocking tone, and she shared a glance with Alex before stepping forward. “Lena-”

 

            “I suggest you start praying,” Lena cut her off, the cherry red end of the cigarette burning down to a stub that she ground underfoot, the day taking on a chill despite the blue skies overhead. “If there’s a God, maybe he’ll listen.”

 

            Striding off, Lena made her way back to the hotel, nodding to M’gann as she breezed past the tables and made her way upstairs. Shutting herself into the room, she threw open the heavy drapes and the squeaking windows, the faint haze of smoke dissipating as a warm breeze swept inside, bringing with it the noise of voices and hooves and laughter, the smell of manure and rain on the horizon. The view of grassy plains, trees and sand stretched out beyond Lena’s vision and she stood at the window for a moment, observing the rolling foothills that led up to the mountain ranges, hiding all sorts of things within them, not just the warrens of old mines and dead.

 

            Throughout the rest of the afternoon, Lena spent her time going over preparations for the next day. She was in and out of her room with frequent haste, begging ink and pens and paper and yellowed maps from various acquaintances in town who disliked her a little less than most. Alex proved a useful force to wrangle the necessary equipment she needed to plot the route through the mine, where the bodies she’d felt would have been most concentrated and paying J’onn for the use of an old wagon to hitch Hecate to for easier removal of the dead.

 

            Later on that night, by candlelight, she spent hours measuring distances of tunnels, plotting a path down to the little clapboard church with its sprawling headstones where the dead would dig their graves. Supper had been brought up to her, filling and hot, with cold beer and bitter coffee to chase it down with, and she stayed up through most of the night, dust-covered and worn, her eyes gritty and burning as she moved the stubby candles closer as the darkness deepened and the room grew cooler.

 

            Fitting in a few hours of sleep before the grey dawn broke, Lena was roused by a banging knock on the door, her hand reaching for the gun beneath her pillow as she bolted upright, bleary-eyed and sore. Half-dressed, she stumbled out of bed, dark hair a bedraggled mess and gun held tightly as her shirt fell to her knees, and unlocked the door, which was still being hammered upon by a heavy fist. Scowling with disgruntlement, Lena yawned widely in Alex’s face, the Sheriff looking alert and refreshed with her badge and guns, a burlap sack slung over one shoulder and a keen look in her brown eyes.

 

            “Shoot, you ain’t ready yet?”

 

            “It’s the crack of dawn, Sheriff. I’ve been at it all night; let a lady have her rest.”

 

            “You don’t need your beauty sleep. Get your pants on and meet me downstairs; I’ll wrangle up breakfast for you.”

 

            Scoffing, Lena ran a hand over her face and turned around, dropping her gun onto the table and yanking on her discarded pants. Washing off yesterday’s dust and braiding her hair back, Lena pulled on her boots, coat and hat and buckled on her gun and belt, looking a little more put together by the time she was striding out the door and locking it behind her.

 

            Her boots thundered on the stairs as she made her way down to the open saloon, where Alex was waiting, boot propped up on a seat as she stood, with Lena’s promised breakfast crowding the table. She gulped down her coffee in three swallows before digging into the runny eggs, thick-cut bacon and bowl of oats while Alex stood over her.

 

            “Hurry up, Doc, we ain’t got time for your gentle manners. Chin up, atta girl.”

 

            Lena slapped Alex’s hand away as her chin was tipped up, hurrying another bite of oats was hastened down. Mouth twisting with annoyance, Lena set her spoon down. “Enough.”

 

            “We got a mine to blow up,” Alex snapped, “and I got prisoners to oversee and crime to investigate, and the like.”

 

            With a droll smile, Lena rolled her eyes, “I had no idea you were such a busy lady.”

 

            Gesturing for her to hurry up, Alex hitched the sack up higher and turned to leave, leaving Lena to scramble after her, the remainder of her bacon and bread in hand as she wolfed it down, shouldering through the batwing doors. Hecate was outside, saddled with her ears pricked and a still demeanour as Alex’s horse, hitched beside her, nosed her with interest.

 

            Swallowing, Lena wiped her greasy hands on her thighs and climbed up into the saddle as Alex unhitched both horses and climbed up onto the back of her own. They rode out to the foothills and Alex lit an oil lamp to light their way through the dark tunnel, the damp and narrow confines of the space making for an uncomfortable trip for two. By noon, they’d ran a line from the cave-in, all the way back down to the mouth of the mine entrance, and shortly afterwards lit the fuse that sent tremors running underfoot as the explosion rocked the mine.

 

            After that, it became Lena’s job and hers alone. She liked the purpose it gave her to get up early, to saddle Hecate and ride her out to the mine, her fingers and hands raw and scraped from hours spent hauling rocks, her softness from relatively no work involving muscles giving way to lean muscles as her arms and back and shoulders ached each night with the effort. Even with a few skeletons to help carry the stone out, it was still weeks of working by lamplight, hunched over with a pick and an ungodly amount of dust and dirt before she got through to the other side.

 

            Before she knew it, another month had passed in Midvale, with the Necromancer out of sight and mind for the most part. And then came the real work as Lena dug out the bodies, rotted away to bones, with a few of the better-preserved ones still in various stages of decomposing. The stench that filled the excavated tunnel was rancid and Lena had to burn local herbs she foraged for to try and make the air sweeter, at the cost of breathing in smoke through a bandana borrowed from Kelly.

 

            Things sped up from there and she was left sitting on the damp earth, filthy and pale as she pricked her fingers and smothered her blood over a handful of teeth, bringing the dead back to life so they could walk themselves out to the plateau and the waiting cart. It was an eerie sight that Lena was glad the townsfolk weren’t around to see, dead climbing into the back of the cart and lying down in the bottom as ordered. Weak and covered in a cold sweat as blood streamed from her eyes and nose, Lena worked throughout the day, until the wide wagon was piled so high that she struggled to blanket the corpses with the canvas sheet. 

 

            The ride back into town was always slower, Hecate plodding along as the shadows lengthened and the air cooled, and by the time she made it to the church just outside the sprawling houses, it would be dark enough for her to work in peace. Under the star-studded sky, she’d sit up on the wagon and tithe even more blood for the magic it leant her, woozy and cold as skeletons dug their own graves by moonlight.

 

            Before she set each one in the ground, Lena took what little personal items they had on them as a means to identify them and marked their spots. Each night, muddy and bloody and pale, she made her way back to the hotel, roaring laughter and music spilling out of the saloon as the yellow light beckoned her to a world beyond her reach, and staggered up the back steps. Lena could read the taut fear in the stiffness of J’onn, M’gann and Nia’s movements as they gave her a wide berth and shooed her up the back staircase so she wouldn’t frighten off their paying customers.

 

            A hot pitcher of water was brought up to her by Nia, along with her supper, and Lena would silently let her set everything down on the table, aware of her monstrous appearance. By the time she scrubbed the blood and dirt away, leaving her pink-cheeked from the scalding heat and vigorous washing, her vision would be swimming and her hands trembling as she sank down heavily onto a dining chair and forced herself to eat. Her appetite evaded her for the most part, and Lena’s prior hollowness sought her out again as her work stripped from her the peace that weeks of working on the ranch without the need of her powers had given her.

 

            It was a searing hot day of gruelling work, no wind making her shirt cling to her back, soaked through with sweat, and the dirt to rime her face between her hat and the neckerchief wrapped around her lower face, when Lena found a body she’d almost apprehensively been waiting to find. She’d worked all day, right through to sundown again, piling the wagon high as she called it a day, and made the trundling trip back across the green pastures and dirt roads, trees whispering to each other as the sickle moon offered little light. 

 

            At the little church, she gouged a cut into her scarred hands, red welling up and running over the handful of yellowed teeth cradled in her palm, and watched the dead rise unsteadily to their feet. Clothes and hair and leathery skin made them almost human in the darkness of night, but their movements were anything but that. The true horror of their appearance was made apparent when she moved along the line, the wan circle of light her lantern gave off illuminating empty eye sockets and lips that had shrivelled and rotted away to reveal the teeth below, fingers held together by sinew and crawling maggots wriggling amidst their flesh.

 

            One by one, Lena forced rings from bony fingers as she swallowed back bile, patted down pants for pocket watches, cigarette cases and money, some small pieces of their life that they’d carried with them. Writing down what each grave’s owner carried on them as blood ran down her cheeks and over her lips in rivulets, she moved from skeleton to skeleton, repeating the process. Until she pulled a photo from one with a woman so achingly familiar to her that Lena’s heart twinged as she rubbed dust and sand off the worn and ragged photo.

 

            Her shoulders slumped as grim realisation knifed through her, and with a flicker of guilt, Lena worked the wedding ring free and directed the skeleton into the grave. She took a little more care with him, making sure he was properly laid to rest before shovelling damp, black earth over him and then the golden brown sandy topsoil, patting the mound down and marking it with a small crucifix from the pile she’d made with sticks and twine.

 

            He was one of the last and after she’d filled the last grave, Lena climbed up onto the front of the wagon and urged Hecate onwards. This time, she unhitched her horse and got her settled and then walked straight past the back door of the hotel, making a beeline for the jail and pausing on the threshold before knocking. A light was on inside and Alex’s muffled voice invited her in. Easing open the door, Lena opened and closed her mouth for a moment as the Sheriff straightened up, mouth dropping open at her appearance as her boots came down off her desk.

 

            “What in the good holy hell. Was you attacked, Doc?”

 

            Lena had the strange urge to laugh, the feeling bubbling up her throat and held back by her inability to speak for a moment. Swallowing around the lump in her throat, she moved over to Alex’s desk. Kelly, who was sitting across from her, the remnants of their supper abandoned before them, shot to her feet and slowly moved behind the desk, her dark eyes wide as fear brimmed in them. There was a stubborn streak of bravery though as her fingers flexed towards the gun on Alex’s desk, as if she thought Lena was one of the things she brought back and meant to put her out of her misery.

 

            “It’s … well, it’s as expected, but … you might want to be the one to break the news,” Lena hoarsely stumbled over her awkward words, holding out a bloody hand with a ring in her palm.

 

            “You’re sure?”

 

            “There was a photo of her.”

 

            Alex didn’t ask for the photo, now tucked safely inside the inner pocket of Lena’s coat, and she gingerly walked over to her to pluck the ring from Lena’s palm. Mouth thinning with grim resignation, Alex nodded and pocketed it.

 

            “I’ll go now. Tell her you found him.”

 

            Nodding, Lena tugged at the faded neckerchief, feeling uncomfortable and helpless. “I’ll leave you to it then. Sheriff. Madam Mayor.”

 

            “Wait!” Kelly called out, twisting her hands anxiously. “Will you see her?”

 

            Lena’s eyes slid over to Alex who shrugged and nodded before she hesitated and echoed the reaction to Kelly. Wrinkling her nose faintly, Kelly jerked her chin to Alex.

 

            “You go and see your sister; I’ll make sure she has a bath.”

 

            Alex let out a snort of laughter while Lena flushed beneath the grime, the stench of decay and damp mud and coppery blood a familiar odour to her but not altogether pleasant. Lena ducked her head as Alex gave Kelly a quick kiss and then donned her hat before stepping outside with Lena and Kelly in tow.

 

            She’d been hoping to escape but Kelly gestured to the Mayor’s office, the modest two-storey brick house lit with lamps a few doors down from the jail. Lena had only been inside a handful of times, and never upstairs, and felt like she was intruding somehow to be in the home of the most powerful woman in town. Kelly’s kindness confused her, and while her fear was expected, Lena didn’t know what to make of her willingness to help. In her experience, people weren’t kind to her for nothing.

 

            “You go on out back and pump some water from the well. It might take a while to boil.”

 

            “Ma’am, I can just wash up-“

 

            “You need a bath, Doc. Not just to look human, but … well, you look like you haven’t slept in days.”

 

            Running a hand over her face, dust and dried blood stuff on her skin, Lena sighed as her shoulders slumped. “It takes it out of me. The magic.”

 

            “I couldn’t imagine why a woman of your status would choose a career like this,” Kelly clicked her tongue as she busied herself fetching a worn shirt and a towel. “The water, Lena.”

 

            Torn between replying or not, Lena hesitated and then turned, making her way back downstairs and out to the back of the house. Her muscles burned as she hauled water in a tin bucket and carried it inside to heat over the fire, pouring it into the tub that Kelly had dragged out in turn. It was the better part of an hour before the bath was filled and steaming, and Lena stripped off her dirty clothes as eager thoughts of being clean swept away her previous objections.

 

            Kelly made tea in the kitchen as Lena scrubbed herself clean, the water growing dirtier with each pass of the cloth and soap, and Lena felt the other woman’s eyes on her. It should have felt discomforting but Lena could sense her curiosity and turned to look at her.

 

            “Sorry,” Kelly murmured, pouring tea from the tin kettle and dragging out a chair.

 

            “How will she take the news?” Lena asked, sweeping aside the apology.

 

            Sighing softly, Kelly shook her head, “she wasn’t that keen on him, truth be told. But … she’s a kind soul and I think she’ll feel … obligated to feel things a wife should.”

 

            “Mm.”

 

            “She misses you.”

 

            Lena’s head jerked around to give Kelly a sharp look, water sloshing as her arm lowered back into the water. “She shouldn’t do. I made every effort to be clear-“

 

            “You miss her too.”

 

            Clenching her jaw as she looked down, Lena’s shoulders bunched with tension. “I’ve never had anyone to miss before.”

 

            “You picked a good one then,” Kelly said with a crooked smile.

 

            “But she did not.”

 

            Scoffing, Kelly waved a dismissive hand, “you’ve earned the trust of the people in town that matter most; I think that don’t make you the worst choice. For what it’s worth, Alex likes you. Well, respects you, at any rate. So do I.”

 

            “That’s kind of you.”

 

            “Wash up,” Kelly reminded her, “I’ll see what’s for supper. It won’t be good; I’m a terrible cook. Too busy running this old town to worry about being a good housewife. And even then, I don’t have a husband and my wife couldn’t care less.”

 

            Arching an eyebrow, Lena smiled slightly. “Wife?”

 

            “Well, she’s as good as. I make the rules here so who says I can’t make them for myself?”

 

            The thought made Lena soften and she was still caught on it as she got out of the tub and dressed in Alex’s borrowed clothes and drained the tea left for her. She was in the midst of emptying buckets of brown water into the ditch behind the house when Kelly came back in with cold cuts of turkey and some bread, the two of them eating by firelight and in relative silence as they let their thoughts consume them.

 

            Eventually, she took her leave as Alex returned, the hour late and the town quieter. She snuck into the stable and saddled Hecate, the mare whickering at the disturbance, before slowly plodding out of town, so tired that Lena imagined she might fall off her saddle.  It was a quiet ride, the night holding a cool edge to it as wan moonlight lit the way and her trusted horse followed the road to the ranch. Kara’s low house was dark when she eventually came upon it, following the long dirt track up to the collection of buildings, but she knew she wouldn’t be asleep yet. Dismounting, Lena let Hecate roam as she crossed the empty yard and climbed up the porch steps.

 

            Removing her hat, clutching it anxiously in her hands, Lena hovered on the porch for a moment before mustering up the courage to reach out for the door handle and let herself if, etiquette be damned. She paused just over the threshold, squinting through the dimness as a low-burning fire cast a wan circle of light over the figure seated before it. Hunched forward, elbows on knees, Kara was scratching Krypto behind his ears as she sipped from a brown bottle clutched in her hand.

 

            At the intrusion, she glanced over at Lena and swallowed, her voice raspy as she spoke. “Why’re you here?”

 

            “I came to … apologise,” Lena awkwardly murmured, shifting restlessly with the urge to cross over to Kara and cradle one of her blotchy cheeks. “And to see if you- if you needed anything.”

 

            Kara let out a hoarse bark of laughter and sheepishly gestured, giving Lena a wry smile, “it ain’t nothing for you to concern yourself with, Doc. Don’t fret none; truthfully, I don’t even know why I’m crying. He was a good for nothing- well, it ain’t right to speak ill of the dead, but he wasn’t- I didn’t- I shouldn’t say it.”

 

            “It’s alright,” Lena softly murmured, crossing over to Kara and sinking down to one knee beside her seat, understanding shining in her green eyes. “Death makes funny things of our emotions. Grief isn’t always quite so straightforward as one might imagine.”

 

            “You must think I’m awful,” Kara muttered, shame making her avert her gaze as she sipped from her bottle and sniffed.

 

            Resting her hand on Kara’s knee, Lena’s expression softened. “I don’t. I couldn’t.”

 

            “Why?”

 

            “Because what would that make me?” Lena asked, a crooked smile, slightly bitter, curling her lips.

 

            Scoffing, Kara rubbed at her cheeks with her sleeve cuff and gave Lena a grim smile, her eyes sad and limned with tears. “I judged you a little too harsh, Lena. You ain’t all bad, you know it and so do I. I think maybe I’m cryin’ because … well, I should feel for him the way I do about you. Guilt … it’s- it ain’t grief. It ain’t right for a wife to not even grieve for her husband.”

 

            “It’s been many months; it’s not so bad that you’re ready to move on.”

 

            “Move on? Ain’t no one to move on with , no matter what Alex says about the other girls in town.”

 

            “You don’t have to move on with someone.”

 

            “I want to,” Kara whispered, reaching out to lightly touch her fingertips to Lena’s cheek as she leaned forward and rested their foreheads together.

 

            Mouth dry and body aching to give in, Lena faltered for a moment and then gave in completely to all reason. This time, she kissed Kara. It wasn’t the surprising spur of the moment kiss from last time - this kiss was soft and hesitant and welcomed, and Lena’s breath hitched slightly at the agonising thought that it would hurt that much more to leave now. 

8. Chapter 8

            Lena was sitting on the edge of the bed, pulling darned socks on and feeling the gentle ache in her limbs as the pre-dawn light filtered in through a crack between the blinds. A hand pressed against her back, warm even through the rough cotton of Lena’s shirt, and she glanced over her shoulder and down at Kara.

 

            A strained smile played on the woman’s lips as she looked up at her with wide blue eyes, the lamplight casting half of her face in its warm orange glow. 

 

            “Must you leave so early?”

 

            “Yes,” Lena wearily replied. “The sooner I leave, the sooner I’ll return.”

 

            “If you return,” Kara murmured, her cheeks flushing pink as she propped herself up on her elbows and ducked her head down, picking at a stray thread on the down quilt. 

 

            Letting out a quiet scoff of laughter, Lena climbed to her feet, the bed creaking beneath the shifting weight, and snatched the pants borrowed from Alex off the floor. Turning as she shoved one foot into a leg, she arched an eyebrow.

 

            “Is that what has you in such a foul mood before the sun’s even risen?”

 

            Her voice was quietly exasperated and a little amused and she studied Kara’s silent embarrassment as she pulled the pants on and laced up the front after tucking in the tails of the billowing shirt. 

 

            “You have a habit of leavin’ me, don’t you?”

 

            “I’m running dangerously low on supplies.”

 

            “And when you’re halfway to where you’re goin’ and decide you’re better off gone from here?”

 

            Sighing, Lena moved back over to the bed and sat down on the edge of the mattress. There was a troubled look clouding her face, pale and drawn from weeks of over-exerting herself with the mine, and she gave Kara a wan smile. One night shouldn’t have changed anything, especially considering Kara’s conflicting grief - Lena regretted her part in the evening a little - but she found herself softening slightly at the dismay in her voice. It wouldn’t do to get attached, but she’d grown fond of Kara, even after weeks of studiously avoiding each other, while finding every opportunity to cross paths to stubbornly ignore one another.

 

            And now this. Lena still harboured that secret thought that she should leave, but she knew Lex would catch her one day, whether in Midvale or a thousand miles away. Stealing from him was a trifling matter in the grand scheme of his plans, and he wouldn’t derail them to hunt her down himself for his revenge, but it was also a matter of pride and wounded ego, and she could imagine his rage. One day he’d get his hands on her and she’d rue the day she’d crossed him - she may as well speed up that inevitable reunion and toss her lot in with the ragged bunch of townsfolk in Midvale. At the very least she might be able to save Kara, and wouldn’t that be a worthy death?

 

            “I told you, I just need more supplies. I’m running low on teeth and everything else was lost in the fire. Look … if it helps put your mind at ease,” Lena said, reaching for the silver medallion hanging around her neck and quickly pulling the long chain over her hand.

 

            She reached out for Kara’s hand and then pressed the medallion into her palm, gently closing her fingers around it. “This is the symbol of my order, bestowed upon us once we officially become a Witch Doctor. It’s … important to me. I won’t leave it behind, so you have my promise I’ll return.”

 

            Uncurling her fingers, Kara stared down at the symbol on it and smiled slightly, quietly pleased with herself. “Okay.”

 

            “I expect I shall return within a week.”

 

            “And if you don’t?”

 

            “Well … perhaps my brother has managed to outwit me at last and finally got the better of me. Don’t mourn me, but don’t forget me,” Lena said with a crooked smile, pulling on her cream duster and reaching for her belt. “Forgetting the dead is like killing them a second time.”

 

            A flicker of irritation passed Kara’s face and she pulled the covers back, her blonde hair waving down her back and her cheeks pink. Sleep still creased her face and she clutched the medallion tightly, the metal no doubt cutting into her palm.

 

            “Don’t say things like that,” she said, that slight drawl to her speech as her brow puckered with concern. “It ain’t a joke, Lena.”

 

            “Well, now, ma’am, it’s not likely to be true either. Don’t you worry about me; I’ve spent years wandering these plains and mountains. Hell, I could creep from one side of the country to the other unseen, if I wished it.”

 

            “You’re mighty sure of yourself for someone who wound up on my doorstep all shot up and the like. What if that happens again? You gonna shack up with the next woman to take you in?”

 

            Laughing loudly as a goading smile curled her lips, Lena cocked her head to the side. “Maybe if they shoot me, but I don’t recall me seducing you.”

 

            “It weren't no … seduction,” Kara spluttered. 

 

            Exhaling softly, Lena finished buckling her belt and sobered up, crossing over to Kara and clapping her hands down on her shoulders. Without her boots on, Kara stood a few inches taller and Lena’s face softened as she thumbed soothing circles against the shoulders of her nightgown.

 

            “Kara,” she said, the name tender in her mouth, perhaps foolishly so. “Nothing is going to happen to me. I won’t stop until I reach the Waypoint and then I won’t stop until I’m back here.”

 

            “I could go with you.”

 

            “No, you couldn’t. It’s a sacred place and a secret we guard with our lives. Besides, you’d only make things more dangerous if it comes to a chase or a shoot out; I’d have to look out for you too.”

 

            “You know, you’re a pain.”

 

            “I know. I’ve warned you away many a time, ma’am; you’d do well to mull it over while I’m gone.”

 

            “Is that right?”

 

            Lena hummed her agreement and then smiled slightly. It felt strange to be standing before someone she’d been as intimate with as any of the other women left in her wake, yet had somehow wormed her way deeper into Lena’s heart, genuine fondness taking root and the expectation that she’d rerun soon. That was unfamiliar and Lena felt uncertain as she stood there.

 

            Mouth opening and closing, she finally pressed her lips together and nodded, squeezing Kara’s shoulder and stepping back. Fetching her boots, she sank to the wooden floor to lace them up and then donned her floppy hat. She had nothing in the way of supplies but would get them on her way through town, stopping to inform Alex of her absence, which left saddling Hecate as the last remaining thing to do.

 

            She did that swiftly, with practised ease, and then made her way back to the porch, where Kara stood in the dark blue of the pre-dawn light. Everything was still very much in shadow and leached of its colour and Lena couldn’t see much but could sense Kara’s disappointment. She knew why, of course, her rather friendly banter lacking the affection the other woman wanted from her, especially after spending the night in her bed, but Lena couldn’t bring herself to give it to her. It was like she was missing that part of herself that trusted, that loved, that could feel things for other people, rather than the distance she intentionally put there instead.

 

            “Well … you stay out of trouble while I’m gone,” Lena slowly said as she mounted the steps.

 

            Scoffing, Kara chewed on her bottom lip and ducked her head, the morning breeze ruffling the cotton of her nightdress. 

 

            “Don’t do anythin’ stupid, now, Doc.”

 

            “Yes, ma’am.”

 

            They both lingered in silence for a moment longer before Lena nodded, boots scuffing on the wooden porch as she turned, and walked down the steps. She kicked up a cloud of dust as she made for Hecate, who was waiting patiently to be off. 

 

            Hauling herself up into the saddle, Lena gathered up the reins and looked towards the dark figure on the porch before she touched the brim of her hat. She didn’t know if Kara saw it but it comforted Lena all the same to have that last farewell.

 

            Wheeling Hecate around, she set off at a brisk trot, kicking up dust that had settled overnight as they made their way down the long path to the main road. It was a few miles into town and Lena got there before the sunrise, dismounting and making her way into the hotel.

 

            The saloon harboured a few drunks around the scarred tables, snoring and mumbling away, and she crept for the sagging stairs, trying not to let them creak too much as she made her way up to her room. She quickly gathered what supplies she could, shoving it all into the knapsack she’d been given for her daily trips to the mine, and slung it over her shoulder before locking the door behind her.

 

            Back outside, she didn’t bother mounting Hecate, just guided the horse by her bridle over to the stately mayor’s office, where she knew she’d find Alex. It was a cool morning and the wind blew sand and grit in her eyes as she made for the back alley and knocked on the door there, too loud in the stillness of the early morning.

 

            Still, it was jerked open minutes later, Alex’s face a scowl creased with sleep as she rubbed at her eyes. “What?” she growled, her hair dishevelled and a revolver in her other hand in case of trouble.

 

            “I’m leaving,” Lena stated.

 

            “You-“

 

            “Briefly,” Lena cut in. “I’m running low on supplies to do my work; I must find a Waypoint and restock before I can continue. It would be foolish for me to let them dwindle any lower, especially if there’s trouble.”

 

            Giving her a wary look, Alex narrowed her eyes. “You mean them teeth of yours? You ain’t going to go pulling them out of people’s heads are you?”

 

            With a derisive snort, Lena arched an eyebrow in a cool manner. “Aren’t we beyond this?”

 

            “Right,” Alex uneasily replied. “What can I do you for, Doc? It’s the crack of dawn and I know you didn’t come here to tell me about your leaving.”

 

            “I need food for the road. A blanket, a pot, a bowl. Just the basics. And I did think you ought to know, on accounts of our agreement.”

 

            “You hopin’ I’d do your dirty work for you and tell my sister?”

 

            Shifting uncomfortably on the stoop as Alex turned from the door to fetch the requested items, Lena watched as she glanced back over her shoulder. Taking in her discomfort, Alex let out a bark of laughter and shook her head.

 

            “Of course. I know I told you to get it all over and done with before we wound up dead, but you’ve got some nerve sittin’ her after burying her dead husband hours before.”

 

            Wrinkling her nose and gingerly ducking her head, Lena shrugged nonchalantly. “I didn’t know him, and to be frank, Sheriff, she wasn’t all that upset about him.”

 

            “Course she weren’t. Well … you break her heart now, Doc, and I’ll put one of your fancy bullets in you and make sure you can’t come back, you hear?”

 

            Rolling her eyes, Lena sighed softly, leaning against the doorframe as she watched Alex wrap food in a bundle, fetching a wedge of cheese from the pantry and a tin of ground coffee. 

 

            “I- you misunderstand our circumstances. I’ll not be dishonourable to her though; I’m … quite fond of your sister.”

 

            “Oh, fond, is it? That’s what you rich folk with them airs and graces call it, is it? Ain’t nothing quite so simply complex as love, Doc.”

 

            Face impassive as she watched Alex drag a scratchy blanket from over the back of a chair and start wrapping the bundle inside it, Lena cleared her throat. She scuffed the toe of her boot along the stone floor just inside the door as her lips twitched ruefully.

 

            “If that were the case,” she murmured. “I’m not in much of a position to form attachments, as you well know. I’m sure that pleases you; I’ll be well and truly gone for good in a few weeks, I should imagine. Should be another month of work at the mine before it’s safe to reopen.”

 

            “And I’ll thank you for it kindly while I escort you over the town limits,” Alex said with a quick grin, walking over to Lena and pressing the bundle into her arm. “But until then … be gentle with her. Lord knows I got enough on my plate without you causing a stir with your dramatics.”

 

            Quietly huffing with laughter, Lena nodded and cradled the bundle in her arms. “Sheriff.”

 

            “I’ll be seeing you, Doc.”

 

            Lena nodded again as she backed out and made quick work of stowing everything in Hecate’s saddlebags as Alex watched from the doorway, looking serious and a little anxious. Lena knew the latter was reserved for her sister, and she imagined Kara would be paid a swift visit that day and delivered a stern warning.

 

            Up in the saddle, Lena gathered the reins up in one hand and touched the brim of her hat before gently digging her spurs into her horse’s flank and urging her down the street. They were slow as they made their way back to the main thoroughfare before Hecate picked up the pace and they tore out of town.

 

            The just-risen sun hung level with Lena’s eyes, watery yellow through the morning haze. The sky was clear and pale above it, a few shreds of white cloud stretched out across the horizon, and it made got a good start to her journey. The air was chill though, the wind holding a bitter edge to it, and Hecate’s breath floated in the air, streaming back towards Lena as the thin haze of fog clinging to the dips in the land slowly dissipated.

 

            It didn’t take long for the day to warm, the cream leather of Lena’s coat holding the heat as it bore down on them. They rode for hours, following the road across the flat landscape, passing the odd outcropping of rocks, past ranches and through another town without pause.

 

            It was lunchtime when Lena came upon a blue-grey smudge of spring water that bubbled up from the prairie, ringed by gnarled oak trees and cattails that waved in the breeze. They’d slowed to a walk a few miles back to give Hecate a reprieve from the gruelling pace and Lena brought them to a stop, taking advantage of the shade and the spring. She drank her fill and ate some of the bread Alex had packed for her, her missed breakfast leaving her starving but the knowledge that she had limited food until she could find her own made her eat sparingly.

 

            They set off again a short while later, riding all through the afternoon at a gentle pace, dusk creeping over the land as she turned slightly westwards, the flatness giving away to rockier terrain that sloped upwards. She’d passed this way before and knew of a copse of trees hiding a jutting bit of rock that offered sparse shelter from the elements. But even sparse was better than none and Lena rode through the dark, no faster than a walk as Hecate’s hooves nicked pebbles as the horse picked a careful path, the white lines of constellations guiding them overhead.

 

            It was hard to see by the time she came upon that patch of dogwood and greasewood, finding her way to the small overhang by memory alone. Once there, Lena swung down off Hecate’s back and set about collecting as much dry wood as she could find and starting a small fire. The orange glow cast a small circle of light over the clearing, it’s warmth taking the edge off the faint chill, and Lena was quick to remove the saddle and brush Hecate down before letting the horse roam to nibble at the grass and plants. She’d buy her oats tomorrow with the little allowance afforded to her by Kelly to buy the necessary supplies she hadn’t been given for the work at the mine.

 

            Eating a strip of jerky and a withering apricot, Lena spread out for the night, but not before she pricked her finger on the razor in the cuff of her coat and finished off a spell in her grimoire. She completed the glyph drawn on the yellowed paper in old blood and then tore the page out, crumpling it and calling on the magic on the page to anchor herself to the bones scattered within a hundred yards of the place. It worked sort of like an alarm system, the spider web of magic connecting her to the bones and the bones to each other crisscrossing the land, and if anyone crossed one of those invisible threads of power, she’d wake with the prickling feeling of being watched.

 

            Satisfied with her measures, Lena scattered the ashes of the page and banked the fire before she pulled the blanket over her and fell asleep. It was strange how she’d spent years on the road, in all manner of conditions - sleeping in a deluge, on soft mud and hard rocks, in snow and sleet and hail, in the dunes of a desert and once in a particularly foul swamp - but found sleep eluding her as she tossed and turned. It was silly to chalk it up to one night spent in Kara’s bed, but the truth was that Lena couldn’t stop thinking about her.

 

            Eventually, she slept though, and woke with the grey of dawn, fog clinging to the trees in pale wisps as early morning light glowed through the branches of the trees. A woodpecker was making a racket and Lena pushed herself up, brushing tangled dark hair out of her face as she watched a chipmunk scurry past and a rabbit bolt. Eating a cold breakfast of bread and cheese, she made herself a cup of black coffee, bitter and scalding, and then saddled Hecate and set off.

 

            The slopes went downhill again after a mile and Lena set off across blonde summer hills, cupped with oaks, whistling softly to herself as they made a leisurely pace. Of course, her guard was never let down, and she chose to conserve Hecate’s energy until she truly needed it. Her gun would suffice until then, and each chamber had been unloaded, cleaned and then reloaded that morning.

 

            She followed much the same routine for the next two days, stopping at a nearby town and finding a man rich enough to barge into the general goods store, disheveled and drunk and grieving, and fall to his knees on the dusty floors to beg her for her services. It wasn’t often people in such small towns could pay with real coin and Lena wasted no time escorting him back to his stately home.

 

            The smell of death permeated the entire home, putrid and sickly sweet, and she was shown to the bedroom where his husband had passed. The man was still in bed, his skin waxen and stiff in his nightclothes. Thumbing the last piedfort coin in her pocket, the spare she always kept on her person in case she lost the tokens of her trade, Lena warranted it was a worthy time to use it, only a day away from restocking her supplies anyway.

 

            Rifling through her grimoire, she pricked her finger and drew on a blank sheet, vivid red bleeding into the thick paper as she swiftly made the familiar glyphs. She’d spent years studying them and could have drawn it with her eyes closed, the sharp, angular line here, the curve line there, the dot and the cross and the sweeping flick. Working swiftly, she forced the dead man’s jaw open, the strength required making her break his jaw - he would be whole and hale soon anyway - and forced the thick coin into his mouth.

 

            Tearing open the cotton of his nightclothes, she refreshed the cut on her finger and swirled matching glyphs over his bare chest, the swirling symbols almost like some foreign script. It was meaningless to those who didn’t know what each line of the glyphs meant, and even then, it was a magic so ancient that they were only taught it was part of the process to revive someone.

 

            With the body as prepared as she could make it, having to forego the opoponax given her destroyed chest of healing tools, Lena burnt basil and rosemary fetched from the kitchens, the smoke used as a tool to summon souls back to the body, and plucked three teeth from her purse. It was a complex web of weaving the magic after that, the spark in the teeth, the blood on the paper, the coin in the mouth and glyphs on the chest. Lena hummed a droning tone as she moved her hands, fingers twitching this way and then that, pulling the spell together.

 

            Blood trickled over her lips as it streaked from her eyes and nose. It was a process that took the better part of an hour, from start to finish, and with each minute the strain became evident on Lena’s face, taut and stony while her shoulders grew increasingly slumped.

 

            Eventually, the man came to screaming. It was how all dead came back to the land of the living and Lena quickly crossed over to the fireplace, stoking the coals she’d prepared and watching as they glowed cherry red, heat radiating from them. 

 

            “Don’t move,” she ordered the freshly revived man, who looked shockingly healthy, given his recent status as a corpse.

 

            Gathering up her tools, she left him gasping and pale in bed and left the room, her part over with. Steps thundering downstairs, she found his husband anxiously pacing in a sitting room and she turned the brim of her gamblers hat in her grasp as she met his eyes, knowing she looked ghastly as his face visibly drained of blood.

 

            “He’s well. You should fetch him blankets and ensure he stays in bed for a day. He’ll be cold.”

 

            He nodded numbly, snapping his fingers at a young maid who hovered in the doorway and quickly turned to do his bidding. Paying her with a double eagle coin, he shooed Lena from his property with a look of fear in his relieved eyes, before he vanished upstairs to his husband without so much as a word of thanks.

 

            Able to buy the things she required from the store, Lena went on her way, putting a few hours between herself and the store before she stopped. Washing at a stream, she caught a wild turkey and roasted it, gorging herself on the meat and beans she heated over the fire before setting her wards and promptly passing out from exhaustion.

 

            Rising late, the day already half over and a fox slinking off with the bones of her wild turkey, Lena groaned as she pushed herself up. Her body protested at the movement, muscles aching as she kneaded her shoulder and let out a low hiss. Making coffee, she grimly rued the delay in her trip and packed up before setting off, aiming to make the most of the remaining hours of sunlight.

 

            The terrain turned rockier now, in the shadows of mountains and ravines, valleys and knolls and twisting paths through foothills. The Waypoint was high up on the slopes of one of the mountains nearby and Lena made for a narrow pass toward the west. She’d covered leagues since leaving Midvale and the scenery was vastly changed. The trail up to the summit was covered in wild blackberries that were just turning ripe. She stopped and ate for a while before continuing the climb.

 

            Stopping on the trail up, darkness falling early and grey clouds blanketing the sky, blotting out any moonlight to offer any light to guide her, Lena drew Hecate a dozen feet from the trail. Aware that word of her involvement with her brother and her status as a Rogue might have travelled far, she resolved to spend the night without a fire and huddled up against Hecate, sleeping as best as she could on a rustling carpet of leaves, relieved she’d be halfway done by mid-morning tomorrow.

 

            Rising early with the sun, she had a cold breakfast and blew some warmth into her cold fingers, missing her gloves more than ever, and readied herself for the last leg of the trek up the mountain. It was a gentle slope all the way up to the narrow pass between two peaks, and Lena could have reached out and touched both sides of the ravine as she passed through, gnarled trees growing out of crevices and shading the rocky path.

 

            The sky was grey overhead and the wind howled through the mountain, eerie and chilling her to the bone, although there was no snow given it was still summer. After a couple of hours, she felt the prickle of crossing over ancient wards and swung down off Hecate, leading her the rest of the way until she reached a dead end. The Waypoint was a narrow crack in the converging rocky walls that had guided her to it and she left Hecate outside as she made for the cave entrance.

 

            She’d only ever been to this Waypoint once before, years ago, and wondered if she’d be familiar to the retired Witch Doctor who served the place. Perhaps she’d remained removed from the news down south, or perhaps one of the protected convoys that travelled from Waypoint to Waypoint with supplies from the East Coast to restock for their order had beaten her there and passed on lies. Lex would have had a hand in spreading the word to as many people as he could so they’d hand her over while he could continue with his mission. Of course, not everyone knew the true Rogue they’d be aiding in the process, but much like Selena, Lena knew some would accept the payment even knowing it was him. What was the state of the Order to a retired Witch Doctor denied the luxury of an ordinary life?

 

            Lena pricked her finger on the cuff of her sleeve, feeling the biting sting of a deep cut opening, and let her other hand stray down towards the bone handle of her gun. Wary and tense, she crept down the long passage and came out into an illuminated cave, the ceiling opening in places to the sunlight above them, so that the cave seemed half-outdoors.

 

            “Greetings, sister. You’re welcome here.”

 

            Lena’s eyes adjusted and took in the cloaked figure of a woman methodically grinding herbs as she weighed them for the little glass vials scattering the long table in the middle of the open cave. Ducking her head, Lena swallowed, her throat dry, and hoped her face remained in shadow.

 

            “Greetings.”

 

            “I’m not sure you’ve ever crossed my path before, child. I’m Jindah Kol Rozz, keeper of the Waypoint. How can I assist the Order?”

 

            “I … waylaid my chest. I have no tokens, my supply of teeth is low and … I’ll need bullets too, I should think.”

 

            Clicking her tongue, the woman set down the pestle, the smell of ground safe perfuming the air. “How does one waylay one of the most important tools of their craft? Reckless idiocy.”

 

            “Indeed,” Lena murmured in agreement, feeling her cheeks heat.

 

            She had her thumbnail gouged into the thin cut on her index finger, keeping the blood flowing as she stood just beyond the entrance to the cave. Lena wasn’t foolish enough to let her guard down.

 

            Magic lay heavily over the Waypoint, so thick it made her teeth ache, her skin humming with its power, but there was something underneath all that power. Something dark and rank, a powerful sense of wrongness hanging over the whole cave. It felt somehow different to the other Waypoints she’d frequented as if the very air of the place was warning her, the ferrous tang of blood, the smell of stale piss hanging in the air as the woman moved around slowly.

 

            Lena watched as she fetched a small empty chest, not unlike the one that had been burnt, and started gathering supplies. Vials clinked and packets of dried herbs rustled, piedfort coins clinking as they were plucked from a clay pot. The woman lit a cigarette as she worked, taking a drag as her cheeks compressed and Lena could see the ghastly shape of her skull.

 

            “Here, child. Your tooth pouch.”

 

            Quickly untying it from her belt, Lena passed it over and felt the humming turn frantic as her coiled body tensed for the attack. The woman gripped her hand tightly, the tooth pouch clutched in Lena’s fist, holding her steady as she lashed out with a small knife.

 

            Lena managed to duck her head, the line of fire tracing across her cheek instead of her throat. Blood ran down her face and she quietly snarled as she tore a page from her grimoire and slammed it against the Witch Doctor’s arm, summoning the magic in a surge of rage.

 

            The old woman screamed as the spell ate away at her flesh, the skin and muscle quickly receding down to the bone as it withered away. Rarely had Lena used a spell so brutal and it gave her pause for a moment as the paper burned down to ash beneath her palm, affording the woman a moment to scrabble for a jar on the shelf and slam it into the side of Lena’s face.

 

            Her vision burst with stars as she stumbled off balance, the left side of her face numb as she dropped her bag of teeth, the sound of them scattering across the floor distant to the ringing sound in Lena’s ears. It took her a moment to realise she’d been struck with a pot of evening primrose oil, the smell cloying as the oil soaked the left side of her, trickling beneath the collar of her coat and soaking into her shirt. A knife hit her next, stabbing through the leather of her coat and down to the hilt in her shoulder.

 

            Drawing in a shallow breath Lena pulled her gun from its holster and pulled back the hammer but it was knocked from her grasp before she could aim it, the bullet going awry and the gun skittering across the floor. She’d lost her knife which left her defenceless, and after the revival yesterday she wasn’t in much of a place to be brawling with an older woman. Not that she had a chance as the woman pulled a sawn-off shotgun from beneath the table and pointed it at her, one skeletal hand reaching up to pull back the forearm and eject a cartridge as a new one was loaded.

 

            “You think I didn’t know you?” she asked with a thin smile. “Your brother is going to be the new order of our kind; he’ll pay handsomely for your head. It’s a pity he won’t be able to bring you back.”

 

            Still unsteady on her feet and breathing rapidly, eyes darting around nervously as she tried to find an out, Lena’s fingertips strayed to her forehead at the mention of being brought back. He’d killed her enough times already, made her suffer tenfold and brought her back for her to want it again. She’d rather be good and dead, finally at rest, than become a plaything for him.

 

            “You’re a fool if you think things will change for us,” Lena ground out, stoic and stubborn as she jerked her chin forward, awaiting her final death as her left arm hung limply at her side, a burning pain in her shoulder.

 

            It didn’t frighten her but beneath it all there was a prickle of regret and guilt - she’d promised Kara she’d return, and there would be no one to explain the truth to her. As far as the rancher would know, Lena had gone back on her word and left her with her medallion as a parting gift. There was a bitter taste in Lena’s mouth as her lips twisted with a slight sneer and she spread her right arm out expectedly.

 

            As she watched Jindah Kol Rozz raise the shotgun, there was the splitting sound of a bullet being fired before she could fill Lena with the small shotgun pellets, and Lena blinked in surprise as she watched the woman’s head snap back. The shotgun fell from her hands as her whole body folded in on itself, crumpling to the floor in a heap as a dark bloodstain started spreading across the stone.

 

            Lena didn’t hesitate as she dove for her revolver and snatched it up before whirling around and catching the newcomer across the temple before they could shoot her. Self-preservation and years of mistrust left her knowing that just because someone had killed the person trying to shoot her, it didn’t mean they were trustworthy and wouldn’t plunge a dagger in her turned back. 

 

            As it was, the woman dropped like a stone, cursing and hissing with pain as the rifle she held skittered across the floor and out of reach. Her hat was knocked back and Lena caught a glimpse of a face that was frustratingly familiar.

 

            “Howdy.”

 

            “Don’t fucking move,” Lena snarled, pointing her Colt at the sprawled Witch Doctor as she stalked towards her.

 

            Raising her hands and swallowing thickly, Sam let out a choked laugh, “you might consider a thank you, on accounts of me saving your ass.”

 

            Scoffing, Lena’s mouth twisted, “I didn’t ask you to.”

 

            “Well, I’ll take it as you owing me then.”

 

            “I don’t owe you shit. What are you doing here?”

 

            Looking a little ashen as her bronze skin beaded with sweat, face a little taut with pain, Sam drew in a laboured breath. “You was right. ‘Bout that brother of yours.”

 

            Lena stiffened, her skin prickling with unease as she adjusted her grip on her pistol, shifting restlessly. Licking her lips, she scowled down at Sam.

 

            “What do you mean?”

 

            “I seen him. Followed him all the way up to Montana. Passed through a dozen ghost towns - dead and pillaged, all of ‘em. Problem was, he was heading back down too. Got me real good, he did.”

 

            She slowly moved a shaking hand to pull aside the cream leather coat of their order she was wearing, exposing a large bloodstain covering the left of her abdomen. Her other hand was pressed against the wound, covered in dried blood. 

 

            “When?” Lena asked.

 

            Drawing in a shallow breath, squeezing her eyes shut and making a low sound of discomfort, Sam shook her head. Pinning her with one boot on her thigh, Lena leaned down and pressed the barrel of her gun into Sam’s abdomen, not quite on her wound but close enough to elicit a small cry of pain.

 

            “Tell me.”

 

            “I- I ain’t likely to get much out in this state, sister.”

 

            “I’m not your sister; tell me what I want to know or I’ll let you bleed out and read it from your blood.”

 

            Letting out a small laugh, Sam grinned. “Heal me and I’ll tell you.”

 

            “Heal yourself.”

 

            “It took everything in me to get here; I ain’t got the strength. And if I die … you’re totally fucked, I’ll tell you that for free.”

 

            Biting back a sound of frustration, Lena huffed and holstered her gun. Dropping to the floor of the cave, she dragged the knife from Sam’s sheath and slashed it across the palm of her hand, fishing teeth from Sam’s pouch and summoning the magic forth as she tore a page from her book.

 

            It burned through her quickly and she pulled the Witch Doctor’s hand aside to press her own fingers to the gaping gunshot wound. It was from a shotgun blast - quite close range - which meant that Lena had to coax forth dozens of tiny pellets. Sam’s breathing turned ragged and she squirmed on the floor but was otherwise impassive, Lena quietly impressed.

 

            Once the wound was sealed, Lena climbed to her feet and moved over to the cave door, ignoring Sam’s rasping plea behind her. Stepping out into the pale sunlight, she made for Sam’s horse and rummaged through her stocked chest, fetching the necessary herbs and making her way back inside. 

 

            Making a little fire, Lena brewed a tincture with willow bark, yarrow, chamomile and some feverfew leaves and dipped a chipped clay cup into it before carrying it over to Sam. She pushed it into her hand and stepped back.

 

            “Drink that.”

 

            Catching the flicker of hesitation in the woman’s hazel eyes, Lena snorted. “I haven’t poisoned you. I’d prefer a bullet; it would shut you up faster. Besides, I still haven’t gotten my information from you.”

 

            Conceding to her latter point, Sam forced the tea down her throat and pushed herself into a sitting position. Chest rising and falling rapidly, she nodded her thanks to Lena and set the cup down.

 

            “Thank you.”

 

            “Talk.”

 

            Lena’s voice was hard and flat and she reached up for the handle of the knife, yanking it free of her shoulder. The pain made her vision dim slightly and she swayed on her feet before reaching up to heal it, palming a tooth from her own supply and smearing it in the blood. 

 

            “I followed him back down. He must’ve known I was followin’ - he’s got a damn big posse with him now, and not all of them’s dead - had scouts and the like. Well, I was ‘bout fourteen days out from here when he got me real good with a shotgun. Lucky they was all camped up for the night or else I wouldn’t have made it far in a chase, I reckon.”

 

            Stooping to pick up the cup, Lena fetched herself some of the tea as Sam talked, draining it to take the edge off that cold feeling of pain. She grunted in acknowledgement of her words and rounded on her.

 

            “What was he doing?”

 

            “Raiding. I didn’t catch him ‘til Montana but I followed him ‘round and back down awhile. He took a train car full of gold from a mine up in Douglas Creek. Shot up the place ‘til they gave it to him, and then shot the rest of ‘em for good measure too. I watched from a distance and brought back as many as I could - least the ones that weren’t shot by no bone bullets. Followed him to the border of Colorado when I got stuck.”

 

            “You didn’t think to heal yourself?”

 

            Giving her a dour look, Sam smiled thinly. “Much like you when you was fleeing me, stopping didn’t seem like the wise choice, now, did it?”

 

            “You could’ve bled to death.”

 

            “I was careful ‘nough not to. I been mighty tired though; I think … I might sleep.”

 

            Lena was silent and watchful, heedless of the blood trickling from her nose and eyes, the tremor in her hands and the hunger gnawing at her stomach. So far, her plan to slip through unobtrusively wasn’t going very well and she felt exhausted and irritable. Running a hand over her face, she pinched the bridge of her nose.

 

            “I’ll leave you to tidy up then.”

 

            “Wha- you can’t leave me here. I saved your life.”

 

            “Yeah? I just saved yours.”

 

            “I’ve got more to say on him, that brother of yours.”

 

            Shooting her a dark look of suspicion, Lena’s lip curled derisively. “Then say it.”

 

            With a choked laugh, Sam shook her head. “No, ma’am. I ain’t giving up my leverage real quick like that. I got a little girl I need to get home to - help me on my way and I’ll give you everything.”

 

            It was rather reluctantly that Lena gave in, nodding curtly and turning to the mess of the Waypoint. She set about taking care of her own stores first, taking the chest and replenishing what she needed, filling vials with herbs and plucking tinctures from the shelves, filling a canvas sack with oats for Hecate and picking up the strewn teeth before scooping out handfuls until it was full.

 

            She didn’t take more than she needed, mindful of the other Witch Doctor’s who would come this way, needing the salted pork and ground coffee, the prunes and crackers and hard cheeses. Still, she had more in the way of supplies than she’d had in months, taking a credit for her monthly stipend to buy new clothes, finding rope and utensils and an extra blanket, everything she could have possibly needed. She packed everything into the saddlebags or strapped it to the back of the saddle, and it was with satisfaction that she finally dusted off her hands and made her way back into the cave.

 

            “We need to get moving.”

 

            Eyes shuttering, Sam leaned against the cave wall, a shaft of sunlight spilling through a natural hole in the ceiling to highlight her wan tan skin. She didn’t look so good, even after being healed and Lena contemplated whether or not she should have killed her first.

 

            “Can’t we rest the night here?” Sam rasped.

 

            “By all means, but I won’t. There’s a dead Keeper here and if someone comes along and finds us both sleeping here, who do you think they’re going to blame?”

 

            “Well … what are the chances of that happenin’, do you reckon?”

 

            Fixing her with a derisive look, Lena made her way over to the bloodstain spreading from the dead body and pressed her hands into the blood. She pulled memories from it, divining snatches of what had happened and feeling a prickle of unease. They weren’t the only Witch Doctors to pass through in recent days and Lena worried about someone else in the area following their trail. 

 

            Climbing to her feet, she moved over to a barrel of collected rainwater, prising the lid off. It was warm and stale with a film of dust on the top but she scooped out a bowl full and washed her bloody hands in it, turning it a pale shade of pink.

 

            “Ordinarily, low, but given recent events, I don’t like our chances very much. I’ll not spend the night here; if you’re too weak to travel far today, we’ll make off the road and set up camp there.”

 

            “Rain’s comin’ in,” Sam drawled.

 

            “Then we’d better get moving so we can find proper shelter.”

 

            Sam’s mouth thinned but she didn’t argue, just jerked her chin at the body. “What about her?”

 

            Lena knew the proper procedure was to wrap the body, a coin in the mouth and the appropriate herbs used, the last rights their Order performed given to the corpse. And yet, she cared for her own self-preservation more than the restless soul of a murdered Witch Doctor and shrugged indifferently.

 

            “She’s a problem for the next one who rides through. Although … we should send a letter in the next town - they’ll need to replace her to keep the Waypoint active.”

 

            Slowly pushing herself to her feet as she groaned, Sam dusted off her hat and picked up the rifle she’d acquired along her travels. It was different to the one she’d shot Lena with, something she was still clinging to with resentment.

 

            “You need anything?” Lena tersely asked.

 

            “Nope. Just came on through to have myself all healed up.”

 

            “Then let’s go.”

 

            Exhausted and in a foul mood, Lena was silent as she made her way out of the cave and swung up into the saddle, offering no help to Sam as she set off and let the other Witch Doctor follow after her. They were known as lone creatures out West, not usually travelling in pairs or bigger groups, and Lena knew they’d attract attention as they travelled and bit back a sigh at the inconvenience. If Lex was keeping an ear out for any sightings of her, whispers of Necromancers passing through town would come back to bite her. She resolved to skirt around any towns and live off the land as best as they could for the next few days.

 

            True to her word, and mostly due to her own bone-deep weariness, Lena led them off the path as soon as they emerged from the steep-walled ravine, leading Hecate through the brush as Sam followed behind on her own horse with a new half-rotted hound to follow after her.

 

            They came to a stop in a secluded clearing, thick brush and trees blocking them from the road, with the sloping land giving them the advantage of seeing anyone approaching from below. There was a rocking cliffside at their back, a portion of it sloping inwards to create a low cleft that would offer them shelter as they slept.

 

            “Here will do,” Lena said, reining in Hecate.

 

            Swinging down from her saddle, boots sinking into the carpet of rotting leaves and moss, she looked around and then looked up at the grey sky. Sam stopped and dismounted as well, a little unbalanced but uncomplaining. They made for wary travelling companions and Lena eyed her shrewdly.

 

            “You was a lady weren’t you?” Sam asked as she started removing her things from the back of her horse. “Why you all out here alone, working your body to the grave instead of … shacked up in some fancy home in a big city with a nice husband and some kids. Hell of a lot safer, ain’t it?”

 

            Rolling her eyes, Lena unstrapped her blankets and the knapsack with her supplies and dumped it all in a neat pile before working the saddle free.

 

            “You don’t know anything about me.”

 

            “Heck, I know you got a mean brother, and that blonde little lady you’re down soft on.” Sam let out a low whistle of appreciation, “what happened there ‘tween you two, anyway? She the reason why you’re out this way?”

 

            “Leave her out of it.”

 

            “Touchy subject, huh? Well, I won’t lie, I don’t envy what’s comin’ your way with that brother of yours. Nasty thing, ain’t he?”

 

            With a scoff of laughter, Lena shook her head as a thin smile played on her lips, stooping down to pick up a log. The wood was slightly damp but she gathered a stack anyway, Sam’s conversation petering out as she rubbed down her horse, attempted to rub down Hecate and earned a swift kick to her stomach - Lena chuckling to herself - and then flopped on the ground.

 

            “You sleep first; I’ll keep watch,” Lena said once she’d cooked herself a small portion of oats and salted pork, guarding her meal protectively as she watched Sam make the most of her stale bread and beans. “We leave at first light. I need to get back.”

 

            “Ah, so it is about that girl.”

 

            “I’m not above shooting you again - and this time I won’t heal you.”

 

            “What’s her name, anyway?” Sam asked, ignoring the threat.

 

            Lena chewed on the inside of her lip as she stared down into her cup of whiskey she’d poured herself from the pilfered flask. Her mouth thinned and she sighed softly. 

 

            “Kara.”

 

            “Well, good luck to you. Speaking from experience, it ain’t all easy to work out when you’ve got a callin’ like this. Here’s to hopin’ she’s a better woman than the man I shacked up with.”

 

            Lena ignored her and sipped her drink and eventually, even though it was barely midday, Sam went to sleep and Lena kept watch. She read the book she’d taken from the Waypoint, flipping through the pages with slow satisfaction as she basked in the peaceful feeling of being on the road and having the downtime to read, her Colt in her lap in case trouble came and the birds tweeting overhead.

 

            Sam slept late into the evening and Lena stoked the small fire and cooked herself food before setting wards and eyeing the Wight hound with unease. She was sure it would alert Sam to any threats if they arose so Lena slowly slept, her own wards protecting her from the other woman in case of treachery.

 

            Waking to the feeling of rain on her face, Lena huddled beneath her blankets and shivered in the chill dawn, the light still a deep blue as the sun struggled to make an appearance. Her breath hung before her when she finally rose, starting a smoking fire that made her cough and finally roused Sam.

 

            Breakfast was a miserable affair and water rolled down the leather of her duster and dropped off the brim of her hat as Lena ate her oats before attending to Hecate. She stroked the mare’s nose and the hollows above her eyes as she whuffed in disappointment at Lena’s lack of apples.

 

            They packed up quickly and Lena sat on Hecate’s back, staring out at the land with a grave look on her face as she worried about flash floods and mudslides from overflowing mountain rivers. Sticking to the high ground as they made their way down slowly, they spent the morning on the narrow back of a rocky ridge where they could see the plains in the nearby distance and the stretch of grey sky over the low hills and valleys, their dark swells glinting with brief flashes of lightning.

 

            Damp and miserable, neither of them talkative, they made their way down and plodded along with weary determination. At the first town they came to, Lena insisted that Sam stay a few miles outside - although she’d truthfully been hoping to shake her off - and mailed a letter at the post office with news of Jindah Kol Rozz’s death. True to her word, mostly due to her desperate interest in what Lex had been planning, Lena returned to Sam and they stuck to their south-easterly course.

 

            Eating lunch in the saddle, trying to make up for lost time, although the roads were muddy and flooded with brown puddles of water, inevitably slowing them further, they made little progress. Her weeklong trip was quickly turning into one of ten days and she wanted to wince at the thought of Kara waiting for her. It shouldn’t have bothered Lena so much - what were they to each other but strangers, really - but it did and she foolishly made onwards through the dusk as sheeting rain plagued them. 

 

            It was pitch black when she felt something off about Hecate’s gait and pulled them over. There was no light to see by and Lena pricked her fingers to heal what she imagined was a stone bruise or inflamed leg, but the problem persisted and they had to make a hasty camp on high ground in case of flooding.

 

            The morning revealed it was a loose horseshoe, the nails worn down and the hoof wall having grown out, and Lena grumbled at the inconvenience. She expected Sam to be on her way then, her strength regained enough to travel alone, but she advised Lena she’d wait outside the next town while Lena found a farrier to shoe Hecate.

 

            It wasted a good chunk of their morning, the slow walk to the nearest town and the hours it took to remove the shoes, file down the hooves and nail on new shoes slipping by with agonising slowness. By the time they were back on the road, the rain had let up, blue skies peering between gaps in the clouds at points, and Sam whistled as they travelled.

 

            “Are you going to tell me now?” Lena asked once they were a day’s ride away from Midvale.

 

            So far, their travelling hadn’t been quite as bad as she’d imagined, Sam sticking to herself for the most part, uncomplaining even when Lena hoarded her food to herself, having the good sense to restock when presented with the opportunity. 

 

            Letting out a quiet laugh, Sam glanced sideways at her from her saddle. “It’s been eatin’ you up, hasn’t it? My silence.”

 

            “A deal is a deal.”

 

            “Aye, and I’ll tell you when we get where we’re goin’.”

 

            “You know where I’m going.”

 

            “So, I’ll tell you when we get there.”

 

            Lena scoffed and gave her a contemptuous look. “They don’t care for outsiders; you know that. Why would you want to go back there, anyway? Their Sheriff will surely shoot you as easily as welcome you, and I know which one she’d prefer.”

 

            Arching an eyebrow at her, Sam smiled thinly, “perhaps it concerns her too. Maybe I got news for the whole town.”

 

            “Well, it’s not going to do them much good, is it? They won’t leave their ranches and their mediocre lives on the word of a Witch Doctor. It’ll be me who has to defend them.”

 

            “Ah, but can you do it alone?”

 

            Falling silent, Lena was stony-faced as they carried on. Sam showed no sign of leaving and Lena was powerless to scare her off, short of shooting her and leaving her for dead, and running the risk of losing out on valuable information.

 

            A few miles later they found a wandering Wight, the stocky man aimlessly walking along the path they cut through, his eyes a milky white and unseeing. With a sigh and the sinking feeling of worse yet to come, Lena pulled her pistol from its holster and raised it at him. The sound of the gun firing started a flock of crows from their perch, echoing faintly in the open countryside and they both looked down upon the dead body as they neared it, knowing Sam was right.

 

            They spent one more night outdoors, everything damp from the recent rains and making for a very uncomfortable evening, her clothes damp and chafing, boots leaving terrible blisters and the food whatever they could manage cold. It was at this point that Lena took a small amount of pity on Sam and shared bread, cheese and some trout she’d caught when seeking a moment alone by the river.

 

            It was a steady pace in a relatively straight line the next morning, cutting across the prairie grass and open fields, past herds of cows and wild horses, skirting ranches and eventually making for the wide road leading into town. It was high noon by the time they slowed their pace, Lena entering Midvale damp and covered in blood as Hecate trotted along the damp thoroughfare.

 

            Making for the hotel, Lena dismounted and hitched Hecate before turning. Her attention snagged on the sight of Kara, who was wide-eyed and pale with surprise and relief, looking tired and a little dishevelled, strands of hair escaping her braid and her hands twisting the fabric of her deep blue skirt. She smiled crookedly at Lena, the brim of her hat shading crinkling eyes and her pace was slow and careful as she crossed over from the porch of the jail where she’d evidently been keeping watch for Lena’s arrival.

 

            “Howdy,” Kara quietly greeted her, shoulders slumping.

 

            “Ma’am,” Lena murmured, touching the brim of her hat and smiling wryly. “I’m sorry to keep you waiting.”

 

            Letting out a shy, slightly embarrassed laugh, Kara gestured vaguely towards the jail as she looked down at the dirt and scuffed a boot through it. 

 

            “I was just- well, ain’t no cause for lies. You already know it, anyway.”

 

            “It’s good to see you,” Lena earnestly replied, shocking herself with the low, tender murmur of her voice.

 

            She didn’t think she’d ever been so forthright and honest with her thoughts and she felt her stomach lurch as her palms turned clammy. Turning back to Hecate, she pretended to check if she was hitched properly and cleared her throat, a slight colour coming into her ashen cheeks.

 

            “Are you … alright?” Kara hesitantly asked, her eyes roaming over the ghastly sight of her.

 

            “Trouble on the road,” Lena muttered, waving dismissively. “Nothing I couldn’t handle.”

 

            “Not without my help,” Sam cut in, boots landing heavily in the soft earth beside Lena as she clapped a hand on her shoulder.

 

            Kara jerked back as shock crossed her face, blinking as she looked at the hand on Lena’s shoulder. Scowling, Lena shrugged it off and roughly pushed Sam away.

 

            “Don’t touch me.”

 

            “You,” Kara exclaimed, eyebrows rising.

 

            “Saved your old biddy for you, Cattle Kate.”

 

            Kara stiffened at Sam’s words, giving her an uncharacteristically scathing look as she haughtily replied, “I’m a rancher. I don’t herd cows.”

 

            “My apologies, ma’am. Much the same to me, ain’t it.”

 

            Lena tried to hide the fact that she was enjoying Kara’s poorly concealed jealousy and turned to Sam. “Time for you to tell me what you know and be on your way.”

 

            “Not ‘fore I have a good mug of beer and some proper food,” Sam eagerly said. “Maybe a bath as well if you’s willing.”

 

            Sighing heavily, Lena gave Kara a regretful look and made for the steps to the saloon before she was interrupted by the sound of Alex shouting out. Turning, Lena narrowed her eyes against the sun as she watched the Sheriff briskly stalk towards her, both guns being freed of their holsters.

 

            “What in the good holy hell,” Alex blurted out, her guns levelled at Sam as she shot Lena an accusing stare as if she’d betrayed them by bringing another Witch Doctor back to their town.

 

            “Sakes alive,” Kara groaned, pinching the bridge of her nose.

 

            Sighing again, Lena put a hand out to stop Sam from hoisting her rifle in defence and her mouth thinned as she gave Alex a grim look.

 

            “I know it’s not ideal-“
