            “What the fuck, Doc? I thought you didn’t like her; last I saw of you two was you shootin’ her in the street and at each other’s throats inside my jail here. Thought you would’ve been glad to see her dead and now you’s bringin’ her into my town. Fucker.”

 

            “She has information and we need all the help we can get,” Lena patiently explained.

 

            Scoffing, Alex jerked her chin at Sam. “She ain’t no great scratch. Truthfully, neither are you, Doc. I ain’t never met a person to get shot up as many times as you - are you sure you even know what you’re doin’, cause I sure ain’t fucking convinced.”

 

            “Alexandra Danvers! Don’t you go on airin’ your lungs like that in broad daylight,” Kelly scolded her wife as she burst out of the saloon. 

 

            Her expression darkened as she folded her arms over the pale pink of her linen shirt. The mayor took in the scene before her as people watched on from the verandahs of their businesses or the alleys between houses where they were pretending to sweep or beat the dust out of a rug.

 

            “Get inside,” Kelly hissed, pointing to the saloon.

 

            Resting her rifle against her shoulder, Sam smiled nonchalantly, as if she wasn’t in the middle of a showdown with half a dozen people who wouldn’t have cared if she died.

 

            “Don’t mind if I do.”

 

            Lena bit back a groan and watched as she walked up the steps and vanished inside, Alex following after her as she shot Lena a dark look. Running a hand over her face, desperately wishing for a bath and clean clothes, but desiring nothing more than to escape the bickering that would ensue, Lena pulled her hat off her head and wiped the dust from her brow.

 

            “It’s good to see you too,” Kara murmured as she stopped at Lena’s side.

 

            Glancing at her, Lena felt oddly shy and shifted uneasily as she ducked her head in a nod. She watched as Kara reached up and fumbled with a silver chain around her neck and Lena’s stomach jolted at the sight of her medallion being pulled from beneath her shirt. For some reason, she hadn’t anticipated the fact that Kara would wear it, and the thought that it had been safely tucked beneath her shirt, warmed by her skin for the past week, felt strangely intimate as she let the triskelion medallion drop onto Lena’s bloody palm.

 

            “I kept it safe for you.”

 

            Curling her fingers around it, feeling the warmth of the metal from Kara’s chest, she smiled unevenly, an ache in her chest as she avoided Kara’s eyes.

 

            “Thank you."

9. Chapter 9

            Inside the saloon of the hotel, Lena sat back from the table slightly, holding a mug of cool beer as if she was there for entertainment and not covered in grime and blood from the road, still reeking of the evening primrose oil and the rancid smell of dried blood. That was typical for Lena in her line of work but she shifted self-consciously before the others gathered around the table.

 

            Alex had one boot up on a chair, hunching slightly as she rested her arm on top, with Kelly to her right, an aura of power about her as if she was keeping her mayoral council from inside the bar. Kara sat across from Lena and kept casting her fleeting glances, taking in the blood soaking the left side of her leather coat, torn from the knife wound, the cuts and bruises on her face that Lena hadn’t bothered to heal to conserve her power, and the dust and sweat from days of hard riding. 

 

            J’onn and Brainy had joined them, while Nia lingered every so often in between waiting tables, and Andrea had come at the announcement of Lena’s return, her companion, Russell, standing protectively behind her as she primly sipped lemonade in her lace gown. As for Sam, she sat at the end of the table, foot up on her chair, smoking as she drank her beer and relaxed. So far she’d given them nothing.

 

            “As I was saying, we was-“

 

            Alex finished rolling a cigarette and sighed heavily as Kelly scraped a match along the side of the matchbox and lit it for her, the sulfurous smell drifting toward Lena. Exhaling a haze of grey smoke, Alex pointed the cigarette at Sam, a hard look in her brown eyes.

 

            “Good God, woman, will you get to the point?”

 

            Giving her a grin, leaned back in her chair before she rocked forward, reaching for her beer. “Why, Sheriff, are you in a rush?”

 

            Lena yanked her sheathed knife out and stabbed it down into the scarred wood of the table, in between Sam’s hand and her mug of beer, without even looking. Andrea and Brainy startled slightly and Kara’s eyes widened a fraction as Lena caught her stare. 

 

            Feeling uncomfortable, exhausted and in dire need of a bath, Lena’s muttered words were tense and frosty. “We’re all in a rush and my patience wears thin. I’ve been on the road for days and I’d quite like a bath, so if you don’t mind …”

 

            Jerking her knife back out of the wood, Lena roughly sheathed it and turned to look at Sam. Her expression was mild, yet pointed, and she reached for her own beer as the other Necromancer narrowed her eyes.

 

            “That brother of yours knows about the mine reopening,” she revealed after a minute of tense silence.

 

            Lena stiffened and set her mug back down, giving Sam a sharp look. Climbing to her feet, chair scraping against the floor, Lena bristled with anger as she clenched her teeth together, itching to pull her gun from its holster as she loomed over the other woman.

 

            “Did you not want to mention that before?” Lena snarled.

 

            There was a ripple of panic and unease in the group, glances exchanged and shoulders tensing as if they expected Lex to sweep through with his shambling army of corpses and skeletons at any moment and shoot them all dead and make off with their gold. 

 

            “I needed my leverage,” Sam cordially replied.

 

            Pulling her pistol free, Lena dug the tip of the Colt into Sam’s dusty cheek as she pulled back the hammer, leaning in close. “How’s this for leverage; you tell me everything, right fucking now , and I won’t blow a hole through your pretty face.”

 

            Across from her, Kara scowled slightly at her words and picked up her beer, burying her face in her mug. No one moved and Sam let out a quiet, shuddering laugh as she raised both hands defensively.

 

            “Easy, girl, that’s all I know. I told you the rest, anyhow. Heard that bit of gossip on a town he’d ransacked on my way up north, so I got to thinkin’ that if they was knowin’ it and telling me, they sure as hell would’ve told him . Especially on accounts of them not having a nice bullet in that head of theirs. Don’t you reckon?”

 

            “What else?” Lena softly demanded, a flat look in her green eyes that must have been threatening enough to convince Sam that she was being serious.

 

            “That’s all. I swear it on my medallion. Now, I don’t know if he knows you’re here, but if I was you, and I had a brother like that putting bounties on my head and the like, I’d get the hell out of town. Hell, I’d get on a ship and go as far as it’d take me.”

 

            Scoffing, Lena spun the gun on her finger and jammed it back into the holster. “Well, fortunately for the good people of Midvale, I’m not a coward.”

 

            She eased herself back down onto her seat and glanced sideways at Alex, who was smoking with a thoughtful look on her face. Looking around at everyone, Lena felt a stab of guilt as her eyelids scraped painfully across her dry eyes as she blinked, aching for sleep. Running a hand over her face, she sighed heavily, feeling the grit of dust and sand on her fingertips.

 

            “He’ll know it’s not open yet,” Andrea said after a moment, haughty and insistent. “We shouldn’t expect him here until the mine is open.”

 

            “Then we could just keep it closed,” Kara said, hands splayed on the table as she shrugged, blue eyes wide and innocent.

 

            Brainy hummed doubtfully, “the mine is the sole profitable aspect of Midvale. We’ve struggled these past months since the accident, and to leave it closed indefinitely would enact mass migration to more populous mining towns. Without the mine … why, I imagine Midvale will be a town of starving and destitute folk who couldn’t pack up and leave. Resources would dwindle, the soldiers would leave - although, I admit to some benefits in that regard - and, why, this very hotel would become a place of empty rooms and empty tables.”

 

            They all took the word of the banker very seriously, and given that the town had come to a deal with Andrea for partial ownership of the mine, neither the heiress nor the Mayor were likely to lose the money they were investing in trying to get it up and running again. There was no Midvale without a mine to offer employment, to keep the small economy flowing with a constant turnover of visitors passing through and deliveries coming by way of the rail car. 

 

            Closing her eyes, Lena breathed slowly and tried to puzzle out what the plan was. Growing up in the grand house of her family, Lena had played chess often, and her brother had been particularly fond of it when he stopped by, taking a vested interest in her education before she’d been sent off to learn the art of raising the dead. He’d likened everything to a game of chess, the logic and strategy of it a crucial lesson for Lena to learn, to which she proved a masterful student. She could almost see the puzzle of the game he was playing, with his grand schemes and dreams of grandeur for himself.

 

            “Doc, what do you reckon?” Alex asked, outing her cigarette. “We ain’t heard your piece yet, and we all know’s you know him better than us.”

 

            Lena’s lip curled as she opened her eyes, a derisive look of contempt crumpling her face. Heaving a sigh as her shoulders slumped, Lena rubbed at her cheek, flakes of old blood falling as she swallowed thickly.

 

            “He needs to be stopped at all costs. He’s a deranged nihilist who’ll bring us to unimaginable horrors. He wants to tear down the order of things, of my kind, even if it kills millions in the process.”

 

            “So, what do you think we should do?” asked Kelly, brown eyes pleading, the fate of her town and her people on the line and her in charge of them all.

 

            Mouth thinning, Lena deliberated for a moment as she tried to parse through the tangled web of too many options.

 

            “Spend too long watching the short game and the long game will kill you,” she muttered, a frown creasing her brow. Her voice was dulled with more than exhaustion. “I caution … not to be hasty. Closing the mine might only hasten our demise here, with what few soldiers and able-bodied fighters leaving for better prospects. I fear it’s too short-sighted to assume he’ll pass us by if we retire from our efforts to start mining for gold again.”

 

            “So, you’re saying we should … do nothing?” Alex asked, disbelief and scorn in her voice as she scowled at Lena.

 

            Rolling her eyes, she sighed softly, calm and thoughtful as she usually was, considering things from all angles as she chose her words carefully.

 

            “No, Sheriff, but I don’t pretend to be an expert in the matter of warfare. I don’t usually hold to making corpses; I usually just bring them back. Any experience I might have with killing … it’ll not help you against the posse he’ll bring with you.”

 

            Alex arched an eyebrow at J’onn, “any ideas, General?”

 

            Blinking in surprise as she looked at the hotelier, Lena gave him an appeasing once-over. Somehow, it made sense that this quiet, observant man had been at war, had been good enough to be a General, and she felt a flicker of respect inside as she watched him think for a moment, falling back into his old profession.

 

            “We’ll need outriders to scout the surrounding prairies. The mountains will be good for watching the northern passes; we’ll have a clear view of the land for miles. We should also consider fences for the town; two ways in and out at either end of the Main Street. Perhaps trenches to stop the dead if they try to breach the wall and barricades that we can put into place at night. We can post a night watch for any trouble. I’d also suggest anyone outside of town moves in for the time being, for safety.”

 

            “My ranch-“ Kara started to protest.

 

            “Damnit, Kara, you can get new horses,” Alex interrupted her, exasperated. “They’ll be fine; he ain’t after a few unbroken fillies now, is he?”

 

            Lena wrinkled her nose slightly but refrained from mentioning that her brother would willingly take all of Kara’s horses, whether to replace some of his own that had rotted through too badly to keep being revived or to sell for a pretty profit someplace else.

 

            “I can’t just up and leave now, can I? What if someone steals in and takes all my things while I ain’t there?”

 

            “Now what’ve you got that’s so important you can’t replace it?”

 

            Mouth thinning as she looked down at her lap, fiddling with her fingers as she wanted to curse herself for her poor foresight, Lena listened to the sisters bicker. It was a few minutes of back and forth before Kara relented and agreed that she’d spend every night at Alex and Kelly’s place while working the ranch during the day when the risk was lower.

 

            “Now, what’re we to do about this one?” Alex asked, gesturing to Sam. “I don’t like the thought of two Necromancers in town. Folks’ll be after my head if they catch wind of this.”

 

            Sam let out a bark of laughter, “don’t mind me, Sheriff. I got a daughter to get home to, and I don’t quite fancy stayin’ here myself with what’s comin’.”

 

            “Well, I won’t cause no fuss tonight on account of you bringing us word, but you rest up and be on your way, you hear?”

 

            “All I need is a bed and something hot to eat and I’ll be gone ‘fore sunup.”

 

            Nodding curtly, Alex donned her hat and pulled down the bottom of her waistcoat. “I better go see about startin’ on these defences then.”

 

            Lena drained her beer and climbed to her feet. “I’ll help.”

 

            Holding up a hand, Alex wrinkled her nose and gave Lena a look of revulsion. “No offence, Doc, but if I get downwind of you once more, you ain’t gonna like what comes up. I ‘ppreciate the enthusiasm, but you need a bath first and a good night’s sleep; you look like one of them dead you’ve brung back. And thanks for takin’ care of my shirt.”

 

            Lips curling wryly, she nodded and their little party dissolved. Andrea stopped her on the way to the kitchens, inviting her to dine with her for dinner tomorrow night, which didn’t seem much like an invitation as she stood in her finery, deep blue dress making her eyes piercing as she commanded her to be there. It was the last thing Lena wanted to do, but she imagined she should be flattered that a lady would wish to dine with her, especially when that invitation was extended to her as she stood splattered with gore.

 

            They parted ways and Lena stepped into the doorway of the kitchen and doffed her hat, giving M’gann an apologetic smile. She watched the other woman’s eyes widen as she cursed and crossed herself.

 

            “What in the good holy hell have you been up to, Doc?”

 

            “I apologise for imposing on you, but I was hoping you might afford me the luxury of a bath. You know, on account of my appearance.”

 

            “That husband of mine is going to get a talking to later,” M’gann clicked her tongue. “Gossiping with the townsfolk while he lets a Witch Doctor sit there looking like she just murdered someone while she frightens off good paying customers.”

 

            “Forgive me.”

 

            “Tub’s out back in the building next to the stables; you can pump the water and I’ll have Nia bring it out once it’s boiled.”

 

            Thanking her, Lena walked out the back door, feet thundering down the steps and her boots sinking into the still damp earth of the narrow alleyway. She could hear the sound of horses shifting in the stables and ducked inside to check on Hecate, who had been given a rub down and oats, looking content, before making her way next door.

 

            It was a storage shed, barrels of beer and clay jugs of whisky in the dim space, and Lena lit a lamp before shifting the tin tub from its hiding spot. A few chickens were clicking around in there, their nests in the coop tucked away in the corner, and she grabbed a metal bucket and made her way out to the water pump to fill it.

 

            It took her the better part of twenty minutes to get the tub half-filled with cold well water while the first bucket load was brought to a boil inside. Nia brought it out afterwards and upended it into the tub of cold water, making it pleasantly warm, but only just, leaving her with a towel and some soap.

 

            Thanking her, Lena shut herself into the shed and stripped off, easing herself into the warm water as dust immediately started rising from her pale skin. Scrubbing herself hard to get the caked-on blood off, Lena was pink from the abrasive soap by the time she felt clean enough to get out. The water was brownish and considerably colder but she felt marginally better. She had to dress in her ruined clothes though and emptied the tub bucket by bucket into the muddy gutter dug along the back of the hotel.

 

            Making her way back inside, holding her hat with her grimoire, gun and bullets and bag of teeth inside it as her wet hair hung around her shoulders, she made her way back inside. M’gann gave her a small smile, patting the wooden table.

 

            “You look better. Sit; you must be starving. I doubt you ate well on the road.”

 

            “Indeed I didn’t,” Lena said with a shy smile, “your cooking was sorely missed, ma’am.”

 

            Snorting, M’gann gave her a reproving look, “those fine manners of yours will only get you so far. But, as it is, you’re a right sight politer than most that come through here. And maybe that owes a little extra kindness.”

 

            She stirred sugar into a cup of lemonade and cut Lena a large slice of a rabbit pie and set it down before her. The food was heavenly and it was all Lena could do to slowly eat it, knife and fork primly poised over her plate. 

 

            “Do you like it here?” Lena asked M’gann after a long pause, the woman humming as she laboured over her recipes.

 

            Glancing over her shoulder, M’gann smiled and nodded. “I do. I’m a lady of my own establishment; I make my own rules and make a nice profit. I had my doubts when J’onn brought me out here, but we have a nice home.”

 

            Nodding, Lena took a sip of lemonade. Giving her a curious look, M’gann cocked her head to the side. “And what about you? Do you like what you do?”

 

            Grimacing, Lena shrugged half-heartedly. “Like is perhaps the wrong word. I don’t know anything else but this career - it’s been in my family for generations - and I was raised to it. I enjoy reuniting loved ones, although, more often than not, my job is that of an executioner for the walking dead and a gravedigger for their final resting place. Would that I could save more of them, but it’s a fickle magic that only gives so much in exchange for life.”

 

            “Can I ask you a question?” At Lena’s hum, M’gann smiled faintly, confused. “You were a wealthy lady before this-“

 

            “I would have been,” Lena interrupted, her expression clouding. “I was too young to have any sort of social status when I was sent away for my training.”

 

            “But if you’d stayed back East, you would have been rich, part of high society. Why I bet you would’ve married a rich man. Most of your kind usually find themselves a nice family to stay on with and make a pretty penny.”

 

            Lena gave her a crooked smile, “I didn’t much like the idea of being a servant for one family, healing a bout of consumption or a broken finger. I didn’t much like the idea of anyone’s company, to be completely honest.”

           

            “Ah, well, that hasn’t much worked out for you, has it?”

 

            Giving her a wry smile, Lena finished her meal and then rolled up the sleeves of her ruined shirt and washed up, scrubbing the sink full of pots and pans and then excusing herself. She carried her piled hat with her worn duster slung over her arm and made her way to the warped staircase. They groaned quietly in the lull of the afternoon, only a few patrons filling the saloon as they drank away the day and kept to themselves, two old men playing cards and a woman smoking as she rolled another cigarette near the sunlight pouring in through a window overlooking the street.

 

            Making her way up to her room, Lena unlocked the door. Her room was mostly the same as it had been when she’d left, although tidied up with the made bedsheets and a fresh pitcher of water near the empty basin. Lena crossed over to her belongings that had been brought upstairs, depositing her hat and coat on the table beside the bags. 

 

            Turning to the bed, her shoulders slumped and she eagerly kicked off her boots and tumbled onto the mattress. Her eyelids were already closing and she was in no rush to open them again for the rest of the day, her body sinking into the soft mattress with relief. She didn’t think she’d ever been so comfortable and couldn’t even be bothered to change - not that she had a change of clothes - before she fell asleep and slept through dinner and all through the night.

 

            She rose before dawn and made her way downstairs, hat tugged down low over her face, her coat looking a little shabby, and her gun strapped on as she dared not venture outside unarmed these days. Standing on the wooden verandah of the hotel, the pale pink dusk creeping in, she found Sam getting ready to depart.

 

            “So, you’re stickin’ around then?” Sam called out as she tightened the straps of the saddlebags filled with supplies she must have bought from the general goods store the day before. 

 

            “There’s nowhere else to go,” Lena said as a crooked smile curled her lips. “And I made someone a promise.”

 

            Snorting, Sam shook her head as Lena walked down the steps and watched her climb up into the saddle. She fiddled with the reins and shifted in the saddle, getting comfortable, before tugging the brim of her had down low and pulling up her neckerchief to cover the lower half of her face, leaving hazel eyes creased at the corners as she gave Lena a bewildered stare.

 

            “You should take my advice and be more cowardly,” Sam gravely warned her, looking down upon her from up in the saddle. “And at the very least, get some help. You ain’t gonna hold the horde off alone; you’re only one woman.”

 

            “Ah, but I’m not just any woman,” Lena murmured, a faint smile on her lips. “I was raised to play this game.”

 

            “And what game is that, exactly?”

           

            “Chess.”

 

            Snorting, Sam shook her head. “You’re perhaps the biggest fool I ever had the misfortune of meeting, but it’ll be a real shame to lose you from our numbers. I hope your spirit finds some rest on the other side.”

 

            “I’ll find no rest until I’ve put him in the ground.”

 

            “Then good luck to you, sister.”

 

            “I hope this is the last time we meet,” Lena said with a sniff, not entirely fond of the woman. Although she had saved Lena’s life this time instead of shooting her, which was an improvement.

 

            “Oh, I don’t doubt it. If I come back this way, I’ll bury the bodies for you.”

 

            Lena quietly scoffed and shook her head, a spark of mirth in her eyes. “How generous.”

 

            Giving her a thin smile, Sam tugged the brim of her hat down low over her face and pulled back on the reins, her horse stepping backwards as the Wight hound obediently stayed at her side. Without another word, the Witch Doctor rode out of town and Lena felt the faintest twinge of regret; maybe it would have been better to ask for help, but she was a solitary creature and didn’t much like the thought of one of her kin around.

 

            Going on her way, Lena busied herself with taking stock of things. She had no experience in true warfare, but she was a fair hand at strategy and had been prone to finding herself in the middle of skirmishes at times - usually, two warring Necromancers who’d staked out territory in the barren western states she sometimes passed through, siding with one of them and helping to fight a host of undead and claim the neighbouring territory before she went on her way with safe passage. It would be a bigger scale when her brother came, a few Necromancers of his own banding together with cowboys who had no one else to tag along with and came in handy with a gun, even if they didn’t have the training to bring back the dead. She expected a few dozen of the truly alive and several hundred of the dead at the most - perhaps even a thousand of them if his rogues had enough skill to manage it.

 

            Walking the perimeter of the town, Lena imagined the wall and trenches and tried to puzzle through which buildings could be left outside and which inside. Would it be better to provide some shelter outside, so they could hide behind it and pick off any approaching dead? Or should they keep them within the boundaries so no one could use the buildings to jump over the wall and infiltrate the town? What was abundantly clear to her as she stopped by the white clapboard church and the rows of freshly dug graves by her own hands - well, powers used by her hands - was that her brother couldn’t get his hands on the dead buried there.

 

            Once the sun was truly up, she made her way back to the hotel and ate breakfast in the empty saloon, coffee waking her up as she ate her way through the large breakfast M’gann had made for her. She joined Lena, eating her own portion, and Lena found that she was perhaps warming to the people of Midvale - or at the very least, she’d spent enough time in close proximity to those that mattered that they no longer viewed her as a threat. They didn’t speak much though, and Lena thanked her and washed the dishes once more, finding herself with too much time on her hands for her liking. She didn’t like to be idle, but until they’d decided on what course of action to take, she wasn’t in a rush to get the mine reopened immediately.

 

            Afterwards, she stepped back out and checked on Hecate before making her way towards the Sheriff's office and doffing her hate as she stepped inside. A drunken soldier was snoring in a cell and Alex was reading the newspaper while she crunched pork rinds with her boots on her desk.

 

            “Do you ever get any work done in here?” Lena asked as she shut the door behind herself.

 

            Lowering the newspaper and her feet, Alex scowled at her. “I’m takin’ a well-deserved break, I thank you, Doc.”

 

            “Oh,” Lena hummed with quiet amusement, taking the chair before Alex’s desk and sitting up straight.

 

            “You here to return my shirt?” Alex asked, holding out the cheesecloth with the pork rinds, which Lena politely declined while rolling her eyes.

 

            “I fear your shirt isn’t long for this world, Sheriff. I’ll be sure to buy you a new one out of my wages.”

 

            Giving her a wary look, Alex’s mouth thinned. “You ain’t here for that now, are you? Cause I ain’t got the money, and if you’re leavin’ again-“

 

            “No, no,” Lena interrupted, “I’m here to strategise.”

 

            “Strategise?”

 

            “For the town’s defences.”

 

            Alex blinked in surprise and straightened up, brushing crumbs off her desk as she leaned forward. 

 

            “Oh, alright then. What’re you thinkin’?”

 

            “We might have to make a smaller perimeter. Do you think any of the outer buildings would be useful as coverage for any fighters we have outside the walls?”

 

            “Maybe. Depends on if we have anyone to fight now, don’t it? What else?”

 

            Lena was silent for a long moment, shifting uncomfortably before she cleared her throat. Her face was stiff and her eyes piercing when she replied.

 

            “We’ll need to make sure the cemetery is within the boundaries of the wall. I know it’ll make for extra work but if he gets his hands on those bodies, it’s an extra few hundred for his army, and … well, we’ll need those ourselves.”

 

            “Hold on a second now, Doc,” Alex slowly said, piecing things together.

 

            “Sheriff, I understand this is a more personal matter for you-“

 

            “We ain’t about to start digging up the dead-“

 

            “Be that as it may, unless you wish for the rest of the town to join them in their own graves, it’s a necessary evil.”

           

            “Disturbin’ their final rest ain’t holy.”

 

            “It’s the only defence I’ll have-“

 

            Their voices overlapped as they cut off each other’s reasonings and Lena winced slightly as she tried to press her case. Tugging at the next of her shirt, she grimaced, uncomfortable with having to ask to violate the final resting place of many familiar loved ones in the town.

 

            Alex shot to her feet, raking a hand through her hair as she grit her teeth, pacing behind her desk. She thumbed her suspenders and scuffed a boot along the floor, sucking the inside of her cheek.

 

            “It’s sacrilege. You know it ain’t right.”

 

            “It’s not about right or wrong; it’s about survival.”

 

            “Folks won’t stand to see familiar faces being used as shields.”

 

            “I think perhaps they’d like death even less,” Lena curtly replied, reaching for Alex’s tobacco and rolling paper on the desk and setting about distracting herself. “It’s the way of my Order; we take death from the ground and pour life back into those still above it. It’s only natural.”

 

            Scoffing as she watched Lena deftly roll a cigarette and light it from the matchbox on the desk, the hiss of it lighting punctuating her words, Alex braced herself against the edge of the desk as she leaned towards her.

 

            “Natural? There ain’t nothin’ fucking natural about that, Doc. I don’t care if it’ll save our asses - it is not natural.”

 

            “What you think is irrelevant,” Lena coolly replied, taking a drag of the cigarette and exhaling the smoke as she handed the cigarette across to Alex, who plucked it from her fingers and scowled as she put it between her lips. “If you don’t want me to use my powers to help, then why am I staying here?”

 

            “Hell, I thought- well, I thought you might bring us back. And I seen you with a gun, so …”

 

            Lena snorted and arched an eyebrow, a sardonic smile curling her mouth. “Alex, he’s not going to stand by and let me revive everyone. He’s not here for a fucking conversation. The second he gets you with one of his bone bullets, that’s it. I can’t bring anyone back from that. It’s what we use to put the dead down for good. Our best bet is to let me use the graveyard and do what I can, and even that won’t be enough.”

 

            “But them fancy powers of yours … I thought you’d just take control of his skeletons and turn ‘em on him.”

 

            “That’s not how it works,” Lena exasperatedly explained with a heavy sigh. “One can overpower the other and take their dead from them, but only if they’re stronger. I couldn’t take them all on - not when he’s bringing a small army with multiple Necromancers to aid him.”

 

            “So is there no hope?”

 

            “Hope is for children and those who believe God is going to save them,” Lena snapped. “You don’t strike me as a fool who believes in hope. You do, however, strike me as someone who wants to save her wife and her sister, and I mean to help you do that if you’ll let me.”

 

            Collapsing back onto her chair and scowling as she sucked in a lungful of smoke and passed the stub of a cigarette back across to Lena, Alex held it for a moment. Waiting patiently as Alex slowly exhaled a haze of grey, looking grim and exhausted, Lena smoked the rest of it and outed it in the ashtray before raising her eyebrows.

 

            “That’s a mighty low blow to use my sister like that,” Alex muttered, a resentful look in her brown eyes. “And Kelly. Hell, you’re one manipulative woman, Doc, and I’ll be glad to see the end of you, but … alright. I’ll let you use the cemetery.”

 

            “Thank you,” Lena said, breathless with relief. “I promise to lay them all to rest once I’m done.”

 

            Giving her a reserved look, mouth turning down at the corners, Alex shook her head. “Just … make sure you put them all back in the right spot, alright? My Pa, God rest his soul, is out there with the lot of ‘em and he best be right back where we put him when you’re done with him, you hear?”

 

            “Don’t worry,” Lena solemnly replied, “it’s a constituent of our profession to treat the dead with the utmost respect.”

 

            After a moment, Alex hummed dubiously. “What else?”

 

            Lena spent the rest of her morning there, Alex dragging out maps while they tried to cobble together some semblance of a plan to enact at their next meeting. Lunchtime came and went as they worked and it was only when Alex complained about being hungry that Lena realised she should leave her to her lunch and her job.

 

            They made plans to reconvene tomorrow and hash out some more ideas at the hotel, roping in J’onn and Kelly, as well as Brainy to crunch the numbers for them with his books from the bank. Feeling woefully unprepared and a little stressed at the prospect of her brother sweeping through the town and massacring everyone before they scrabbled together some defences, Lena briskly walked across the street to the hotel.

 

            Lost in her thoughts as she made for the stairs, hoping to shed some layers before joining the later patrons enjoying lunch, she was oblivious to anything else around her. Gripping the bannister, she hauled herself up the stairs and ran a hand through her hair as she held her hat in her other hand, turning over the possibilities of her brother’s plan.

 

            As she stepped onto the landing that circled the interior of the upstairs, Lena caught sight of someone leaning against the carved balustrade. Her steps slowed and she pressed her lips together, her stomach swooping slightly. 

 

            Kara looked up and smiled softly, pushing off the balustrade and wringing her hands nervously before her. “Hi there.”

 

            “Good afternoon, miss,” Lena murmured, feeling shy and uncertain as she stepped in closer, fishing her keys out of her pocket. “Can I invite you in?”

 

            Some of the nervous tension in Kara’s shoulders bled away at the invitation and she nodded eagerly, stepping forward as Lena unlocked the warped wooden door and shouldered it open. Turning, she watched Kara step inside, dust motes swirling through the shafts of sunlight spilling in through cloudy windows. There was an intense look in Kara’s eyes, her face stiff with worry, and her voice was hoarse when she spoke.

 

            “You’re alright?”

 

            Giving her a thin smile, Lena nodded but that wasn’t convincing enough for Kara. She crossed the space between them with sudden urgency and grabbed the blood-soaked collar of Lena’s borrowed shirt, jerking it aside as her blue eyes trained on the place where she expected to see a deep knife wound, worthy of so much blood. 

 

            Instead, there was only the smooth, unmarred skin of Lena’s shoulder. Kara couldn’t help touching it, spreading her palm over the place where the stab wound had been as she exhaled sharply, her blue eyes softening as the hard worry vanished. There was no mark, no scar – Lena had nothing to show for the violence that had been done to her. She never had anything to show for it, no matter what she endured.

 

            Letting out a strained laugh, Kara removed her hand, cheeks pink as she looked down. “I know I shouldn’t be surprised, but I thought- well, I’m glad you ain’t hurt. I mean, you was hurt, I know that, but … I’m glad you’re safe.”

 

            Lena bit back a smile, tasting blood from the effort it took to keep her expression impassive, and she swallowed thickly. “I’m glad to be back.”

 

            “Growing fond of us, huh?” Kara asked, pink-cheeked as she twisted her hat in her hands. 

 

            “Perhaps,” Lena coyly replied, looking down at the worn tabletop as she pressed her palm against it. 

 

            “You look tired.”

 

            Looking up, Lena gave her a weary smile, “too much trouble on the road to stop.”

 

            “You ought to consider a new career path, Doc. I still don’t quite know what it is that brung you out here to the dust and plains; ain’t you ever thought about a nice house and balls and pretty dresses?”

 

            Cocking her head to the side, Lena gave her a searching look. “Is that what you dream of?”

 

            “Me? Shoot, no, ain’t nothin’ for me but horses and guns and nights at the saloon, but … there’s something mighty fine about you, and I ain’t clever enough to see what it is that you get from being up to your elbows in blood and death.”

 

            “Ah, well, I have the pleasure of reuniting people with their loved ones, on occasion.”

 

            Quietly scoffing, Kara raised her eyebrows as she crossed her arms over her chest, wrinkled shirt sleeves rolled up to reveal bare forearms corded with muscle. “Don’t tell me you’re all sentimental about death, now. I know you better than that.”

 

            “Do you?” Lena shot back, her eyes mystified and her faint smile goading as she arched an eyebrow. “Is there a more comforting thought than having one’s dear departed close at hand? Being able to reunite the lost with the living? Death loses its sting, its permanence, and life acquires a lesser value and not quite as much meaning. No longer is there a before and an after, but an unending constant.”

 

            “And I bet you think that life ought to have more value and meaning now, I reckon.”

 

            Dragging out a chair, Lena sank down onto it and gestured for Kara to take a seat at the table, their encounter leading to more thoughtful conversation than she’d anticipated. But Kara was right; Lena thought that to bring someone back too many times was to disrupt the natural order of things - if no one died and more were born, that would inevitably cause socio-economic collapse, and was one of the lessons she’d had to learn in her training and had caused her to deny any offers of permanent employment with one such rich family looking to live on forever. Kara was more perceptive than she gave her credit for.

 

            “I do believe so, yes. Would we cherish life more to know that we only had one chance? Would we try to enjoy more experiences, knowing we had limited time to enjoy them?”

 

            “Ah, I think you’re right there, Doc, but the folks that can afford to pay for your services usually don’t give a damn, if it means they get to live for longer. They get rich and live forever while the poor folk die in the gutters from things even a common doctor could’ve saved ‘em from if they’d had the coin. Frankly, some of your kind only exist to give the rich more time to get richer. Ain’t that the sorry truth.”

 

            “You just opened the door on the darkness of the human soul,” Lena said with a rueful smile. “People will do anything for money.”

 

            “Not you though.”

 

            A flicker of slow surprise crossed Lena’s face and she propped her chin up in her hand. “Oh? How have you come to that conclusion?”

 

            Giving her a wry grin, Kara leaned back, “you surely can’t care about money when that pretty voice of yours speaks of a hell of a lot of it, enough to buy you a fancy education ‘fore you trained for this. And since you been here, there’s been more talk of what kind of lady you must’ve been. But here you are, same as the rest of us, covered in blood without two pennies to rub together; if you cared about money, you’d be decked out in finery in a big home back east, eating fine food and drinking champagne from France.”

 

            “I’ll let you in on a little secret - champagne isn’t all it’s cracked up to be.”

 

            Kara let out a loud laugh, tipping her head back as her eyes creased at the corners, “well, I’d still like to try it.”

 

            “Once this is all over, perhaps I’ll stop by again and bring a bottle for you.”

 

            Shaking her head, Kara smiled grimly, her cheek dimpling, “this ain’t the kind of place to drink something so fine.”

 

            Leaning in closer, Lena’s face softened and there was a warmth in her chest. “Then, I shall have to take you with me and buy you a fine dress and take you to a ball so you can try it while you listen to music and dance with New York’s finest.”

 

            Wrinkling her nose, Kara grinned as she flushed with delight, “ah, you’re teasing now, Doc.”

 

            “I’m not known to tease,” Lena murmured, a thoughtful look creasing her brow. “Although, I do wonder how my mother would react to me bringing someone like you back with me.”

 

            “Someone like me? Why I feel I should be offended.”

 

            “Not at all, I mean it as a compliment,” Lena quickly assured her, feeling her cheeks warm with a blush at how forward she was.

 

            “Oh. How’s that?”

 

            Mouth opening and closing, Lena let out a strained laugh and looked down at her lap. “I find you … warm . It’s not often I encounter people who treat me with anything but disdain, and while the good people of Midvale have been more welcoming than most, I find … you are a beacon of sunshine in this sorry hole.”

 

            “Doc, if you go on saying such fine things to a lady, I might begin to think you might actually care for me.”

 

            Lena clicked her tongue and let out a scoff of laughter, replying quickly before she could stop herself from being so honest. “Of course I care for you.”

 

            Kara’s teasing smile died on her lips as Lena stiffened, a lump closing up her throat. She pushed her chair away from the table and turned, pausing before walking over to one of the windows overlooking Main Street. Shoulders stiff, she gripped the chipped edge of the windowsill and peered through the warped yellow glass, waving away the irritating fly as it buzzed around her face.

 

            “Things could be worse,” Kara lightly said after a moment of thick silence.

 

            “Yes, I’m intimately familiar with that thought,” Lena muttered as her stomach twisted.

 

            Loathing, shame, and anger rushed through her as a series of escalating internal temperatures, and she pressed her cool hand to her brow, closing her eyes. The anger, when it finally came, was a relief. It was the cleanest and hottest of the emotions; it scoured her of everything else that might have lingered. As much as everyone else hated her, she hated herself even more, and yet she had stubbornly refused to die, out of no choice of her own, but now that she might actually die, she found it rather troubling to think she would die alongside someone she’d grudgingly come to care for. 

 

            And all Lena could think of was how she should have killed her brother when she’d had the chance, that white-hot anger inside her making her head pound as her knuckles whitened on the windowsill. Would she have been afforded the luxury of lingering, indulging in getting to know this rancher who’d caught her unaware and by surprise, or if the threat of the town’s demise hadn’t hung over them would she have even bothered to stay longer than it had taken to heal from Sam’s gunshot wound?

 

            “Why are you so afraid of letting someone in?” Kara quietly asked when Lena didn’t elaborate.

 

            She almost didn’t expect a response then either, but Lena glanced down at the floor instead of turning to look at her, drawing in a rattling breath. “I … I’m afraid to be an imposition.”

 

            Kara’s chair legs scraped on the floor and her boots thudded across the floorboards as she closed the gap between them. Her palm was warm through the cotton of Lena’s dirty shirt and she could feel the ridges of the Necromancer’s spine and the knots in her muscles. 

 

            “Impose on me,” she whispered.

 

            “You don’t know what you’re asking for.”

 

            “You’re a fickle one, Doc. One second you’re talkin’ about taking me to a ball and now … well, here we are again with you pushin’ me away again like you don’t give a damn.”

 

            Lena’s mouth twitched and she ducked her head, still feeling Kara’s hand pressed between her shoulder blades. 

 

            “This only ends two ways, and neither of them is good for us.”

 

            “And you’re content with livin’ in danger your whole life?”

 

            Quietly laughing, Lena pressed her lips into a hard line and was silent for a moment. “I’ll let you in on a little secret; sometimes, when someone lives in danger for too long, the only time they feel alive is when death’s breathing over their shoulder.”

 

            “Then you must be feelin’ quite alive right now.”

 

            Turning slowly, Lena gave her a long, searching look and swallowed thickly. Kara’s blue eyes were clouded and brooding and it brought a small smile to Lena’s lips as she reached out and tweaked her chin, laughing softly. It was a rare laugh and Kara’s frustration melted slightly.

 

            “Ma’am, I do believe I am, but for once in my life, it’s not from the danger.”

 

            “I-“

 

            Lena cut her off with a swift kiss, closing her eyes as she felt the warmth of Kara’s chapped lips beneath her own, reaching up to cup her cheek as she exhaled, shoulders dropping. And Kara melted into the kiss as well, her fingertips warm as they gently brushed Lena’s cheek.  As she kissed her slowly, luxuriating in the novelty of it, Lena was struck by the thought that it was the kind of kiss she could have lived for. The kind of kiss worth dying for. And she might at that yet, to keep Kara safe.

10. Chapter 10

            The sky was dark beyond the curtained hotel room and the air was close, the rumpled blankets strewn across Lena’s waist, leaving the rest of her bare as she propped herself up on her side. Her dark hair splayed over the pillows and there was a rather grave look on her face as she stared down at Kara, who lay on her stomach.

 

            Lena had struck a match and lit a lantern a short while ago when the dusk had started to blur the shapes of things. The glass on it was tinted yellow, and it varnished the room in warm amber tones, turning Kara’s skin golden as she lay silently. 

 

            They’d been content to silence for a while, but Lena’s thoughts weighed heavily on her mind, almost tangible as it blanketed them. Eventually, Kara couldn’t hold her tongue.

 

            “What’re you thinkin’ so hard about?”

 

            Letting out a heavy sigh, Lena pursed her lips faintly and reached out to brush Kara’s unbound hair off her back. She was silent for a moment, thoughtful.

 

            “I didn’t imagine I would ever say this but you ought to listen to your sister,” Lena murmured as she idly stroked her fingers over the expanse of Kara’s back.

 

            “Well, Doc, that is a surprising sentence. Now, what exactly should I be listenin’ to her about?”

 

            Snorting, Lena’s trailing touch stilled and she rolled onto her back, swiping her thumb and finger across her eyelids as she listened to the sound of the fiddle and piano drifting upstairs from the saloon. Raucous laughter and voices were muffled but the floorboards shuddered faintly.

 

            “You know what it is I speak of. You should move into the town proper; it’ll be safer for you.”

 

            “And leave all my horses? No, thank you, ma’am.”

 

            Pushing herself up onto her elbows, Lena let out a huff as Kara opened her eyes, eyelashes fluttering as she blinked. Rolling onto her back as well, she stretched her arms widely.

 

            “Forget the horses, Kara,” Lena muttered with frustration, her voice tense with concern. “Or better yet, stable them in town and let us use them as a defence. Forty on horseback will do better than forty on foot against an army of the dead.”

 

            “They’re not even broken yet. I can’t bring forty wild horses here and keep them in a stable.”

 

            Pushing herself up, Lena scowled, “whether or not they’ve been broken is irrelevant; your safety is paramount here. But if you care so much for them, I shall continue to break them while I’m here.”

 

            “Won’t you be busy with the mine?”

 

            “The mine’s reopening will be delayed, as discussed. And if it convinces you to stay in town, then I’ll prioritise the horses.”

 

            “It’s all a little much, don’t you think? And ain’t we expecting your brother to come down from the north? I’d surely be safe in my ranch on the opposite side of town.”

 

            “Why are you so opposed to the idea of being kept safe?” Lena bitingly asked.

 

            Blinking in surprise as she sat up, looking young and naïve as her eyes widened at Lena’s reproachful tone and her cheeks coloured slightly, Kara frowned. 

 

            “I’m opposed to the idea of being told what to do. By you and my meddling sister. Now, I admit it’s a shock you both see eye to eye on this, and I should be so flattered that you can admit you care enough about my well-being, but I ain’t some damsel. I might not be a mighty fine shooter like yourself but I know my way around a rifle damn fine, Doc.”

 

            Scoffing, Lena threw back the rumpled bedsheets and climbed out of bed, her scarred back taut with annoyance. Stooping down, she fished her pants from the floor and started dressing.

 

            “Well, I’ll be glad to know you had the skill to take down three of the undead before you were dragged from your home and had a bullet put between your eyes. That’ll be some comfort to offer your sister when I tell her I can’t bring you back while we’re holed up behind our walls here.”

 

            “I ain’t asking you to do what you can’t. If that’s the case-“

 

            “You’re being foolish. Is your opinion of yourself so high that you’ll get yourself killed to go against a reasonable command?”

 

            “Well, I see now that your opinion of me isn’t that high.”

 

            Shooting her a contemptuous look, Lena pulled on her coat and buckled her gun around her waist. Snatching up her keys, she waved dismissively in Kara’s direction as she stalked towards the door.

 

            “You can see yourself out once you’ve dressed.”

 

            “Aw, come on, you can’t be mad like that.”

 

            That only caused to make Lena rankle, gritting her teeth as she yanked the door open, Kara softly swearing from the bed before she called after her. “Lena.”

 

            Shutting the door behind herself, Lena tucked her keys in the pocket of her duster and raked a hand through her hair, hastily starting to plait it as she made her way downstairs. Bristling and hard with anger as her flat gaze scanned the room, she made for the batwing doors leading out to the mild night. She was cut off before she reached them by another meddling Danvers.

 

            “Where are you off to in a hurry?” Alex drawled.

 

            “For a walk. To clear my head.”

 

            “You seen my sister 'round here?”

 

            Lena stiffened slightly, a muscle twitching in her jaw as her eyes strayed up to the mezzanine. “She’s dressing.”

 

            “Ah. And she’d be the cause of your frustration, I imagine?”

 

            Lips twitching with a hint of a wry smile, Lena looked at Alex, green eyes bright with a spark of anger. “It would seem to run in the family, Sheriff. If you’ll excuse me.”

 

            Pushing past her, Lena stepped outside, the wooden planks groaning underfoot as she strode across the verandah and down the steps. Making right, she walked down the dark street, sidestepping patches of churned mud and stagnant brown puddles, drunken shouts and laughter spilling out of streets leading off the main thoroughfare, where the less reputable gambling dens, saloons and brothels were situated. 

 

            Feeling restless, Lena stalked through the streets with an eye for strategy, noting places that would offer a good defence, a sloped roof that would be good for shooting from, a place to hide a few townsfolk. She might not have been much in the way of a soldier, planning for large battles, but Lena had grown up as a Necromancer, riding through towns and learning how to fight in duels, looking for any advantages - cover to work a spell, patches of land that had a higher chance of preserving bodies - and knew the things that would slow the dead.

 

            With the plans to build a wall encircling the town, the main street through the centre would be the spot they needed to defend the most, and with the way Lena saw the churned up street turn into a muddy mess when it rained, she knew the logical choice would be to flood it and let the mud slow down the dead. That would require more water than she imagined they could get from the wells on short notice upon invasion and she was thoughtful as she walked. That house there would be a solid safe house for people, while that shack near the outskirts would be flattened beneath a horde of skeletons, as flimsy as it was.

 

            She walked the perimeter of the town, pausing near the church and cemetery set just beyond the confines of the town proper and letting her magic flow into the ground. Midvale was a relatively new town in comparison to what she’d travelled through in the eastern states, built for the sole purpose of the mine, yet there was a surprising number of dead buried near the church - not all of them from the mine collapse, and not all of them neatly contained in the rows of headstones, predating the creation of the cemetery by decades if her magic was accurate in its assessment of bone density and depth. It was more than she could accurately handle, but even throwing the dead at her brother in a desperate attempt to keep him occupied while she tried to think of a way to save this inconsequential town was better than nothing.

 

            Ducking down a dark side street, the hour growing late and her stomach rumbling with hunger, Lena tried to skirt past a group of soldiers sitting on upturned crates and barrels, the group of them rowdy and drunk outside of the gambling den. She could only imagine how much they’d had to drink with little else to do stationed out in the middle of nowhere, and she didn’t go undetected in her recognisable coat. 

 

            “Look who we have here,” one of them called out, sounding smug and pleased, and not quite as drunk as the others.

 

            Lena’s eyes slid over to him as she walked past with her hands in her pockets, and there was a flicker of recognition there. She remembered him from before, his hatred for her and his soldiers gathered around as he spewed vitriol in the middle of the street. Lockwood.

 

            “Word 'round here is that you’re to thank for the dead coming upon us.”

 

            “No, sir,” Lena brittly replied, “but I’ll be to thank when you come out of it alive.”

 

            He was tall as he loomed over her, the smell of whiskey enveloping him in a sour cloud as he narrowed his eyes, his carved cheekbones making his face seem sunken in the dark. His mouth curled in a sneer and his dark eyes shone in the lamplight spilling out of a grimy window and Lena’s hand itched to ease her Colt from its holster. She could feel the malice but wasn’t keen on starting a shoot out in the middle of the street at night; she was a dead shot, even blindfolded, but there were too many people about. She could heal injuries, but she would rather save herself the headache.

 

            “I’ve crossed paths with your kind before. The only thing I’ll thank you for is finding a nice home for my bullet.”

 

            A ghost of a smile graced Lena’s lips and there was a serene feeling spreading through her chest. She’d been here before, a hundred times, the fear, the anger, the blame. All of it laid upon her as if she embodied the entirety of her Order. Sure, she’d known some who took advantage of their training and abilities, running in the same crowd as her brother, committing unspeakable crimes with the dead at their command, but she knew plenty more who laboured over their trade, digging graves in New York so the streets and graveyards didn’t overflow, who fixed bones quicker than a doctor, even if it cost a lot more, who would stand there bleeding from their mouths and nose and eyes as they brought back as many dead as possible after carriage accidents and fires, working with flesh sloughing off bones and mangled corpses. They were the ones who endured the horrors of the world and painstakingly tried to stitch it back together as carefully as possible. But none of his anger was new.

 

            “Don’t stand there smiling at me you twisted bitch,” he snarled, reaching out to grab her arm in a vice-like grip. “There ain’t no Sheriff around now to protect you. No one here will breathe a word if I put you down like a stray dog in the gutter.”

 

            “If you can,” Lena murmured, steel in her soft voice.

 

            He laughed, the sound rough and surprised, a gleam in his eyes, “you don’t frighten me.”

 

            Lena paused, her eyes roaming over his face as she tried to glean the truth from his expression. The hollowed-out cheeks, the dark eyes, the drunken state and dishevelled appearance, this exiled soldier who hated her more than he feared her. Her face softened minutely.

 

            “Who did you lose? Who did they fail to bring back for you?”

 

            A snarl tore from him as he lashed out and wrapped a hand around her neck. “Stay out of my head.”

 

            “It’s written on your face,” she whispered, reaching up to touch a pale cheek, slightly sunburned from standing guard outside.

 

            He flinched away from her, his expression darkening as his fingers tightened. She swallowed thickly beneath his touch, her lips turning down faintly at the corners in a grimace. Truthfully, she pitied him, although she’d never lost anyone she’d cared about, had never cared about anyone to begin with.

 

            “Let go,” she softly ordered him.

 

            Face twisting with anger, he tightened his grip further and Lena suppressed a sigh, a flicker of regret welling up inside. Not a violent person by nature, Lena hated confrontation unless necessary, but she wouldn’t allow someone to intimidate her, no matter how much she pitied them. Her fingers curled around the cuff of her coat sleeve, the sting of the hidden blade skimming her fingertips as she dug it in deep enough to draw blood. 

 

            As he bore down on her, the other soldiers jeering and laughing as they smoked and drank near the wall of the gambling den, Lena snagged a tooth from the pouch on her belt and rolled it in the quickly drying blood on her fingertips. She could feel the spark of bones nearby and summoned it forward, an arm scrabbling up through rain-softened mud to grab the ankle of the man choking her and pull his drunken form off balance.

 

            Unfortunately, he fell forward, slipping in the mud and bowling Lena over in the process. She landed on her back, fist instinctively curling around the smoking tooth, some subconscious part of her brain trained to keep ahold of it like a lifeline, knowing that it was the difference between life and death at times. As his hand painfully drove into her stomach, Lena groaned and curled on her side as she kept the skeleton coming, dragging itself bit by bit from the earth.

 

            It spooked a few soldiers as it came forth, yellowed bones clotted with black earth, and they scrambled over their feet in their haste to make themselves scarce. Lockwood pushed himself off her and drew a knife, slashing at Lena’s throat and managing a thin line against the pale expanse of it as the skeleton yanked him back by the collar of his coat at the last second.

 

            Grabbing another tooth as it started to rain lightly on her, Lena touched the shallow cut on her throat and coated the canine with blood before calling forth another nearby skeleton. There were panicked shouts now, and a woman screamed as she stepped out of a saloon opposite and saw the undead, this one a little fresher with leathery skin covering it in patches, along with the rags of its clothes. 

 

            Scrambling to her feet, Lena drew her revolver and pointed it in the air, firing off a warning shot before she glared at the handful of remaining soldiers. Her skeletons walked around her in a shambling circle of defence, empty eye sockets leering at the onlookers, jaws with missing teeth clacking in an eerie manner that made one man look like he was about to keel over. He did a moment later, before a woman dressed in uniform with her rifle pointed at Lena lowered the gun and slunk back into the shadows.

 

            “Captain,” one of the men said, tugging on Lockwood’s sleeve to make the drunk man leave, and Lena watched as bitter resignation crossed his face. 

 

            She let the teeth in her palms burn to ashes and the skeletons stop, swaying unsteadily on their feet. Fixing Lockwood with a hard stare, she watched him hesitate, and as she busied herself with holstering her gun, he lashed out and punched her squarely in the face. As the other soldier forcefully dragged him away this time, Lena cupped her hands around her broken nose and cursed as blood spilt over her chin and from her busted lips. Around her, her skeletons collapsed to piles of bones and Lena folded a moment later, pitching forward into the mud as her vision dimmed and the pain crept in.

 

            Laying in the middle of the road as her vision swam and the pain of drawing on her power, with the pain and suffering that came with using the dead, from taking from someone else in exchange for what her magic offered, Lena breathed in the damp smell of dirt as the rain pattered onto the filthy back of her coat. Cheek pressed into the mud, she breathed through bloody lips as people watched from alleyways and doorways without lifting a finger to help. The white-hot pain of her broken nose made her feel nauseous, her skin a sickly pallor in the dark, and after a few minutes of foggy consciousness, she passed out amidst the bones of the old skeletons.

 

            When she woke, it was considerably drier and Lena was comfortable. Her fingers were searching for her gun, for her knife or teeth, before she’d even fully regained consciousness, so aware of the change in her surroundings. Blinking as the grey of the room arranged itself into the shapes of furniture, a banked fire burning a dim red amidst the coals, Lena frowned. It wasn’t her room at the hotel, nor the jail or Kara’s ranch, and the furniture didn’t look as fine as that of the Mayor’s house. That was the sum of her interior knowledge of Midvale, which begged the question where was she?

 

            Sitting up, Lena ran a hand over her face and winced as pain blossomed on her face and her eyes shuttered as her hand fluttered around her nose. It was definitely broken but she didn’t have a tooth in the vicinity so it would have to wait, in favour of her safety.

 

            Swinging her legs out of bed, they hit worn wooden planks which groaned as she stood, the room pitching slightly. Lena thought she might have a slight concussion but it was nothing she couldn’t fix with a tonic and some blood. Catching her bearings, she shuffled towards the door a moment later and opened it, finding herself staring at a short hallway with stairs at the left end.

 

            Making her way to the top of the staircase, she frowned and gripped the polished wood of the bannister and walked downstairs. Feeling bare and vulnerable without her gun, Lena was wary as she rounded the end of the staircase and stepped into the open doorway of an open kitchen.

 

            Kara was sitting at a table, peeling potatoes while a lit stove behind her held a bubbling kettle of water. She looked up at Lena’s arrival and gave her a tentative smile. Lena’s eyes fell onto her clean and patched up coat hanging over the back of a chair, her belt with its numerous attachments neatly folded on the tabletop.

 

            “Mornin’,” Kara softly murmured in greeting.

 

            “I- what …”

 

            “Querl Dox found you lying in the street and fetched Alex. Some girl said it was Lockwood.”

 

            Grumbling under her breath, Lena touched the stinging slice across her neck, feeling the thin bandage wrapped around her throat. Grimacing, she ran a hand through her unbound hair and resisted the urge to wrinkle her nose.

 

            “Why was you wanderin’ all alone so late?” Kara sighed, “you know what folk here are like. They don’t all mean well; you could’ve died.”

 

            Clenching her jaw, Lena’s lips twitched with dissatisfaction. “I didn’t want it to be one of them. It would’ve caused an uproar that wouldn’t have benefited anyone. And I’ve told you before that a bone bullet would kill for good, so I wouldn’t have been able to bring them back either. I … hoped to de-escalate the situation.”

 

            Snorting, Kara gave her a fearful look, setting down the small knife and dumping a potato into the growing pile in the pot. Crossing her arms over her chest, Kara pursed her lips.

 

            “You don’t de-escalate with men like Lockwood. He’s bad news, I tell you. You’re lucky he didn’t slit your throat good and clean.”

 

            Lena let out a quiet scoff of laughter. “He’s lucky that I showed restraint. Nothing more than smoke and mirrors to frighten them off.”

 

            “Smoke and mirrors? You was found with bones around you; Alex nearly had a fit when she saw it.”

 

            “Then it’s fortunate for me that I have an ally in the good Sheriff,” Lena drawled.

 

            Clicking her tongue, Kara shook her head. “Why’re you bein’ like this? You ain’t that foolish or reckless.”

 

            “No, indeed, I leave the part of the fool up to you,” Lena murmured, a faint pout forcing the corners of her mouth down.

 

            Loosing a long, gentle sigh, Kara gave her a grim look. “Are you really so mad at me?”

 

            Freezing for a moment, Lena took a slow step closer, and then another, looking nonchalant as she closed the gap between them. Standing over Kara, she frowned slightly, a solemn look clouding her face, and reached out to cup Kara’s chin in her calloused hand.

 

            “Furious,” she murmured, letting out a quiet huff of laughter as she gave Kara’s chin a gentle, affectionate squeeze.

 

            Reaching up to encircle her wrist with her hand, Kara stared at her with wide blue eyes, mournful and meek. “And what if I’m furious at you?”

 

            “I’m used to inspiring such feelings in people,” Lena shrugged indifferently. “Although not usually born from concern.”

 

            “It’s not concern that makes me so darn mad,” Kara muttered ducking her head down as her cheeks heated and Lena’s hand was left to fall limply back at her side. “Well, not only.”

 

            Lena didn’t reply, turning away slightly and letting her attention wander around the room. The kettle was boiling properly now, a plume of steam hissing from it, and she took in the neat patchwork curtains covering the window overlooking the street beyond.

 

            “Where am I?” she asked after a long minute of silence.

 

            “My Ma’s house.”

 

            Lena’s face furrowed with confusion, which only made her broken nose hurt, the pain blossoming on her face and bringing stinging tears to her eyes. “You have a mother?”

 

            “Don’t everyone?”

 

            “Very amusing,” Lena muttered, blinking rapidly, her teeth aching in her pounding head as she rubbed at her forehead. “You’ve never mentioned her before.”

 

            “Ain’t been no cause before.”

 

            Resisting the urge to roll her eyes, Lena moved toward the table and fished out a tooth, using the hidden razor in the coat cuff to cut her fingertip. She moved over to the sheet of polished metal serving as a mirror and looked at her reflection, healing herself slowly as she straightened her nose in the process, making sure it healed straight. It was agonising and she thought she might crack a tooth as she knitted her face back together, not bothering with the small cuts and scrapes, a waste of the energy it would drain to heal them.

 

            Wriggling her nose as she finished, Lena felt the dull ache of lingering pain but was otherwise satisfied and set about removing the bandage from her throat. Balling it on the table, she dragged out a chair and took a seat, watching as Kara quickly finished off the remaining potatoes and then climbed to her feet.

 

            She made tea for them both and Lena was watching her fill her cup when she heard the front door open. Turning slightly in her seat, shoulders taut and stiff, she watched as a blonde woman entered, looking frazzled and in a rush, and then watched her pause as she took in the sight of Lena sitting at the kitchen table.

 

            Slowly rising to her feet, Lena faced the woman with a reserved look on her face as Kara stood as well. “This is Eliza Danvers,” Kara introduced her. “And this is Miss Lena Luthor.”

 

            “Yes, the Witch Doctor,” Eliza replied, her blue eyes trained on Lena. Her tone held no fear or judgement.

 

            “Pleased to meet your acquaintance, ma’am,” Lena murmured, wishing she had her hat in her hands to twist the brim. Instead, she clenched her hands into fists at her sides.

 

            Eliza ignored her as she stepped forward, blinking as a small look of awe crossed her face. Lena drew back slightly as Kara’s mother came closer but she didn’t quite step back and froze as Eliza reached out, unafraid, to cup Lena’s chin, tilting her head side to side.

 

            “Well, ain’t that something? Perfectly healed.”

 

            Kara looked wary as she drifted closer, unsure of how Lena would react to her mother’s forwardness, but Eliza withdrew her hand a moment later and Lena’s lips twitched, her eyes unreadable. Shaking herself out of her amazement, Eliza smiled slightly, stepping back towards the door.

 

            “I can’t stay; the baby’s close to coming. I just need more rags.”

 

            Eliza was already out in the hallway as she spoke and Lena looked over at Kara, a perplexed look on her face. “The baby?”

 

            “She’s something of a healer too, usually helping deliver children for the women in town. Not quite a doctor but I thought it’d be safer to bring you here.”

 

            Hurrying back the way she’d come, rags bundled up in a woven basket in her arms, Eliza hesitated and looked at Lena. “I’m glad to finally meet you and sorry I can’t stay longer.”

 

            “Thank you for your kindness,” Lena murmured, still standing. “I hope you’ll forgive the intrusion, ma’am.”

 

            Giving her a small smile, Eliza nodded. “You ought to come round here for supper one night. ‘Specially now that Kara’s comin’ to stay here for a while.”

 

            Lena hesitated and then glanced over her shoulder to find Kara busying herself with the potato peels, gathering them into a pot to throw on the decomposing pile of scraps for the garden. Turning back to Eliza, Lena gave her a wan smile and nodded.

 

            “I’d like that. Thank you.”

 

            “Kara, make sure you lock up if you’re leavin’,” Eliza said to her before she made a swift exit, leaving the two women alone in the kitchen.

 

            Sinking back down onto her chair, Lena’s eyes tracked Kara’s movements across the kitchen before she spoke. 

 

            “You look like her,” Lena murmured.

 

            Kara let out a quick laugh, her eyes creasing at the corners as she grinned as if Lena had told her a funny joke. She didn’t wait to clue her in on her amusement as she wiped her hands and dragged her chair back out and sat. 

 

            “Funny that, seeing as I’m adopted.”

 

            Lena’s stomach dropped. “You never mentioned that either.”

 

            “Weren’t no cause for that either. She’s my Ma, plain and simple.”

 

            Taking a sip of her tea, the heat making the cuts inside her mouth sting, Lena’s mouth twitched at the corners. Kara stared at her, bathed orange by the light of the stove, and tried to piece together the furrowed look on her lover’s face.

 

            “Why does that look like it bothers you?”

 

            “It doesn’t.”

 

            Choking on a laugh, Kara wrinkled her nose as she smiled slightly. “Yes, it does.”

 

            “I’m adopted too, is all. In a sense.”

 

            Leaning forward as surprise crossed her face, Kara blinked. “Really?”

 

            “My Papa wasn’t a good man, nor a faithful one, which is how I came to be. My Mama has always resented raising a child that wasn’t her own, which is why she sent me away to train at such a young age. We were never close, and we don’t see much of each other.”

 

            The admission made Lena feel restless as she shifted in her seat, the weight of what she’d divulged not lost on her. It wasn’t something she’d ever shared with anyone. Lena didn’t have friends, only acquaintances or family, and so she’d never revealed that to anyone and felt rather unbalanced by her forthright honesty. How to explain Lillian to someone who didn’t know her mother?

 

            “I- well, that’s-“

 

            “I’d prefer not to talk about my mother,” Lena murmured, raising her cup of tea to her lips again.

 

            Kara nodded and sipped her own tea, her blue eyes frequently glancing back over at Lena. Setting her cup back down, Lena ran a finger over the grain of the wood and swallowed, keeping her eyes down.

 

            “You’re staying in town?”

 

            “I- that is … you were right, to an extent; it’d be foolish to not stay where we can protect each other. And I’d hate for you to think so poorly of me, now, Doc.”

 

            Lips twitching with a small smile as a glow of warmth spread through her, that not of frustration and worry loosening in her chest, Lena looked up. 

 

            “I could never think such a thing of you. I only grew frustrated because I- because I-“

 

            Cutting off, Lena pressed her lips into a flat line, her brow furrowing with a clouded look as she struggled. Clearing her throat, she opened and closed her mouth and gave up as Kara let out a quiet laugh. Looking up, Lena’s frown deepened as Kara’s face softened, eyes creasing at the corners.

 

            “Good Lord, is it such a struggle, Doc?”

 

            “Yes, it is,” Lena whispered, feeling her cheeks warm. “I’m not a sentimental sort, nor have I ever been so with anyone else.”

 

            “Well, you’re mighty warm with me.”

 

            “Do you really think so?” Lena quietly snorted.

            

            Laying her hand on the table, palm upturned and fingers reaching, Kara smiled slightly as she nodded. Glancing down at it and then back up, Lena hesitated before slipping her hand into Kara’s and letting out a short laugh, lapsing into a sigh.

 

            “Perhaps I shall be more so with you, and frank at that, once we come through this ordeal unscathed. I’ll even settle for alive , if I must.”

 

            “Then I’ll try my darn best to make sure I survive to hear what it is you have to say to me.”

 

            Her fingers curled around Lena’s and they both remained that way for a prolonged moment, pink-cheeked and shy, before Lena pulled her hand back and picked up her teacup.

 

            “You needn’t worry,” Lena insisted, “I’ll make sure no harm comes to you.”

 

            “That ain’t a promise you can make. ‘Specially not if you find yourself in harm’s way.”

 

            “I can promise it and I will,” Lena haughtily replied, setting her cup down firmly as a muscle twitched in her jaw. She swallowed thickly, raising her chin and fixing Kara with a piercing stare. 

 

            A smile creased Kara’s face as she propped her chin up in her hand, early morning sunlight painting her golden. She looked soft and sweet and Lena had the urge to kiss her, alongside a pang of fear that she couldn’t protect her from what was coming.

 

            “Is that right? And how’re you managing that, Doc?”

 

            “If I must, by any means, I’ll come back from the dead for you.”

11. Chapter 11

            Exhaustion seemed to be a permanent state for Lena as the days crept past and work began around town. The trench started as a shallow ditch, dry dirt and sand crumbling as a few soldiers and townsfolk started shovelling it out, and it became a wide hole beyond where a hasty wall was being erected, hands blistered and full of splinters as trees were felled from the nearby mountains and repurposed from collapsing huts. The whole thing was a flimsy, shambling mess and Lena didn’t think they’d manage a deep ditch or fortified walls around the entire town before trouble descended upon them.

 

            Still, she was up before dawn, hitching Hecate to the wagon she’d commandeered for her mine work, ordering skeletons found out in the wild to fell trees, to push the piles of dirt up against the base of the snaking wall to shore it up, adding some support. She worked harder than everyone else, whose fears weren’t enough to fuel them, ignorant to just how brutal her brother was, but she knew and she was up before dawn and home nearing midnight every day as she worked and worked and worked.

 

            The only time she saw Kara was when she insisted on jumping up in front of the wagon and accompanying her to chop trees, or standing beside her in the deepening trench, side by side shifting earth until they were filthy and tired. There was something to be said for watching Kara roll the sleeves of her cotton shirt up and work beneath the sun, tanned and forearms corded with muscle from years working the ranch. Lena would sneak glances at her and watch, not even realising she’d stopped what she was doing, the skeletons stilling as blood ran down her face until she burned through the teeth clutched in her fists and bones clattered to the ground, the magic binding them together undone.
