            However demanding Kara’s work was, Lena’s was positively gruelling, and she was grateful the rancher was with her, helping her up onto the wagon, wiping her bloody nose and cheeks with a damp rag, making sure she ate and drank enough and steering the wagon back into town as Lena dozed, swaying with the jolting motion through the rutted tracks. Lena would leave her back in town once it started getting dark out and return to her work alone.

 

            Kelly and Alex had been the driving force behind getting the townsfolk and soldiers to pitch in, all of the people who hadn’t left with the mine closure, but were lacking any other work without the mine, finding themselves digging or chopping or fixing tools and making food. It was slow progress and there weren’t enough people around to help speed things up, but at least they were trying. J’onn watched over them all with militaristic power, Lockwood trying his hand at stealing back control with his rank, only to be quickly cowed as anyone with common sense ignored him. 

 

            On the rare nights that Lena returned early, borrowed clothes filthy and the pale skin of her hands somewhat reddish where the fresh blood had been rubbed in instead of off, she would find herself in the saloon of the hotel, drinking beer and eating whatever was put in front of her while she conferred with the handful of people who had assumed control. As the Mayor, Kelly was naturally always there, with Querl at her side rattling off figures and budgets, Alex keeping the peace and the law, while J’onn discussed defensive tactics with Lena as they tried to combine his military training with her knowledge of how an army of skeletons and undead could be utilised. 

 

            Kara usually came for company, while Andrea avoided the conversations completely - she’d been scarce and abrupt when anyone managed to get ahold of her, out of her depths as an heiress hoping to strike gold and finding death in her path instead. The mine had been effectively abandoned, for the time being, leaving townsfolk on the verge of starvation if they didn’t resolve things soon. Lena didn’t bother telling them that it wouldn’t matter; they’d either be dead or back in the mine once this all blew over.

 

            “What do you reckon?” Kara asked one evening when Lena had returned early with her and they’d gone upstairs to her room to wash off the dirt and eat in the peace and quiet.

 

            “About what?”

 

            “Do you think we’ll manage?”

 

            Lena didn’t want to lie to her but she didn’t want to give Kara no hope for what was to come. Setting down her cornbread, she sighed softly and rubbed her thumb over an eyelid, hunching forward.  “I think … we’ll do everything we can to hold them back.”

 

            “But will it be enough?”

 

            “It’ll have to.”

 

            It was a glum conviction and she was running low on teeth as she went through her stock with shocking speed, not just in logging and digging but in fixing injuries sustained while everyone else worked too. She had to resort to slyly stealing a pair of pliers and tearing the teeth from skulls she brought forth for work, refilling her pouch and hoping no one questioned why the skeletons were all toothless. 

 

            She grew silent and restless, her exhaustion permanently weighing her down. Kara hovered around her, her nervousness evident, her touches gentle and fleeting reassurances even as she let Lena dwell in her brooding moods. If they did talk, it was mostly Kara regaling her with stories about her childhood in the town, of summers spent picking apples and shooting wild turkeys, learning how to rope a horse and bake bread. 

 

            It was vastly different to the cramped and fetid childhood of Lena’s, half of it spent in graveyards and around bloated dead bodies as she learned the theoretical side of her practice and then the physical side. The earlier years were lost to dim memories of a switch rapped against her knuckles during etiquette lessons, days spent learning to sew and sketch wildflowers and herbs, all intended to prepare her to be shipped off to be trained as soon as she was eligible. Her mother had been cold and unfeeling and the thought of her teaching Lena to bake an apple pie and letting her run free through New York was laughable.

 

            It didn’t stop her from imagining what it would have been like, enjoying a childhood free from the responsibility and fear of raising the dead. Witch Doctors were more common on the East Coast but it didn’t mean they weren’t feared as equally as respected by the upper crust of society, keeping them youthful and healthy while being shunned from the presence of the very people who filled their pockets the moment their services had been rendered. Lena was glad to have left it as soon as possible, trading the cramped cities for open fields and mountains, seeking the childhood that Kara had experienced as she made herself useful whenever possible.

 

            “You should take a day off,” Kara said to her on Tuesday night, walking over to where Lena was sitting at the table, the hour passing midnight as the orange glow of the fire bathed the Witch Doctor’s haggard face in its light.

 

            Kara set a small glass of the bottle of wine they were sharing down before Lena, standing behind her chair and ducking down to press a kiss to the pale skin of her bare shoulder. Blinking and shifting slightly, Lena turned her head as she reached for the glass, taking a sip, the wine thick from the tannins.

 

            “There’s too much work to do.”

 

            “Running yourself into the ground ain’t going to help no one. Least of all you. My Ma told me to ask if you wanted to come for Sunday lunch after church. Course, I ain’t expecting you to go to church but it might do you a bit of good to take a day off and eat a proper meal. I know M’gann’s none too pleased with you leaving her food untouched - and she takes a lot of pride in her cooking, so …”

 

            Tilting her head back, Lena gave her a thin smile, eyelashes fluttering as she closed her eyes. Reaching for Kara’s arm, warm and soft beneath her callouses as she gently smoothed her fingers over her skin, Lena exhaled softly, almost a sigh.

 

            “If it’ll make you happy then I’ll come for Sunday lunch. But I’ll not waste the day; there’s too much to be done as it is.”

 

            Humming dubiously as she considered it, Kara nodded. “Fine, how ‘bout you work the mornin’ and then take the afternoon off. Maybe have a proper bath.”

 

            Making a quiet choking sound, Lena arched an eyebrow. “Are you saying I smell?”

 

            Wrinkling her nose slightly, Kara gave her a sheepish look. “Of blood. You always smell like it a little, but these days it’s like you’re a walkin’ corpse with all of it dried on you like that.”

 

            “I’ll be fresh as a daisy on Sunday,” Lena promised, rubbing at her forehead as a headache blossomed behind her eyes.

 

            “You ought to rest now, Doc.”

 

            “I don’t imagine I will.”

 

            “Would you if I stayed?“

 

            Dropping her hand, Lena gave her another suggestive look. “That depends on the manner of your stay.”

 

            “My intentions are innocent, I promise,” Kara impishly grinned, reaching out to cup Lena’s cheek and stroke her thumb over her sharp cheekbone, which had become more prominent over the past couple of weeks. “I know you ain’t been sleeping well.”

 

            Feigning nonchalance, Lena took a sip of her wine and stared at the fire. “And how do you know that?”

 

            “Cause I ain’t blind,” Kara murmured, her fingertips straying up to the dark circles beneath Lena’s eyes. “Is it nightmares?”

 

            Turning her head aside and ducking it down to let her dark hair hang between them, Lena’s lips twitched regretfully. “It’s nothing for you to fret about.”

 

            “But I will.”

 

            “Well, you shouldn’t,” Lena shot back, head rising and wine glass touching her lips before she knocked it back and swallowed the mouthful.

 

            Slowly sinking to her knees beside the chair, Kara looked up at her with deep concern etched onto her face. Her fingers dug into the rough cotton of the skirt Lena was wearing and she tried to catch Lena’s eyes.

 

            “Tell me about them.”

 

            With a resigned sigh, Lena closed her eyes and leaned her head back against the chair, gripping the arms of it as she felt her pulse jump at her jugular. The fire was warm on the bare skin of her chest and she could feel how damp her hair was at the nape of her neck.

 

            “Oh, they’re all much the same,” she dismissively replied. “I die. Over and over. They’re not so much nightmares but memories.”

 

            “Lena-“

 

            She picked up Kara’s hand and turned it, pressing a light kiss to the inside of her wrist and gave her a tired smile.

 

            “Come. Let’s sleep.”

 

            Lena climbed to her feet and untasted her skirt, letting it puddle to the floor before Kara stopped her, hand on her shoulder and a panicked edge to her searching gaze. She didn’t speak for a moment and Lena stared at her expectantly.

 

            “You don’t have to hide it from me.”

 

            “I know,” Lena said, fleetingly pressing a hand to her cheek. “It’s not my intent. Once you’ve been killed once, it’s all much the same.”

 

            She was blasé about it but there was a hollowness to her stare that didn’t go unnoticed by Kara. Truthfully, Lena was often troubled by the memories of what she’d endured at her brother’s hands, but death was the least troubling. He’d killed her, yes, many times over, and brought her back in perfect health, but it was what came before that plagued her and weighed heavily in her memories.

 

            Lex had always been one for games; part of Lena’s training had been spent on long days trekking across rough terrains answering his riddles and philosophical questions and listening as he waxed on about dilemmas and impasses and how he’d solve them with her superior intellect. He was a learned man and prided himself on being so much cleverer than anyone else. Nothing angered him more than Lena’s failures, which he deemed weak, and above that, her triumphs, outsmarting him to his embarrassment.

 

            The punishments were always severe and she could remember the feeling of bullets pummelling into her. Sometimes the pain would last hours, her teeth, her grimoire, her razors and knives taken from her so she couldn’t heal herself. They’d make camp and he’d sit beside the fire, eating as if nothing was amiss, while his sister languished in agony, her own blood pooling beneath her as her breaths turned laboured and shallow and her skin took on a deathly hue. Sometimes she’d slip away from the blood loss, other times if he was feeling particularly vindictive, it would be a painful death where he’d shoot her multiple times in soft places that weren’t immediately lethal. If he was impatient and irritable, she’d get a swift death, a bullet right through her brow, the split-second agony of her skull shattering before her brains were splattered across the desert or mountain they were one staying with her long after he’d brought her back.

 

            Sometimes Lex would torment her with talk of her final death. This would be it, this one. He’d palm a bone bullet with a plain iron one and make her believe that she was going to die for good this time for her failure, her hubris, her smugness. She believed him too, a part of her relieved that she might be free of his games, but he never used a bone bullet, kept a separate rifle loaded with them and an ordinary pistol holstered at his waist. He’d sometimes leave her dead as long as he could before she was almost out of his reach, and she’d come to a while later, moved from the spot of her death after being flung over the back of her horse and led onwards. 

 

            His mercurial moods were terrifying, to say the least, and Lena didn’t know how to explain to Kara how afraid she was. Not that he’d target her - she’d long since gotten used to that feeling of pain, of fear of death, even gotten used to the prickling discomfort of burdening herself with the pain of the dead every day - but that he would know she cared for Kara, that he’d pluck it straight from her blood and make Lena watch as he brutalised her instead. He would know her deepest feelings from just one glance.

 

            Squeezing her eyes shut, Lena shook her head for a moment and then walked over to the bed, climbing onto it and worming her way under the blankets. Kara climbed in beside her, sitting up as she shed her shirt and dropped it to the floor where the rest of her clothes lay. Burrowing into a pillow, Lena stilled at the feeling of a warm arm thrown across her back and closed her eyes, slowly relaxing and allowing herself the secret thought that she could get used to that.

 

            The week passed by in a blur, the town bisected by a wall that encircled the church and graveyard, the moat deeper and almost connecting, sharpened stakes pounded into the ground. With a couple of hundred warm bodies and a few skeletons in Lena’s retinue, which she kept away from the main body of the townsfolk. She would usually use them for logging and then once the townsfolk and soldiers had finished for the day, take them to town and oversee them as they shovelled dirt aside with hands by moonlight, the usual sounds of revelry greeting her from outside the walls.

 

            By the time Sunday came around, she was relieved for an excuse to take a break from work without the guilt of knowing that some of these people would die unless she devoted as much time as possible to the task. Lena knew the ragged pace she was setting herself wasn’t feasible and she slept late on Sunday morning, well past dawn, before she got to work with some manual labour, shovelling with her own hands and adding the dirt to the growing piles heaped against the bottom of the fence, making a slippery slope that would make it hard for anyone to scale the walls, let alone skeletons and rotting corpses.

 

            Still, Lena woke that morning with cold dread coiling in her stomach, leaving her staring at the ceiling for a while as she tried to make sense of it. The sheets had scratched at her skin and exacerbated the terrible prickling that had spread across her body, the sense of foreboding leaving her uneasy long into the morning as she ruminated over it, slamming the heel of her boot down on the shovel and working a clod of damp earth free with a pensive look on her face.

 

            It wasn’t often such feelings came to her with such an overwhelming warning but she knew not to ignore them when they did. The last time she’d been filled with that sensation that something was off on such a gut-deep instinct she’d been trekking through the Appalachians and the forest had gone silent. A rogue Necromancer had slaughtered a small town and was using the bodies to ransack the place and target travellers and it was only the result of being well-tuned into her surroundings and herself that had allowed Lena to put a bullet in him and cut the strings of his power before the dead could overwhelm her.

 

            She set her concerns aside but was on guard all day, the web of her power cast wide around her as she kept tabs on anything moving around her. By the time she finished up, all was still and it was a cloudless Sunday and Lena dusted off her dirty hands as she walked through the deserted streets.

 

            Most of the town was at church and Lena made her way around the back of the hotel, ducking her head into the kitchen to find Nia taking a break, sewing on the back step of the kitchen as a narrow shaft of sunlight illuminated the alley. She gave Lena a small smile, her deft fingers pulling the needle through the cotton.

 

            “You’ll be needing a bath, I suppose.”

 

            “That would be welcome. Thank you.”

 

            Waving a hand in the general direction of the shed with the tub, Nia pushed the needle back through. “Help yourself.”

 

            Nodding, Lena went to pump some cold water and lug the buckets back to the kitchen to heat over the fire, hovering uncertainly as she rubbed at her blisters. Eyeing her, Nia cut a thread and shook out the floral shirt she’d mended, satisfied.

 

            “You ain’t wearing that, are you?”

 

            “Pardon me?”

 

            “To lunch.”

 

            “How do you know what my lunch plans are?”

 

            “Small town and friends gossip. You’ll want to do better than filthy clothes if you plan to make an impression.”

 

            Mouth opening and closing, Lena paced a few steps in the alleyway, flexing her fingers in an agitated manner.

 

            “I don’t own much. Any clothes I did have were lost to the fire.”

 

            “How about you ask that lady upstairs. She seems fonder of you than I’d expect.”

 

            A flicker of amusement crossed Lena’s face as she smiled thinly at the thought of borrowing one of Andrea Rojas’s expensive dresses. “I haven’t worn a fancy dress since I last had the displeasure of dining with my Mama. I don’t imagine it would agree with me; my skirt will have to do.”

 

            Sighing, the young woman rolled her eyes and climbed to her feet. “Is the art of romance all lost on you, Doc?”

 

            Spluttering as she haughtily raised her chin, Lena grimaced. “Well, romance is hardly to be concerned with here.”

 

            “You’ve been invited for lunch with her family. Kara ain’t one to invite anyone over - well, she is but you ain’t just anyone is my point, you hear?”

 

            “What’ll you have me do? Sew myself a nice new skirt from the upstairs drapes?”

 

            “I don’t imagine you’re good at needlework.”

 

            Bristling, Lena gave her a wolfish smile. “As it happens, I am. Too many years spent sewing bodies up and the like.”

 

            Humming dubiously, Nia sidled over to her and stood shoulder to shoulder with her. “That’ll work.”

 

            “What-“

 

            Lightly tapping her on the shoulder as her mind wandered elsewhere, Nia turned away and gave her a dismissive wave over her shoulder. 

 

            “You take a bath; you smell like a pigsty.”

 

            “How kind to say,” Lena snorted, rolling her eyes.

 

            Fetching her boiling pail of water, she lugged it out to the tub, which she’d already filled with cold water, and poured the steaming bucket in. Once it was pleasantly warm, she shed her filthy clothes and stepped in, dust rising to the surface as it washed off her skin.

 

            The water was quickly brown and Lena was trying to gouge the dirt from beneath her fingernails when the door barged open. She startled, splashing water as she hastily reached for her gun, heart hammering until she realised it was Nia, her arms full.

 

            “Here, scrub yourself with this. Honey’s more pleasant than shit.”

 

            A bar of soap splashed into the water and Lena fished the slippery bar out before working it into the flannel and scrubbing the suds over her skin. She worked the soap into her hair and once she was as clean as she’d get, she climbed out, wrapping herself in a towel to eye the bundle left for her.

 

            One of Nia’s rose-pink shirts with small flowers in the pattern and a dove grey heavy skirt, buttoning at the front. There was a paisley navy neckerchief as well and Lena felt tidier than she thought she’d been in years, the clothes fitting rather well, as judged by the young woman waiting for her in the kitchen.

 

            “Well, now that’s much better, Doc. You’re real pretty when you ain’t covered in blood and walkin’ ‘round everywhere scowling, you know.”

 

            “A by-product of the job, I’m afraid,” Lena said, holding a damp armful of clothes she’d just rinsed off in a bucket of cold water.

 

            “You go in and sit there near the fire while I fix your hair for you.”

 

            “That won’t be necessary.”

 

            “It weren’t a request. Mrs Danvers is a respectable woman in town and you ain’t about to have dinner with her looking all scraggly - even if my clothes do make you look less like a vagrant.”

 

            Suppressing a sigh, Lena dumped her belongings in a pile by the fire and busied herself polishing up her scuffed boots as Nia combed her hair free of snarls and braided it simply down her back. 

 

            “Much improved.”

 

            “Thank you.”

 

            “Go on now, you best be heading off. They’ll be back from church now.”

 

            “Why aren’t you there?” Lena enquired, raising an eyebrow.

 

            Giving her a wry smile, Nia fiddled with the comb in her hand. “Me and the Lord got some things to work out. I imagine you feel the same, else you’d be there too.”

 

            With a quiet laugh, Lena nodded. “It’s not in my beliefs to worship something that isn’t real.”

 

            “You’ll get struck down for that if you say it too loudly,” Nia quipped, her sarcasm making Lena laugh again, louder. “Go on, now.”

 

            Nodding again, she reached for her hat and stopped short of setting it on her head at Nia’s cry of objection. “I didn’t do your hair all nice and tidy for you to muss it, Doc. No hat.”

 

            Sighing, Lena left it on the table and reached for her belt, grimoire, gun and teeth hanging off it, and was cut off by Nia again. “No gun! Heavens, Doc, is that your idea of a parlour trick, raising the dead at lunch for entertainment?”

 

            “It’s for protection.”

 

            “The most you’ll need protecting from is a full belly after eating too much.”

 

            Rolling her eyes, she removed the pouch of teeth and kept that at the very least, reassured that she’d be able to cast her magic if necessary. She donned her coat against Nia’s judgement though and gave the girl a crooked smile as she ducked out the back door.

 

            Setting off through town, feeling clean and tidy and smelling sweetly of the honeyed soap, Lena basked in the warmth and tried not to focus too much on the thought of lunch. Lena wasn’t afraid of much, if anything really, but the idea of sitting down to dine with Kara’s family was an uncomfortable idea, even if she was already familiar with most of them. It was the intent behind it and Lena wasn’t sure she was quite ready for something so meaningful but she was in far too deep to bow out gracefully, and truthfully, she didn’t want to. This was a glimpse of an ordinary life that was just beyond her fingertips and she was fascinated by the idea of it.

 

            She was halfway across town when a wolf whistle sounded behind her and she turned, rolling her eyes at the sight of Alex, wearing clean denim pants and her best shirt beneath a brown waistcoat on accounts of it being Sunday. Her gun belts were still slung around her hips, two pistols holstered, and Lena’s mouth thinned with exasperation as she turned back around.

 

            “Don’t you ever take off the damned coat, Doc?” Alex asked as she fell into step beside Lena.

 

            Glancing over at her, Kelly on the other side, biting back a smile, Lena frowned slightly. “Tool of the trade, Sheriff. It’s got my razors in it; it could be the thing that stands between life and death.”

 

            “Y’all are always so … gloomy. I reckon you spend too much time with the dead; you ought to lighten up a bit.”

 

            With a withering look, Lena rolled her eyes. “We’re on the brink of another war - this time fought by rogue orders of Necromancers against me - and you think I ought to lighten up? I should be off setting traps to slow down the horde, not … sitting down for lunch.”

 

            Alex grabbed Lena’s arm and pulled her to a stop in the middle of the street, pointing a finger at her as her expression turned grave. “Now, this here’s important to Kara, and that’s my Ma you’re dinin’ with, so you best pretend like you’re having the time of your fucking life, you hear me, Doc? They’re both tough ladies but they’re kind, and you’re gonna let them have this one nice lunch, alright? God knows they ain’t had enough of them ‘round here.”

 

            Reaching up, Lena pushed Alex’s hand away and her hard eyes flickered with amusement. “I wouldn’t be doing it if I didn’t know it meant a great deal to your sister. Now, will you stop pestering me so we can arrive on time?”

 

            Nudging her as she let out a scoffing laugh, Alex lurched into motion and Kelly shook her head, looping her arm through Lena’s and leading her along. Feeling awkward at being dragged into the middle of this family and their friends when she’d spent so many years going at it alone, Lena arrived at Eliza’s doorstep sweating beneath her coat tugging at the neckerchief carefully knotted around her neck.

 

            Kara opened the door, all smiles and eagerness. Alex brushed past with Kelly, leaving Lena standing in the shade of the awning, looking small and shockingly meek. At Kara’s softening gaze, Lena rolled her eyes and gave her a crooked grin as she sarcastically greeted her.

 

            “Howdy.”

 

            Snorting, her eyes creasing at the corners with amusement, Kara reached out to snag the leather of her coat. “That’s a terrible accent, Doc. You ought to stick to your airs and graces. Come on.”

 

            Dragging her inside and shutting the door, Kara hesitated as Lena started unbuttoning her coat, pulling it off to reveal her borrowed clothes. A bewildered look of amusement crossed Kara’s face as she gave her a once over.

 

            “What are you wearing? Is that … pink?”

 

            Flushing slightly, Lena’s mouth thinned as she gestured to herself. “Nia.”

 

            “Ah.”

 

            “She was … concerned that I would look like I hadn’t made an effort. Which, quite honestly, I would have,” Lena said with a quiet laugh as she spread her arms.

 

            “You look nice,” Kara said. “All the time, though. I mean … I think you’re real pretty.”

 

            Arching an eyebrow, Lena gave her a cool look of amusement, “I hardly think that’s the truth, ma’am. You’ve seen me covered in blood and worse.”

 

            “It might make you smell like a rotting corpse but it don’t mean you still ain’t pretty. Now, let me take that coat of yours and get you a drink.”

 

            “Oh, I-” Lena said, jamming a hand into one of the bigger pockets inside her coat. “I brought this.”

 

            She thrust the bottle of moonshine out to Kara, who took it with a mild look of surprise. “This from J’onn?”

 

            “Yes. I wasn’t sure what to bring but one mustn’t turn up empty-handed.”

 

            Kara smiled and hung Lena’s coat up before taking her hand, calloused palms rough and familiar, and pulling her into the kitchen where the sound of voices and banging pots filled the space. Eliza greeted her warmly and Alex proclaimed she wasn’t all that bad when Kara set the moonshine down on the table, and in short order they were all sitting around the table, the surface crowded with food.

 

            Lena helped herself to a small portion and wielded her knife and fork with the delicate table manners of one who’d been forced to endure numerous dinners growing up, back straight and her chin never dipping as she brought the fork to her lips. She was silent as she listened to the chatter about gossip overhead at church, the inane mechanisms of small towns going over her head as she enjoyed the food and the opportunity to rest her weary body.

 

            “They’ll be thankful for it in the end, won’t they, Doc?”

 

            Blinking, Lena turned to Kara as a politely inquisitive look crossed her face. “Pardon?”

 

            “I was saying the townsfolk will be thankful for the wall in the end, won’t they? Some of ‘em love to complain about a hard day’s work, but it’ll keep the dead out.”

 

            “I- yes, well … with a bit of luck,” Lena murmured as her brow furrowed.

 

            “She’s a dead shot, Ma, you should see her shoot,” Kara eagerly continued as she praised Lena. “I reckon we’ll be able to hold ‘em off, as long as they don’t get inside .”

 

            Eliza eyed her with a modicum of wariness. “I’ve seen you outside the walls with those skeletons. It’s … surely something.”

 

            Giving her a thin smile, Lena cast her eyes back down to her plate and cut a small piece of beef. “I know it’s an unpleasant reality to be confronted with, ma’am. I don’t pretend to be oblivious to how people view my craft, but I’ll argue that it is necessary at times and can be useful, whatever people may think.”

 

            “And where are you from?”

 

            “New York City, ma’am. At least, I was born and raised there, but I’ve not lived there for quite some time.”

 

            “You sound …”

 

            “Rich?” Alex supplied, arching an eyebrow as she refilled the cups of moonshine, their early afternoon lunch quickly heading towards a night of rowdiness if they continued down a path of drink and chatter.

 

            Eliza laughed softly, “I guess that’s a fair way to put it. What do your parents do?”

 

            “My family … has an established business in the craft. My father was involved in the family business of oil and railways, and my mother was predominantly in healing. I’m sure you well know the path my brother has taken of late. I can assure you, that’s a most unusual manner of practice, but he’s ever been too ambitious for my liking.”

           

            “And you’ve chosen a path of healing as well,” Eliza pressed. “I think that’s admirable.”

 

            “You know Miss Rojas in town?” Kara eagerly piped up. “Lena brought her Pa back one time.”

 

            “Is that right?”

 

            “I’ve brought back a number of people,” Lena murmured, taking a sip of her drink as she shifted beneath the scrutiny. “It just becomes another element of the job after a while.”

 

            As if sensing her unease, Kara swiftly diverted the topic and captured Kelly in conversation about some news read in that week’s paper about flooding in a neighbouring town. Grateful for the opportunity to fade back into the background, only occasionally dragged back in for an opinion on something she didn’t have much of an opinion on. 

 

            After eating, she helped clear away the leftovers, covering the piece of beef with a clean cloth and scraping scraps into Krypto’s bowl as the dog lounged by the fire. She rolled up her sleeves and insisted on scrubbing the dishes, Kara drying them off and putting them away, and once she’d been shooed from the kitchen, she followed Alex outside.

 

            “You seem gloomier than usual, Doc. Everythin’ alright?”

 

            “I … have this feeling,” she haltingly confessed.

 

            “A feeling,” Alex snorted, her eyebrows rising and falling quickly as she put her cigarette between her lips and lit a match, the sulfurous smell enveloping them as the tip turned cherry red. “Well, let’s not get too worked up about that, now.”

 

            Shaking her head as her eyes clouded with worry, Lena folded her arms over her chest. “It’s more than that. I’ve had them before, on occasion, some … sensation that something is amiss. It’s not just usual intuition, it’s more , and I expect we’ll hear news we’d prefer not to before the day is out. Mark my words.”

 

            “Why, you sound like an old harbinger of doom, speaking like that.”

 

            “I don’t find it amusing,” Lena murmured, a shiver wracking her as the day seemed to get colder for a moment. “Have the scouts been reporting back to you?”

 

            “Mhm,” Alex hummed, a stream of grey smoke pouring from her mouth. “Nothing unusual as of yet.”

 

            Mouth turning down at the corners, Lena gave the wooden pillar holding up the roof of the verandah a reassuring pat. “You might want to double it.”

 

            Slipping back inside, Lena stood beside Kara in the kitchen, her fingertips brushing against the back of her hand, and felt the prickling unease quieten for a moment. Looking up, Kara’s gentle face creased with a smile, her cheeks rosy and blue eyes bright with delight as she stared at Lena, who managed a reserved smile in response.

 

            “Do you like sweet potato pie?”

 

            “I’ve never tried it.”

 

            “It’s real good.”

 

            Lena gave her another faint smile and nodded, the pie starting to turn golden in the old oven as it baked. They hovered for a moment before Kara led her through to a small sitting room, a loveseat against one wall, which they squeezed onto, knees touching, while Eliza arranged a tray of tea. The wallpaper was a faded yellow and a small fire was smouldering from that morning and Lena didn’t feel too out of place as she allowed Kara to stir sugar into her tea and add a splash of milk. Cradling her saucer on her knees, Lena politely replied to Eliza’s cautious questions about her life, her plans, and if she liked it in Midvale.

 

            They ate the pie, which Lena had to agree was good, and the afternoon was dragging on towards night by the time she left, earnestly thanking Eliza for inviting her and allowing herself to believe for a brief moment that she would have been pleased for her daughter to end up with someone like her. Lena was well aware that she was far from the ideal partner but she was grateful for the other woman’s welcoming warmth nonetheless.

 

            “I’ll walk you back,” Kara said as Lena donned her coat just inside the door.

 

            “I’m not likely to get lost, you know,” Lena softly snorted. “And your incorrigible sister and her lovely wife will be with me.”

 

            “It ain’t about you getting lost. Maybe I just want to spend a little extra time with you, Doc.”

 

            Lena could stop the smile that twitched her lips as she stepped outside, fixing the collar of her coat and walking down the steps to the dirt road. Kara looped her arm through Lena’s as she happily accompanied her down the street, drawing a few looks, and not all of them kind, and Lena felt her stomach twinge a little at the act of walking arm-in-arm with someone, so simple and ordinary. It was nice.

 

            It was nice all the way back through town, Kara’s hand slipping into Lena’s at some point, the day warm and the sun intending to linger for a while yet as the lazy Sunday dragged on until they were just around the corner from the hotel. Shouts could be heard and Lena’s hair stood on end as she glanced at Kara and the two of them took off running, Alex already in action at the commotion. They breezed by Kelly, whose small heeled shoes weren’t suitable for running through the soft mud of the street, and came to find a pale, trembling man stumbling off the back of his horse as Alex reached him.

 

            “I seen it. I seen it, I’m tellin’ you,” he babbled, ashen and wide-eyed.

 

            “Speak sensibly, man, or I’ll knock it into you,” Alex brusquely demanded, snapping her fingers in his face. “What’re you yellin’ about?”

 

            “He was dead. Walkin’ around like he wasn’t but he was . I swear it.”

 

            Lena went cold as she heard his words, shouted in the street before Alex clapped a hand over his mouth, hissing for him to be quiet as she gripped him by the lapel of his jacket. Alex glanced over at her and Lena hesitated before she quickly crossed the gap to the hotel, boots thudding up the steps as she flung the batwing doors wide open, startling the duo of ladies she breezed past as she anxiously walked to the kitchen.

 

            “You took your time,” Nia noted, scrubbing glasses at the sink as Lena barged in.

 

            “Where are my guns?” Lena asked, ignoring her.

 

            Nodding at the bundle, left out of the way, Nia frowned slightly. “Everything alright?”

 

            Dashing forward, Lena snatched up the belongings tucked inside her hat. She swiftly buckled on the belt, the familiar weight of her Colt and her grimoire balancing out either side, and slapped her wide-brimmed hat on her head, making back for the door.

 

            “Don’t leave the hotel,” she threw over her shoulder.

 

            “Don’t ruin my clothes!” came the distant reply as she wound through the tables.

 

            Pushing back out into the street, Lena found a small crowd gathering as the pale man lay face down with Alex’s knee in his back, multiple voices clamouring over each other as Alex tried to calm him down while he shouted incoherently and Kelly tried to direct people back inside. Striding right past them, Lena grabbed the reins of the man’s horse and pulled herself up into the saddle, bringing the horse around and then to a stop as a hand grabbed the reins.

 

            “What are you doing?” Kara asked, a flicker of panic in her eyes.

 

            “Stay here,” Lena said, covering Kara’s hand with her own and squeezing before she peeled her fingers off and kicked her heels to the horse’s flank. 

 

            He was slightly bigger than Hecate and built for speed instead of endurance, which meant that the gruelling pace Lena put him through quickly tapered off. She wasn’t one to push a horse to its breaking point and allowed the gentler pace as she made for the mountains, aiming for higher ground.

 

            Nothing seemed amiss as she followed the beaten path she’d taken dozens of times now, but there was that feeling of unease that had dogged her since that morning and she wasn’t willing to take any chances. Climbing higher through the trees, she cast her magic wide, feeling for the telltale signs of reanimated skeletons or corpses, the prickle of magic felt in all things brought back. The trees were dark as they shadowed the path and Lena brought the horse out onto a plateau she’d been using to canvas the area, the sun sinking over the horizon like a copper penny as everything was bathed in an orange glow.

 

            She narrowed her eyes, letting her power ripple down the ridges of the sloping path, seeking out anything moving with that odd, shambling gait. And there , a few miles away, a black dot moving slowly, aimlessly. It could have been an ordinary person, too far away from her to feel the bones, but no person of sense would be walking from town to town across exposed terrain. 

 

            Suspicious, Lena urged the horse onwards and took a steep path down the side of the mountain, branches whipping at her cheeks and the switchback path making it a slow descent. She was wary of broken legs laming the horse and hindering her pursuit but eventually, she came out in a ravine on the north-facing side of the mountain range, cutting a westerly path and rounding the tip of the foothills to head south. 

 

            It was a wight, shambling along freely, and Lena exhaled a sigh of relief as she relaxed on her saddle, slowly the borrowed horse to a trot as she gained on the corpse. At the very least, it meant that there was no one in the vicinity controlling the corpse, which looked to have been a fresh one upon death, although it was rotting now, the flesh putrifying as it sloughed off the bones in places. She could handle an escapee who’d managed to get ahead of the main host, not needing to be puppeted about like the skeletons who weren’t given the same autonomy as wights.

 

            Still, it was with a sinking stomach that Lena knew they had weeks, if not days before they’d be set upon more than one dead, and a few more alive at that. At least now she had a rough idea for their time frame, that stab of panic flaring up like an old friend as the peril of her brother’s wrath lit a fire beneath her. They needed to get a move on with their defences because trouble was coming, whether they willed it or not.

 

            As she came down upon the wight, Lena unholstered her gun and pulled the hammer back as she aimed it at the brow of the dead man with milky white eyes. Her mouth was a hard line as she fired a single bullet into him, watching his body crumple as a few crows took flight, disturbed by the sound.

 

            Dismounting, Lena knelt beside the corpse and reached out to touch a chalky cheek. Grave wax had started to form, a crumbly white substance that accumulated on the fat deposits of some corpses, and it bothered Lena that she dated the corpse at three weeks old, barely. They were running out of time. 

 

            Climbing to her feet, she shaded her eyes and looked to the north, as if she’d see an army approaching, outriders watching her, but she was utterly alone. Standing in a field at the bottom of the mountain at sunset, Lena watched the sky purple and listened to the birds chirping in the trees, oblivious to the impending danger.

 

            She didn’t move, not even when the sound of hooves grew increasingly louder behind her. Lena already knew who it would be, and knew Kara would’ve accompanied her against her gentle instructions - admired her, even, for coming anyway, although it made her heart lurch in her chest to think of her throwing herself into danger so willfully - and Lena was deep in thought, trying to cobble together a plan to survive what was coming as Alex knelt beside the corpse and Kara made a retching sound and the foul smell.

 

            “What’s this?”

 

            Lena narrowed her eyes, a brooding look of concern as she stared out at the sprawling plains and fields and hills, the rotting smell of the body fouled the air. She wiped the sleeve of her coat over her cheek, flecks of black blood smearing across her pale skin. They were both looking at her and she felt her stomach twinge with dismay as the inevitable arrived.

 

            “This is the beginning.”

12. Chapter 12

“I’ll need to visit the Waypoint again within the next day or so,” Lena told Kara, stroking her blonde hair as she stared up at the ceiling.

 

            “Again?”

 

“As a rule, we only take what we need, and leave what we can. I’ve burned through a lot of my teeth since the last trip and … well, I think just this once it wouldn’t be frowned upon for me to loot as much as possible. He’ll only take it for himself anyway.”

 

“Will they let you take that much?”

 

Lena winced slightly, her eyes closing. “We killed her.”

 

“Oh. Right.”

 

“They won’t have found a replacement yet.”

 

Kara pushed herself up, an unbuttoned shirt slipping down her shoulders as she looked down at Lena with worry in her eyes. Her face was cast in shadows as thin fingers of sunlight poked through the curtains, but the tension in her expression was palpable.

 

“I’d like to go too.”

 

Freezing momentarily, Lena pushed herself up and gave Kara a long, piercing look. Eventually, she raked a hand through her dark hair as it fell around her face, head ducked down to study the worn sheets as she picked at a stray thread.

 

“I don’t think you should. It’ll be dangerous; I’m heading north - towards him. A whole army.”

 

“You shouldn’t go alone.”

 

Looking up, Lena gave her a strained smile, her eyes pleading. “I don’t want you to put yourself in harm’s way.”

 

“But it’s alright for you to do it?”

 

“Yes.”

 

Kara let out a quick laugh and cupped Lena’s chin, “you seem to get into more trouble when you’re out all by yourself, Doc, and I don’t like it. I don’t like it one bit.”

 

Catching her hand in her own, Lena gave it a gentle squeeze and slipped out of bed. Reaching for her abandoned clothes, she dressed quickly, neatly fastening buttons and smoothing out creases before washing her face at the basin and finishing off the dregs of wine. Sucking on her teeth for a moment, she turned to look at Kara, who was dressing at a slower pace.

 

“Trouble is a side-effect of my job; yours is … a nasty bruise from a stubborn stallion with a swift kick. Splinters and blisters and sunburns.”

 

“Well, you make me sound all soft like.”

 

Smiling thinly, Lena sighed as she braced her hands on her hips. “You’re far from soft Miss Danvers - you’re tough as nails and kind to boot, which is why I- I would never stop you from making your own choices. I only wish you’d choose … better.”

 

Grinning Kara brushed her hair back and swiftly started loosely plaiting it out of her face. “Does that mean you’ll let me come?”

 

Making a vague sound of amusement at the back of her throat, Lena smiled tightly. “You’re so stubborn that I don’t believe I could stop you from following after me even if I told you not to.”

 

“I reckon you’re right there, Doc.”

 

Lena softly clicked her tongue and sighed before walking over to Kara. She sank onto the edge of the bed and nudged her hands for Kara to let the loose strands of hair go before she picked them up and tightly plaited it down her back. Afterwards, she pressed her hands against Kara’s shoulder blades, feeling the rise and fall of her chest.  Resting her chin on her shoulder, Lena’s hands ghosted down the sleeves of Kara’s shirt and she closed her eyes, exhaling in a resigned sigh. “Promise me you’ll listen. If I tell you to run, you run.”

 

“I ain’t a coward.”

 

“I don’t think that you are. Only … my mind has a terrible habit of falling to distraction whenever you’re around. If it comes to a fight … I would be more concerned with what you’re doing, if you’re safe, than what was before my very eyes.”

 

Kara hesitated for a long moment before audibly swallowing and turning her head slightly, nose brushing Lena’s cheek. “I promise.”

 

She kissed her cheek then and climbed to her feet and Lena gave her a faint smile before following after her. They made their way downstairs for breakfast, Lena feeling tired and a little washed-out from too much work and not enough rest. She wished she could sleep for a week but they couldn’t spare the time. As it was, she was perhaps cutting it a little close to fetching supplies. She imagined she might beat her brother to the Waypoint by a day or two, which meant she needed to leave as soon as possible.

 

“We ought to go tomorrow,” Lena said as she spooned porridge into her mouth, glancing across the table at Kara, who lounged in her chair, holding her bowl in hand.

 

“Tomorrow? Alright. Well, I s’pose I should let Alex know.”

 

“I don’t envy you that task,” Lena said with a short laugh, taking a swig of coffee and luxuriating in the splash of cream; they wouldn’t have that on the road.

 

Kara wrinkled her nose and her eyes creased at the corners. “Aw, she’ll be alright, Doc. She’s just a little protective.”

 

“Yes, I’m intimately familiar,” Lena muttered. “You should pack your belongings and spend some time with your mother.”

 

Nodding, Kara pushed her empty bowl back and climbed to her feet, chair legs scraping across the warped floorboards. “Alright. I’ll see you later, then?”

 

“Yes, ma’am,” Lena said with a faint smile.

 

She finished her own breakfast while brooding over Kara accompanying her, trying to run through the worst scenarios imaginable so Lena could come up with premeditated solutions. Afterwards, she made her way from store to store, racking up a tab to be paid by the town at a later date, and took Hecate to a farrier to make sure her hooves were in good condition - she couldn’t afford a delay to re-shoe her again like last time.

 

It was almost lunchtime when Lena made her way back to the hotel and walked upstairs, bypassing her room and knocking on another door. Voices went quiet and after a moment the door opened to reveal Russell, his suit jacket abandoned and his shirtsleeves rolled up. He looked surprised to see her and hesitated.

 

“Miss Luthor.”

 

“I’m here to see Miss Rojas.”

 

He glanced over his shoulder, deeper into the suite, and then opened the door to admit her. The curtains were parted, letting in wide swathes of sunlight, and Andrea was sitting at a table spread with sheets of paper. She looked up at Lena’s arrival, a flicker of worry in her blue eyes even as she smiled. The blue of her dress was bright against the faded room, speaking of her wealth and upbringing, and Lena imagined this life for herself if things had turned out differently.

 

Doffing her hat, Lena twisted the brim in her hands. “I’ve come to inform you I’ll be out of town for the next week.”

 

“Pardon?” Andrea asked, paling as she half-rose from her seat, the singular word a faint gasp.

 

“I need to restock while there’s still time. I admit, I’ve procrastinated longer than I should have; I imagine there will be mere days once I return before we’ll be set upon.”

 

“You can’t leave,” Andrea imperiously replied as she sank back down onto her chair.

 

Lena let out a short laugh and gestured off-handedly. “I’m not here to deliberate my going - that’s already been decided and I don’t take orders from anyone but myself and my Order - my concern is the mine.”

 

Mouth thinning, Andrea gave her a dressing down with her eyes, displeasure on her face. “Yes, you’ve been rather unfruitful there, I must admit. My promised fortune diminishes with each day I’m yet to see gold in my hands.”

 

Smile growing a little wider, Lena cocked her head to the side. “You’ll have your gold once this is all over. But while I’m gone, I would recommend rigging the mine shaft with explosives. The Sheriff has dynamite that you might make use of.”

 

“Now why would I do that? You’ve put a lot of effort into unblocking the mine; that sounds awfully counter-productive to me.”

 

“The mine can be dug back out again; the gold can’t be recovered once he’s taken it. It’ll also create a more direct route for him to take if what he really wants has been denied him.”

 

“Drive him directly to town?” Andrea innocently asked, arching an eyebrow slightly before she laughed, leaning back in her seat. “I thought we would hope for the opposite.”

 

“This is going to come to a head either way, ma’am. It would benefit us to be prepared and direct our strength from a vantage point. I don’t imagine you’ll abandon your investment-“

 

“On the contrary, I’ll be leaving town in a few days myself.”

 

Freezing, Lena narrowed her eyes a fraction. “No, you’re not.”

 

“Miss Luthor-“

 

Walking over to the table, Lena planted both hands firmly on it, fixing Andrea with an unwavering stare. “Now, you listen to me, good and well - you will not abandon this town and come back to reap the rewards once trouble has passed. Do you hear me? You’ll not see a single nugget of gold, if that was your intention.”

 

Lounging, Andrea smiled thinly. “Is that a threat, Doctor?”

 

“I’m not in the business of threats. But you should think twice about crossing me; we had a deal.”

 

“Business is business. You clear the mine out and get it in working order, you get paid. If you don’t intend to live long enough to complete your job, I’ll find someone else to do it.”

 

“And the town?” Lena countered, arching an eyebrow. “Is your intention for it to be wiped out so you can attain complete ownership of the mine?”

 

“As I said, business is business. Either way, I make my money in the gold mine.”

 

Scoffing as her eyes darkened with anger, her face hardening as she flushed, Lena grit her teeth. “And fuck everyone else.”

 

“Well, I think that’s quite enough, Miss Luthor,” Russell said, reaching out to grab her arm.

 

Lena elbowed him in the stomach, eliciting a sharp exhale as he stepped back. Andrea rose from her chair, a flash of anger in her eyes, and Lena straightened up, squaring her shoulders.

 

“I would encourage you to leave as well,” Andrea softly said. “You’re a well-bred lady; don’t die out here in some backwards, deserted town for people that aren’t yours, and money that you don’t need. Run back to your mother and hide behind her skirts; perhaps she can spare you from your brother’s wrath. It’s your only hope.”

 

“I’m not a coward,” Lena snapped, pointing a finger at her in warning. “But you listen closely, ma’am; you step a foot out of Midvale and I’ll make sure that mine never reopens.”

 

Giving her a fleeting smile, Andrea tugged at the lace cuff of her dress. “I might believe your threat if you would survive to carry it out. I suppose this will be the last we see of each other.”

 

“I’d consider it a pleasure if it was,” Lena roughly replied before jamming her hat back down onto her head and stalking downstairs.

 

She ordered herself lunch from J’onn, who filled a tin mug with beer and set it down before her, his dark eyes appraising her for a long moment before he ventured a question of concern. Assuring him she was fine, although her sulking tone betrayed her, Lena retreated to a table and bristled with anger and annoyance as she ate. Her solitude was broken halfway through by the batwing doors admitting a tense Sheriff making a bee-line straight for her.

 

“What in the God damn hell are you thinking, Doc? I thought we was in agreement,” Alex disgruntledly greeted Lena, hauling a chair out and planting one boot firmly on it.

 

“Sheriff.”

 

“Don’t you Sheriff me, Lena Luthor.”

 

Humming faintly, Lena cocked her head to the side and narrowed her eyes slightly. “That’s possibly the first time you’ve called me by my name.”

 

“I’ll call you a lot worse if you drag my kid sister into an early grave, I’ll tell you that.”

 

Mouth thinning, Lena sighed and wiped her hands on the thighs of her pants. “I’m not pleased about it either,” she admitted. 

 

“You told me you was goin’ to keep her safe.”

 

“And I stand by my promise,” Lena earnestly replied. “I’ll do everything in my power to make sure she doesn’t come to harm. But she has her own mind, Alex, and we have to be content with letting her make it up.”

 

Scoffing, Alex’s mouth thinned. “I don’t like it when you’re right.”

 

“It must be difficult for you to know I often am.”

 

“I think I might just kill you by the end of this trip.”

 

Freezing, Lena stared at her blankly for a second before swallowing her mouthful of food. “No.”

 

“No, what ?”

 

“No you’re not coming.”

 

“I weren’t askin’ for permission, Doc.”

 

“Just as well; you wouldn’t get it,” Lena curtly replied, picking up her knife and fork again before warily eyeing Alex. “Two is already one more person to look after than I’d hoped. I’ll not be responsible for another life, nor allow another reason to be delayed.”

 

Scoffing, Alex rolled her eyes and collapsed down onto the chair. Leaning forward, she braced her arms on the scarred table. “Like I said, I weren’t askin’ permission. If she goes, I go. And you don’t need to worry about keeping me safe. I do just fine myself.”

 

“Perhaps against drunken soldiers and chicken theft.”

 

“Don’t go making me feel small , Doc. I know you and the law ain’t in agreement, but you know as well as I it ain’t all drunks and petty theft.”

 

Clearing her throat, Lena reached for her beer and Alex jerked it out of her reach, scowling. Rolling her eyes, Lena’s mouth thinned.

 

“You can’t leave. There’s something I need you to see to while I’m gone.”

 

“And what’s that?”

 

“I need you to lock up that conniving lady and her little associate and keep them there until this whole thing is over.”

 

Alex’s eyebrows rose a fraction. “Miss Rojas? She offended you some?”

 

“Oh, she’s planning on doing a lot more,” Lena quietly seethed. “Blind robbery is more like it. I have a plan, though.”

 

“I ain’t locking up an innocent woman.”

 

“Oh, now you have morals about that?” Lena snorted. “And what crimes have I been guilty of?”

 

Pointing a finger at her, Alex gave her a grim look. “I could've had you tried for shootin’ someone, you know. That was a crime, make no mistake.”

 

Waving a hand dismissively, Lena reached for her cup and Alex moved it even further away. “Be that as it may, I need you to do me a favour.”

 

“I’ll do you a favour if you agree to let me come. Otherwise, we’re gonna leave here pretending like I ain’t gonna follow you anyway, and you ain’t gonna do what it is you want me doin’. Why do I have a feelin’ like it ain’t entirely legal?”

 

“It’s not,” Lena curtly replied.

 

Hesitating, Alex lifted the cup to her lips and drained the rest of Lena’s beer, setting it down firmly and rising to her feet. She smiled sharply and held her calloused hand out.

 

“We’ve got a deal then, Doc.”

 

“Won’t your wife be upset?”

 

“Kelly? No, she knows how to lay down the law. It ain’t the first time I’ve gone running off into trouble as well; she just used to join me before all this mayoring happened.”

 

“Well …”

 

“What time we off then? Kara said dawn. Crack of or we waitin’ until we can see where the hell we’re going?”

 

“Crack of, if not earlier,” Lena sighed, scooting her chair back. “I’m going to need you to bring as much dynamite as you can carry as well.”

 

“I’ve got a hell of a lot of it.”

 

“Good. We’ll need it.”

 

Alex hesitated, her brow creasing momentarily as doubt blossomed in her eyes. “Now, Doc, what’s this plan of yours?”

 

Giving her a tight-lipped smile, Lena tucked her chair pack in and picked up her hat. “I won’t ruin the surprise for you.”

 

Touching the brim of her hat, she left Alex grumbling beneath her breath as she ordered another beer from J’onn, apparently not satisfied with Lena’s dregs. As for herself, Lena carried on out into the afternoon sunlight and ferreted out the rest of the necessities before making her way back up to her room and carefully packing everything as efficiently as possible.

 

She bought new overalls, the denim kind like Kara’s, and left it out with the new shirt before tucking a spare one in with an extra pair of socks. It was familiar and allowed a moment of reprieve from planning and worrying. She had a small cooking pot, enough dried food for a couple of extra days, a sparse medical kit and the tools of her trade.

 

Lena didn’t see Kara for the rest of the day and she slept fitfully, worrying about bringing her along, before waking to the darkness of early morning. Changing into her new overalls and shirt, she donned her battered coat and hat, tucking the hems of the pants legs into her boots, and hauled her knapsack onto her back. Pocketing her key and patting her gun reassuringly, Lena descended through the dark hotel, a step groaning loudly and the front door squeaking as she slipped out.

 

She rounded the building to the stables and saddled Hecate, stowed her bag and then got into the saddle. Rounding back around to the front, Lena remained seated as she waited a few minutes for the other two party members to arrive. She heard the trundling sound first and bit back a sigh as she watched as Kara and Alex arrived on the cart Lena had been using for her work.

 

“Absolutely not,” Lena firmly greeted them.

 

“What’s wrong?”

 

“We need to be quick. A cart is the complete opposite of speed.”

 

“It’s the only way I could bring all the explosives,” Alex explained, twisting in her seat.

 

Bringing Hecate around to the back of the cart, Lena’s stomach jolted at the sheer amount of dynamite Alex had scrounged up for her. Giving the Sheriff a long look, a glint in her green eyes, Lena grunted.

 

“We’ll risk it but we might have to cut our losses at some point.”

 

“Alright then.”

 

“Let’s get moving.”

 

She flicked her reins and urged Hecate into motion, bearing right once she was out of the town. The cart immediately slowed them down, despite the two horses pulling it, and Lena grew impatient as the sun started to rise, painting the landscape lavender and soft orange.

 

“Hey, Doc, where was you leading us anyway?” Alex called out after a while.

 

“To the mine,” Lena shouted back over her shoulder.

 

“The mine? What in the lord’s name are we headin’ out there for?”

 

Lena didn’t reply, just kept urging them on, ranging ahead to scout out the land at times. A few miles in, she spotted a shambling wight and split the stillness of the morning with a dead shot between its eyes, not bothering to bury the body as she galloped back to reassure the duo that it was nothing to worry about. It was, in fact, a big thing to worry about, with a few more spotted over the past few days by the townsfolk they sent out scouting.

 

Eventually, they made it up to the mine though, and Lena dismounted and made for the cart. Tugging back the canvas flap, she hauled a crate of dynamite off it and started trudging towards the mouth of the mine shaft.

 

Alex caught up to her first, grabbing her arm. “Hold on now, what’s this all about?”

 

“Miss Rojas saw fit to enlighten me on her plan to leave town until this blows over. She’s under the impression she’ll have her gold either way. Whether it’s over the town’s dead bodies or by my hand. I don’t intend on letting her get the mine without a struggle.”

 

Blinking as she opened and closed her mouth, Alex was silent as she gave Lena a curt nod and then went to fetch her own crate. Kara carried an oil lamp a safe distance ahead of them as they burrowed into the dark a while.

 

“So, how does this help us, exactly?”

 

“Lex won’t stop here first. And he won’t get the gold. Miss Rojas will need workers to dig it back out again, and it might offer a big enough reprieve for any survivors in town to stake their claim on the mine before you lose the only profitable resource out here. She’s betting on everyone dying first. Called it business.”

 

“Well,” Kara sighed.

 

They wasted an hour rigging the explosives, but it was worth it to listen to the stone-shattering sound as the lit fuse split apart the fractured rock of the mine shaft. Lena worried about the structural integrity of it once it reopened, but that was a problem for a day they might not live to see. Still, she felt vindicated as they carried on their way.

 

The day grew hotter as the miles vanished beneath hooves and wheels, the blazing-hot, grass-scented wind blowing in their faces as they wound north. Overhead, spun-sugar clouds drift across the cornflower blue sky and Kara started to whistle.

 

“No whistling,” Lena called out.

 

“Ain’t you a spot of sunshine,” Alex drawled.

 

“We’re not on a leisurely ride. We need to be as quick as possible. A cart and three of us slows us down immeasurably.”

 

Alex laughed, “am I intruding on your lover's trip?”

 

Rolling her eyes and scoffing, Lena pulled up beside the cart, slowing Hecate to a brisk trot. “I’m not in the business of romance but even I wouldn’t seek to endanger any lovers of mine.”

 

“Had a lot of them, have you? Good thing I’m here to chaperone. Wouldn’t want any untoward behaviour with my kid sister, now.”

 

Kara elbowed Alex. “Very funny.”

 

Heaving a sigh, Lena’s cheek dimpled with an exasperated grimace. “Are you quite done having fun?”

 

“You don’t have to be all glum about it, Doc,” Alex said with a click of her tongue. “Maybe you ought to lighten up. Being miserable won’t make it go any quicker.”

 

“Yes, but it may allow me to spot danger before it reaches us,” Lena countered in a clipped tone, her magic fanning around them as she remained on edge.

 

To say it was a long few days was an understatement. She set a gruelling pace that made her think the cart might splinter apart from the motion, only allowed a few hours of sleep per night, leaving Alex and Kara to take turns sleeping beneath the canvas in the wagon - Lena politely refused the offer of a turn - and spent half of the time ranging ahead and looping back around, picking off strays and raising all the dead she found to put a bullet in them, denying her brother more skeletons for his army.

 

The weather was hot and Lena grew increasingly paler, almost grey in the face with dark circles beneath her eyes as she focused on the task ahead. Her stolen moments with Kara were a soothing balm that offered a brief break from reality - cooking dinner together, collecting firewood and pointing out plants and animal tracks as they occasionally walked through the rocky terrain of the mountains.

 

Eventually, they made it all the way to the Waypoint, the stench of death so strong that they all had to tie bandanas around their mouths and noses before stepping inside. Lena was unafraid, but the other two followed her into the cave with uneasy fear tensing their shoulders.

 

Making quick work of sealing a barrel of teeth and rolling it towards the tunnel, Lena stopped as she watched Kara and Alex take in the space. Giving them a wan smile, she cocked her head to the side and raised her eyebrows.

 

“Not what you were expecting?”

 

“I have to say, it’s a right sight more organised than I imagined,” Alex commented, rubbing at her forehead. “And y’all have these all over?”

 

“We do. They’re tended to by retired Witch Doctors - like her,” Lena jerked a thumb at the dead body and Kara wrinkled her nose. “Here. Get this on the wagon.”

 

Sifting through supplies, taking stacks of empty grimoires and crate after crate of bone bullets that would fit rifles and pistols alike, Lena wondered if it would be enough. As she lined up barrels of teeth, she knew she wouldn’t be able to get through them all before she killed herself with the effort, as she took bags of Piedfort coins for revival, she knew she’d never get the chance to bring back even a fraction of the townsfolk with them unless she made it out alive too. 

 

By the time they’d ransacked the entire Waypoint, taking sacks of oats and chests of cured meats, pots of coffee and tea and bags of dried fruits, enough to last the town a few extra days in a siege, it was bare inside. Lena considered blowing the cave to pieces as well but decided against it as she looked around the place, taking in the remnants of a clay pot, the cloying scent of oil making her scowl with the memory. Perhaps she should blow it up, but there would come a day when another of her kind needed to restock, and everything she’d taken would be replaced.

 

“Are we bringing this down?” Alex asked as Lena climbed back up into the saddle.

 

Face clouded with thought, Lena shook her head. “No, ma’am, but I was thinking we might bring down the whole damn fucking valley.”

 

Giving her a crooked smile in return, Alex tugged her hat down lower on her face. “You know what, Doc, I was thinkin’ the same fucking thing.”

 

Sighing, Kara shook her head as she rolled a cigarette for her sister, lit it and puffed for a moment, before exhaling grey as she passed it off, her blue eyes burning into Lena’s. “I reckon letting you two get acquainted was the biggest mistake of my life.”

 

“Oh, no, ma’am,” Lena crookedly smiled, “I believe that was not shooting me dead when I showed up on your doorstep.”

 

Cheeks flushing pink, Kara cleared her throat and shifted. “Now, how many times are you goin’ to bring that up, Doc? It was an accident.”

 

“I think I’ll bring it up until the day I die,” Lena laughed, putting her heels to Hecate’s haunches. “That just might come a lot sooner than we think, so consider yourself lucky.”

 

Setting a recklessly fast pace back down the mountain, wheels bouncing off rocks and both women jolting on the bench seat up front, Lena glanced down into the ravine that carved the main path through the mountains and tried to plot how to blow it up. In the end, it was Alex who led the way, sending Kara off to plant explosives on one side of the ravine while she did the other.

 

In the meantime, Lena busied herself with raising as many of the surrounding dead as possible and had them congregate in the pass. The three of them made a swift exit with the cart and horses and lit the fuse a safe distance away, watching as dust and smoke billowed from the explosion as it shook the day. It would undoubtedly be seen for miles around, black against the blue sky, the sound echoing through the mountains and perhaps setting off a chain reaction of landslides, and Lena was pleased with herself, thinking of how many dead would be sacrificed to dig the path free. They’d bought themselves a few more days, at the very least.

 

Still, they didn’t slow their pace for the entire ride back. It was slower than Lena would have liked, although they’d traded off the rest of the dynamite for the supplies, which evened out in the end, and they returned to Midvale within a week of setting out, sweaty and slightly sunburnt in Kara’s case, all three of them looking in dire need of a bath and a good meal.  Lena didn’t get further than dismounting from Hecate before she was accosted in the street though, a bristling woman decked out in finery emerging from the saloon.

 

            “You blew up my mine?” Andrea yelled, storming down the steps.

 

“Miss Rojas,” Lena drawled nonchalantly.

 

The slap was quick and surprising, Lena’s cheek flooding red as she let out a quick laugh. Cocking her head to the side, she smiled thinly.

 

“Oh, ma’am, you’ll have to do more than that if you think to hurt me. Even death itself lost its sting after the first couple of times.”

 

Blanching as horror crept into her face, Andrea floundered for a moment before turning her attention to Alex. Clicking her fingers, she gestured at Lena. “You. Sheriff. Make yourself useful; arrest her.”

 

“Hm, I don’t know about that, ma’am,” Alex hummed. “You see, I was with the good Doctor here this past week. I don’t recall no explosives being set off. Do you, Kara?”

 

Scratching her chin, Kara wrinkled her nose and squinted. “Me? No, I don’t recall none of that.”

 

Lena fought hard to keep a smile off her face as she watched the heiress silently fume. Giving Lena a scornful look, her brow furrowing, she clenched her hands into fists. 

 

“You’d better get me my gold once this is all over.”

 

“But of course, ma’am. I have an agreement with the Mayor,” Lena cordially replied, clasping her hands behind her back. “Will you be staying in town until then?”

 

Andrea’s mouth thinned and she looked down, brushing a hand over her skirts. “As a matter of fact, we were just about to leave .” She sniffed derisively, glancing around. “I trust that the town will honour the deed to the mine when the time comes.”

 

“Oh, you bet,” Alex agreed, thumbs tucked in her belt.

 

“Good day then, Miss Rojas,” Lena breezily replied before making for the steps of the hotel.

 

For all her nonchalance, there was the uneasy feeling that she’d perhaps pushed the woman too far. The woman who knew all of the details of their planning. Trying to squash that prickling unease, Lena made for her room as Kara followed after her, her mind latching onto the fate of the rancher’s. She was loath to let anything happen to her, especially over her own idiocy, but knew that there wasn’t much she could do except hope that she was around to revive Kara and anyone else she’d grown fond of. But if she wasn’t, on the off chance that attempting the impossible paid off, she set her mind to the process of bringing back the dead and wondered if anyone untrained could pull it off.

 

Unlocking the door, Lena breezed inside with a sudden purpose as Kara followed her inside, shutting the door behind them.

 

“Heavens, it’s a hot one today, Doc,” Kara said as she plucked at the front of her paisley shirt, dust clouding from the dirty denim overalls she was wearing on top.

 

Lena ignored her as she walked over to the windows, slamming the warped framed glass shut and drawing the curtains tightly over it. The room was dim and dingy without the sunlight highlighting the faded grandeur of the hotel, and it was made stiflingly hot as Lena stoked the fire, a wall of heat radiating from the hearth.

 

“Now what in God’s good holy name are you doing lightin’ a fire now,” Kara exclaimed, wiping at her sweating brow.

 

Lena grabbed the small chest of her new supplies and fumbled through the items until she came up with a mortar and pestle, a small bowl and a little paring knife. “Anyone can use Necromancy; it’s not a closed practice so anyone can learn. I don’t have the years it takes to train someone properly, but I can give you a Hail Mary in case things go awry.”

 

“Now, hold on a minute-”

 

Grabbing the small knife in a white-knuckled grip, Lena slashed the blade across her wrist, cutting deep to get the blood flowing fast as it trickled into the small bowl. Kara let out a panicked cry, reaching for an abandoned shirt hanging over the back of a chair and grabbed Lena’s arm as she tried to stem the blood flow. Pushing her hand away, Lena set the bloodied knife down and reached for a tooth, looking a shade paler as she healed herself.

 

            “Don’t do that,” Kara snapped, eyes wide.

 

“It’s alright,” Lena dismissively replied, fumbling with the buttons on the cream leather duster she was wearing over the blue gingham shirt.

 

Shrugging out of it, she pulled the shirt untucked from the overalls and started unbuttoning that as well. Kara watched her undress and frowned. “Did I misunderstand what’s goin’ on here?”

 

Rolling her eyes, Lena tossed her shirt onto the floor and then reached for Kara’s overalls, unclipping them and then unbuttoning her shirt. They were close enough for Lena’s somewhat frantic urgency to bleed through, visible in the way her throat bobbed as she swallowed, the clammy sheen of sweat on her ducked head. 

 

“Pay attention,” Lena ordered her, tearing open the front of Kara’s shirt and then moving over to the table.

 

Dipping her finger in the bowl of blood, she tore a sheet of paper from her grimoire and reached out with her free hand, cold fingers wrapping around Kara’s wrist and pulling her closer. “The glyphs look like this. You do a line, like so, and a dot here.”

 

She dipped her finger in the blood again, painting the spell on the page as Kara watched beside her, her shirt clutched tightly in her fist and a nervous air about her as her eyes occasionally flitted to the windows and door. The room was unbearably hot and Lena could feel her restlessness, but it was too important for her to keep her locked in the dark. She would give her whatever fighting chance she could.

 

“There are matching glyphs for the body,” Lena informed her as she dipped her finger into more blood and then turned to Kara, fingertips touching her sternum and leaving a swipe of dark red against Kara’s tanned skin.

 

Making a sound of protest, Kara stumbled back a step but Lena closed the gap as she clamped a hand down on her shoulder. Meeting her frightened eyes, her own stare hard and intense, Lena’s mouth tightened at the corners.

 

“Listen to me, you must pay attention. This could save someone’s life. Think of your sister.”

 

“I don’t-”

 

Expression clouding with grave worry, Lena reached up to cup Kara’s face, touching their foreheads together briefly. “It’s highly probable you couldn’t do it anyway - it’s complex and long, but … if you know how, then maybe- if I- you could save other people if I-”

 

            “Stop.”

 

Pulling back, Lena scooped up the bowl from the table and sniffed, nudging her dark hair off her sweating brow with the back of her hand before she forged onwards, painting patterns on Kara’s skin. Her voice was quiet but clear as she instructed her, a stream of knowledge rolling off her tongue as she explained the swirling patterns and lines and dots, told her about the thick Piedfort coins to put in the mouth and which herbs to burn to guide the soul. She told her she needed three teeth, but probably more for a novice who didn’t have the control to weave the blood magic effectively, and she’d need to use her own blood to make it work. Kara listened with a pinched look of panic and fear on her face, blue eyes wide and childishly naive as she stared back at Lena, trying to keep up.

 

Once Lena had painted the symbols on Kara’s chest, she grabbed Kara’s hand and dipped it into her blood before gently pulling her forward. “Your turn.”

 

Lena guided Kara’s fingers over her sweat-slick skin, going through the motions as she tried to envision the sprawling glyphs in mirror image. Kara watched her hand move under Lena’s direction with a queasy look of horror, her dry lips parting and her breaths shallow. 

 

“You have to say the words too,” Lena hoarsely explained, her throat getting dry as she started to chant, her tone droning on as the dry air of the room gave her voice a gentle rasp.

 

Afterwards, she made Kara repeat it all back to her, fumbling through the process, making the wrong marks on the torn out pages - which was already rather sparse with the amount of half-finished spells Lena had been creating in preparation - and burnt the correct herbs, perfuming the room with grey smoke pluming from the fireplace. 

 

“There are also nine things about being brought back from the dead you should be aware of,” Lena said, a tremor entering her voice as she stared at Kara was a flicker of darkness in her eyes, memories stirring there. “They’ll be cold. They’ll wake up screaming - they all do. Their entire body will throb, but the pain will eventually subside; being brought back is never painless. They shouldn’t get up immediately; they’ll be nauseous and they need time to adjust to being back in their body. They’ll be very cold; blankets or a fire help. They won’t remember how they died, and they shouldn’t ask. I- I remember, but only as someone who has the self-awareness of the practice. Tell them not to ask you how you performed the ritual. It’s considered bad luck.”

 

“I- wha- okay …”

 

“That’s enough for today,” Lena eventually said, sweat running down both of their faces, making the blood streaky as the symbols blurred at the edges.

 

Moving over to the pitcher of water and the empty basin, she filled it and dipped a clean cloth into it, wringing out some of the water and crossing back over to Kara. Lena gently wiped her face clean first before moving on to her chest, rubbing firmly at the drying blood as it flaked away. The basin was pink by the time she was almost finished with herself, Kara pushing open the curtains and windows to let cool air and blinding sunlight inside. Lena put the fire out with the rest of the jug of water, the wood spitting as the small fire guttered, and she pulled on her shirt as she breathed in fresh air.

 

“I don’t want to use that, Doc,” Kara murmured, shifting uncomfortably.

 

“I know,” Lena sighed with resignation, moving over to the window and bracketing Kara as she gripped the windowsill on either side of her, looking out at the quiet midday street. “I’m praying that you won’t.”

 

“Praying to who? You don’t believe in nothin’.”

 

Pressing a kiss to the shoulder of Kara’s shirt, Lena closed her eyes. “I believe in myself. That’s enough.”

13. Chapter 13

            The next few days were a scrambling mess of planning and panic. Those who wouldn’t be able to fight for one reason or another were sent on the road to the next town over, bearing letters to be passed on to the surrounding areas, and they saw a small trickle of soldiers and nearby townsfolk who’d caught wind of their predicament heading into the city. There weren’t many, but it was enough to offset the numbers they lost as ranchers and miners showed up with their rifles and explosives and food, knowing their towns would be next.

 

            Kara and Nia escorted Lena out to the pastures beyond Kara’s ranch, fanning out to keep watch for anything untoward as Lena canvassed the area for the corpses of dead horses and cows and anything else big.
