She found a few skeletons of creatures she didn’t know, some of them with short arms and long tails, others with stockier but with horns that didn’t belong to bulls. The trio escorted them all home, where Lena disassembled them on the main street, stowing their bones away for future use.

 

            Under Alex’s eye, explosives were laid out in a large web, all of them somewhat connected to trigger a chain reaction, while shallow trenches were filled with tar and oil and pikes, hoping to slow the army down. Everyone was put onto rations, and it made for a tense atmosphere in the town, drinking watered-down beer as they chewed dried meat from anything they slaughtered to keep out of enemy hands.

 

            Up in her room, Lena opened the windows, the heat suffocating as her shirt clung to her back. She was wearing dirty overalls, which seemed to be all she lived in lately, her coat always slung on top as the sun baked the cream leather and the cuffs grew stained with too much of her blood spent on the concealed razors. 

 

            The last day was spent in a frenzied mess of preparation, barrels of bullets hauled up onto the parapets, sandbags and wood stolen from the beams of abandoned homes used to shore up the gates. Once the sun started to disappear, the last few townsfolk labouring to get the hard work done called it a night, including the unlikely group of friends who dusted off their blistered hands and headed back to J’onn’s hotel for food and drink.

 

            Lena wasn’t sure how the rest of them managed to keep their spirits up, laughing and joking as if the end of the world wasn’t about to arrive on their doorsteps, and she was silent and pensive as she nursed a cup of moonshine. She felt numb and empty, too tired to think or feel much, and managed to sneak out for a reprieve, standing on the front verandah and leaning against the railing as she breathed in the dusty air. The sky was vivid with lingering streaks of fuschia and lavender and Lena imagined this might be her last moment of peace.

 

            The batwing doors creaked open behind her a few minutes later and she listened to the sound of boots on the wooden planks, crossing over to her. She caught a whiff of Alex’s oiled leather and tobacco smell before she glanced over at her, watching as the Sheriff started rolling a new cigarette.

 

            “Reckon we’re ready?” Alex muttered.

 

            “We’ve done all that we can.”

 

            “Mm, will it be enough though?”

 

            Lena’s brow creased with concern, her mouth turning down at the corners. “Only time will tell, but … I’d not think so.”

 

            If she was surprised by Lena’s honesty, Alex didn’t show it as she scraped a match along the side of the box and touched it to the tip of her cigarette. Shaking the match out, Alex tossed it into the churned-up dirt of the main street and slumped forward onto the railings.

 

            “Least we got those fancy bullets of yours. Gives us a fighting chance, don’t it?”

 

            “Don’t give them to anyone who can’t shoot well,” Lena said, her mouth a grim line as she squinted at the horizon. “I’ll not waste valuable bullets.”

 

            “Well, hell, what’re they supposed to do then?” Alex asked, nudging the brim of her hat up as she folded her arms over her chest, the end of her cigarette clamped between her lips.

 

            Lena looked at her, taking in the evident worry, and frowned slightly. “They can have regular bullets. It won’t take them down for good, but they’ll be hard-pressed to do damage without any arms or legs. And the Necromancers will be using them as cannon fodder.”

 

            “Wish we had a couple of cannons,” Alex grumbled, sucking her teeth with dismay.

 

            “We’ll make do,” Lena said, inhaling deeply and then letting out her breath, glancing sideways as she smiled wryly, “and if not, well … I never thought I’d die fighting in the middle of nowhere beside a Sheriff, but …”

 

            “You know, you ain’t half bad for a Witch Doctor,” Alex hummed, exhaling a plume of grey smoke and passing the cigarette over to Lena.

 

            Letting out a short laugh, leaning against the railing, Lena’s eyebrows rose and fell quickly as she hesitated, lifting the cigarette to her lips. “For a Sheriff, you’re not too bad yourself.”

 

            Turning, leaning her back against the railing, elbows propped up on top and legs crossed at the ankle, Alex fixed her with a long stare as Lena smoked and avoided meeting her gaze. She could feel how weighted it was, some sense of precognition she didn’t need to dip her fingers into blood to read.

 

            “You know, she won’t say it but she loves you.”

 

            A muscle twitched in Lena’s jaw as she nodded, lowering the cigarette and narrowing her eyes. “I was afraid of that.”

 

            “Might not be much cause to be ‘fraid now,” Alex gloomily replied. 

 

            Lena’s thoughts weighed heavily on Alex’s words all evening, and she retired early, hoping to sleep as much as possible before she burned herself out. Conflicted between the need to be fully rested for when the fight arrived and doing as much as possible to defend the town, Lena found herself sleeping in fits and starts, stolen hours here and there and the occasional deep sleep that stole away half the day when she crashed and burned. 

 

            But she slept that night, with Kara sprawled across the other half of the bed, an arm flung across her waist, and was spared any restless dreams. In the morning, she thought perhaps her mind had known what was coming for them and had offered her one last reprieve, but when the shouts started just after dawn, that wasn’t the first thought on Lena’s mind.

 

            Tripping over her feet as she hauled her overalls on, hopping to shove her feet into her boots, Lena was snatching up her belt and hurrying out of the room as Kara groggily asked what was happening. Lena was already passing the other closed doors lining the mezzanine and took the stairs two at a time, barrelling outside. Alex was pulling a waistcoat over an untucked shirt, squinting as Kelly followed her outside, the Mayor looking harried as she loosely held a rifle in her hands.

 

            The trio converged as they ran towards the locked gate on the north end of the town, and Lena darted off to the rickety ladder leading up to the platform building against the wall. Hauling herself up fast enough to earn a few splinters, she had her gun in hand and the hammer pulled back by the time she peered over the top. Finding herself looking at one of the scouts on horseback, pulling the stallion in tight circles, she frowned. The man looked up at the sight of her.

 

            “I seen ‘em! All of ‘em! Heading right this way.”

 

            “How far?” Lena shouted down.

 

            “Passing through a valley near the mountains. Eight miles, I reckon.”

 

            Cursing, Lena pulled back and called down to open the gate to admit him before she descended the ladder. Running a hand over her face, she met Alex’s troubled stare. “Looks like this is it.”

 

            “Eight miles? How long’ll that take them, do you reckon?”

 

            “Hours yet,” Lena rasped.

 

            Hands on her hips, Alex hummed as they watched the people who’d been standing guard barricade the gate once more. “Ain’t no cause for a fuss then,” she said, reaching out to clap Lena on the shoulder. “May as well have breakfast.”

 

            Kelly scoffed, rolling her eyes, and looped her arm through her wife’s as Lena walked on ahead. A moment later they saw Kara rushing towards them, looking frazzled as she tried to smooth down her unbound hair, rifle in hand and a belt of ammo slung over one shoulder.

 

            “What’s goin’ on?” she asked, her accent thickening from sleep in a way that made Lena’s heart ache with the urge to protect her.

 

            “We’ve a few hours yet,” Lena murmured, cupping the side of her face and then pulling her into stride. “Nothing to be done until then.”

 

            “Oh,” Kara softly replied, her arms lowering with a mildly dazed look in her blue eyes as if she hadn’t anticipated things actually coming to this.

 

            Word spread quickly through the town, and by the time the sun was fully in the sky the platforms were packed with people watching the army approach, a few people had tried to leave through the equally guarded south gate and Alex had to arrest two people for trying to steal food. It was organised chaos as people watched the inevitable approach, shouts flying back and forth, people loitering near their posts with their guns, rifles cracked open to load with plain bullets.

 

            Lena watched from one of the platforms, standing stiffly the whole time while Kara came and went, bringing food, replenishing her canteen of water, badgering her with nervous questions about how long, how many, would they survive. Lena didn’t have answers and couldn’t even recall what she answered, but all she knew was that when the army made itself clear, indistinguishable from the grassy plains, the hills and mountains and desert patches, it was worse than she’d hoped.

 

            As the hours dragged by, cold fingers of horror splayed across Lena’s spine as she watched the advancing army. They were a shambling mass of corpses in varying stages of decay, and as the wind blew across the open land, it brought the smell of them rushing into Midvale. The air was rank and more than a few people coughed and retched, although Lena was used to it and was stoic as she stood rigidly on top of the flimsy platform erected against the rough-hewn walls. 

 

            They seemed even more pathetic now, the thickness of felled trees suddenly insufficient to keep out so many dead trying to force their way in. How long would it take ten thousand corpses to scrabble their way through bark and wood before they gouged their way through the entire trunk? It was a question Lena didn’t have the answer to, and she hoped their bag of tricks would allow for some errors in miscalculation. 

 

            Watching as they approached, she felt her stomach plummet and grew restless with agitation. She hadn’t realised she was anxiously drumming her fingers on the leather cover of her grimoire until Kara grasped her hand in her own, stopping her. Lena glanced over and gave her a weak smile, unable to muster any confidence as she feared she’d set the town up to die.

 

            “Lena.”

 

            Her brother’s loud voice spilt from a hundred rotting corpses who still had vocal cords of some use, the sound eerie as it seemed to come from everywhere as the army reached within earshot. She felt Kara’s ripple of unease as if she’d been struck by lightning, from beside her but wasn’t concerned as she reached out to gently grip her elbow. To fear him was natural, it was what he expected, and she didn’t want to give him that satisfaction 

 

            “It’s puppetry,” Lena said with a sneering twist of her lips. “It’s an amateur trick. Nothing to be frightened of.”

 

            Kara still looked uneasy as she glanced at Lena’s impassive face. Tearing a page from her book and slitting a fingertip, Lena flipped to a blank page and hastily wrote down an identical spell, the glyphs swirling together as she snorted at having to waste a page on such a small thing, something the children had used to cause mischief in the early days of their apprenticeship in the halls beneath the graveyard, with nothing but the dead to play with.

 

            “Lex,” Lena ground out, a few of her own recent corpses calling out across the decreasing space between both armies. “You should leave this place, brother. It is mine.”

 

            “Tut tut. Your manners are a disgrace; what would mother think? You ought to share, dear sister. Especially with your family.”

 

            “I’m not amused. Take your army and leave.”

 

            “I should think not. After all, you did steal from me. Now, I think I shall steal from you, take from you what you hold dear. Although, this pathetic town is hardly something worth dying over - are you sure you’d like to throw your lot in with … miners and ranchers?”

 

            Lena’s lips thinned with a fleeting smile as she licked her lips, tasting the dry dirt in the cracks as she squinted to the very back of the army, where her brother would be hiding. “Why don’t you come and have a proper talk, like a real man, brother? We’ll even extend our good generosity to a nice mug of beer for you. I know how you like your vices.”

 

            The laugh that fell from the mouths of the corpses was chilling, somewhat broken and inhuman. “You cannot goad me, Lena. I’m not some gullible imbecile.”

 

            “You could’ve fooled me,” she replied, the words coming out laced with mockery as she grinned.

 

            “Enjoy your mockery. It will be cold comfort by the time I’m through with you. Unless you’d like to reconsider. I’m a lenient master, as you well know; hand over the mine and what gold you have and I’ll allow you to live.”

 

            Humming as if considering it, Lena hardened herself against her brother’s needles, trying to prey on her doubts. “A tempting offer, but I must decline. We both know you’ll not stop here; tell me, what is your endgame?”

 

            “It’s but a simple goal; I’ll create a new order of Necromancers - ones who sit above society, not below - and take everything that has been denied us by these primitive fools who think we’re something to be feared. If that’s what they think, then I’ll show them fear as I break this country and remake it in my image.”

 

            “You’re a narcissistic fool,” Lena shouted back, raising her voice as her pale cheeks coloured with anger. “You’re a coward, and when I kill you, history will forget you even existed.”

 

            Her brother’s cold laugh slid down her spine and made the hairs on the back of her neck and arms stand on end, a chilling sensation that she’d already lost leaving Lena feeling terribly unbalanced for a moment. But she wouldn’t go down without a fight and clenched her teeth hard enough to make them ache dully as she listened to his reply.

 

            “You know, when you’re dead, I’m going to command you to kill every single one of your friends. Do you think they’ll know you’re dead, or just think you finally turned into a proper Necromancer, like they always feared?”

 

            Crumpling the paper in her hand instead of replying, Lena let it fall to the wooden planks underfoot and turned to look at Alex, a flinty look in her eyes. “Are you ready?”

 

            “How close we lettin’ them get?” the Sheriff asked, puffing on the end of her cigarette as she touched a lit match to the tip of it and shielded it with a cupped hand.

 

            “Maximum damage.”

 

            Nodding, Alex leaned against the top of the wall and narrowed her eyes. “Hell, they sure do walk slowly, don’t they? I reckon we’ll be here another fifteen minutes ‘fore the first ones are even in range.”

 

            “We have time,” Lena murmured.

 

            “You got that gun of yours ready?”

 

            Lena instead picked up one of Kara’s rifles leaning against the wall, giving Alex a crooked smile. “I thought I’d make use of my marksmanship skills with the rifle for the time being.”

 

            “You better be as damn good with it as you are with that,” Alex muttered, jerking her chin towards the Colt holstered at Lena’s waist. “Once we blow them to hell, I’ll head on over to the other side of the gate with Kelly. J’onn and M’gann have the platform over.”

 

            “Nia and Brainy?” Kara asked.

 

            “Guarding the south gate, God bless ‘em. It’s as safe as can be without cuttin’ them out of the fight entirely. And you know they won’t sit idly.”

 

            “I reckon those two’ll have something up their sleeves,” Kara snorted.

 

            Making a sound of agreement at the back of her throat, Alex blew a smoke ring and sighed heavily. “I hope so. Any extra help would be a fucking miracle right about now. You think he’d pack up if you gave him back the money you stole?”

 

            Alex added it as an afterthought, her eyes sliding to Lena, who scoffed, eyebrows rising. “You know that he wouldn’t.”

 

            “And what did you do with it all? I know you ain’t got two coins to rub together, so what’d you do with it? Stash it somewhere out in the wild? Melt it down?”

 

            “Wouldn’t you like to know,” Lena said with a fleeting grin.

 

            “As a matter of fact, I would . That gold could’ve bought us an army, could’ve maybe brought the law down on our side for a fee.”

 

            “If you have to pay the law to do their job, they’re not people to trust. We should get ready, Sheriff. No amount of gold will save us now.”

 

            Humming in agreement, Alex leaned against the wall and they waited in tense silence, the lone cry of a bird cawing overhead and the wind rustling through town cutting through it. There was an air of unease in the townsfolk who were perched along various points of the wall, all of them anxiously awaiting their deaths, and Lena felt a pang of pity for them.

 

            It felt like an eternity as they watched the skeletons and corpses come closer, blotting out the land as they stretched across the horizon like an ugly stain. Eventually, Lena deemed them close enough for their traps to be strung.

 

            “Sheriff?” Lena lightly asked as she turned to her, “would you like to do the honours?”

 

            “Doc,” Alex said, grinning fiercely around her cigarette as she raised a stick of dynamite to the lit tip of it, lighting the thin string on fire as it smoked for a moment before catching. “It would be my absolute pleasure.”

 

            Holding the lit explosive, Alex cocked her arm back, eyeballed the approaching horde and the shallowly submerged explosives covered with sand and dry grass, the long cords of the bundles running back towards the walls and into a ditch, waiting to be set alight. Alex lobbed the stick of dynamite as hard as she could and Lena prayed to no one that her aim was true, watching it twirl through the air with bated breath before it landed squarely in the patch of oil.

 

            For a moment, nothing happened as the dead shambled towards them, and then the oil exploded with a plume of unfurling orange, sending black smoke skywards as the fire traversed the lengths of the ropes with speed. A few moments later, a chain of explosives detonated, moving further away from the wall as one batch set off the next, set off the next, fanning outwards from the patch of oil.

 

            It was with satisfaction that Lena watched a chunk of her brother’s forces get blown to pieces or incinerated by the fires, beyond repair for even the most skilled Necromancer. It would be a bitter blow to his ego and she could feel his fury in the air, malodorous and tangible, a threatening aura that spoke of revenge. But at that moment, watching patches of bones split apart and to the musical sound of explosives and the taste of gunpowder on her tongue, Lena only felt the sweetness of striking the first blow.

 

            They’d blown apart perhaps a third of his forces, which was no small dent, even if it didn’t even the numbers at all. Still, it was a victory, and Lena would claim it, her chest loosening slightly with the triumphant feeling that emboldened her; perhaps they stood a chance now. This part had gone off without a hitch, and maybe he wasn’t quite so prepared or well-equipped as Lena had imagined, but she didn’t want to get ahead of herself just yet. She’d seen small battles between Necromancers change swiftly, sometimes with the addition of just one skeleton. 

 

            The fact that he had spread himself and his recruited rogues too thin trying to control so many dead would also give them an edge, but the few hundred Lena could stretch herself to if necessary would put her at a disadvantage too. Still, she knew her brother wouldn’t deploy them all at once, would probably send a thousand in until the ranks thinned too much to give Midvale a leg up on him, and then send in reinforcements. It was smart, it was strategic, and her brother had always excelled at that, had never really seemed cut out for healing and reviving the dead like most of their order. 

 

            Lex had always been too ambitious for anything other than a power grab that would give him control and money, just like their grandfather poaching the oil and railroad industry with tireless labourers to line his own pockets. It wasn’t exactly frowned upon, and there were many factions within the orders of Necromancers, with Witch Doctors being the most accepted in society - which said a lot - but Lena had always thought training in such powers to only help oneself was distasteful. 

 

            It seemed even more distasteful as she watched her brother’s army press onwards, regrouping to fill the gaps in the ranks, crossing the distance between the town and the open plains. A few of the soldiers had taken up posts beyond the wall, climbing down ladders set down on the other side so they could lay flat on rooftops with their rifles, occupying as many vantage points as possible. Lena would have been out there herself if not for the need to stay close to her own army of the dead, which paled in comparison. She hasn’t even pulled them from the ground yet but could feel how few bodies were buried in the cemetery in comparison. A mere thousand or two at most, and most being the loved ones of the townsfolk who would resent her the moment she exhumed their corpses to fight in their defence.

 

            She was already weary of the battle and it hadn’t even begun yet, but a few minutes later once the vanguard crossed into her rifle range, she let off the first shot and watched as a skeleton collapsed to pieces, swiftly lost underfoot as the army advanced. That seemed to be the catalyst for things to fully kick off, gunshots beginning to ring out through the early afternoon as those trusted with bone bullets thinned out the front ranks. Each sharp crack was another chance to save someone else, one less body to worry about, and Lena shot with methodical swiftness, striking home with each one.

 

            Alex left at some point, kissing her sister’s cheek and vanishing to the platform a dozen feet away, on the other side of the road coming in through the gate. They’d put all their best shooters in the centre to take on the main assault, and a few of the more mediocre ones on the further sides of the town, picking off anyone who tried to surround the town.

 

            Sighting down the barrel of the rifle, Lena pressed it firmly against her shoulder and fired off another shot, the bone bullet striking in the middle of the brow bone of the old man, his skin withered away to clumps clinging to bone. He went down, never to rise again, and Lena jerked back the bolt handle and slammed another bullet into place. On and on, she aimed and fired and took down another body, hearing similar shots split the shockingly quiet day as the army kept approaching.

 

            No matter how many they took out, there were always more though, and Lena fired as quickly as possible, running the rifle to empty and swapping with the rifle Kara hurriedly reloaded, sitting on the floor of the platform to stay out of sight. Sending off another shot, Lena flinched sideways as the tip of the wall exploded in a shower of splinters, tasting the metal and gunpowder of a fired bullet as she let out a low whistle as she dropped to the floor of the platform.

 

            “We’ve got a live one,” she said to Kara with a wan smile, trying to muster as much nonchalance as possible. 

 

            “Shit.”

 

            “Oh, don’t worry about that,” Lena waved a hand, dismissively, as Kara exchanged the rifle in her hand for the newly loaded one.

 

            She took the rifle and paused before leaning in to swiftly kiss her bitten lips, giving Kara a roguish wink before she drew in a deep breath and sharply exhaled. Quickly removing her hat from her head, Lena thrust it up over the wall and heard the crack of a pistol, the hat almost flying out of her hand from the impact of the bullet tearing a hole through it. Lowering the hat, she eyed the angle of the bullet and used it to determine the shooter was off to her left.

 

            In a smooth motion, she propped her rifle up on top of the rough trunk before her and located the man with ease. His movements were smooth and precise as he wound through the bodies, a neckerchief covering his nose and a gun in his hands as he struggled with a stuck chamber. Lining him up, Lena took him out with one bullet and felt a prickle of relief; the living were a greater threat to them at the moment, their autonomy affording them some unpredictability. At least the dead couldn’t think for themselves - even the wights who walked without command couldn’t string a thought together.

 

            Each time she popped her head up, Lena made a few swift shots in succession but her main focus was on the ones who weren’t dead, trying to pinpoint any Necromancer lurking in the bulk of the army to control those at the front. The more of them she could take out, the more she’d incapacitate her brother’s army, leaving him with more bodies than he could properly control. The first she saw was a stocky man, fair-haired and dressed in green, his clothes too pristine to be anything other than new, his movements too smooth to be dead. He was looking right at her.

 

            Lining up the shot, Lena fired it and watched as he raised a hand, the other one reaching for his gun stilling as he twitched his fingers and jerked the skeleton beside him into the path of her bullet. It shattered the skull and the man let go of his control, pulling his gun from its holster and raising it.

 

            Lena was already on the floor of the platform, breathing heavily as sweat soaked her back and brow. “Shit.”

 

            “What?” Kara frantically asked, pulling her rifle from her and handing her the reloaded one.

 

            Blotting her forehead as she raised her hat, Lena’s mouth thinned. “Necromancer.”

 

            “Did he see you?”

 

            “Of course he saw me. It’s fine, just stay down, alright? Don’t come up.”

 

            Kara mumbled her assent and Lena inhaled sharply, tearing a page from her grimoire and grabbing a small fistful of teeth from the barrel they’d stored up there for her. Dragging the heel of her palm across the razor in the sleeve of her coat, Lena let the blood run into her hand as she tightened her fist and started speaking the spell, her power reaching out to the patch of the dead where he’d been lurking. She could feel him there, each bone in his body, the calcified spots of old injuries healed over. Closing her eyes as she kneeled, Lena ground her teeth together and pulled .

 

            It was a difficult spell, one that was hard to contain, to control, and she would’ve been just as likely to kill herself as her opponent if she’d been anyone other than a Luthor. Instead, she overpowered his resistance with relative ease, burrowing into his bones, feeling the fibres from where she crouched, straining her reach as she felt the blood pour down her face.

 

            His scream was a slow thing, distant at first and then growing in pitch as she took control of him, perhaps one of the most invasive spells a Necromancer could perform, and not strictly allowed by Witch Doctors, but which Lena had been made privy to under her brother’s tutelage. Slowly but surely as his screams turned violent, Lena pulled his bones apart - not at the joints, but from the very fibres, splintering him apart from the inside out. It was a spell she’d never had cause to use, but nothing could be spared in war. If the townsfolk thought it an atrocity, let them see if they felt similarly after she’d killed her way to their safety.

 

            She felt him die a moment before his body virtually exploded, blood and muscle splattering as he was undone from the inside. The sound of nothing but gunshots and rattling bones felt deafening as she screams cut off and Lena pushed herself to her feet, letting a few burnt-out husks of teeth clatter to the platform as she picked up her rifle, glancing over the top of the wall to watch as a few hundred bodies collapsed with no one to control them.

 

            Seizing the opportunity, Lena snagged more teeth from the barrel and wiped the blood from her face to power it before reaching out to raise the dead and turn them on the advancing crowd. She managed them all, scattering them throughout the crowd at intervals before rifling through her grimoire, splayed in her lap as she left bloody thumbprints on the edges until she found the correct page. Tearing it with frantic fingers, Lena scrunched it up and rose to her feet, feeling the thrum in her veins as she pulled on the heat within the teeth she burned through and channelled it into the marrow of the dead.

 

            There was a pause before the bodies went up in flames, bones splitting and cracking as fire blossomed outwards, catching on the dried scraps of clothes and patches of hair of the surrounding dead. It was destructive, especially when she could’ve used them to bulk out their own army, but she wouldn’t be able to mobilise them all at once, and as she watched some of the lit ones stumble into the shallow pits of oil and tar, setting them alight too in another chain reaction, it made her feel vindicated. The fires would eat away at the army at a slower rate than the explosives, but it would amount to more than a few dozen reduced to ash, along with the few hundred she’d poached. 

 

            Still, it was never-ending, and the afternoon wore on, leaving Lena feeling ragged and worn out as she pushed onwards. The first assault reached the walls, falling into the trenches and spearing themselves on spikes, while others tried to clamber up the walls, to no avail. It offered easy targets for those without bone bullets, blasting apart limbs and skulls with ordinary bullets, incapacitating the skeletons in the process. It made it easier for Lena to take them for herself then, the cord of magic cut as the losses were abandoned, and she used them to scour for Necromancers.

 

            She found another one in the middle of the army, a woman with dark hair on the back of a skeletal horse, and lost almost all of the dead she sent to drag her down as the woman tore them apart and overwhelmed Lena’s attack. Frustrated, Lena spent the next three hours honing her attack on her, before she finally managed to seize control of the horse and buck her from the saddle. When the Necromancer was down, Lena detonated a skeleton and listened to the woman scream as her skin burned, trying to pat it out with her hands as the teeth she was using slipped from her grasp. Her army dropped momentarily, and Lena used that pause to take them for herself and stampede the woman, before casting a wide net through the fray, cutting off a portion of the advancing army from the remainder behind it.

 

            It was getting dark and the shots were still ringing out by the time Lena was relieved by Vasquez and one of the better shots in town. Climbing down the ladder, feeling sore and irritable, Lena doffed her hat and sniffed, tasting blood at the back of her throat.

 

            Gathering on the verandah of J’onn’s hotel, they all gave each other weary, concerned looks. Lena took the canteen offered to her and drank with relief, the looks everyone gave her rolling off her back as she envisioned her bloody face, imagined what they’d thought of the screams, the fires, the violence. She was everything they’d always thought her to be as she’d torn through the bodies as quickly as she could, but she couldn’t bring herself to care, knowing what the alternative was.

 

            “So, that’s it for today?” Kara asked, brushing her sweaty hair back and running her palms on her thighs.

 

            “Oh, no, he won’t let up,” Lena stiffly replied, wiping her sleeve across her sweaty brow. “It’ll be an all-night assault. I imagine he’s hoping to overwhelm us quickly, but the longer we hold out, the more we deplete his resources. He hasn’t even begun to show his abilities yet. We’ll need to take shifts.”

 

            “The soldiers will be used to long hours,” J’onn said, “they can man the walls tonight. Get the less experienced folk to bed; they can do the day watch when they can see what they’re shooting at.”

 

            “Don’t waste the bullets tonight,” Lena cautioned him. “We’d be better off blowing through our explosives first and trying to thin the ranks out.”

 

            He nodded and went off in search of Lockwood and his cronies, his old military experience garnering some respect from the soldiers in town. Lena rubbed at her eyes and sighed before meeting everyone else’s eyes in turn.

 

            “You should sleep while you can,” she murmured.

 

            “And you?” Kelly softly prompted.

 

            Shaking her head, Lena sighed, “someone needs to stay up and watch over things, and none of you can command an army of the dead, or sense someone else’s army. I’ll know his movements. If he means to encircle us, we’ll know.”

 

            “You ought to sleep too,” Kara murmured, pressing a hand to the warm leather of her coat, between her shoulder blades. “You need your strength a hell of a lot more than we will to do what you can.”

 

            Reaching out to touch her elbow, Lena gave her a thin smile, “I’ll sleep tomorrow.”

 

            Lena conveniently forgot to mention at what time though, staying up all through the night as she picked off skeletons in the dark by feeling alone. Her brother wouldn’t have risked anything extreme in the dark, where he was as blinded as she was, so it was a purely physical assault, trying to break through the gates and clamber over the walls to no avail. Most of the bullets used up were ordinary, splintering bodies apart for them to be snatched up by Lena and reassembled, turned on the army they’d been a part of moments before.

 

            She fired off shot after shot with her rifle, slower now that she had to reload herself, and the ground was littered with piles of broken bones when dawn rose to highlight the damage she’d inflicted. Still, she kept going, silent when Kara arrived, holding a bowl of oats and a cup of weak coffee, taking over for Lena for a while as she shovelled down her breakfast. Once she was finished, she took up the other rifle and the two of them fired in unison, Kara a decent shot as she picked off any close by, while Lena targeted certain spots.

 

            “You should rest now,” Kara told her after an hour had passed.

 

            “I’ll rest later,” Lena dismissively replied.

 

            “Lena-”

 

            Ducking down and turning, Lena gave her a placating smile, touching her fingers to Kara’s cheek. “Don’t worry about me; I once spent three days holding a point guard in a skirmish in Montana. No rest, no food.”

 

            “Just because you can doesn’t mean you should.”

 

            “Wise words,” Lena hummed in agreement, her fingers smoothly loading the rifle before she went back at it.

 

            She managed to locate another two Necromancers out in the army, but they were too far out for her to reach them, weaving on horseback through the ranks as they tried to split the army and encircle the town. The townsfolk on the east and west walls made quick work of the dead trying to inch around, and Lena could almost feel her brother’s frustration as the head-on approach failed. If he kept this up, eventually the waves of the dead he threw against the walls would give out as the town picked off too many of them, but there was that chance that the walls would buckle first, allowing them to flood the streets.

 

            But Lena knew her brother, and if the straightforward approach didn’t work, he wouldn’t waste time on patience, he would turn to his tricks. The first came as the sun peaked overhead, a quartet of dead horses dragging a sparking sled of explosives right towards the gate. Lena picked off one of the ones on the left, dragging the horses off balance as they veered to her right. Still, by the time the dynamite exploded, the horses had made it to the outlying buildings on the east side of the town, where a few soldiers were holed up on the rooftops, taking out about a dozen of them in a shower of splinters and smoke.

 

            Lena let out a sharp hiss through her teeth, watching as the black cloud dissipated and charred bones and the skeletal remains of what had been the homes of a few townsfolk left a dark stain on the land. Still, they’d avoided the gate being blasted open, so it wasn’t as bad as it could have been, although she felt guilty for saying so, but when J’onn echoed her thoughts an hour later at an impromptu meeting, she realised that they could only view it as the cost of war.

 

            By late afternoon, Lena was flagging though. For all her talk of being able to go days without rest, Lena had let too much blood, felt weary right down to her bones after raising so many dead, after being called away from the wall to heal some injuries for those who’d been shot by the dead that were armed. They shot with deadly aim under the guidance of the Necromancers and more than one person bit it with a bone bullet in them before Lena could gouge it out and heal them. Another cost of war.

 

            Eventually, she stole a few hours of sleep, right before dusk when their small army could still see, could still shoot their enemies. Holed up in her room at the hotel, Lena was almost feverish as she drank a tonic she ground up for herself, knocking herself out as her body tried to regain as much energy as possible. When she woke to the deep blue tint of night creeping in, Lena made herself another tonic, grinding up the herbs with water and downing the bitter liquid as it shocked her system back to life.

 

            With a meal of dried pork and potatoes, a jug of water and some coffee, she was back outside in yesterday’s clothes, pulling back the bolt handle as her boots crunched through the layer of settled dirt. Catching sight of Kelly, Lena made straight for her, giving her a resigned look as she dipped her head.

 

            “Ma’am. Have I missed much?”

 

            “You haven’t been gone long enough to miss much at all, Doc,” Kelly disapprovingly replied, her eyes flitting over Lena’s face, taking in the pink tinge of blood she hadn’t washed off properly, the dark bruises beneath her eyes and the shocking pallor of her skin. “Shouldn’t you be resting more?”

 

            With a hollow smile, eyes creasing at the corners as she flashed her teeth, Lena ran a hand over her face. “I’ll have enough time for that when I’m dead. Which might very well be soon. Where’s Kara?”

 

            Kelly nodded to the platform on the right of the gate, where Alex had taken up post so far. Lena squinted, taking in the two sisters, alternating popping up and shooting beyond the wall while the other reloaded. 

 

            “They’ve been at it since you went to rest,” Kelly said with a sigh.

 

            “J’onn’s saddled up a few of the soldiers to take them through the south gate and drive a wedge into the army from the west,” M’gann said as she approached, wiping her hands on her britches, her cracked pistol over her arm.

 

            “You’re riding with him?” Lena asked, nodding in response to his wife’s confirmation. She hesitated as she drummed her fingers on her grimoire and nodded again. “I’ll saddle Hecate.”

 

            Kelly’s arm darted out to snag the sleeve of her coat, “Lena-”

 

            Gently prying the Mayor’s hand off her sleeve, Lena cocked her head to the side and raised her eyebrows. “Ma’am-”

 

            “She’s going to follow you,” Kelly murmured, her voice low and frantic, throat bobbing. “And then Alex will follow, and I’ll have no choice but to follow.”

 

            “None of you should follow.”

 

            “No, indeed, none of us should , but we will. You’ll be of more use in here - you’ve said it before.”

 

            Pointing to the wall, Lena’s mouth thinned. “There are seven thousand corpses out there; I can’t let a hundred men on horseback ride out with no cover. That’s suicide.”

 

            “J’onn’s a seasoned soldier, he wouldn’t lead men to die.”

 

            “No,” Lena agreed, “and his tactic is good, but there are Necromancers out there too. Did you see what I did to that man yesterday? That woman? Yes? I’ll not let that happen to anyone here. I can’t heal that.”

 

            Kelly paused and her eyes darted over to Alex. “I’ll tell them you’re still in bed. It’ll give you enough time to get out before we barricade the gate again.”

 

            Hesitating between letting Kara know and keeping her safe, Lena nodded as she swallowed her guilt. Hurrying to the stables, she saddled Hecate with the practised efficiency of someone who had done it a thousand times before in a rush before she hauled herself up into the saddle and brought Hecate out into the alley at a trot. She gripped her rifle in one hand and the reins in the other, manoeuvring her way out onto the main street, finding J’onn and M’gann on horseback waiting for her.

 

            As the trio trotted towards the south gate Lena heard a shout behind her and squared her shoulders as she winced. She could imagine Kara’s anger, later on, eclipsing the worry she currently felt, and knew it’d be better to ask for forgiveness than reason with her to stay behind. But she had no cause to ask forgiveness, because a moment later, she felt someone bump her arm and had to bite back a group as she saw that Kara had caught up to their gentle trot, sweating and panting as she gripped the straps of the saddlebags and heaved herself up behind Lena.

 

            Unable to do anything but scoot forward to make as much space as possible, settling in for an uncomfortable ride, Lena suppressed a sigh as Kara perched awkwardly behind her, one arm wrapping around her waist and her lips brushing Lena’s ear.

 

            “You thought you could leave without me, huh?”

 

            Grunting with irritation, Lena followed the small horde of soldiers milling about near the gate as they parted to let them out. The sound of the gates thudding shut behind them, and the shuddering planks of wood slamming back into place, followed them as the horde kicked up dust, forming a ribbon of riders rounding the west side of the town.

 

            “You hold on tight,” Lena shouted over her shoulder. “And you stay with me.”

 

            “Always.”

 

            Her heart was doing something funny in her chest as panic set in, an unfamiliar feeling for Lena, and she found herself even more stiff and alert as she took to the point of the charge, bringing them around in a wide arc. She kept it relatively close to the front of the enemy army, not wanting to leave the soldiers surrounded by the dead on all sides, and Hecate trampled the first few corpses in a leaping gait. Around them, the dead reached for Lena, soldiers overtaking her as they wielded clubs and cleavers, dismembering for blunt force damage before they turned to their guns. 

 

            Lena slipped her rifle into the saddlebags, willing the jutting end to stay put as she cut her fingers and pulled a page from her grimoire, reaching out for the binding threads of the Necromancer controlling them and cutting the link to those surrounding her. She then used them as a barricade, pushing the crowd away from her as the swarm tried to drown her, Kara and her horse. 

 

            Feeling her holster lighten a moment later, the sound of it firing made her right ear ring as Kara blasted apart the skull of a corpse that had managed to clamber over the one pushing it back. As Lena spread her web out further, stealing from the enemy as she carved a rift for the soldiers to trot back and forth freely, picking off as many as they could while lobbing sticks of dynamite into the fray, Kara fired the Colt for anyone near enough to be a threat, her fingers scrabbling at Lena’s gun belt to reload once the chambers were empty.

 

            “How are we doing back there?” Lena asked, her voice hoarse as she sweated buckets, blood trickling from her nose and over her chin.

 

            “Dandy,” Kara flatly replied, firing off another shot. “What’s the plan, Doc?”

 

            “Sit tight, Miss, I’m looking for someone to take out.”

 

            It was J’onn who found the next Necromancer though, a weedy man dressed in all black who’d blown the heads off three soldiers with a sawn off shotgun as he used the dead like a shield. Lena managed to overpower him and with the sharp twist of her wrist, snapped his neck like it was no more effort than the motion to skip a good stone across a flat body of water. He went down quickly and J’onn put himself at risk forging through a throng of the dead as he tried to put a bullet in the Necromancer.

 

            As Lena watched, he was dragged from his saddle and she cursed loudly, pausing a moment before glancing over her shoulder at Kara. Hesitating, she exhaled sharply and then nudged her out of the saddle, wincing as Kara’s feet struck dirt before she keeled over backwards from the impact.

 

            “Sorry!” Lena called down before Hecate reared up and she carved a path through the army.

 

            It took all of her mental power to keep that safe spot open for the soldiers within as she thundered through the crowd towards J’onn, but even still, the dead broke through as her skeletons were pulled apart. Hoping the line would hold while Kara was safely enclosed within, Lena bent low over Hecate’s neck, having to yank her foot from the stirrup to lash out with a sharp kick every so often, breaking jaws and clavicles in the process.

 

            Pulling up sharp at the pile of corpses burying the spot where J’onn had been, Lena found herself embroiled in a game of tug-of-war for a moment as the skeletons tried to whisk away the Necromancer so he could be revived by her brother, while she snatched up a few skeletons to stop them. Hecate managed to trample a few, but Lena was worried her horse would accidentally injure J’onn, so after emptying her rifle into the decomposing faces and quickly reloading, she jumped from the saddle and forged forward on foot.

 

            Catching a glimpse of the limp man in black, Lena fired her rifle until she’d thinned the gap enough to catch the fresh corpse in the temple, blowing blood and brain matter over the skeletons carrying him, before they turned their attention to her. Their grasps were painfully tight as she pushed through them and almost tripped over J’onn as his arm grabbed her ankle. Relief shot through her, sharp and clear, and she soaked a few teeth in blood and flung her arms wide with an indecipherable shout, the spell creating something akin to a shockwave as the skeletons all stumbled backwards a few feet.

 

            Reaching down, Lena hauled J’onn to his feet, finding him dusty and limping a little as he cradled his ribs - possibly broken, she assessed - but otherwise fine. Lena whistled sharply and Hecate fought her way towards her, allowing Lena to help J’onn up into the saddle before slapping the horse’s rump to send her onwards.

 

            Clinging to her magic to maintain her control, plucking more teeth from her pouch to replace the burnt-out husks that disintegrated in her palms, Lena forged onwards, batting the dead aside with the butt of her rifle. She fell a couple of times, the taste of blood filling her mouth as she bit her tongue, and had to scramble backwards, pointing the rifle ahead before she blew the head off a suspiciously fresh corpse that filled the air with the rotting smell of its innards as it crumpled.

 

            Closing the gap back to safety, Lena fired off a shot and whirled around, hand raised as she clenched her fingers around a torn piece of paper and reduced half a dozen of the dead into ashes in a ten-foot radius around her. She could taste the blood on her lips, feeling it running from her eyes and down her cheeks, knowing how terrifying she must look, but she didn’t stop. She wasn’t tireless, but she fought as if she had all the energy in the world, as if she could single-handedly defeat the horde. 

 

            And then a shot fired and she found Kara instinctively, pushing towards her to urge her away as fear distracted her. Lena couldn’t afford to be distracted, and Kara could fire from the parapets just as well - perhaps even better with the length of her rifle making it unwieldy so close to the approaching masses of the dead. She’d only taken a few steps towards her when another shot rang out behind her, missing Lena entirely as she watched it burrow into the thigh of the woman before her and felt the world narrow to the sound of Kara’s cry of pain.

14. Chapter 14

            Lena barreled into her just as Kara collapsed.

 

            Leg giving out, shock etched on her face as her blue eyes widened, her lips moving soundlessly as her rifle slipped from her grasp, she clutched at her thigh, where a red stain was already blossoming. Kara’s name fell from Lena’s lips as she bore the brunt of her weight, trying to keep her propped up as the teeth tumbled from her hand, her grasp on her magic fading as dozens of skeletons crumpled to bones. 

 

            The advancing army swarmed the soldiers who’d ridden out with her, and they pulled back, cursing, while Lena’s attention was solely on Kara. She’d been shot in the thigh, the bullet stuck in her leg as she bled - fast - and Lena was consumed by the panicked thought that Kara would die if she didn’t get the bullet out. Lena wouldn’t be able to bring her back.

 

            Hauling her over her shoulder, gritting her teeth at the effort, Lena half-dragged her back towards the fence, the toes of Kara’s boots creating two shallow grooves in the dirt and grass as her limp weight was helpless against Lena’s strength. Sweating and breathing heavily beneath her burden, Lena forged a path back towards the walls, a bullet striking the dirt beside her as it missed before another one scraped the top of her shoulder, searing her with pain. It was shallow and would bleed slow enough for her to not be concerned at the moment. It did make it more difficult to tow Kara along though, her bunched shoulder protesting.

 

            “Alex,” Lena shouted, cutting through the gunfire of the abnormally quiet battle. “Alex, open the fucking gates.”

 

            They wouldn’t do it, wouldn’t risk losing their flimsy defence to let the duo inside, not even if it was the Sheriff’s sister. Alex hadn’t even known Kara was out there - or at least didn’t have any prior knowledge before spying her on the back of Lena’s horse. But Lena was frantic, dragging with all of her might, her muscles burning and weak, and in a last-ditch effort as the walls loomed closer, she grabbed a fistful of teeth from her waist and bit into the soft part of her thumb, hard enough to draw blood, leaving her teeth stained ghoulishly red.

 

            Raggedly breathing, a filthy, sweating mess with a heart that felt like it was going to pound out of her chest, Lena dragged the nearest skeletons to her, their bony hands hard and pinching as she willed them to lift her and Kara. Born aloft by a sea of bones, they uplifted each other to form a perilous structure raising the two living women up to the top of the wall. Lena was oblivious to the moment the townsfolk realised it would be that easy to overwhelm Midvale, too relieved that she was spilling onto the platform that Alex had control of, Kara letting out a small cry as she sprawled heavily onto the floor.

 

            “She’s been shot,” Lena managed to get out, already dragging Kara towards the ladder by the collar of her shirt.

 

            Alex was pale and leapt to attention, hauling herself over the side and dropping onto the ladder, landing heavily on the dirt ground below as she reached up. Lena nudged Kara’s legs out from under her, watching as her lover’s face contorted with pain, still clinging to consciousness through it all, and lowered her over the side until her strength gave out. Kara fell like a sack of stones, Alex breaking her fall with much puffing and cursing as she collapsed beneath her waist, no doubt earning a handful of nasty bruises.

 

            Jumping down, knees aching in protest as a puff of dust rose around her, Lena was hauling Kara up, Alex taking half of her weight as she jammed her shoulder into Kara’s armpit, and they made a swift bee-line for the hotel. A few of their friends peeled away from the fray, their rapid footsteps following as they all converged on the front porch. Lena didn’t dare waste time getting Kara upstairs, onto a bed or somewhere similarly comfortable. There was no time for that, no time for anything but sending Kelly to fetch her chest where she’d stowed it just inside, near enough for easy access.

 

            Alex helped lower Kara down onto the sun-warmed wood, a gasp of pain slipping from bloodless lips as Kara made a low sound of agony at the back of her throat. Already dropping to her knees beside her, Lena felt her throat close up, guilt eating away at her. She’d never wanted Kara to go out with her; she should’ve listened to her instinct.

 

            “Can you save my leg?” Kara asked, her face grey with a sheen of sweat, twisted with pain as she lost too much blood too fast.

 

            “I’ll do you one better,” Lena muttered as she dragged her chest across the wooden porch of the hotel, opening it up and plucking a Piedfort coin from amidst the medical paraphernalia. 

 

            Kara’s eyes were wide and Lena gave her an agonised look of apology, gripping the coin in her fist as she struggled to swallow. The thigh of Kara’s pants were soaked with dark blood and Lena knew that a femoral artery wound would kill someone quicker than she could heal them, and she concluded that Kara had been shot pretty damn close to it, even if she was still drawing breath. That wasn’t what worried her though, not entirely. She could bring someone back if they’d been shot, but it was the bone bullet that would make it impossible for her to do that which had Lena’s face pinched with panic.

 

            She’d never felt so frantic in her life, tearing open the seam of Kara’s pants with her bare hands, ripping stitches to expose the pale skin covered in vivid blood. “I need you to trust me, Kara,” she said, her voice trembling as her hands shook like never before. “Do you hear me? I need you to trust me. It’s going to hurt, but I’ll make it better, alright?”

 

            Yanking a knife from the sheath at her waist, Lena’s eyes darted up to Alex, Kelly and M’gann. “I need you to hold her still.”

 

            They immediately grabbed arms and legs, while Lena pinned the injured one, wincing as she gouged the tip of the knife into the bloody mess of the bullet wound. Kara’s shout was ragged and ear-splitting as she strained against them, the tendons in her neck taut as she went shockingly white. M’gann knelt at her head and lifted it into her lap, quietly speaking to her as she held her still.

 

            “Can’t you just heal her?” Alex stiffly asked through her teeth, struggling to keep her sister pinned.

 

            Blood made Lena’s hands slick as she parted flesh to the sound of Kara’s broken screaming, wanting someone to gag her but knowing it wouldn’t lessen the guilt or her pain. “No,” Lena firmly replied, her voice low and trembling. “If she dies with the bullet inside her … I can’t bring her … back.”

 

            Lena prised the bullet from the muscle of Kara’s leg, bringing forth a fountain of blood, worsened by the damage inflicted by her knife, and Lena tossed it aside impatiently, holding out a shaking hand as she beckoned to Alex.

 

            “Give me your gun.”

 

            Unholstering it with a mystified look on her face, Alex handed it over and Lena brushed her hair out of her face, sniffing and clearing her throat as she pulled the hammer back and then pointed it at Kara’s forehead.

 

            “Trust me,” she softly pleaded as Kara’s blue eyes met her own.

 

            Unable to speak, her face so white that she would be suffering a long while if Lena healed her and let her recover herself. She would be helping by speeding things along, bring her back to full health instead of merely healing the wound and leaving her weak. Kara understood that and shallowly nodded, but before she could shoot her dead, Alex’s hand snatched out and grabbed Lena’s wrist as she realised what she intended to do.

 

            “Hold on now, Doc-”

 

            “Sheriff, let go-”

 

            “I’m not letting you shoot my kid sister.”

 

            Exhaling roughly as frustration and impatience lashed through her, Lena pulled herself forward, her eyes bright with a manic look as she bared her teeth. “She’s going to die either way. She’s lost too much blood . You can either let her suffer a few minutes longer, or you let me do my job.”

 

            “Damn you,” Alex snapped, letting Lena go.

 

            She fell back hard on the wood, bruising her tailbone as she was left with the Sheriff’s gun, mercifully loaded with plain bullets, as Lena carefully checked. There was a scowl on her face and her stomach swooped, Kara’s eyelashes fluttering as she dwelled on the edges of consciousness, a spreading pool of blood beneath her, and then she shot her in the forehead.

 

            Everyone startled slightly at the casual display of murder, Kara’s entire body going slack the moment the bullet struck her on the brow, and they all sat back numbly before Lena roughly gestured them away. Scrambling through the chest of her tools, she grabbed fistfuls of herbs and piled them on the wood, thrusting a hand out.

 

            “Matches?”

 

            A pack was dropped in her hand and she lit one with the stench of rotten eggs before lighting the pile on fire, smoke billowing from it as she inhaled the aroma and wafted it towards Kara. Reaching out, Lena tore open the front of Kara’s shirt and Alex made a sound of indignation.

 

            “At least show her some dignity.”

 

            “Fetch blankets,” Lena dismissively replied. “You’re no good to me here.”

 

            Sniffing as she wiped at her face, her eyes bloodshot even if they were dry, Alex seethed, unable to look at her sister’s dead body as she channelled her fear into hatred. “You’re cracked. The whole lot of you. We’re in this mess because of you.”

 

            “Go,” Lena harshly replied, fumbling out of her leather duster and rolling up her sleeve before slashing the knife across her arm and then letting it clatter to the boards beneath her. 

 

            “If you don’t bring her back, I’ll kill you myself.”

 

            She had the blood-slick coin in her hand and worked Kara’s stiff jaw open, still slack enough for her to work it open instead of breaking it. Lena didn’t think that would go over well with Alex. Forcing the thick gold coin into Kara’s mouth, she then dabbed at the blood on her arm and started tracing out the sigils and runes she’d been raised with. The smoke made her throat raw and dry as she said the words, ignoring the activity around her as she fell into the familiar trance-like state of her work.

 

            It was the first time she’d done it for someone she cared for, someone she loved , for that was what it was, even if she couldn’t voice it. Her hands trembled for the first time in her life and she was seized with fear that it wouldn’t work. She’d gotten the bullet out intact, had removed the magic that would stop her from being revived, so there was no logical reason why it wouldn’t work, but Lena was suddenly filled with a cold dread that this would be the time her magic failed her. 

 

            The herbs burned, paper torn from her grimoire in her fist with three teeth, blood flowing freely from her hand, and Lena intoned the spell of the dead as everyone else watched on with horror. Gunshots split the day and Alex had returned with blankets, restless and tense as she watched behind Lena, hands balled into fists. Sweat ran down Lena’s face, mingling with blood as she kept going, reeling the soul in as she wove the body back together.

 

            M’gann crossed herself in a rather amusing pious gesture as the bullet in Kara’s head wormed its way back out, flesh and bone and brain matter knitting itself back into shape, the muscle of her rent thigh repairing itself before her skin smoothed out. By the time the teeth had burned themselves out and the spell died on Lena’s lips, Kara looked as if she was sleeping.

 

            And then she woke up screaming, just like they all did, her body going taut on the wooden planks as her eyelids fluttered, eyes rolling beneath them. A small, broken cry of relief escaped Alex, who leaned over to brace her hands on her knees, hat toppling off, while Lena anxiously crawled forward to cup Kara’s face in her bloody hands, leaving two grim prints on her cheeks.

 

            “Don’t move,” Lena gently urged her, tender relief ripping through her as her eyes smarted. She told herself it was the smoke of the herbs, fanned by her urgency. “You’re alright.”

 

            A hoarse cry fell from Kara’s lips as she came back to herself, and Lena knew she would be aching fiercely, a lingering pain in her limbs. Clammy and still a little pale, Kara moved slowly as Lena helped ease her up, holding a hand up to keep Alex at bay.

 

            “Best not get too close.”

 

            Ignoring her, Alex loyally knelt beside her sister, hands gripping her as she looked at her with a haunted look in her eyes, trying to reconcile the dead body with the very much alive person before her eyes. Mouth thinning with grim exasperation, Lena studied Kara for a moment and then shifted out of the way.

 

            And then Kara turned aside and retched, her whole body convulsed by the effort, and vomited right into her sister’s lap. Kelly heaved and turned away as the air turned sour with the smell of it, but Lena was used to all things foul and messy and just climbed to her feet, ducking inside to fetch a bottle of moonshine from behind the bar.

 

            She re-emerged, prying the cork from the ceramic jug, while Alex cursed and tried to mop at her legs with her untied neckerchief. Lena just gave her a slightly smug look of condescension and handed the moonshine to Kara, before tenderly wrapping her in blankets as the shivers set in and carefully buttoned up her shirt for her, draping her own cream duster over her legs.

 

            “You don’t remember so don’t ask,” Lena reminded her and Kara nodded, looking ghostly with shock.

 

            Her hands shook as Lena gathered them up in her own bloody ones and she kissed Kara’s scarred knuckles before giving her a regretful smile.

 

            “You need to rest. Eat and drink; it’ll help calm you. And then go inside and sleep.”

 

            “You need to rest,” Kara rasped, finally speaking for the first time.

 

            “All in good time.”

 

            Climbing to her feet, Lena sheathed her knife and grabbed her abandoned rifle before she turned to Alex. The Sheriff still looked a little stunned and Lena softly sighed, stooping to pluck a tonic from her chest and then palming it off.

 

            “Make her drink this. You take a break; I’ll handle it from here.”

 

            Numbly nodding, Alex’s face crumpled and she turned towards Lena, her eyes not seeing her. “Thank you.”

 

            Nodding, Lena paused and then fetched Alex’s pistol as well, shoving it into her holster for her and clapping her on the shoulder. Kelly fell into step beside Lena, her own rifle in hand, and let out a low whistle as she shook her head.

 

            “I’ve never seen anything like that, Doc. Eerie, isn’t it?”

 

            With a wan smile, Lena tugged her hat down low over her face and then pulled back the bolt on the rifle, sliding a bullet into place. There was a slump to her shoulders and a tremor to her hands as waning adrenaline still coursed through her. Nothing had ever rattled her so much and she felt weak with relief.

 

            “That’s just a day of work for a Witch Doctor,” Lena airily replied.

 

            Hauling herself up the ladder with the weary air of someone sick of fighting and death and blood, Lena took up a post and surveyed the battle. The soldiers she'd ridden out with were holding their own, J’onn still on Hecate’s back, cradling his ribs as he bellowed orders and regrouped before making another mad dash through the vanguard of Lex’s army. It was a tactic they’d used a few times already, the dusty plain littered with splintered bones and bloated corpses that filled the air with their rancid smell.

 

            Taking stock of things, Lena started her methodical shooting with Kelly similarly taking action beside her. Wilting beneath the heat, the strain of too much magic and not enough sleep to keep her going, Lena shot and shot, eyes bloodshot, face ghastly, and nothing but sips of water, whisky and shared cigarettes rolled by the Mayor to see them through it.

 

            Lena had already spent too much blood but she had to spill a little more, reopening the angry bite mark to make a sudden pushback against the advancing army. The collapsed bones knit themselves back together in a woven wall, creating a flimsy barrier that made it easier to pick off the dead as they clambered over, dropping to a bullet or impaling themselves on spikes of flaming patches of oil. It was tedious work and Lena could feel the pressure of a headache pounding behind her eyes and at her temples, while her shoulders ached with the repetition of levelling the rifle and firing.

 

            Alex joined them what must have been well over an hour later, two bowls of food stacked and a lit cigarette between her teeth. She sat on the edge of the platform, puffing smoke as Lena shovelled feed into her mouth.

 

            “How is she?”

 

            “Sleepin’ … well, like the dead, ain’t it?”

 

            “She’ll be alright. It’s better in the long run.”

 

            “Aye.”

            

            Accepting the cigarette, Lena inhaled deeply and exhaled a plume of grey, before taking a swig of dank water hauled from a well and tearing a bite off her salted pork. The afternoon was dragging on and she knew she’d have to sleep soon to make it through the night without nodding off. As if sensing her line of thought, Alex narrowed her eyes and took a swig of whisky, flicking ash off the dwindling rolled cigarette.

 

            “You look a rotten sight, Doc. You ain’t about to drop dead, are you?”

 

            “Not yet.”

 

            “I reckon you ought to take a break now.”

 

            Reluctant to give in, to be weakened by something so mundane as exhaustion, Lena let out a weary sigh. “I should.”

 

            “Go on then. I’ll take over.”

 

            “Fetch someone to wake me before dusk. We’ll trade off then.”

 

            “Yes, ma’am.”

 

            “And get J’onn back inside before then. No good routing them if we lose all our good soldiers in the process. If I know my brother, he’ll tire of their little attacks sooner rather than later.”

 

            “You don’t need to tell me about war, Doc. We’ll sort them out and keep everyone safe. You just worry about sleeping and taking a bath.”

 

            “I’m not the one who smells of vomit.”

 

            Sniffing derisively, Alex gave her a disgruntled look. “You might’ve warned me.”

 

            With a sharp smile, Lena cocked an eyebrow. “I tried, but on account of your prejudice and distrust, I thought you rather deserved it, didn't you?”

 

            Flipping her off, Alex grumbled beneath her breath and Lena chuckled, leaving her rifle up there to be used before climbing down the ladder. She sucked at a splinter on her way back to the hotel, pausing at the spot where she’d shot Kara and sighing heavily.

 

            Pushing through the doors and moving through the empty saloon, the sounds of battle muffling behind her, Lena wearily plodded upstairs. Her room was unlocked and she stepped into the dim space, a fire blazing and the dark outline of Kara’s form huddled near the fire. It gave Lena pause and she doffed her hat, shoulders slumping, before shutting the door behind her and kicking off her muddy boots.

 

            “You should be sleeping,” Lena softly said.

 

            Making a distracted sound of agreement, Kara half-turned, tracking the sound of Lena’s footsteps padding over the creaking floorboards as she rounded the table. Dropping to a knee at Kara’s side, a listless sigh slipped through Lena’s lips as her face crumpled with anguish.

 

            “Are you alright?”

 

            “You know that I am,” Kara said, smiling as she rubbed absentmindedly at her bare thigh.

 

            She was wearing one of Lena’s clean shirts, hanging down to mid-thigh, exposing the smooth skin of her leg. Lena placed a gentle kiss to her soft skin.

 

            “Forgive me. I know it hurt, but-“

 

            Kara softly hushed her, her face bathed in orange light as Lena looked up. “You saved my life. It ain’t no small thing, that. Thank you, Lena.”

 

            “I would have gladly given my own if it had saved you,” Lena murmured, casting her eyes down at the vulnerability she bared.

 

            “It didn’t feel how I thought,” Kara mused. “It ain’t what you said.”

 

            “I know. I didn’t want to frighten you,” Lena whispered, her voice ragged with guilt. “It’s not something one can easily explain either. Forgive me.”

 

            “There ain’t nothing to forgive,” Kara murmured, leaning down to kiss Lena’s greasy hair.

 

            Lena hummed, the sound frayed and exhausted, and she pressed her fingers into her eyelids, exhaling sharply. Turning her head, she placed her cheek against Kara’s thigh and felt her hand rest on her head, some of the worry knotted in her chest easing a little.

 

            “Kara,” she whispered.

 

            “Mm?”

 

            “If I- if I asked you to run … would you? Would you do that for me?”

 

            Her response was slow to come, halting and strained. “We- we can’t leave everyone.”

 

            “No, I can’t, but you-“

 

            “No,” Kara cut her off. “I ain’t a coward. I ain’t going to run while everyone stays.”

 

            Eyes squeezed shut against the fear that sat in her stomach like a stone, Lena swallowed thickly. “Alright.”

 

            There was a momentary pause before Kara spoke, her voice a whisper and her face crumpled. “Why would you ask me that?”

 

            And Lena couldn’t bear to lie to her, so she told her the truth. “Because I’m frightened.”

 

            There had been moments she’d felt fear, but it had all seemed secondary to the cause. Lena’s fear for her own life was something that existed outside of herself, the number of times her brother had killed her just to bring her back again taking the edge of fear off of it, to the point where Lena had wished for its permanency at times. Sure, she woke up screaming like the rest of them, and had the unfortunate memory of how it all happened, but it had never seemed like such a terrifying thing to her if she’d died while roaming the wilderness. God knows enough people tried , and while she had enough self-preservation to flee or fight back, Lena had never really been all that concerned for her own being.

 

            But Kara, the people she’d come to care for, the town she’d unwillingly dragged into this mess, even if the mess was coming for them regardless of her presence, filled her with so much fear. It felt debilitating, her chest tight as she struggled to breathe through the fear of getting the entire town killed. It was the responsibility of so much life that got to her - Lena had never been responsible for anyone but herself and her horse, let alone someone she loved.

 

            It was a shocking show of weakness for her to admit her fear, and she thought it would spread to Kara, its rotten taint killing what little hope still lingered. Instead, Kara just drew in a shaky breath and let her fingers glide over Lena’s hair, ducking her head down to whisper.

 

            “Then I’ll be unafraid for both of us.”

 

            The air was expelled from Lena’s lungs as she turned her head, pressing her face into the warm skin of Kara’s thigh. She wanted to cling to the clean cotton of her shirt but was such a mess that she just curled her hands into fists. As if sensing her state, Kara clicked her tongue.

 

            “You’re filthy.”

 

            “It hasn’t been a good day.”

 

            “It will be better tomorrow.”

 

            It was easy for Kara to say, meaningless in the grand sense of things, considering the army beyond the walls that they were trying their best to keep at bay while being slowly picked off. But as the words settled over her mind like a warm blanket, Lena was struck with the thought that it would be better tomorrow. It wouldn’t be over, but it wouldn’t be quite so dismal.

 

            Pushing herself to her feet with great effort, Lena sagged and wearily started to undress, unbuckling her belt, undoing the denim overalls and the stained shirt. The basin of water was clear in the corner of her room and she quickly dirtied it, scrubbing her bloodstained hands with the soap. 

 

            Kara moved to her side a minute later, still looking a little pale and haunted, dark circles beneath her eyes, and took the cloth from Lena’s hands. Standing still, Lena closed her eyes and allowed her to wipe the cloth over her face, removing mud and dust and dirt and sweat with gentle passes. Out from beneath the layer of grime came the coldly beautiful face of the Necromancer as she subjected herself to the careful touch of the rancher.

 

            Once she was as clean as she’d get without a hot bath, Lena pulled on one of her dwindling clean shirts and sank onto her bed. A cloud of dust billowed from the sheets and the air was close and stifling in the room, but she was too exhausted to care about the state of things. The hotel, with its lump mattresses, warped floorboards and faded grandeur, was a luxury that she didn’t intend to waste as she fell asleep with Kara beside her.

 

            Waking to the darkness an indeterminable amount of time later, feeling only slightly more rested, Lena slowly sat up. She drew in a deep breath and then exhaled, her eyes feeling gritty and heavy as she ran a hand through her hair. Kara was still sleeping beside her and she leaned over to kiss her head before slipping out of bed.

 

            It was dark beyond the windows, the crack of gunfire sputtering nearby, and Lena frowned with annoyance. She should have been woken already. Hurriedly dressing, she snatched up her coat where Kara had left it and donned her hat before making her way down to the street below, striding down to the north gate with long steps.

 

            Her feet thundered on the ladder as she rushed up it, watching as Alex ducked back down to reload and glanced up at her. A thin, guilty smile crossed the Sheriff’s face as her fingers halted and then redoubled their effort.

 

            “Howdy, Doc.”

 

            “I told you to wake me.”

 

            “And I ain’t in the business of following orders,” Alex nonchalantly replied, tapping the star-shaped badge pinned to the vest she was wearing. “I give ‘em. That’s what this means.”

 

            Ignoring her, Lena snatched up her abandoned rifle and then moved towards the wall, peering over the top into the blackness of the night beyond. She reached out with her magic, taking stock of things and finding that her flimsy barrier of bones had been breached in a dozen places. Calling on the threads of her power, Lena willed the bones to shift, a tidal wave of collagen, calcium and marrow rising up and consuming the front ranks of her brother's army, swallowing them into the churning mass as the bones solidified into a new wall. 

 

            They couldn’t see much but she could sense it all, the only pair of eyes her army had as he set his against her with full force. Lex’s patience was wearing thin after the second day of fighting began slipping into night, and she could feel the press of his army as contingents peeled away from the main force, slowly but surely encircling Midvale. Lena conveyed his actions to Alex, who barked hoarse orders as fires were lit and they tried to waylay the army by any means.

 

            It was too dark to send riders out and Lena tried her best to hold the tide back, Hecate ferrying her back and forth between the east and west walls, while their best shooters perched on rooftops beyond the walls, gunning down swarm after swarm. 

 

            It was a long night and they yielded the strip of land almost straight to their walls, and halfway around Midvale, the trap closing in around them. Lena knew that once it was light enough for her brother to see, to assess the layout of the town and the state of his army, reviving what he could and what she hadn’t stolen for her own defence, he’d devour the town. It would be a simple thing, leaving the townsfolk with no way to escape while the dead swarmed over the walls in an endless flow, trampling people dead, down to the very last one. She’d seen firsthand the chaos he’d unleashed on other towns, wights and piles of bodies left in his wake, and she was desperate to save Midvale from the same fate.

 

            By the time the first sliver of dawn cracked over the horizon to the east, Lena was depleted, swaying on her feet as her knees felt like they would give out at any moment. Caked in fresh dirt and blood, woozy from losing too much of her own, her chest rose and fell quickly as she finished casting another spell, drawing a nearby cluster of skeletons and corpses into a tight group and then letting her power shred through them, gore splattering over her as she stood atop the walls. 

 

            They’d tried coming over in duos and trios, corpses lifted by skeletons, and the ground inside the gate was littered with broken bones and rotting corpses that had been ripped apart by Lena’s magic, the air fetid with the smell of their decay. It clung to her, nothing new but not altogether pleasant, and Alex had long since moved to the platform on the other side of the gate, picking off those that came over there while she stayed upwind of Lena. 

 

            “He’s going to swarm us,” Lena hoarsely shouted as soldiers pulled back from their perches, trading off with the less skilful shooters for their day shift.
