            “We’ve still got the dynamite,” Alex called back, looking calm and indifferent as she reloaded. “May as well use it while we can, I reckon.”

 

            Lena considered it. “They’re close enough. We should confer with J’onn.”

 

            “He’s sleepin’ off the ribs.”

 

            Cursing, Lena slung her rifle over her shoulder, making for the ladder. “Hold down the fort, Sheriff.”

 

            “You’ve got it, Doc. Hey, bring me back some tobacco, would you? Running a bit low.”

 

            Lena rolled her eyes and watched as Kelly jerked Alex sideways, out of the line of a bullet. Alex swore over the wall and shot back, letting out a quick laugh when her bullet struck home. 

 

            Hurrying towards the hotel, Lena snagged her chest and barged her way through the batwing doors, leaving them swinging behind her. Feet thundering upstairs, she called out until a door creaked open to reveal M’gann’s exhausted face.

 

            “Doc?”

 

            “I’ve come to heal him.”

 

            There was a moment of hesitation before M’gann opened the door to admit her. Their room was more homely than the rest of the hotel, with books and paintings and rugs around the open space, doors to bedrooms and an office leading off it.

 

            “He’s in there,” M’gann said, nodding to one of the doors and moving over to the kettle she was boiling for tea.

 

            Knocking before entering the room, Lena gave the ex-soldier a wan smile. “Forgive me, I should’ve come sooner.”

 

            “How’s it looking?” he asked, ignoring her apology.

 

            “Dire,” Lena gravely replied, setting her chest down at the foot of the mattress and opening it up.

 

            She rattled off numbers and military tactics her brother was employing, although she wasn’t an expert herself and couldn’t judge what his true intention was. All she knew was that he had a lot more dead and less patience and was ready to overrun them for a swift victory.

 

            As she mended J’onn’s ribs and ground up herbs for a tincture to aid with his healing, they exchanged ideas as they tried to cobble together a plan. She mentioned Alex’s ploy for the explosives and he wearily agreed - preserving their stores wouldn’t be much use if they weren’t alive to use them.

            

            By the time she was finished, his ashen face had a bit more colour in it and he was dressing without holding his side. M’gann handed Lena a cup of tea, which she gulped down in three scalding mouthfuls before chewing on dried peppermint leaves to stifle her headache and revitalise her. Leaving the couple to ready themselves to rejoin the shabby army, Lena made her way to her own room to check on Kara.

 

            She found her already awake, midway through getting dressed and looking better than Lena did. Kara just clicked her tongue and shook her head at the sight of her.

 

            “For such a well-bred lady, you sure love gettin’ yourself in a state, Doc.”

 

            “Ah,” Lena shrugged, spreading her fingers as she looked down at her bloody left hand. “Not much to be done about it, I’m afraid. If we survive, a hot bath will be the first order of business, I think.”

 

            “And will we?”

 

            Wincing slightly, Lena couldn’t meet Kara’s eyes. “There have been worse odds.”

 

            “And certainly better.”

 

            Lena’s smile was rueful when she looked at Kara, her green eyes sad and already somewhat defeated. But she would go out kicking and screaming, to the very last breath, until her brother put a bullet in her brain and made sure she never rose again.

 

            “The day is young,” Lena blithely replied, waving a hand. “We’ll turn it around.”

 

            Looking a little pale with apprehension, Kara gave her a stiff nod as she pulled on one of her scuffed boots. Lena hovered a moment before telling her she’d go and fetch them breakfast, slipping down to the kitchens to raid the slim provisions their rations provided, a watery porridge and yesterday’s bread whipped up by M’gann just before Lena had arrived.

 

            She spooned a small amount into her own bowl and gave Kara the rest of her portion before wolfing down her own, ferreting out some tobacco for Alex, and then meeting Kara in the dingy saloon. It was a dismal place without music and laughter and shouting, the smell of beer pervading as early morning sunlight started to lift the grey inside. Kara ate quickly and Lena anxiously paced as she listened to the gunfire outside.

 

            Walking outside, she slowed on the decking as Kara marched onwards, and then darted forward to snag her arm. A lump got caught in Lena’s throat as Kara turned, eyebrows rising with anticipation. Letting go, she fumbled at her neck and removed her medallion, curling her fingers around it as she worked the lump down, swallowing against the tightness in her dry throat.

 

            Picking up Kara’s hand, she pressed the medallion into her palm and curled her fingers around it. “Here.”

 

            “Why are you giving me this?” Kara whispered, her breath hitching as her eyes widened with worry. “You’re not- you’re not going again, are you?”

 

            Lena gave her a strained smile, eyes creasing at the corners. “No. No, I’m not going anywhere. I just- I would like for you to have it. It’s one of my most treasured possessions.”

 

            “Then you ought to keep it,” Kara tried to protest, pushing it back into Lena’s hands.

 

            Shaking her head as she curled Kara’s hand back around it, squeezing tightly, Lena gave her another smile, this one tender and genuine. “No. It’ll be safe with you.”

 

            What Kara didn’t know was that there was a superstition amongst Witch Doctors and the medallions of their order. It was said that it held their souls, and while Lena didn’t believe it, if they were going to die, she wanted to leave her soul with Kara. She didn’t tell her that though, just raised their clasped hands to her lips and kissed her knuckles.

 

            Kara hesitantly nodded and then slipped it over her head, tucking the medallion beneath her shirt and placing a hand over it. She swallowed thickly and gave Lena an earnest look.

 

            “I’ll look after it. I promise.”

 

            Nodding, Lena opened her mouth to say something else when they were interrupted. A shout came from the south and she whirled around, already stepping down to the rutted main street to watch as Nia ran towards her, skirt flapping and a ghostly look on her face as she breathed sharply.

 

            “Doc, we’ve got company. And it ain’t lookin’ good,” the young woman breathlessly told her, coming to a stop before her as she bent over, bracing her hands on her knees.

 

            As Kara put an arm around her shoulders, their heads ducked together, Lena visibly paled and took off as fast as she could, leaving them both behind. Her rifle bounced against her back and a stitch formed in her side, her legs burning from the exertion, and she came to a skidding halt at the bottom of the platform that Querl was standing on, watching whatever lay beyond.

 

            Scrambling up to join him, Lena’s chest rose and fell quickly as she squinted against the blue plains, cursing the slow-rising sun as she brimmed with anxiety. But she could feel with her magic and wanted to scream herself hoarse at the tangible feeling of a couple of hundred dead being led by two very much alive beings. He’d penned them in on both sides like a hammer and an anvil, and her mind strayed to the townsfolk they’d sent to the towns beyond for safe refuge, wondering if they’d been burnt down and slaughtered on the way.

 

            Still, she hedged her bet that she could put a bullet in one of the Necromancer’s, evening the odds a little to take on the other one. If they were proud enough, Lena thought she might even be able to take them on in a formal duel, a chosen skeleton each and a quick draw before she shot them dead.

 

            The butt of the rifle dug into her shoulder and she licked her cracked lips as she squinted, watching the shapes reveal themselves as the column advanced. Lining up the shot, she waited a moment later before she fired with a crack, hoping her aim was true as she shot blindly into the hazy blue morning.

 

            She missed.

 

            “Well, ain’t that a sorry welcome,” a familiar voice shouted from the shadows.

 

            Lena’s stomach plummeted and she pulled the bolt back, slamming another bullet home as she grit her teeth. Kara was just pulling herself up onto the platform, standing at Lena’s shoulder to see for herself, with Alex not far behind, when the head of the small force was finally close enough for Lena to make her out in the dim light.

 

            Sam tipped her head back and smiled, folding her arms over her chest with a pleased look on her face. “And here I thought you might’ve been glad to see me.”

15. Chapter 15

            “Don’t move,” Lena firmly ordered, keeping the gun level.

 

            Sam’s laugh was quick and cut through the sounds of the early morning, the bluish dawn lightening as the sun peeked over the horizon. There was another person beside her, dressed similarly in the coat of their order, and it was a few moments before Lena could place him.

 

            “Spheer?”

 

            “Always a pleasure, Lena,” he replied, touching the brim of his hat, his words clipped and decidedly English. 

 

            She couldn’t see his face but she could hear his amusement and flushed indignantly. Lena had been training in New York at the same time Jack Spheer had arrived fresh off a long voyage from London and entered the underbelly of the cemetery as well. They hadn’t been friends - Lena didn’t have friends and kept her own company - but they’d bled together, been sick together, shivered through long winter nights spent digging graves together. That forged a rather reluctant bond between people and they’d always been cordial whenever their paths had crossed.

 

            “What are you doing here?”

 

            “Came to answer the call, of course.”

 

            “Passed along your message,” Sam shrugged. “He’s the only one that seemed interested in dying. All that English gentleman nobility bullshit. Hell, he convinced me to come with him so … guess it’s a day for idiocy.”

 

            Lena was silent as she weighed their words, her natural inclination to mistrust people creeping up on her now. Sam had shot her, hunted her north until Lena had passed out in Midvale, and Jack … well, he was alright, but that wasn’t enough cause for Lena to trust him right now. Give two Necromancers entrance to the town and they could just as easily turn and slit the throats of everyone in there. Lena was no gullible Trojan; she wouldn’t let the horse inside unchecked.

 

            Gesturing with her rifle, Lena jerked her chin towards the duo. “Prove it.”

 

            “Let us in then,” Sam said, raising her eyebrows.

 

            “Not a chance,” Lena said with a cold laugh. “You shot me-”

 

            “You ain’t still caught up on that, are you? You shot me back . I say it’s even.”

 

            “I told you we were never to meet again.”

 

            Rolling her eyes, Sam gave her an uneven smile, “yeah, well, I didn’t plan on coming back this way until the dust had covered your bones, but … here I am.”

 

            “I don’t like this,” Alex muttered in Lena’s ear. “We can’t trust them.”

 

            Lena wasn’t sure the Sheriff was the best judgement on who to trust or not. She’d put Lena in jail a few times, and she’d been the only thing holding back the army of the dead for the last two days. Not everyone was what they seemed, and Lena knew that Necromancers were as ordinary as the rest of them, but perhaps Sam was a shade more annoying, on account of the bullet she’d put in Lena.

 

            Still, a helpful nuisance was better than no help at all. Lena knew if it came down to it, she’d be able to kill Sam, was more powerful and had more skill. And Jack had only ever been devoted to his healing, heading out west with the others of their kind who wanted to travel. He’d come from old money, his family landed gentry back in England, and this was more of an adventure for him than a means to make a living. Unlike Lena, he could go home and regale the upper class with stories of his time out in the wild west before settling down with a nice practice in the countryside and a generous income as the heir to a gold mine down in Cornwall. 

 

            Lena would rather die out here in Midvale than ever go crawling back to Lillian, begging for a stipend and a quiet life in the gilded house she’d been removed from the moment she’d been eligible. Lena hadn’t even seen her in a few years. But the memory of that scorn, that cool contempt and lofty bearing was enough to make her feel small as she considered all of their options.

 

            “They’re trying to encircle us,” Lena called back. “Hold them back and then we’ll talk about it being even .”

 

            “Any dead to spare?” Jack asked.

 

            Lena’s mouth thinned. She wouldn’t give up a single skeleton under her control. Not when it would thin her numbers and potentially provide her enemies with more bodies to overwhelm her once the tide had turned. Letting out a quick laugh, she arched an eyebrow.

 

            “I’m not in the business of sharing.”

 

            He nodded, a polite smile on her lips. “Perhaps I remember your generosity differently. No matter; we’ll cut the heads off the hydra.”

 

            “Careful. There are more than nine,” Lena darkly warned him.

 

            Her brother had dozens of Necromancers with him - less now since Lena had picked off the easy targets - as well as thieves and runaway soldiers and a few people hoping to pick over the town once it fell. The latter had no skill with the dead, but they were a nuisance, shooting at the townsfolk over the top of the walls, trying to knock soldiers from their saddles and make off with the horses. They’d lost a few soldiers to them, her brother annoyingly arming them with bone bullets that made it impossible for Lena to revive the people they lost.

 

            Two more on her side would make all the difference in the world against the thousands of dead she’d been facing alone. While the armed townsfolk were useful in thinning out the ranks, they weren’t really helpful against the magic that made it so the other Necromancers could keep reanimating corpses and skeletons that hadn’t been permanently put down. Lena couldn’t afford to be picky with her allies - if that’s what they were.

 

            Still, as she watched, wary and tense, Sam and Jack conversed amongst themselves and then split in half, one leading a column of dead around to the western fork of the advancing army, while the other went east with the remainder. Lena watched them go, waiting for a trick, but as morning arrived and wind whistled through the town to the chorus of gunfire, nothing else made a sound.

 

            “Well …” Kara said after a moment, hands in her pockets as she rocked on her heels, rifle clutched in the crook of her elbow.

 

            Alex gave Lena an unimpressed look. “If they turn on us … the deaths are on your head.”

 

            Mouth thinning, Lena sighed and removed her hat, running a hand over her face. “I know.”

 

            “Good,” Alex nodded, appeased with the fact that Lena would take the blame.

 

            She clapped her on the shoulder and made her way back down the ladder. Lena lingered a moment, Querl leaning against the wall in his woollen suit as he chewed a piece of jerky and watched her before she sighed heavily and moved to the ladder.

 

            “We’re all grateful, you know,” he said in his contemplative way of talking, as if he was thinking aloud. “I don’t imagine anyone has said it, but we’d all be dead already without your help.”

 

            Humming dubiously, her head above the platform as she clung to the rough-hewn ladder, Lena’s cheeks dimpled with dismay. “Or maybe he would’ve followed me north if I’d run that way instead.”

 

            Querl frowned slightly, “we both know it would’ve delayed the inevitable.”

 

            Lena hesitated and then nodded. “Quite right.”

 

            Slipping down the rest of the ladder, she followed the rutted road back to the other side of town, hauling herself up onto the platform where Kara perched. Crouching beside her, Lena closed her eyes and felt for the threads of magic, not just before her, but on either side.

 

            “How’s it looking?” Kara anxiously asked.

 

            Forehead puckering with a confused look of surprise, Lena hummed. She could feel Jack’s forces slam into the encircling army on the east, a brutal act of pure aggression as he drove them back. To the west, she felt Sam’s army collide with the dead on her side with a little more delicacy. She was wily and smart, and Lena kept track of her weaving path, small clusters of the dead overwhelming the enemy and adding them to her own forces. While Jack destroyed, Sam poached, and Lena felt a prickle of satisfaction.

 

            “Today is better than yesterday,” Lena said with a crooked smile.

 

            Kara’s expression brightened and Lena inhaled deeply before she reached out for her own army tucked safely behind the walls. She’d mostly kept the townsfolk back, intended as a last resort, but now she thought a quick apologetic prayer and brought them forth from their resting places, swarming up the walls as she let blood soak her hands and the fistful of teeth in each one. Expending too much energy, Lena went on the offensive.

 

            Teeth bared, blood streaking from her eyes and nose, dribbling over her lips and staining her teeth, she tore a path through the army, seeking out anything alive. Lena wasn’t the bloodthirsty kind and had rarely been so vengeful and ruthless, but if ever there was a time for it, it was now. The first she found was a young woman picking her way through Lex’s army to steal wedding bands, belt buckles, necklaces and anything else that was even remotely of value. She didn’t have time to react as she was ripped apart, limb from limb, by a hoard of dead, her screams quickly silenced.

 

            Sitting with her back to the tree trunks of the wall, her knees drawn up to her chest, Lena stared sightlessly ahead as she felt, rather than saw, the battle. Managing to take down two more thieves tagging along, and a Necromancer as well, causing a sudden halt in the front right of the army as a few hundred bodies dropped dead, Lena was breathing heavily. Pages were torn from her grimoire and burnt down to ashes or lay crumpled around her, blood soaking into the paper, and she could feel the slowly creeping army gain ground over them.

 

            Her brother’s gang managed to tear down a couple of the buildings beyond the wall, soldiers swallowed by the dead, and a few of them posted themselves on top of the roofs, staking out a vantage point as they shot the villagers and threw waves of the dead against the walls. They were starting to breach with more frequency now, scrambling over the tops to be shot by those lingering in the streets, nursing flesh wounds or taking a break from the monotonous shooting. Everyone was exhausted and tense, screams and shouts filling the air, soon followed by smoke as fires were set.

 

            Eyes stinging from the smoke as she breathed the acrid taste of it, Lena listened to Kara’s babbling descriptions of what she was feeling beyond. Alex had lit the pitch in the trenches on fire, which was the source of the smoke, and had taken out the teetering pyramids of the dead, who were busy using each other to hoist themselves up onto the wall. It offered a quick reprieve to shoot the ones near the top who had fallen inside the perimeter. 

 

            Deciding now was as good a time as any to bring out the bones of some giant creature, some of them missing which spoke to their age, Lena summoned her dead to ferry them over the walls for her. On the other side, she assembled one into what looked like a giant bear, only three times bigger with a thick jaw, and the other which looked like a drawing of an elephant she’d once seen in one of her father’s encyclopaedias about India and Africa, but it was twice as big with long curved tusks, and Lena didn’t think there had ever been elephants in Colorado. 

 

            They were bigger than anything else her brother had brought with him, bigger than the bears or mountain lions, or even the dead horses being ridden. That also made them easier targets as Lena controlled these strange creatures with their brittle bones, the mammoth remains swaying its tusks side to side, flinging anything in its path aside as it stomped. The remains of the giant ground sloth similarly stomped its way through the left side of the army, and Lena knew they wouldn’t last long but endeavoured to cause as much damage as they did.

 

            She could hear the distant shout of her brother and his posse, scrambling to take down the two beasts. The dead swarmed over them, climbing into the rib cages, scrabbling at bones, tearing them apart in little brittle fragments. Lena kept them together with all of her force, soldiers and any volunteers from the townsfolk following in the wide path she cut through the army as they shot any dead in sight, cut down in return as they were shot by the very much alive people strewn amidst the dead, or swallowed up by the Necromancers controlling the horde.

 

            Eventually, the mammoth and the ground sloth went down beneath the ropes of a few bandits, and bullets riddled them as they ensured they never rose again. But it had allowed Sam and Jack to carve up most of the sides in a pincer movement which did more to annoy the Necromancers controlling those sections than anything else. But even with their help, Lena could tell that it was a losing battle.

 

            When the two Witch Doctors grew tired, spending all their energy on turning the tide, they retreated a safe distance until Lena reluctantly let them inside. From then on, it became a routine of watches, two of them fighting at a time, while the other slept and healed whoever they could and revived anyone who’d died without a bone bullet in them. For periods at a time, Midvale was filled with the screaming sounds of those brought back to life, and their numbers thinned as they were laid up on bed rest to recover their strength. 

 

            The rest of the day slipped by and Lena stayed up through the night and into the next one. Even when it was her turn to rest, she couldn’t quite bring herself to turn over the battle to Sam or Jack. She didn’t quite trust them. She would sit on the hotel porch and eat her rations and lightly nap as the sounds of battle raged around her.

 

            They only held out for two more days before their defeat became imminent. The walls were almost overrun with the amount of dead that breached it, always shot down before they could do any harm, but slowly overwhelming them all the same. And their barrels of bullets were quickly depleting too, their dynamite stores running out with a final stick thrown by Alex. Rations ended up lifting as they realised there was no good hoarding food for the dead, and there was a general air of despair filling the town as more dead joined the enemy or were dragged back inside with bone bullets in them to be buried. No one had the time or energy to dig graves though, and Lena was reluctant to waste her energy on commanding skeletons to do it for her, so the bodies were laid out in empty homes, covered in swathes of fabric as flies buzzed around and a putrid stench started stemming from them.

 

            On the second day, Jack was captured by Lex as he tried to flank his army with a couple hundred of his own dead, trampling through the little makeshift camp her brother had set up. Lena felt the life gutter out of three Necromancers and felt Jack burning brightly, but he never returned. Sam knew it too, standing on the other platform beside the gate and slowly turning her head to look at Lena. 

 

            “They’ll take us tomorrow,” Sam said later on with chilling certainty. It almost seemed prophetic, and Lena knew it too, but then they all did as hope waned.

 

            “I suppose you’ll be wanting to take your leave again now?” Lena wryly asked her, arching an eyebrow.

 

            Sam let out a quiet chuckle, pouring water over her dirty hands and washing away some of the blood. They trembled slightly and she kept her head ducked down. “It’s too late for that, isn’t it?”

 

            “Didn’t you say you had a daughter?”

 

            “Yes. Ruby.”

 

            “She’ll need her mother as she grows.”

 

            Giving her a wry smile, Sam shrugged. “What we need and what we get are two very different things, ain’t they?”

 

            Mouth thinning, Lena swallowed thickly. “If you left … would you take some people with you? Not far; just a few towns over and then I imagine they’d fair well on their own.”

 

            “This about that rancher?” Sam said with a gleeful smile. “Well, ain’t that a damn thing? Finding love at the end of it all.”

 

            “Her family too,” Lena nodded. “I’ll convince them all to go. Tonight. As many of the survivors that will go.”

 

            “He’ll feel us leaving.”

 

            “I’ll buy you time.”

 

            “Alright then. At midnight.”

 

            Feeling the guilt of leading more people to their deaths lessen, Lena let out a sigh of a breath. Rubbing her forehead, she turned and went to seek out Alex. She was with her mother, who was tending to some of the injured. Kelly and Nia were there too, and Brainy was pacing outside.

 

            “May I speak with you?” Lena quietly asked Alex.

 

            The Sheriff followed her out and they rounded the building, away from Brainy. Lena pressed her fingertips to her eyelids as she ducked her head.

 

            “We’ll fail tomorrow,” she confessed.

 

            “We still have time to turn it around,” Alex firmly objected.

 

            Shaking her head, Lena gave her a thin smile. “No. It’s inevitable. Jack is taken and Sam … she leaves tonight.”

 

            “What? That cowardly-“

 

            “It’s at my request,” Lena gently interrupted. “She’ll take people with her for me. Get them to safety.”

 

            Alex let out a short laugh and arched an eyebrow, “you think she’s goin’ to leave you here all by yourself?”

 

            “If you’re with her, then yes.”

 

            “Like hell am I leavin’ this place,” Alex scornfully replied, crossing her arms over her chest. “I got more right than you to fight for this town. I was born here, raised here. Ain’t nothin’ for me away from this place.”

 

            “But there could be. You could take Kelly and your mother, and Kara. Settle down somewhere new. J’onn and M’gann could open a new hotel. Nia and Brainy would go too. I urge you to consider it,” Lena quietly pleaded.

 

            Alex clapped a hand on her shoulder and gave her a solemn look. “Doc, I ‘ppreciate you trying to save us all, but we ain’t lookin’ to run away. We threw our lot in with you, live or die, the day we chose to stay when half the town left. Ain’t nothin’ for it now. And we might just win yet.”

 

            “She could die, Alex.”

 

            “We all could. Probably will. But don’t we deserve to die fighting for each other? For our home? You ain’t got one of them, so might be that it’s different for you, but … you’re here, fighting for this town, so maybe … you’ve chosen to die for a place that feels like home too. It ain’t a bad way to go, is it?”

 

            “No, not at all,” Lena murmured, her shoulders slumping.

 

            “I’ll ask the questions in case anyone does want to go, but I can’t imagine I’m wrong. I’ll round up anyone else we can get out too. Anyone who won’t stay.”

 

            “Have them at the south gate before midnight.”

 

            After that, she went off to sleep in her bed for one last night. Kara was out fighting and Lena knew that Sam would cover the walls while she slept, and would keep them safe until it was time for her to leave. Lena would need her strength more than anyone else in the following days, and she took a tonic that knocked her out cold, sleeping through the afternoon and into the evening as her body tried to repair itself.

 

            She would’ve liked Kara there beside her, would’ve liked to feel her warmth and her touch once more, indulged in how it felt to sleep beside someone else as it healed some of the loneliness in her heart. But she slept alone and slept deeply, knowing that it wouldn’t matter tomorrow. 

 

            Waking an hour before midnight, Lena went through the motions of getting ready, reloading her weapons, stocking up on teeth and running through the thinning grimoire. She ate a hearty, late dinner and drank some moonshine from a jug on her table to calm her nerves and then made her way downstairs. The hotel was lit and a few of them lingered at tables, having a drink. There was a mournful air to the group and Lena nodded as she joined them.

 

            “Will any of you go?” she asked, a plea in her voice.

 

            One by one, they all shook their heads, a grim air of resignation settling on their shoulders. She nodded and then sighed heavily. They were free to make their own decisions, even if she strongly objected to their choices. 

 

            She left them to enjoy their last drinks then and walked out into the night, making for the gate where a cluster of people waited for Sam. The Witch Doctor arrived shortly after, abandoning the wall while soldiers manned it. They had decided to stay as well and a few of them now lifted the wood from the barred gate and hauled the doors open.

 

            “Thank you for your assistance,” Lena said to Sam, the woman looming over her from horseback.

 

            “I’m not sure I did much but delay your death a few days.”

 

            Letting out a hoarse laugh, Lena’s chin dimpled in a wry smile. “Well, we fought our hardest. At least we can say that. It was always inevitable though.”

 

            “You might still win,” Sam said, her doubt clear in her voice.

 

            Lips pressed together to hold back a bark of laughter, Lena’s eyes creased at the corners. “Mm. I intend to try my hardest, still. But you should be off now. Safe travels.”

 

            “And you, sister.”

 

            Lena touched the brim of her hat and stepped back as Sam led the group out through the gate. She had a host of dead, half of which she’d come with, encircling them protectively, and Lena wondered if they’d live long enough to come and reclaim Midvale once Lex was through with them all. Perhaps they’d rebuild it one day.

 

            She watched until she couldn’t see beyond the small circle of light the torches offered, which wasn’t for very long as the darkness of midnight quickly veiled them, and then oversaw the gate being barred once more. Then she lingered there for a moment longer, feeling the battle behind her, on the north side of town, and found herself reluctant to join it. Lena would’ve preferred peace.

 

            “Do you want some company?”

 

            Turning slowly, Lena’s face softened with an aching smile. Kara hung back, looking pale as she fiddled with her fingers. 

 

            “I would always like your company,” Lena murmured.

 

            Taking slow steps forward, Kara paused before her and then wrapped Lena in a tight hug. It held the pieces of her together for a moment and Lena exhaled as her body deflated, holding her rifle in one hand as she returned the hug.

 

            “I’m sorry,” Lena whispered.

 

            “It ain’t your fault.”

 

            “I thought I could’ve stopped him.”

 

            “We’ll keep trying,” Kara insisted. “We ain’t dead yet, are we? Or if we are, I think death ain’t that bad if you’re here.”

 

            Choking on a laugh, Lena pulled back, her eyes bright and yearning. She touched Kara’s cheek and smiled crookedly.

 

            “In another life, we’d be dancing at balls together, you and I.”

 

            “Sipping champagne?”

 

            “Yes, champagne. Fine dresses. Lovely music. Good food. I wouldn’t let anyone else dance with you.”

 

            “I wouldn’t want to dance with anyone else,” Kara whispered. “I wouldn’t want anyone else but you.”

 

            Smiling, Lena reached out and touched the medallion hanging from Kara’s neck. Then her eyes lifted to meet hers and she let out a short sigh and leaned in to kiss her. She savoured it; it might be their last one.

 

            “I should go,” Lena said, jerking her chin towards the fight. “They’re circling.”

 

            Dawn was breaking by the time Midvale was completely surrounded. Anyone they’d had outside the walls, fighting back and causing trouble, was dead. There were a couple of hundred left within the walls and an increasing amount of dead to choose from. Lena threw them at the enemy with reckless abandon but it still wasn’t enough.

 

            By mid-morning, the dead walked the streets as the fight came to them. People laid on rooftops picking them off and had made traps of pikes and wire strung between buildings to lop off skulls or cut through kneecaps. It was madness and people started to board themselves inside as all hope was finally lost.

 

            Lena had long since given up the walls, knowing that to stand before the unending wave of the dead would only lead to her being overwhelmed by them as they climbed over. Instead, she hid behind a barrel near the Sheriff’s office and picked off stragglers while her own dead went hand-to-hand. Every time she cut the threads of control or put one down, three more arrived, until soon enough Lena was out of teeth and had spent far too much blood.

 

            When defeat seemed imminent and the gate was moments from being split open, she gathered her friends in the centre of town and gave them agonised looks. Worry seized her and she couldn’t do much but offer them a chance to hide while she faced her brother and hoped for the best.

 

            “Board yourselves inside,” Lena gravelly ordered them, her green eyes wild with anger and fear. “Don’t come out until I tell you to, and shoot anything trying to get in.”

 

            They all hesitated, an uneasy moment of silence as the gate shuddered at the north end of town. It was certain death for Lena to remain outside alone and they all knew it. Kara started to talk, an argument on her lips, before Alex spoke over her, surprisingly objecting to Lena’s orders as well.

 

            “You’re no help to me here,” Lena dismissively replied, trying to keep the tremor out of her voice.

 

            She was frightened, she realised. Here, now, at the end of it all, she finally had a reason to live and it made for a bittersweet realisation. Kara’s ashen face flushed with anger as she took a step forward, grabbing the collar of Lena’s filthy shirt as she loomed over her.

 

            “I ain’t leaving you out here by yourself. He’s coming.”

 

            Covering her hand with her own, Lena gave her a strained smile, eyes creasing at the corners. “I know. But once I kill him it’ll all be over.”

 

            “Lena.”

 

            Eyes sliding past Kara, she watched as reluctant defeat crept onto Alex’s face. She met Lena’s eyes with a hard look, a grim set to her jaw as she nodded. Feeling the knot loosen slightly in her chest, Lena’s smile grew a fraction as she reached out and touched Kara’s face, both hands cradling her gently.

 

            “I could not say it before, and I will not say it now, but … I will say it after,” Lena murmured, her facade cracking momentarily before she gathered her composure.

 

            She had a tooth clenched between thumb and forefinger and faint smudges of blood marked Kara’s jaw where she touched her. Feeling every inch of her body with her magic, Lena gave Kara an apologetic smile as she stopped her lungs, cutting off the oxygen to her brain as her blood pressure plummeted.

 

            “Forgive me,” Lena whispered, bearing the brunt of Kara’s weight as her body went slack and she passed out.

 

            Alex quickly stepped forward and relieved Lena of her sister’s body, J’onn getting the other side and propping her up. 

 

            “That’s one way to do it, I guess,” Alex muttered.

 

            “You’ll have to keep her inside the room,” Lena hoarsely instructed her. “No matter what. Even if you have to tie her up. She can’t come out here; he’ll know, and he’ll use her.”

 

            Nodding, Alex’s face rippled with a conflicted look. She hesitated and Lena blinked back the stinging feeling in her eyes as she watched Kara’s head loll.

 

            “Doc?”

 

            Alex’s voice was so soft that Lena’s eyes widened a fraction with a mild look of surprise. Mouth twisting ruefully, Alex swallowed thickly and wiped her hand on her thigh before holding it out.

 

            “I’m real sorry it has to end like this.”

 

            Lena’s eyes stung fiercely and she let out a choked laugh as she reached out to grip Alex’s hand, seeking comfort in it. “Me too.”

 

            “You know, I don’t say it often, but … I was wrong. About you. I hope it’ll come quickly for us if it has to end.”

 

            Face taut, Lena nodded and cleared her throat. “I lied. There is something more, once we get to the other side,” she lied, offering up a small bit of peace as the gate started to splinter. “I’ve seen it before. It’s- it’s light and warm and peaceful. It won’t be so bad for us all. We’ll go together.”

 

            A faint smile curled Alex’s lips and she nodded once more, a flicker of pity and sadness in her eyes. “Thank you. You’re a brave woman, Lena Luthor. A good woman.”

 

            She didn’t reply, just cleared her throat and glanced off towards the gate. Dead swarmed over everything now and the town was filled with screams and shouts. Lena glanced back at the people she’d come to respect, and one she’d come to love, held between them as she was limply carried towards the hotel. Her only regret now was that they hadn’t run when she’d told them to. 

 

            If her brother had an ounce of mercy inside her that she could pander to, Lena would, for Kara’s sake. If she couldn’t kill him, she would kneel and beg him to spare everyone.

 

            Awaiting her fate, and almost certainly her death, Lena licked her cracked lips and stood in the middle of the street. She used what little strength she had left now, the shallow pool of power remaining in her blood as her heart sluggishly pounded it through her body, to order the skeletons still under her control to barricade the hotel. They moved in lurching steps, pushing heavy water barrels in front of the doors that M’gann had locked over the swinging batwing ones, piling sandbags around it and benches and rocking chairs. They did the same at the back door leading into the kitchen, blocking them inside. It wouldn’t be enough if Lex’s band wanted to get in badly enough, but Lena hoped it would deter them a while. 

 

            It was five minutes later that the gate finally caved. It wasn’t enough for her brother’s army to flood the town, he had to ride in through the gates, gloating as he trotted along at a slow pace. He stopped two dozen feet from her, his face shaded by a flat-brimmed hat before he took it off and tossed it into the dust.

 

            “You’ve lost now, little sister,” he softly called out, cool amusement in his words. “As you knew you would. But you fought valiantly; I admire your courage, even in light of your folly.”

 

            Swinging out of the saddle, boots thudding into the baked dirt with a rising cloud of dust, he was sweating in his trim black suit. Taking a few slow steps forward, Lex clapped, the sound mocking in the chaos of the town as the dead streamed in without opposition now.

 

            “You haven’t won yet,” Lena couldn’t resist retorting, a sneer of derision twisting her face.

 

            “Come now, we both know you were never going to win,” he said with a fleeting laugh. “You’ve always been more interested in saving people, in healing-“

 

            “That’s the purpose of our Order.”

 

            He let out a withering sigh. “That is not the only Order. But they’re all cowards. I thought perhaps you would have understood, but you never did love the power as much as I did. What a waste.”

 

            “You love your dead things so much - I’ll help you join them,” she snapped, yanking her pistol from its holster and raising it.

 

            She fired off a shot and her stomach lurched as her brother crooked his hand in a careless gesture, a man in scruffy clothes fiddling with teeth suddenly jerking across the few feet to her brother to take the bullet for him. It struck him straight in the chest, his teeth spilling from his hands before he went limp. Lex clicked his tongue and let the body crumple, the easy violation and waste of human life leaving a sour taste in Lena’s mouth.

 

            Gritting her teeth, she pulled the hammer back again and took a step forward, firing. He jerked another body, and then another as she kept shooting, advancing on him as she trembled with anger. Caked in mud and blood - some of it her own - one shoulder slumped lower as her left arm hung at her side, dislocated. The barrel of her gun was smoking by the time the sixth body crumpled to the ground and her brother fixed the cuff of his faded tailored jacket, stepping over them and smiling smugly.

 

            A few feet separated them then and Lena still had the gun trained on him, trembling slightly in her hand as she swallowed. Her throat was dry and she felt cold fear slither down her spine, sweat dripping into her eyes as she found herself weaponless before her brother, knowing he would kill her without hesitation.

 

            Lex wasn’t particularly tall or strong, but he was still bigger than her, and when his hand snatched out and tore her beloved Colt from her grasp, Lena was helpless to stop him. He carelessly tossed it aside and sneered, taking a slow step forward. He laughed softly and Lena stiffened. 

 

            Then she remembered she had a knife still sheathed at her thigh and slipped it into her hand, launching herself at him. He caught her hand and averted the blade but Lena let it fall into her left hand, the dislocated arm screaming in protest as she forced it to move. Her aim was off though, and even though she was aiming for his jugular, she didn’t slash deep enough when the knife bit into skin, skating a shallow cut along the side of his throat.

 

            The rotting fingers of a corpse grabbed at her, the knife knocked from her hand, and then more dead hands grabbed her. Her legs were kicked out from under her even as she struggled, and by the time Lena had been forced to her knees, bloop caking her face, her breaths quick and shallow and her dark hair coming free of its braid, Lex had plucked a handkerchief from his pocket and was dabbing at the shallow coat. It only served to enrage Lena.

 

            The knife was just in front of her, close enough that she could’ve struggled, fought against the dead who her brother would’ve set upon her. Instead, she knelt on the hard ground with a bitter taste in her mouth as she wrestled with the grief of confronting her brother. He’d taken her from that cemetery and made her believe that she belonged with her family. It had been a short-lived dream, but it had made Lena happy for a while, and now she wanted him dead. But there was that corner of her heart that hadn’t forgotten the moments he’d been kind to her, not even after he’d killed her. She looked up at him with sorrowful green eyes.

 

            He clicked his tongue and let out a soft laugh, his dark eyes shining with victory. “Oh, look at you. So … pathetic. Even after everything I’ve done to you, you still look at me with love . I knew you would always come back to me.”

 

            Lena hated that he was right. She hated him but she loved him too. The former just eclipsed that love. But now, when he’d forged the last pieces of his monstrous plan into place, feeling nothing for her, not even a flicker of affection for his sister, who’d been loyal and in awe of him, until she hadn’t. 

 

            Still, she was unwilling to drop down into the swamp of pure hatred that was waiting for her, just over the edge. But hatred burned so easily, and he’d tried to take away from her the only thing that had ever brought her even a moment of peace. Lena silently vowed that he wouldn’t leave this place alive. No matter what happened to her, she would take him with her.

 

            “It’s a pity,” he said, pressing his lips together in a thin line, a hard look on his face. “We could have done so much together.”

 

            “You’re going to lose,” Lena said through a mouthful of blood and bile, sweating beneath the sun as she stayed on her knees, her whole body aching.

 

            “Lose? No, I should think not. This is the beginning of my victory. This here, dear sister, is the empire of the dead,” he said, spreading his arms wide to the chaotic mess surrounding them. “And I am its master.”

 

            The dead were tearing apart buildings, and his Necromancers on horseback were setting fire to the general goods store, the bakery, the tailors, careening down the main street with flaming torches. She watched as some of them kicked open doors to a chorus of screams, dragging people out into the street and shooting them. Lena was horrified beyond the capacity for rational thought, her mind reeling as she felt faint beneath the crushing weight of her defeat.

 

            “You could have stopped this,” he said, “if only you’d set your pride aside. Now look - they’re dying because of you.”

 

            “Please,” she whispered, the sound ragged and desperate.

 

            He quietly chuckled. “I wonder, would you die to save them?”

 

            “Yes,” Lena said, her voice barely audible as it came out strangled. She licked her lips and tried again, her heart twisting awfully in her chest as the panicked thought of losing Kara filled her with pain. “Yes.”

 

            "Would you die for me?" he asked, his voice rising at the end with intrigue.

 

            "Again?" she rasped.

 

            The memory of the bullet hitting home, of putting her down, again and again, flashed through her mind. There had always been nothing on the other side, and a part of her welcomed that relief of emptiness. It might have been a comfort for Alex, for her friends, but it was a lie and Lena was glad that her existence would cease, that nothing else would be demanded of her once her soul became untethered from her body for good. She was tired. So very tired.

 

            “Yes,” she said, balling her hands into fists in her lap, shoulders curving inwards as she knelt, defeated.

 

            She waited, anticipating her death as Lex let out a quiet huff of laughter. He jerked his own gun from its holster and Lena’s stomach lurched at the sound of the hammer being pulled back. He stepped forward, her downcast eyes looking at his muddy boots, and she felt the barrel press against her shoulder.

 

            Stiffening, Lena clenched her teeth as she braced herself for the gunshot, but it was still blindingly painful when it came. Swallowing a scream as it shattered bone, making her vision white as nausea clawed at her, a ragged, breathless choking escaped her instead. Spitting bile as the breath got caught in her throat and her body went slack, curling forward as she breathed quickly, Lena squeezed her eyes shut.

 

            “Did you think it would be quick?” he asked with cold amusement. 

 

            He crouched before her and reached out, cupping her chin. Lena jerked her head away from his touch, a scowl on her grey face as she looked at him with hatred. There was nothing in him that could be saved. 

 

            “We’re beyond that now,” he murmured, “now, you live and watch as I kill them all, one by one, before your very eyes. And then, after you’ve begged for your death, I’ll make you suffer some more before I-“

 

            A shot cut through the moment and Lena blinked as Lex stumbled off balance, on his hands and knees in front of her, straining against the effort it was taking not to scream. His face reddened with rage as he pressed a hand to his shoulder blade and Lena frowned, turning her attention to the hotel. A window was slid open, a rifle balanced against the windowsill, and Alex was frowning as she smoked, Kelly’s worried face beside hers.

 

            Seizing the moment, Lena drew in a rattling breath and tensed before leaping at her brother. Using her good shoulder, she knocked him off balance, sending him sprawling backwards, and drove her knee into his stomach. He gasped for air, raising his gun in a jerky motion before smashing it into the side of Lena’s head. She bared her bloody teeth, a quiet snarl building in her chest, and grabbed his wrist in her right hand, trying to break his grip and then biting his hand when she couldn’t.

 

            He cursed her as he dropped the gun, using his strength against her as he forced Lena back and simultaneously used her to sit up. Jerking his head back, he smiled as he smashed his forehead into her nose, Lena feeling it break with a rush of warm blood cascading over her mouth and chin. 

 

            Spitting a mouthful of blood into his eyes, she wrapped a hand around his throat as he let out a roar of frustration, wiping at his eyes. Her grasp was feeble and Lena felt his fingers grab her braid, yanking down on it and forcing her head back to an awkward angle that made her choke for air. Dragging her sideways so she sprawled beside him, Lex rolled over and quickly staggered to his feet before stomping on her stomach.

 

            Lena retched curling in on herself, and she heard another shot fired off. It would be hard for Alex to hit him when they were rolling in the dirt like children, risking Lena getting struck by a misaimed shot. This one missed Lex by inches but he paid it no attention as he grabbed Lena by the back of her neck and dragged her to her knees.

 

            He had a tooth in his hands then, looming over her before he let out a quick laugh, turning to look up at the hotel, pinpointing the source of the firing. He spread a hand theatrically and grasped his magic before commanding it.

 

            “Shoot me, if you like, but I will take her with me,” he called out.

 

            Lena silently prayed Alex would call his bluff. Even if he wasn’t bluffing, which he wasn’t, it would put an end to it all and save those that survived. Lena had already made her peace with her death, a somewhat bittersweet and resentful peace but peace nonetheless. For Kara, she’d gladly die and take her brother with her.

 

            Still, she knew he wasn’t bluffing and couldn’t stop the cry of agony that fell from her lips as he demonstrated that. She felt her alone crack and slammed a hand over her mouth to keep a sob in, blood dripping down her face as her bones cracked and bent. He would break her apart slowly, and in the end, the Sheriff couldn’t bring herself to let the bane of her existence die.

 

            “Alex,” Lena softly sobbed, a plea in her name, but it wasn’t loud enough for her to hear it.

 

            Instead, she had to end it alone, feeling her body’s weary resistance as she commanded it to move. Inhaling sharply, Lena pried her thick lips apart and reached to the loose molar at the back of her mouth, prying it free with a sharp pinch of pain and coating it in the blood already covering her face.

 

            Shallowly breathing as Lex made the bones in her right leg fracture, cracks radiating through her tibia as vomit clawed up her throat, splattering over the dirt beneath her as she hunched over. Clutching the tooth tightly in her hand, Lena suddenly seized control of a dozen of his dead that had crumpled to bones as he gave up the majority of his control, allowing his remaining crew to wreak havoc while he dealt with his sister.

 

            Now, the closest ones were Lena’s and she managed to fling them at her brother. He was caught off guard, teeth knocked from his hand, and Lena took a long minute to climb to her feet as Lex went under beneath a pile of bodies. Swaying on her feet, Lena grabbed the skull of the closest one and knocked its teeth out, cupping them in her palm and then turning her attention to her brother.

 

            He shattered the yellow bones of a particularly old skeleton’s leg and sickeningly pulled the flesh off a relatively new corpse, the putrid smell of it making Lena want to heave as Lex made a sound of disgust. Commanding them to drag him to his feet, Lena stalked forward in a shuffling gait, her breaths a shallow wheeze as she dealt with broken ribs and perhaps a punctured lung. Trembling all over, she spanned the distance separating them and curled her fingers into a fist over the handful of teeth, punching him across the face.

 

            It was for her own satisfaction more than anything else and Lena felt the ground shift beneath her as vertigo hit. Knees buckling, she stumbled and then righted herself. Sniffing as she wiped her face on her sleeve, blinking back the grittiness in her eyes and swallowing the sour taste of bile and the coppery tang of blood, she let out a strangled laugh.

 

            “You have always underestimated me,” she calmly told him. “You won’t live long enough to make that mistake again.”

 

            Reaching out, she wrapped her hands around his throat and sagged against him. Her dead held him in place while her weight slowly dragged them both down to the ground. The dirt was hard beneath her knees and Lena’s hearing turned tinny as she fought for her own consciousness. But she wouldn’t give in until he was dead, until she’d choked the life out of him.

 

            She had no gun, no grimoire for spells, no knife to gut him. Just her hands. They would suffice to do what needed to be done. 

 

            And she would’ve succeeded too, if not for the sound of carriage wheels rattling into town at break-neck speed with a dozen horses in pursuit. Lena had almost crushed Lex’s windpipe by the time the four horses pulling the carriage stopped and nine Witch Doctors swung down from their saddles and stepped out of the carriage.

 

            Lex’s fingers scrabbled at her face and her hands, his nails scraping her skin raw, creating tracks through the grime, but Lena didn’t let go. Not when the Witch Doctors sought out the other Necromancers and cut the threads of power, and took control of their own dead to render them immobile.

 

            Not until she found her body in someone else’s control, the violation yanking her back against her will. Her fingers slipped from her brother’s neck with a sinking feeling of regret, and a flash of surprise as an angry voice cut through the din.

 

            “Stop this at once. "

16. Chapter 16

            Lena blinked back dizzying black spots as she pushed herself up, her body protesting with the effort. Her left arm felt positively numb by now, her head pounding with a headache and a tremor in her aching muscles as her body fought to remain conscious. She’d spent too much of her blood to fight anymore. But she knew that voice.

 

            Struggling onto all fours, hissing as she put weight on her left hand, Lena staggered to her feet. Lurching forward, she took in the sight of the intimidating woman in a crimson riding dress, a matching hat with a lace veil and silk flowers on her head. She wore a cream leather coat with crimson piping and Lena let out a frayed laugh as she swayed, watching as a pair of crimson leather gloves were removed.

 

            “Mother,” she mumbled through thick lips.

 

            Lillian’s eyes were cutting as she glanced over at her daughter, her face pale and haughty with anger. Clutching her gloves in one hand, Lillian motioned with her other hand and Lena’s feet skimmed the ground as her body obeyed the summons of her mother’s power. For all of Lena’s power, she was helpless to resist Lillian, one of the Councillors of the Order and decades of experience and increasing power over her daughter, leading Lena to surrender to her. Even if she had been able to outmatch her, Lena was tired and spent and was willing to give in without a fight.

 

            Her brother was dragged over to their mother as well, his suit rumpled and dirty, the black hiding his bloodstains, but they were assuredly there. He couldn’t resist Lillian either, and so brother and sister stood before her, stiff and helpless in her control as her power left them immobile. Lena felt like a child again, thinking back to all the chastisements she’d endured under similar circumstances. She swallowed thickly, feeling a little faint.

 

            “Brawling like squabbling children. Have you no shame?” Lillian snapped, her voice low and aghast.

 

            Lillian was a proud woman, powerful and haughty, a little arrogant and thin patience that wouldn’t suffer the embarrassment that came with two children darkening the Luthor name. Word would spread and it would look bad for her, as well-respected as she was. Lena imagined that was the purpose of her sudden appearance in Midvale, far from New York City. It must have rankled her mother a great deal to have drawn her months of travel away to sort it out personally. 

 

            “There’s no shame in taking our natural place in the world order,” Lex said.

 

            “You’ve razed two dozen towns, you foolish boy .”

 

            “Come now, mother.”

 

            Lillian clenched her left hand into a fist and Lex let out a choked sound as his throat constricted, cutting off any further reply. Then Lillian turned her scathing attention to Lena, her eyes giving her a contemptuous once-over.

 

            “And you … I had thought you were too weak to turn to such idiotic pursuits of power. Instead, I hear rumours of you slaughtering your own kin and stealing gold. Did I not give you more than you deserved , allowing you the privilege of being trained when others would have shipped their husband’s bastard off to less savoury places? This is how you repay my kindness?”

 

            Letting out a strangled laugh, Lena smiled thinly. “You’ve assumed the worst of me once again, mother.”

 

            Repeating the clenched fist with her right hand, Lillian choked off Lena. Both of her children were left gasping and quietly choking around the sensation of ghostly hands closing around their throats, sagging beneath the fleeting strength of their bodies as they were held aloft against their will. Looking around with a severe look on her face, taking in the fires and destruction and death, Lillian’s eyes glanced over the Witch Doctors she’d ridden with and jerked her chin.

 

            “Clean it up.”

 

            They all moved off, fishing teeth out of their pouches, tearing pages from their grimoires, red staining their fingers as they did her bidding. Lillian unclenched her fists and let Lena and Lex fall to their knees, touching their throats as they drew in ragged breaths. Heeled boots scraping up dust, she walked around them in a circle, disdain on her face as she shook her head.

 

            “You’re both a discredit to the Order. I should strip you of your medallions and put a bullet in you where you kneel, but unfortunately, that’s not for me alone to decide.”

 

            “You’d kill your own cherished son,” Lex asked, his voice an amused rasp as he looked up at Lillian and smiled.

 

            The three of them knew she would never truly harm her son. He was undoubtedly her favourite - it hadn’t even been a contest. Lillian would pin it all on Lena if she could, but she’d been tasked with taking him back to New York to stand trial. And his blood would reveal everything she grimly wished would stay hidden. They’d execute Lex for his crimes and there was nothing she’d be able to do about it but watch. Lena knew her mother would only show a flicker of the same sadness for her daughter’s fate if she was to meet the same end, but Lena knew her blood would reveal an honest cause. Not the corrupt version that had spread wide, influenced by her brother’s misdeeds.

 

            As she knelt in the dirt, sweat and blood dotting the ground before her, Lena blinked as the sun baked the shoulders of her shirt and she spied something small and cream trodden into the ground. Listening to her mother and brother converse, she slyly pried the thing from the dirt and brushed off the earth with a thumb, revealing a perfect little incisor. Lena clenched it in her fist and swallowed thickly.

 

            “It’s out of my hands now,” Lillian said in a clipped tone, annoyance sharpening her face. “You’ve sealed your own fate. I always expected more of you than this. A baseless butcher. There were a dozen other ways you could’ve seized power, yet you chose the path of a fool, thinking bloodshed would carve an easier path to the top. Perhaps my leniency towards you made you soft and complacent and allowed your ego to reign unchecked.”

 

            “You and I both know there is so much more we could be doing,” Lex said, arching an eyebrow. “They shun us for our help when they should fear us as their betters.”  

            “Be that as it may, this was not the way to do it.”

 

            “No? Violence makes people listen. Gold makes people listen.”

 

            “And pride gets people killed.”

 

            “Mm, yes, look at our dear Lena. Too proud to run, too proud to admit defeat until it was too late.”

 

            Lillian was still pacing around them in a wide circle, her eyes flitting between the two of them with a hard look of anger. Holding the tooth in her closed fist, Lena bided her time, waiting for a complacent moment before she could attack, holding the gift of one last chance to end it in her hand. She stayed on her knees, curled inwards as she breathed slowly against the pain flooding her body before she finally lashed out.

 

            It was reckless and dangerous to her own well-being, but she wouldn’t allow her brother to leave Midvale alive. Calling on the spark of magic she felt her brother’s body, free of her mother’s control, and thrust her hand out. He stiffened, shock on his face as his spine arched and his chest seemed to pull towards Lena.

 

            Teeth gritted against the effort as sweat dampened her forehead, Lena heaved with all of her effort, watching as realisation dawned on Lex as his suntanned face went shockingly white and a slow scream of pain built in his chest. It felt like minutes but it was only mere seconds, too quick for Lillian to stop her as she covered her mouth, gasping, and wrenched open her brother’s ribcage and yanked out his still-beating heart.

 

            There was a long moment of silence as he teetered on his knees, a mess of blood and flesh and bones gaping open to the world, before he crumpled to the dust, no life in his eyes. The heart lay before Lena and she stared at it before turning aside and retching before stiffening at the cold feeling of metal pressed to her forehead.

 

            “Drop it,” her mother ordered her, her voice ice cold.

 

            Letting the remains of the half-burned tooth roll from her palm, Lena splayed them for Lillian. Empty. Holstering her gun, Lillian used her own teeth to hoist Lena back to her feet - just a little bit higher than she was tall, to leave the toes of her boots scuffing at the dirt for purchase - that invisible hand clamped around her throat once more. She still wasn’t as tall as her mother and Lena stared up at her, inhaling sharply through her nose as a muscle twitched in her clenched jaw.

 

            Lillian’s slap was quick and stinging, and if she wasn’t already filthy it would have turned her pale cheek red. Disbelief and shock were clear in her mother’s eyes but her face was hard with anger as she tried to keep her composure, looming over her daughter as the sudden loss of her son sank in.

 

            “You stupid girl,” Lillian scornfully berated her.

 

            “You may think so, but it’s justice all the same. I won’t apologise.”

 

            “Are you really so callous in the cold-blooded murder of your own brother? The man who mentored and taught you?”

 

            A small laugh escaped Lena and she swallowed the bitter taste in her mouth. “If I wasn’t in such poor shape, I would celebrate it.”

 

            Lips twisting derisively, Lillian was silent as she bristled with quiet rage. There wasn’t much she could do though; her son would have met the same fate in a different state. This just sped up the process. Dropping her command of Lena’s body, she allowed her daughter to crumple to the ground once more and then clicked her fingers at a young man shepherding the dead back out of the gate. Despite the thinned numbers of Lex’s army, there were still a few thousand dead about the place, and thousands more beyond the breached walls. It would take weeks to bury them all, months to repair what had been damaged. At least she could be glad that the survivors would be around to do so.

 

            “Cuff her,” Lillian instructed the Witch Doctor. “And find me the others who aided this attack.”

 

            Lena didn’t move as her hands were bound in heavy manacles and she was hauled to her feet by her dislocated arm, her shoulder screaming in protest but helpless against the hands that led her to the wagon with the iron cage.

 

            “No,” Lillian said as the man made to open the door to the cage. “In mine.”

 

            He nodded and led Lean to the fine carriage instead, opening the door and ushering her inside onto a plush bench. Left inside the warm interior, outside of the harsh sunshine, Lena’s body went slack and she closed her eyes against the pounding headache and body riddled with pain.

 

            Listening to her mother shout orders outside, she waited patiently and five minutes later the door to the carriage opened as her mother climbed in and sat across from her. Pounding the ceiling of the carriage, it lurched forward into motion. It was pulled by horses that had been turned into wights, which meant that they didn’t tire and would run endlessly until their bodies fell apart, and thus, Lena left Midvale chained across from her mother without a word to Kara or any of her friends left behind.

 

            With the other prisoners crammed into the cage, they rattled along the rutted road out of town with haste, the retinue in cream and crimson with their dead steeds leaving behind the broken town without pause. Nursing her many wounds, Lena was pale and clammy, a fever taking root, as she slumped against the side of the carriage, her eyelids closed, and felt her mother’s gaze on her.

 

            “I won’t apologise,” Lena stubbornly muttered, peeling open one eyelid as she was confronted with her mother’s icy demeanour filling the carriage.

 

            “No, I don’t suppose you would,” Lillian hummed, “you’ve harboured a grudge against your brother for years; I imagine you’re glad.”

 

            Lena touched her forehead, where he’d put a number of bullets, and her lips twitched with a faint smile. “I am.”

 

            Lillian didn’t say anything, but Lena could hear her disapproval in the clearing of her throat as she shifted. After a moment she spoke again, the topic moving on from Lex. “You’re filthy . I thought you would have composed yourself with more pride than a slovenly beggar wallowing in her own filth.”

 

            “Oh, well, don’t worry,” Lena drawled, “only half of it is mine.”

 

            “You’d do well to keep your blood inside. We’ll have need of it once we arrive at the cemetery.”

 

            With a frayed laugh, the gravelly sound of her voice a weary sigh, Lena looked at her mother beneath surly eyebrows, feeling like a petulant child. “That would be easier to do if I was allowed to heal.”

 

            “I don’t imagine you could lift a finger in your state. Look at you. No coat, no gun, no book, no teeth. No respect for yourself. You disappoint me, Lena.”

 

            “But haven’t I always.”

 

            With a twist of her lips and a reviled once-over, Lillian plucked a tooth from her pristine pouch belted at the waist of her dress and tossed it to her daughter. It softly struck Lena’s lap and fell between her thighs and Lillian gestured dismissively to it.

 

            “Heal yourself then. And hold your tongue, if you know what’s good for you.”

 

            Mouth thinning, Lena swallowed a sigh and fumbled with the tooth, holding it tightly and struggling to grasp onto the spark as her waning strength was reluctant to hand itself over to her healing. She could only do half a job anyway, no herbs and tinctures to aid her, to clean out the wounds and help take the edge off her pain. Still, she knit her broken bones back together, stanched a few open wounds that were soaking blood into her clothes, and smoothed away a number of bad bruises and aches and pains.

 

            Her shoulder was a lost cause though, dislocated and hanging at a nauseatingly low angle as the dull throb of pain made Lena feel sick. Now that her adrenaline was fading, she could feel everything keenly and she knew that unconsciousness would soon swoop in and bear her away. At least she didn’t have to try and stay in the saddle, although Lena probably would have preferred to lay in a ditch on the side of the road and sleep for the next two days instead of being bounced around in the carriage.

 

            The tooth burnt down to ash in her palm and she swiped it on the thigh of her overalls feeling her mother’s eyes crawl over her. Clicking her tongue, Lillian shook her head at Lena’s poor effort to heal herself. 

 

            “I’m tired,” Lena ground out, frustration making her words sharp. “Or have you forgotten I’ve spent the last week trying to stop Lex from slaughtering an entire town?”

 

            “That remains to be proven.”

 

            “I’m sure you’ll have my blood for it.”

 

            “And your brother’s.”

 

            Opening one eye to give her a shrewd look, Lena hummed. “Did you bring him with us?”

 

            “Of course I did,” Lillian scoffed. “And I have his blood as well. The truth will out.”

 

            “And then you won’t treat me with such disdain. Not when you see what your precious-”

 

            Lena cut off with a barely contained groan of pain, the sound scraping her throat at the effort it took not to scream, as Lillian thrust a hand out and then yanked it back, the motion dragging Lena’s limp arm back into her shoulder socket. She looked grey for a moment, breathing shallowly through her nose as she curled inwards, black spots dancing across her field of view. 

 

            Swallowing the taste of bile, she eventually straightened up and scowled at Lillian as she rolled her sore shoulder. “That wasn’t very nice.”

 

            “Then you shouldn’t be surprised.”

 

            After that, her pain somewhat lessened, Lena tried to sleep. She was uncomfortable on the bench, her body still aching and her cuffed hands and the narrow padded bench making it hard for her to twist herself into a comfortable position. Lena didn’t dare put her filthy boots up on the seat and had to settle for leaning against the side of the carriage, sunlight cutting across her face, bouncing with the motion of it and making her neck stiff when she finally gave up a few hours later.

 

            Lillian was quietly reading when Lena woke, stretching and softly cursing as she scowled past the sleepy look on her face. The right side of her face was pink where she’d been leaning and she rubbed at her eyes before splaying her fingers, remembering how dirty she was.

 

            “Will we be stopping?” she asked her mother.

 

            “Eventually. I would imagine so.”

 

            “When?”

 

            “What does it matter to you? You’re a prisoner; you’ll do as you're told.”

 

            Mouth thinning, Lena fixed her with an exasperated look. “I’ve done nothing wrong. It’s unlawful to clap me in chains and haul me back home for no crimes.”

 

            “That remains to be determined.”

 

            A prickle of anger flaring hot, Lena bit back a short sigh. “Am I to starve and sit in my own filth for the next six weeks?”

 

            “No,” Lillian curtly replied, her eyes still glued to the page as she slowly turned it. “It would offend my senses to sit in here with you smelling like a sewer.”

 

            “How about you put me in the cage then?”

 

            “No.”

 

            “Why?”

 

            “You’ll have food when we stop. And clean clothes,” Lillian said with a weary sigh, ignoring Lena’s question. “Now, quiet. I’m trying to read.”

 

            Petulant and brooding, Lena was left to her own thoughts, and as usual, they naturally turned to Kara. She wondered if she was angry that Lena had caused her to black out, if her friends had recounted everything that had happened, if they were now realising they’d won and numbly going through the motions of cleaning up the battle and putting everything to order. Lena wished she was there to command the dead for them, clearing the streets, rebuilding the destroyed homes, laying their loved ones to rest back in the churchyard graves she’d dug them out of. 

 

            Instead, she was caked in her own and her brother’s blood, sitting with her aloof mother and awaiting her fate which would take weeks to arrive. Their journey would be swifter with the undead horses that didn’t need to rest, so long as someone was awake to urge them onwards with magic, and she sat disgruntled and quiet as she tried to pretend she was asleep.

 

            She did sleep though, her exhaustion catching up with her and leaving her to rest, despite how uncomfortable it was. There was little else to do, and Lena had gone so many days without proper rest, on top of all her energy spent controlling the dead, that she slept almost the rest of the day, waking for brief bouts when they hit a rock or a rut before slipping back into unconsciousness. Despite Lillian’s talk of food and clothes, neither were forthcoming until the following dawn when the retinue came to a stop.

 

            “Out,” Lillian ordered her before adding in a withering tone of annoyance, “and don’t try anything foolish; you’re severely outnumbered.”

 

            Lena deigned not to inform her mother that she’d faced worse odds in Midvale. Instead, she stiffly hunched over inside the carriage and lurched out onto an empty road. A wind was blowing and a landscape of sun-bleached trees and open prairie lands teeming with life greeted her. She licked her dried lips and shook out her legs, tipping her head to the sun and inhaling the dust and smell of plants.

 

            “There’s a stream nearby,” Lillian gestured dismissively.

 

            “I know it,” Lena stiffly replied, familiar with her surroundings. 

 

            They were miles east of Midvale, cutting a path through the wide swathe of land between the sloping mountains on either side, before they hit the taller mountains just beyond. It would be the quickest way east, although not the easiest, and Lena was familiar with the dense mountains and endless trees of Colorado, the small plains and creeks and lakes. If she thought she’d have even the slightest chance of escaping, she would have been able to survive off the land long enough to traverse the distance back to Midvale without getting lost, but it was the escaping part that brought her up short.

 

            Under her mother’s watchful eyes, as if she didn’t trust anyone else to deal with her daughter - probably a wise decision on Lillian’s part - Lena wove through the bushes and over rocks before carefully making her way down the sloping banks of the narrow stream. Trees shaded the dark water as it slowly trundled past and she turned, holding her hands aloft.

 

            “I can’t bathe if I’m cuffed,” she reasoned.

 

            As if weighing the benefits of Lena being clean and the cons of allowing her to be uncuffed, Lillian was silent for a moment. She had a ring of keys attached to her belt and she looked sharp and dangerous as she unhooked it, walking over to her daughter and unlocking the heavy manacles. 

 

            “Let me remind you that I have no qualms about shooting you.”

 

            “I would expect nothing less,” Lena softly replied, her lips twisting wryly.

 

            Lillian arched an eyebrow and shoved the bundle of worn clothes into her arms. “Be quick. We aren’t lingering.”

 

            Nodding, Lena set the clothes down on a dry rock and then swiftly peeled off the clothes plastered to her skin. For all their Order were used to the stench of decay and blood and vomit and all manner of unsavoury odours, she knew her mother had only relented to uncuffing her because it was unbearable to be confined in the carriage with the smell of the blood and gore coating Lena.

 

            Now, she waded into the stream, turning rigid against the freezing temperatures of the run-off from the mountains, and quickly submerged herself. It was shallow and Lena squatted as she roughly sluiced water over her arms and face, trying her best to wash away the worst of the grime as she violently shivered. Without the luxury of soap and hot water, she didn’t feel truly clean as she waded back out mere minutes later, drying herself off with her old clothes and dressing in the loose shirt, pants and socks Lillian had provided.

 

            Pulling on her scuffed boots as she sat on the rock, Lena stiffened as Lillian’s hand lightly touched her shoulder. “Sit. I’ll braid your hair.”

 

            “Do you even know how?” Lena snorted.

 

            “Of course I know how.”

 

            “I don’t recall you doing my hair as a child.”

 

            “Why would I? We had servants for that.”

 

            Lena made a low sound of amusement at the back of her throat but was still as she let Lillian tease apart her knotted hair and tightly braid it. She had to resist grumbling and whining whenever Lillian snagged a knot or pulled too hard, out of a desire to not sound like a child. Once her mother finished, Lena looked miles better than the vagrant picked up from the middle of the road in Midvale the day before, better than she’d looked in days.

 

            Still, her mother clapped the manacles back on her and nudged her back towards their convoy, where breakfast was being doled out. The prisoners were given a small amount in the back of the cage and Lena sat on a rotting tree trunk as she ate her own portion with a glowering look on her face, the pork and porridge the usual fare she ate on her own travels.
