It was nothing luxurious but she was hungry and ate it without complaint before chasing it down with the bitter coffee she was handed.

 

            Her day took on a routine of periodic stops and enough sleep to help Lena recover what strength she’d lost. Lillian even went so far as to heal her daughter completely as Lena shifted uncomfortably and tried to mask her winces as the days went on, and they rode in tense silence for the first two weeks. Resigning herself to her imprisonment as she was unwillingly dragged back home, Lena didn’t fight it. It would have been a lost cause anyway.

 

            As the third week passed by, Lillian produced a pack of playing cards and they passed the time playing games, although the tension remained. Lena couldn’t remember the last time she’d spent such a prolonged period of time with her mother. It was dreadful. But not as bad as she’d imagined. Although Lillian was still a little standoffish on account of Lena killing her son. They both knew that his fate would have been death, or worse, anyway, so it was really a mercy that she’d shown her brother, and one Lena secretly thought he’d been undeserving of. She never voiced those thoughts to her mother though, but their conversations were rife with snide comments and stony comments about Lena’s actions. 

 

            It was a long journey, cutting through valleys and across mountain paths, then as the land turned flatter, across endless stretches of fields and ranches and small towns, past mines and lakes and snaking rivers. Lena was bored out of her mind and missed the freedom of riding Hecate wherever she wanted. Most of all she missed Kara. She kept that secret tucked away inside her heart though, loathing the idea that her mother could taint it with her knowledge of something her daughter cherished. Lena liked to say they were estranged; Lillian spun a different tale in New York City, of her willful daughter off practising their noble craft, until the story of her going Rogue had come flooding in from out west. 

 

            Weeks after leaving Midvale, they finally rolled into New York City’s crowded streets, the crooked buildings plunging the narrow streets into shadow, the grey smog of coal and the thickness of the pollution making Lena’s stomach sink with resentment for being brought back there. Children shone shoes and hawked newspapers on street corners, wagons made the churned-up roads impassable and the city was overwhelming. An autumn wind swept in off the harbour with the smell of rotting fish, brine and sewage, and Lena shivered as they pulled outside the overflowing cemetery she’d been trained inside, the cold seeping through the cotton of her shirt.

 

            Still cuffed - her good behaviour over the weeks of travelling hadn’t earned her any lenience - Lena was led along one of the winding paths through tombstones, the grey evening encroaching making the shadows darker and the place seem ominous. It wasn’t anything out of the ordinary for Lena though, the sight of novices in their uniforms striking a pang of nostalgia, while the looming mausoleum leading underground brought only weary annoyance. 

 

            Walking down the wide paved steps leading below ground, Lena didn’t feel any fear as she squared her shoulders and raised her chin in a haughty manner. They all knew her here and she knew they were just in their laws, so she had nothing to fear. Lena wasn’t some warmongering Rogue like Lex had tried to paint her. The only thing she’d done was retaliate against her brother, antagonise him into turning his attention south, where whispers of her in Midvale had reached him thanks to that insufferable English reporter. No one would find her guilty or convict her of any crimes - they would see the truth in her blood.

 

            Still, it felt like every Witch Doctor in the city and surrounding states had convened in the cemetery to watch as Lena was escorted into the main hall in heavy cuffs. Despite her serene disposition, it did make Lena feel a little apprehensive as her mouth went dry, her eyes glancing around the round chamber. Tiers of curved benches ringed the room and there was a wide, shallow bowl set upon a raised stone platform in the middle, where Lena was led over to as Witch Doctors crowded into the stands, overlapping whispers filling the space.

 

            The members of the Council stood at the far end of the room, conversing amongst themselves, and turned their attention to Lillian as she strode in ahead of her daughter. They flocked to her, one of the more powerful and notable members of the Council, and they conferred quietly for a moment while Lena was forced to her knees on the stone platform bearing the shallow bowl. 

 

            The manacles were undone and each wrist was clapped into the ones bolted to the stone platform, leaving Lena with little room to move as she stared into the empty depths of tarnish brass. Her mother started speaking a moment later and she listened to the sound of her steely voice while keeping her head bowed.

 

            “On behalf of the Order, the Council brings forth Lena Luthor on charges of broken oaths. The truth of the matter shall be settled through the power of divination, for the Council to decide whether to rule in favour of guilt and innocence. Does anyone object?”

 

            It was a routine procedure and no one made a sound inside the packed hall, curiosity creating a palpable hum of excitement. With no objection forthcoming, Lillian gestured to a Witch Doctor standing beside the platform as she walked towards her daughter, claiming the task herself. The other Witch Doctor held aloft something wrapped in scratched leather and pulled it back to reveal a long, curved blade.

           

            Taking it from the man, Lillian climbed the few steps onto the platform and touched the top of her daughter’s head, her pale fingers almost gentle for a moment as Lena leaned back against her skirts, her green eyes flickering with doubt as she looked up at her mother. 

 

            And then Lillian placed the curved edge of the blade to Lena’s neck and swiftly cut her throat, letting her choke on her blood as it spilt into the bowl before her.

 

 

            Kara tossed a chair aside and threw her weight against the dresser that had been used to block off the door. It was a solid, heavy thing and she couldn’t move it by herself and found her friends too slow as they aided her in removing the blockade they’d built while she’d been out cold. Stepping back, Kara paced for a moment, hand pressed to her forehead, and then suddenly turned towards the window overlooking the main street.

 

            The window was open from where Alex had been shooting, and Kara could see the Necromancers getting ready to leave, with Lena tucked inside the carriage in chains. She was going to kill her for knocking her out but that required getting her hands on her lover, which was proving harder than anticipated. At the sight of a dozen cream coats on horseback, preparing to leave, Kara grew desperate.

 

            Climbing out of the window, she stood on the shingled roof of the verandah for a moment, catching her balance, before the carriage lurched into motion and desperation caused Kara to pitch off-balance. Sliding down the wooden shingles, she pitched forward once she’d reached the edge and landed heavily on the packed ground. Her ankle gave way beneath her with a shooting pain up her leg, followed by Kara slamming her head against a small rock, splitting the skin above her eyebrow and knocking her out cold again.

 

            Fifteen minutes later, she was scowling and pale as she held a bloody rag to her bloody face and let Eliza tightly bind her broken leg while she scratched Krypto beneath the chin. Tense and restless, Kara kept swallowing the lump in her throat as she itched to jump to her feet and be off.

 

            “Don’t be stupid,” Alex cautioned her. “You’ve got a broken leg , you can’t walk.”

 

            “I’ll be on a horse,” Kara argued.

 

            “The whole time?”

 

            Giving her sister an irritated look, Kara scowled. “No, but I can’t just let them take her, can I?”

 

            “Kara, they’ll shoot you dead, and I don’t imagine they’re sweet on you enough to bring you back.”

 

            “I don’t care. I ain’t letting them take her. She saved us; it’s the least I could do.”

 

            “You can’t go by yourself-”

 

            “She need not go alone.”

 

            The last comment came from someone else - a man, and very English - and the group gathered in the saloon of the hotel looked up to see the beaten Witch Doctor that had briefly held his own in their defence. Jack gave them a weary smile, cradling his ribs and breathing heavily from his walk into town, breaking free of his makeshift prison as the dead holding him captive were reduced to bones as Lex’s control slipped. 

 

            He plucked a tooth from his recovered belt and healed Kara’s ankle with his blood before meeting her eyes. His own were dark and solemn and trustworthy. “I can travel with you.”

 

            “You don’t know where I’m going.”

 

            “They’ll take her back to New York. To stand trial.”

 

            Kara didn’t ask how he knew Lena had been taken. He’d clearly been eavesdropping outside for a while, and now he dropped down onto a chair, looking spent as he ran a hand through her messy hair, smoothing it back into place.

 

            “Trial?” Kara spluttered. “She’s done nothing wrong.”

 

            He shrugged, “it’s the way of our Order.”

 

            Alex snorted, “you ever thought maybe it ain’t right?”

 

            “Be that as it may,” he said with a grim down turning of his mouth before he climbed to his feet and raised his eyebrows in a polite look. “I can escort you, though, if that’s your intention, miss.”

 

            “She ain’t goin’ nowhere with you. We don’t even know you.”

 

            Letting out a quick chuckle and giving them a winning smile, he shrugged again, the sight almost arrogant but coming off as charming on him. “Nor I you, and yet, I got myself captured in defence of your … lovely town.”

 

            His eyes roamed around the saloon, taking in the much-faded grandeur of the weathered town. Its state had only worsened with the battle spilling into its streets but it felt oddly peaceful now. It was a warm day and the wind gently blew through town, the muffled sound of birds cawing and people talking outside.

 

            “Fine, but we need to leave right now,” Kara agreed after a brief hesitation, climbing to her feet and finding her ankle supporting her weight with no problem.

 

            “We’ll do fine by ourselves,” Alex stubbornly insisted.

 

            “We?” Kara echoed, her face clouding. “You can’t leave. You’re the Sheriff.”

 

            “I have a Deputy for a reason.”

 

            “Alex-”

 

            “Where you go, I go.”

 

            “Kelly,” Kara exasperatedly turned her attention to the Mayor.

 

            Holding her hands up defensively, Kelly shrugged and gave her a thin smile. “Don’t look at me. We’ll all sleep better if you go together. Vasquez will manage just fine in her absence, and we’d very much like our Witch Doctor back, don’t you agree?”

 

            Kara had no argument for that and in short order two packs had been assembled, M’gann filling them with rations, J’onn with some moonshine, Kelly pressing coins into their hands while Querl gave them a writ to be cashed at banks along the way. Krypto was restless and wanted to accompany them but by the time she’d kissed her mother goodbye and swung up onto the back of the gentle saddled horse that didn’t belong to her, Kara was itching to be off as swiftly as possible. 

 

            Jack was already in the saddle, in his cream coat and a bowler hat, and Kara had found Lena’s ragged one up in her room and decided to don it as well. She’d recovered Lena’s beloved pistol as well, the grimoire, relieved of most of its pages, and had the medallion she’d been gifted hanging around her neck. Alex gave her a sharp look at the sight of her sister masquerading as a Witch Doctor but kept silent as Jack did the same.

 

            The trio were off at a gallop after that, already more than an hour behind the carriage that had torn out of town with haste. But they couldn’t sustain the gallop for long, or the canter, unless they wanted to run their horses into the ground. Jack could always revive them, of course, but it was cruel, so they resorted to long stretches of trotting and walking and Kara could feel Lena slip further away from her with every mile they slowly traversed.

 

            “We should’ve taken a train,” Kara said as they sat around a fire, bathed in orange light.

 

            They’d made camp in a small cleft in a shallow valley, the sloping mountains and thickets of trees bearing the brunt of the wind as they huddled, tucked behind a finger of rock stretching out into the valley. Kara had unsaddled Hecate and brushed her down when they’d stopped, caring for Lena’s horse with tenderness and attention as she smoothed the velvety soft nose and sparingly shared the withered apple she’d been eating with the horse.

 

            Now, after a dinner of stew, made with whatever had been readily available in their packs and what Jack had ferreted out from the teeming wildlife around them. He’d managed to snap a rabbit’s neck with his power before it had even known it was caught and returned with small purplish potatoes he’d pulled up, along with wild garlic. 

 

            “It’ll take about a week to ride to Promontory before we can catch a train bound for New York,” Jack said, adding more wood to the fire. “And that’s not accounting for Lex Luthor slaughtering half of the northern towns. I’m not sure if he made it as far north as the top of Utah, but considering the railroad … there’s a good chance. Not to mention the horses.”

 

            Alex was leaning back on her elbows, against her pack as she blew smoke rings. “I heard they’re dangerous. You ever ridden on them?”

 

            Jack ducked his head in a nod and then fished a flask out of his pack. It was a mild night, the stars out and the sound of wolves howling in the mountains drifting down to them. The horses were hitched to a low tree branch and they nibbled at the grasses and plants carpeting the valley floor.

 

            “A few times. I prefer horseback or stagecoach. As does most of my Order.”

 

            “There. It’s settled. We go by horse,” Alex said to her sister.

 

            Kara grimaced with frustration, her blue eyes clouded with worry as she gripped the medallion tightly in her hand. “It won’t be fast enough.”

 

            Still, onwards they went, both sisters a little apprehensive around Jack, although Kara warmed to him quicker than Alex did as the days slipped past. They both had to admit they wouldn’t have known the first thing about getting to New York City without him, merely struck out eastwards and figured it out once they’d hit the coast. But Jack had spent years travelling about, enjoying his bout of freedom before he’d inevitably be called home to London to marry, and he was confident as he took the lead.

 

            He knew winding mountain passes that cut through what they would’ve had to otherwise ride around, and where the closest rivers were whenever they needed to refill their canteens and camp for the night. After a couple of weeks, they reached land flatter than Kara had ever seen, no looming mountains nearby and the ones behind them fading to nothing, until they eventually passed further than Alex had ever been before. Through open fields and forests and yet more mountains, across undulating hills and shallow fords as the weather turned cooler and they spent many days riding through the downpours, their clothes plastered to them, they went onwards.

 

            Twice they were brought to a stop, when Alex’s horse had thrown a shoe and was brought to the closest farrier, and again when Kara was struck by a fever and Jack insisted they spend the night at a hotel after healing her. The three of them were worn ragged and needed a night in proper beds, although Kara was loath to delay any longer. She’d had to resign herself to Lena reaching New York ahead of her by days, if not weeks. They’d had undead horses and a host of Necromancers to keep them running. In comparison, the trio had Jack and three very much alive horses they were opposed to abusing.

 

            Autumn was far colder on the east coast Kara discovered as they finally crossed the border into New York to storm clouds and leaves in a riot of fiery colours. The terrain was different to home and she ached for the comfort of her ranch and the warmer climate, thinking anxiously of Lena as they ambled along a hunting path. What if she didn’t want to come back with Kara? What if they’d already killed her and her body had been rotting underground for weeks?

 

            The thoughts soured her mood and she grew even more tense and silent as the miles passed by. Even the eventual arrival at the bustling, awful city of New York didn’t inspire any relief or eagerness in her. The city was cramped and choking with pollution, affronting Kara’s senses as she looked around with wide eyes, aghast at the squalor and noise, the sight of more people than she’d ever seen in her life. 

 

            The trio were brought to a clopping walk through the muddy streets as a dismal rain fell around them, grey puddles and streaks of coal dust leaching the colour out of the surroundings. Jack seemed unbothered by the weather and they didn’t draw nearly half as many looks as Kara had anticipated. She supposed the city was used to the sight of Witch Doctors coming and going from the cemetery, but she did catch sight of a few people crossing themselves.

 

            “What is it you intend to do now?” Jack asked, sidling up alongside Kara and leaning across the gap to make himself heard over the noise.

 

            “Take me to the cemetery,” Kara instructed him, a stubborn set to her jaw.

 

            “They won’t allow you entry.”

 

            Her eyes were bright with determination and Kara smiled, her eyes creasing at the corners and her cheeks dimpling as her appearance gave off something altogether more innocent than her intentions. She wasn’t a violent person by nature, but they’d have to kill her to keep her away from Lena. They might at that.

 

            “I look the part,” Kara said, gesturing to herself in her borrowed Witch Doctor coat.

           

            “You must understand that I can’t-“ Jack started before Kara cut him off with a small laugh.

 

            “I wouldn’t want you to get into trouble because of me. Thank you for guiding me here though. You can’t know how grateful I am.”

 

            Jack touched the brim of his hat and then hesitated. “Might I ask why?”

 

            Giving him a quick grin, Kara shrugged slightly, a faint pink blush in her cheeks. “I love her, don’t I? I don’t think I could say that if I didn’t come after her.”

 

            “Then I wish you luck,” he said, nodding, “and if you have further need of my assistance, I’ll be at my lodgings near Central Park.”

 

            He produced a calling card and handed it over before he tipped his hat and trotted off on his horse. They watched him go, still in the saddle, and then looked at each other.

 

            “You’re a fool, you know,” Alex said.

 

            “Yeah,” Kara sighed. “I’d be a bigger one if I didn’t do it.“

 

            “Yeah,” Alex sighed in response.

 

            “You’ll watch the horses?”

 

            Rolling her eyes, Alex’s mouth thinned and she swung down out of the saddle as Kara similarly dismounted, reaching for the bridle.

 

            “If you die,” Alex started, a panicked look in her brown eyes as rain dripped off the brim of her hat, “I’ll pay them to bring you back so I can kill you again.”

 

            Flashing her an easy smile, which did little to convince Alex that she wasn’t actually terrified, Kara rolled her eyes and spread her arms. Water pinged off Lena’s leather coat and her stomach tied itself into knots as she hugged her sister and tried to emulate her courage.

 

            “I’ll be back shortly.”

 

            “Try and make sure it’s with her. I ain’t ever been somewhere this big; I don’t like it. Too many people around. I’d like to go home sooner rather than later.”

 

            “I don’t like it either,” Kara murmured, even more apprehensive than Alex, who’d seen a great deal more of the states than Kara had. “I’ll be quick.”

 

            They parted ways with solemn nods and Kara hurried through the cemetery in the gloomy weather. It was just past noon yet the day was grey and the sight of crooks gravestones and mausoleums, overgrown paths and an abundance of moss and lichen covering the trunks of twisted trees felt ominous. Kara had never liked death, had never thought it was anything other than what it was, but here it was something else.

 

            Trying to behave as if she belonged, as if she’d walked the path to the biggest mausoleum a hundred times before, been trained in the underbelly of the place, she pushed onwards. It was only the sight of a few children in the early stages of their training as they tended the graves and seemed to appear from nowhere that led Kara in the right direction. Two of them were hurrying up the paved path as they hunched their shoulders to the rain and Kara followed after them.

 

            They led her to the stone steps disappearing downstairs, beneath the black earth and away from the bustling city beyond the confines of the sprawling cemetery. As her boots scuffed the steps on her way down, they glanced back at her and she watched wary fear cross their faces at the sight of her before she smiled and they tentatively returned it.

 

            She didn’t get very far along the wide hallway, stumped at which direction to follow and intent on following it to the end, when a trio stepped out of a doorway and made towards her. Two of them glanced at her as they neared each other, the conversation carried on, and Kara thought she’d perhaps gotten away with her disguise before one of them stopped.

 

            Tall and imposing with a sharpness to her features, Kara realised she knew her. There was a flicker of suspicion on the woman’s eyes too as she narrowed them, stopping as she stepped into Kara’s path, her eyes dropping to the medallion around Kara’s neck.

 

            “You’re no Witch Doctor,” she haughtily confronted her, reaching out to grasp the medallion with an affronted expression on her face. “Where did you get this?”

 

            At her demanding tone, Kara bristled and pulled it from her grasp. “It’s mine,” she defensively replied.

 

            Letting out a sharp laugh, the woman raised a hand, her fingers curled into a limp fist as if she was about to caress Kara’s cheek. She was wearing a ring with a sharp point on it and Kara didn’t realise until her cheek stung as the woman raked it across her skin. A bead of blood welled up and Lillian reached up to wipe it away, and in a gesture that left Kara horrified and reviled, she tasted it and smiled slowly.

 

            “Ah. It is you,” Lillian said with amusement. “You’re a long way from home.”

 

            “Where is she?” Kara softly demanded, shoulders taut and her body bristling with fear and anger.

 

            She was hyper-aware of the other two on her left, watching the exchange as they waited for the confrontation to yield some results. They would have known Kara was helpless against the three of them, even if she’d had powers to begin with.

 

            “Far from your reach,” Lillian replied.

 

            Taking a menacing step forward, Kara swallowed thickly. “If you’ve done anything to her-“

 

            “I’m her mother,” Lillian said, taking Kara by surprise as she receded a step, appraising the woman with renewed interest. “She is mine to do with as I will.”

 

            Kara opened her mouth and Lillian raised a hand, rolling a milk tooth between her fingers, her eyes trained on it as she made an obvious threat. Then her eyes slid to Kara and she smiled faintly before jerking her chin towards her.

 

            “Go. Now.”

 

            Wanting to stay and argue, wanting to search every room in the sprawling underground warren, wanting to slap the woman before her for her actions, Kara felt utterly powerless. She considered resisting anyway but realised she’d most likely end up in a cell or dead just to do away with the inconvenience, and then she’d be no use to anyone.

 

            Reluctantly nodding as she bristled against the order, she made to turn but froze as Lillian continued to speak.

 

            “Remove the coat and the belt. And the medallion. They don’t belong to those outside the Order.”

 

            Quietly scoffing, Kara shed the coat, balling it up and tossing it to her feet. It was riddled with holes and tears, scratched and weathered from years of use and shootouts. She imagined Lena would need a new one anyway so it was an easy thing to give up. She’s brought it as a disguise. Unbuckling the belt was a little harder to swallow, her fingers fumbling with it as she grit her teeth against the guilt of handing Lena’s gun over to her mother.

 

            When she’d dropped that to the ground too, all that remained was the medallion. This was where Kara stubbornly objected, curling her hand around it protectively.

 

            “There’s your coat and your gun and whatever spells she had left in there.”

 

            “The medallion,” Lillian frostily pressed.

 

            It was warm in her palm from where it had lain against her skin and Kara jerked her chin up, swallowing thickly against her fear. “I’m afraid I can’t give you that.”

 

            “It doesn’t belong to you,” Lillian hissed, stepping forward as Kara retreated. “She studied for years for the privilege; you have no claim to her soul.”

 

            Momentarily confused, Kara just gripped it tighter and shook her head. “She gave it to me. I’ll not part with it until I return it to her own hands.”

 

            Sneering, Lillian’s mouth twisted and she flicked her hands dismissively at Kara. Stiffening as she expected an attack, for her heart to burst in her chest or her bones to fracture and force their way through her skin in the horrifying display she’d seen between Lena and Lex. But it was just a plain dismissal.

 

            “Go. Before I change my mind,” Lillian flatly ordered her.

 

            Not needing to be told twice, Kara stalked back the way she’d come from, taut with frustration but considering herself lucky she’d kept her life. It had been risky sneaking into the cemetery to try and track Lena down and she’d anticipated getting caught at some stage - Kara had just hoped it would’ve been after she’d freed the woman who could help them get back out alive.

 

            The rain had gotten heavier by the time she re-emerged, the afternoon sunlight dimmed by black clouds, and she splashed back down the path to Alex. Her sister was smoking as she held the reins of the horses in one hand, restlessly waiting. Her shoulders went slack at the arrival of Kara, although there was a grim set to her mouth at the lack of Lena in tow.

 

            “That was fast.”

 

            “It’s her mother,” Kara murmured.

 

            Blinking, Alex straightened up, dropping her damp cigarette to the ground and grinding it underfoot before replying bc, her words coming out with wisps of smoke.

 

            “Oh. Well … that’s good, isn’t it? At least she won’t hurt her.”

 

            Giving her a despondent look, Kara looked like she was on the verge of tears. “She don’t like her mama.”

 

            “Oh. Still … surely. Right?”

 

            Mouth turning down at the corners, Kara pulled her hat off and ran a hand through her hair. Water soaked into her shirt, making the faded blue seem almost black and she felt defeated and exhausted.

 

            “Let’s find a place to stay and some food before we figure out what’s next, alright?” Alex suggested, raising her eyebrows.

 

            Sighing, Kara reluctantly nodded and hauled herself up onto Hecate, patting the horse’s damp neck. They set off through the streets and into the slums of the city, where their coin would stretch further. Still, they were reluctant to find somewhere too cheap, afraid their horses might vanish under the touch of thieves and they might find their bellies full of holes as they were robbed at knifepoint. 

 

            After asking around a bit, flashing her shiny Sheriff’s badge - which wasn’t entirely useful as they were out of her jurisdiction, but instilled fear all the same - Alex led them to a relatively clean hotel. Their rooms were above a hole-in-the-wall place called Noonan’s, the air thick with tobacco smoke and the sound of an accordion as someone played rather poorly. The horses were stabled out back by a groom kept on hand and the two of them nursed cups of tea and ale and ate their first decent meal in weeks.

 

            “How about we ask Spheer?” Alex suggested as she slipped a bone from her lamb.

 

            “I thought you didn’t trust him.”

 

            “You get the measure of a man when you travel with him. He could’ve slit our throats every night for two months if he’d wanted to.”

 

            “I’m starting to think you ain’t that put out by Witch Doctors as you say,” Kara wryly replied.

 

            Giving her a drill look, Alex sipped her ale. “Well, they ain’t all bad. Same as normal folk, ain’t it?”

 

            “I think that’s what she was trying to show us the whole damn time,” Kara dismally murmured. 

 

            “Well, we’ll believe her when we get her back,” her sister replied, clapping her on the shoulder. “Now where’s that calling card?”

 

            “It’s-“ Kara started, going to pat the pocket of her coat, only to realise she didn’t have it anymore. Groaning, she gave Alex a sheepish look. “Gone.”

 

            Grumbling a bit, Alex finally presented the idea to wait for Lillian to emerge from the depths of the cemetery and then following her home. Once there, Kara would find a way inside and threaten Lena’s location out of her. Alex offered to do the threatening herself but Kara was rather stubborn and insisted on conducting the heroics herself.

 

            They hastily finished their food and had the horses saddled again before settling in for a miserably long evening spent waiting in the rain and cold. They’d bought Kara a scratchy woollen coat from a secondhand store to replace her leather one and as the night wore on, the light waning and the streets emptying somewhat, although they were still thriving with the nighttime activities of the more unsavoury citizens of New York, she grew wetter and shivered on horseback as they waited.

 

            It was a few hours to midnight when a carriage pulled up outside the cemetery gate with those dead horses pulling it, and the sisters retreated a way down the road, watching. They weren’t sure if there were others at the Order with identical stagecoaches but at the sight of a tall figure in a cream coat, Kara decided to take the risk.

 

            As the driver commanded the dead onwards and the carriage started trundling down the street, the two women followed at a distance. They kept pace as they wife through the throngs of foot traffic clogging the muddy streets, rain lashing them as they trampled through wide puddles and peered through the dim light of gas lamps and carried lanterns trying to keep up. They almost lost the stagecoach twice but they managed to tail it all the way back to a rather quiet street.

 

            They were unfamiliar with New York City but they could tell that Fifth Avenue was incredibly wealthy, with mansions bigger than any buildings they’d ever seen before. Kara didn’t know the street had been styled Millionaire’s Row, but she hedged a bet and guessed that Lena was a lot richer than she’d made out she was. Suddenly, taking in the size of the house and guessing at the number of people inside, it didn’t seem like such a good idea to storm it and hold Lena’s mother hostage. But Lena had been reckless on a number of occasions for Kara; she owed it to her to do the same just this once.

 

            They stopped in the shadows across the street from the house the carriage stopped outside of, pale stone seeming to glow in the moonlight, making the mansion ghostly and foreboding. Dismounting as her stomach knotted, Kara stood beside Alex and looked up at her. Unholstering one of her guns, Alex handed it over to her and looked a little pale in the darkness.

 

            “Be careful.”

 

            “I will.”

 

            Crossing the street as soon as the carriage pulled off to be housed around back, Kara glanced around as she neared the gated front of the house. There were lights on inside and the gate had been locked behind Lillian, which gave Kara no other option but to awkwardly clamber over it, wincing in anticipation of the spikes but managing to make it safely over the top. She landed with a quiet thud, masked by the sound of rain, and crept up to the front door before using the bronze knocker.

 

            A few moments later, a sharply dressed butler with milky white eyes opened the door and Kara hesitated. She knew what a wight was and that they were rather autonomous, but it still surprised her to find out that the man had been kept as a servant. It made sense she supposed - he would never leave, couldn’t tell a soul about any of the ongoings in the house and didn’t need to be paid.

 

            Still, it was eerie as she stepped inside, dripping water onto the marble floor of the foyer, which led into an expansive entrance hall through wide doors standing open to the opulence beyond. With Alex’s gun in hand, Kara wiped the rain on her wet sleeve and sniffed as she walked inside, steeling herself now. The hardest part was over.

 

            “Who is it, Corben?” Lillian’s voice drawled through a doorway leading off to a sitting room.

 

            It was drawing closer and Kara adjusted her grip on the gun, swallowing thickly as she pointed the gun at the butler. She had to remind herself that he was already dead, and she wouldn’t technically be killing him if she shot him. Lillian emerged a moment later and paused before a sharp smile crossed her face.

 

            “You again.”

 

            “Where is she? Is she here?” Kara asked, her words short and blunt.

 

            “Naturally,” Lillian said, gesturing off-handedly as she arched an eyebrow. “It is her home.”

 

            “Where?”

 

            “You presume much, entering my home and demanding answers from me.”

 

            Without pause, Kara shot the butler, the sound too loud in the foyer as it seemed to echo slightly. The wight crumpled to the ground in his pressed tails and Lillian’s mouth thinned.

 

            “Really, must you? Good help is so hard to find. I had to kill him myself.”

 

            “The next one will be in your head if you don’t answer me,” Kara warned her.

 

            Lillian just cocked her head to the side and smiled, seeing through Kara’s threat and into the doubts beyond. It didn’t matter anyway - Lillian wasn’t above the violating invasion of controlling Kara’s body, using it against her as she forced her hand to turn, pressing the barrel to her own temple.

 

            “Or perhaps it will be yours.”

 

            Mouth dry and heart fluttering in her throat, Kara licked her dry lips. “Please.”

 

            “I was generous before because I recognised you from my daughter’s blood and saw that she foolishly had grown fond of you, but I’m not a merciful person by nature. We’re healers, yes, but I’m not soft. My service is an honourable profession but there’s a darkness to our art if required. I’ll give you one more chance out of pity - leave. She doesn’t belong with people like you. Lena is a good girl, soft and with a deep-rooted insecurity, which I imagine is how she fell vulnerable to your … certain charms. But she is better bred than you are and I won’t see my only living child squander her potential for some dusty, forgotten mining town on its way to destitution. Good evening, Miss Danvers. Do not tempt me further.”

 

            The strange hold on Kara’s body suddenly went slack and she found herself in control again, jerking her arm away from her head as she gasped, shaking for breath. The gun clattered to the floor and Kara stared at Lillian with wide eyes. There was a brief moment where she wasn’t sure what she was going to do before they were interrupted.

 

            “Mother? I heard shots.”

 

            Kara’s stomach dropped at the sound of Lena’s voice and she whirled towards the stairs. Feeling weak with relief, Kara’s shoulders slumped as she roughly exhaled, her eyes stinging as she smiled at Lena. Only this was a far different Lena to the one she was used to, the worn shirts and pants and scuffed boots replaced with a high-necked dress with a slightly fuller skirt than she’d seen her in before. It was lacy and finely embroidered, a green so dark it almost seemed black in the dim lighting of the foyer. Her hair was carefully curled and pinned and Lena had lost the lean edge of poor food and insufficient sleep from her long travels. The entire effect was rather stunning for a moment as they stared at each other.

 

            “Kara?” Lena eventually said, her voice soft and bewildered as it drifted down to her.

 

            “Lena,” Kara wearily replied, the sound of her name tasting sweet as her throat constricted around it.

 

            Lena’s footsteps were quick as she descended the rest of the grand staircase, hurrying across the foyer to grab her face in her hands, green eyes roaming over her with a panicked look in her eyes. Then she turned and put herself in front of Kara, as if she could hide her from Lillian, her hand tightly gripping one of Kara’s wrists.

 

            “Hurt her and I’ll kill you,” Lena haughtily told her mother, not having to question the context of the moment.

 

            “Always so melodramatic,” Lillian scoffed. “See the girl out and return to your room.”

 

            Kara grabbed Lena’s arm, standing close behind her as her heart pounded in her chest with the thrill of seeing her again after so many weeks. It hardly seemed real.

 

            “Pack your things,” Kara told her, “we’re leaving.”

 

            There was a tense moment of silence before Lena slowly spoke. “Will you stand in my way?” she haltingly asked her mother, doubt colouring her voice.

 

            “You’re better than this. Your brother led you astray and then you went further down this foolish path of adventure when you should have been here, benefiting from your family name and money.”

 

            “I don’t want to be here,” Lena sharply objected. “Now, I asked you a question; will you stand in my way? We’ve had our differences but I mean you no ill will unless you force my hand. Let me leave freely and I’ll think kindly of you for it.”

 

            “Think kindly of me?” Lillian laughed. “Oh, you delusional little girl. Do you think I care about how you think of me? I’m your mother; your opinion of me is irrelevant.”

 

            “And yours of me. They’ve judged me innocent and yet you insist on keeping me trapped here out of some revenge for taking your son from you. I did him a service. You know his fate would’ve been worse in their hands. Now, I ask you to repay my kindness and leave me be.”

 

            Stiff and silent for a moment, Lillian jutted her chin forward and stared down at her daughter with contempt. “Walk out of that door and you remain dead to me from that moment onwards.”

 

            Reaching down to pick up Alex’s gun and pressing it into Kara’s hand, a spark in her eyes as she smiled with wry amusement, Lena closed her fingers over it and then glanced down at the floor behind her. She didn’t look at Lillian, just swallowed thickly and spoke to the marble instead.

 

            “Then I hope you take comfort in the fact that you never cared for me enough to grieve your loss.”

17. Chapter 17

            The wide front doors burst open with a loud bang, two women hurrying out into the night, hand-in-hand as they ran down the slippery steps and made for the gate. Rain soaked them almost immediately and Kara struggled with the locked gate, her heart pounding in her chest as adrenaline coursed through her, before they were out on the pristine street beyond the gilded mansion and running across the road to the shadowed figure on horseback.

 

            Kara pulled Lena to a stop at Hecate’s side and grabbed her face in shaking hands, fiercely kissing her as an elated laugh built in her chest. Pulling back, Kara looked at the blurred shadows of Lena’s face and touched her fingertips to her face as if assuring herself that Lena was real and let out a shuddering laugh of surprise as the knot of tension in her chest went slack.

 

            “Howdy, Doc,” she murmured, her voice rough and weak with relief.

 

            Darting in to kiss her again, chaste and quick, Lena quickly hauled herself up onto the back of her horse, patting Hecate’s neck as she smiled. “Hello, old girl.”

 

            Glancing up, she peered through the dark at Alex and a flicker of surprise crossed her face. “Sheriff. Surprised to see you all the way out here.”

 

            “Well, I weren’t likely to let her go runnin’ off all by herself, now, was I?” she wryly replied. “Good to see you, Doc. You’re lookin’ … grand.”

 

            Lena rolled her eyes slightly, irritation flashing up her spine at the voluminous, tailored skirts and delicate embroidery, her singular dress costing a small fortune. It felt silly and frivolous as Kara pulled herself up behind her, and Lena cleared her throat, shifting uncomfortably as she drew her shoulders back.

 

            “Where are we off to? So I can get out of these damned clothes.”

 

            She could feel Kara’s laughter behind her and Lena felt her body relax, glancing a parting look at the colossal house and praying she’d never see it again. Alex led them back to the cheap accommodation they’d paid for and despite the fact that she was swapping grandeur and unlimited wealth for a lumpy narrow mattress and bed bugs, Lena couldn’t have been happier to sink down onto the edge of the bed and unbutton the top few pearls at her throat, kicking off her small heeled boots and falling backwards onto the bed.

 

            “Well, that’s certainly improved my evening,” she said to the ceiling, heavy footsteps thudding overhead as tiny dust particles rained down on her. “I must admit, I’m very shocked to see you here.”

 

            “Did you think I’d let them take you without a fight?” Kara asked, sinking down beside her.

 

            The difference was amusing, highlighting all the ways they should never have even met, let alone fallen in love. One so prim and polished and oozing wealth, the other travel-worn and wiry in darned clothes and accumulated filth. Lena sat up and smiled at Kara, taking her hand.

 

            “Yes, I had hoped you’d avoid doing anything so reckless and stupid as confronting my mother.”

 

            “I didn’t know that was your ma,” Kara said, wrinkling her nose, “she’s a real frightening lady. But I wouldn’t let that stop me. I’m just surprised I ain’t dead yet.”

 

            “She’s known to play the long game.”

 

            “Do you reckon we’ve been followed?” Alex asked, jerking aside the curtain covering the small window and squinting through the night beyond.

 

            “We have a tenuous relationship; I don’t imagine she’ll come after me unless there’s something to concern herself with. Say, a rumour that I’d gone rogue and slaughtered a town of innocents. That would draw her out from her den. Otherwise, I’m as inconsequential to her as a fly to a horse.”

 

            Alex hummed dubiously and moved away from the window, taking in the small quarters and then at the two women. “Well, it’ll be a tight squeeze alright. I say we head off at first light; ain’t no cause to stay longer than we need to. Big cities are rife with all sorts of trouble.”

 

            They all readily agreed but Lena insisted on going to the cemetery in the morning before leaving, needing the familiar weight of her gun, the comfort of the coat she’d worn for half of her life, the smell of blood and paper and leather at her waist. She had no intention of coming back to New York again, if luck was on her side, but she wouldn’t give up her trade. There would be enough work out west to keep her occupied, and enough horses at the ranch to fill the spaces between the urgent requests for healing and resurrections.

 

            Lena felt safe in her assumption that perhaps Midvale would allow her to stay awhile, maybe even stay forever, and she couldn’t stop staring at Kara, a fierce look of protectiveness and love in her eyes as she watched her shed her wet coat, hanging her hat on the bedpost, smoothing her forehead. She looked exhausted and limp, her smile when she met Lena’s eyes small and relieved.

 

            There was a palpable hum of tension, of excitement, filling the room but they didn’t talk much. With only two narrow beds, Kara and Lena lay pressed up against each other and Alex snuffed the gas lamp out on the small table set between the beds, plunging them into darkness as they listened to the muffled noise of the street outside. 

 

            The three of them slept deeply and the sky was a shade lighter than Alex would’ve liked when Lena roused them. Pulling on coats and boots and grabbing packs, they were out of their room and saddling their horses in the stables before heading back to the cemetery. It was a place that never ceased to function, always operating and occupied by a stream of Witch Doctors and those who’d yet to earn their medallions coming and going at all hours. The sprawling graveyard was still relatively quiet in the grey of dawn as Lena went alone up the path alone.

 

            Stepping underground, she walked the stone hallways, making a stop at varying rooms that she’d come in and out of over the years, but not for some time now. In the weapons space, she requested another Colt pistol and some bullets and was handed a holstered one with a pristine bone handle, a belt of bone bullets to match. In another room, she acquired a new pack and all the trimmings of tools and preserved foods for lengthy travels, and in another, changed out of her dress and into the new denim pants and a maroon linen shirt, pulling on a brand new leather duster, just a touch too long at the sleeves, and packed the spares and her dress away. 

 

            She got a new grimoire, a new bowie knife, a new hat and boots and a chest filled with herbs and tinctures and Piedfort coins. It was everything she’d lost along the way and she ran her hands over her newly restored items with satisfaction. Outfitted in the hardy travelling clothes and spurred boots that would lead her out west, Lena lastly got a new writ for a monthly stipend to be cashed at banks along the way. That was safely tucked into an internal pocket of her new coat and she shouldered her pack and carried the small chest under her arms before making her way back outside.

 

            There was another piece of paper in hand, and as Lena reached Alex and Kara where they anxiously waited beyond the threshold of the cemetery, a thin veil of mist making the early morning eerier as Kara fretted over her return, she handed it over to Kara and set about fastening her belongings to Hecate’s saddle.

 

            “What’s this?”

 

            “A horse. We’ll need another one to travel with. Hecate won’t be able to carry both of us for long.”

 

            “I don’t have enough money-”

 

            Giving her a small smile, Lena raised her eyebrows slightly. “You can thank the good Order for taking care of that. Come on; our stables are housed near the docks.”

 

            Lena let Kara pick out her new horse, standing back as she watched her discuss the stud of this horse, and how many hands another was, the rancher eyeing them critically before she settled on a buckskin mare with a black mane and socks. Kara was brimming with excitement over the acquisition of a new horse and Lena’s mouth twitched with suppressed amusement as she stood beside the restless rancher and watched the horse get saddled and kitted out with new tack.

 

            When they were finally ready to go, Lena mounted Hecate and held the horse in check as she waited for Kara. The three of them set off at a brisk walk, weaving through the packed city with Lena taking the lead. She led them through a warren of streets before the city fell away to nature, a bitter grey day awaiting them as. It was a few miles before Alex pulled up beside her, face furrowed with confusion.

 

            “We’re heading south.”

 

            “Well spotted.”

            

            “You plannin’ on taking us the scenic route back home or what?”

 

            “Lot of mountains between here and Midvale,” Lena replied.

 

            Alex snorted, rolling her eyes. “You reckon? We sure just crossed every single one of ‘em to get here.”

 

            “How was the snowfall in the passes?”

 

            “Light.”

 

            “Speaking from experience,” Lena wearily sighed, “it won’t be light for much longer. We’re too far north to cut a quick path south-westerly. If we pass through the Blue Ridge mountains and then cut west once we reach Tennessee, it’ll be quicker.”

 

            Alex made a disgruntled sound but didn’t argue; Lena undoubtedly knew the area better than she did but Lena couldn’t blame her for being annoyed at being parted from Kelly for longer. It would result in a quicker trip, but the detour didn’t feel that way, especially after weeks of non-stop travel already.

 

            Still, Lena was insistent on them making south for the first portion and then cutting west through the Smoky Mountains as the Appalachians tapered off in Tennessee. Then they’d strike a southerly route through the flat prairies of Arkansas before heading in a more northerly direction afterwards. Still, it would take a little over two months to get home if all things went well, and Kara and Alex had just spent the same amount on the way to New York.

 

            They rode forty miles the first day before stopping at Saugerties, following the banks of the Hudson River away from the city. The trees had turned as autumn swept in and it was a town where the ice industry thrived, although they made camp beyond the limits of civilisation, unsaddling the horses and freeing the small clearing of rocks. 

 

            Alex cleared her throat and wiped her hands on her pants, raising her eyebrows slightly. “I’ll get firewood. Might take a while. A long while, so, uh, don’t worry if I’m not back.”

 

            “Do you need help?” Kara asked.

 

            “No. Uh, no. You stay here.”

 

            They both watched Alex stalk off into the woods with her guns holstered at her waist, and Lena glanced at Kara with wry amusement on her lips.

 

            “Well …”

 

            “She’s in an awful hurry to collect firewood,” Kara said, rubbing the back of her neck.

 

            “It’s an important task.”

 

            “Mhm.”

 

            They stared at each other for a moment before Lena took a few nonchalant steps forward, a coy look on her face. Reaching out, she pressed her hand to Kara’s chest, just over her collarbone, feeling her pulse as her whole body seemed hypersensitive, tuned in to every fibre of Kara’s body. Every breath, every beat of her heart and flow of blood, the marrow in her bones and the movements of tendons and muscles as she stood still before Lena. It could be disorienting at times, to be so aware of other people, but it felt exhilarating then.

 

            “I still feel like you’re not here,” Lena murmured, her face creasing with confusion. “I didn’t think- you already have your life, so-“

 

            “You thought I’d forget you?” Kara softly asked, a slow look of dismay softening her face.

 

            Slowly shaking her head, Lena’s mouth turned down slightly at the corners. “No, not forget. But it is a long way to ride for a Witch Doctor.”

 

            “It ain’t so long for someone you love,” Kara haltingly replied.

 

            “No, I don’t suppose it is.”

 

            She glanced up, away from the hollow at the base of Kara’s throat, and met her eyes. Shadowed apprehension clouded Lena’s green eyes and she licked her lips, parting them to speak before Kara spoke first.

 

            “Are you alright?” she quietly asked, reaching up to cup Lena’s cheek. “I mean, you look it, but … what did they do to you? Are you-“

 

            Lena reached up and touched her throat, the ghost of the memory of a knife cutting her throat lingering as she dwelled on it. Clearing her throat, she smiled crookedly.

 

            “Nothing that hasn’t been done to me before,” she assured her. “They held a trial and deemed me innocent. My mother annoyingly confined me to the house for a probation period. I’ve healed numerous broken bones and ailments since I’ve been back but I haven’t been allowed a foot behind the front door. It’s a good thing I enjoy my own company or it would’ve been maddening.”

 

            “Did she treat you well?”

 

            “Just fine. She’s not a brutal person unless necessary; her preference is the mental side of things. She’s a cold woman, and I’d think she didn’t have a heart if I hadn’t seen her love my brother so dearly, but it’s negligence, not beatings that have caused me pain at her hands.”

 

            “I won’t let her cause you any kind of pain now,” Kara promised.

 

            A grin cut across Lena’s face as she arched an eyebrow. “Is that so?”

 

            “Aye,” Kara smiled in return, “I’ll take you far away from her.”

 

            “Kiss me then,” Lena murmured, stepping in closer.

 

            Letting out a quiet laugh, Kara obliged, and then Kara relieved her of her brand new clothes and weapons and boots and Alex was a long time collecting the firewood. They were both dressed again and Lena was pulling on her boots, sitting on the gnarled root of a tree, as she watched Kara try and wipe the dirt off the damp wool of her coat.

            

            “Kara?”

 

            She hummed in response and Lena swallowed thickly, her throat tight and a twisting feeling in her stomach. Climbing to her feet, she walked over to her and opened her mouth, no sound coming out, and then cleared her throat.

 

            “I … told you I could say it before. That I’d say it after. Well, it’s belated and I hope you’ll forgive me for it, but … I love you.”

 

            Kara blinked in surprise, her lips barely moving as she replied. “Oh.”

 

            “Oh,” Lena laughed, her eyes creasing at the corners as she smiled. “Yes, I rather think that’s an appropriate response for words that have never passed my lips before. I don’t think they ever will again unless I say them to you.”

 

            Kara grabbed the front of Lena’s coat and dragged her forward, pressing a bruising kiss to her lips that left them tingling once she pulled back. Her blues eyes creased with laughter and then the sound built in her chest and fell from her lips, filling the small clearing as blue jays burst from the canopy of trees, startled by the noise.

 

            “Yes, I think I can forgive you, Doc,” Kara mused, reaching for the end of Lena’s braid and giving it an affectionate tug.

 

            “Good.”

 

            “Hey. Can I get a hand?” Alex’s voice drifted towards them.

 

            Kara gave her a rueful smile and softly sighed as Lena snorted. “She’s not very subtle.”

 

            “No, she’s not,” Kara agreed before walking off into the trees.

 

            They huddled around the fire later that night, sharing whisky and the meal that Lena cooked for them when it became apparent that both sisters were equally quite bad at cooking on the road. All of them were tired and a little sore but Lena was glad to be back in the saddle, glad to trade in meals prepared by one of Lillian’s few human staff for the salted pork and beans that cowboys favoured.

 

            Sleeping earlier and rising earlier, they were off again, on a slogging trip that felt monotonous to her but was exhilarating for Kara, who’d never travelled more than a few towns away from Midvale. Even Alex was unfamiliar with the east coast, and didn’t find the same charm in it that her sister did as Lena led them through valleys and rolling fields of wildflowers in late bloom.

 

            They’d been at it for more than two weeks by the time they reached the Smoky Mountains, turning their backs on the Appalachian’s, which had proved painfully long as they traversed the narrow game trails with trepidation. Despite Lena’s ability to mend broken bones and revive animals, they were all wary of the horses spooking and breaking a leg, causing unwarranted pain. Even worse if one of them threw a shoe without a farrier in nearby sight.

 

            Two weeks later they found themselves in Memphis and took a day to rest at a hotel while Lena paid for the horses to get re-shod and their stores replenished. It was a lazy day of indulging themselves in their vices, gambling and drinking through the afternoon and eating better than they had in months - for two of them, anyway - and they slept soundly in a proper bed, rising late and nursing hangovers as they irritably set off.

 

            It was encouraging that they were halfway home though, and following the winding Mississippi River south before cutting through the flatter lands of southern Arkansas was an easier trek than the trip so far. Without the undulating mountains that had seemed endless as bitter winds and freezing downpours assaulted them, they were in warmer country now, even as the end of the year rapidly approached. Winter was well and truly underway and while the weather was still cold, it didn’t have the same edge as the cold fronts of the Atlantic Ocean.

 

            Passing through Oklahoma and the northern part of Texas, red rock and shrubbery guiding them through plateaus and ravines, they came upon Colorado and watched the terrain become familiar. There was an urgency to them now, home within site, and they were making fifty miles a day, filthy and half-starved and saddle-sore. 

 

            San Luis gave way to Alamosa as they traversed the mountain basin, shallow creeks and rivers and wetlands filling the arid valley. Fields of long yellowed grass disappeared beneath their horses' hooves and they encountered hundreds of birds making their home in the habitat as the surrounding mountains fed into the basin. On their last night passing through the wet meadows and dry uplands, Alex shot a mule deer to see them the rest of the way home and they left the scraps for the coyotes skulking about before enjoying fresh meat after days of fish and waterfowl.

 

            It was another three days of rigorous riding before they finally reached Midvale. It almost didn’t seem real, and Kara let out a ragged sound of relief as they slowed on the road into town, splashing through puddles and thick mud from recent storms.

 

            “Oh, home,” Kara softly exclaimed as they passed by the beaten track to her ranch.

 

            The thought of that ranch with its little kitchen and comfortable bed, Kara’s boots beneath the bed and her guns lined up inside the door, and the little pantry with jars of preserved fruits and dried herbs sounded like heaven. Heaven would have to wait a while longer though as they continued on to town, the three of them sitting straighter than they had in weeks, their shoulders no longer bowed with exhaustion as renewed happiness filled them.

 

            Trotting into town with wary looks on their faces as they eyed the modified walls, now expanded beyond the outer buildings initially not enclosed within, they took in the sooty buildings repaired with new planks of wood, stark against the old worn planks. There were strangers in the streets, drinking and smoking and carting goods, and children kicked a ball around. The smell of fresh bread drifted from the bakery and women whacked sticks against rugs to shake out the dust, soldiers loitered in their uniforms and the butcher plucked pheasants outside the open store, sitting on a barrel as feathers littered the wooden boardwalk linking the row of stores on the main street.

 

            They slowed outside the hotel and before Alex could even swing down from the saddle, her wife burst out of the Mayor’s office and sped across the street. Lena dismounted at a slower pace as the two women kissed and held each other tightly, quietly speaking, and after Kelly had given Kara a fierce hug her eyes alighted on Lena.

 

            She smiled brightly and surprised Lena with a brief hug. “It’s good to have you back, Doc.”

 

            Nodding, Lena gave her a small smile and glanced around. “You’ve tidied up a lot since I’ve been gone.”

 

            “Mm, four months is a long time to change things. The mine’s even been open and running for two weeks now. About damn time.”

 

            Eyebrows rising in surprise, Lena hummed appreciatively, “well, I guess that all worked out in the end then.”

 

            “Any trouble?” Alex asked.

 

            Waving a hand dismissively, Kelly rolled her eyes. “Nothing we couldn’t handle while you were gone. A few less people spending the night in jail, I warrant, but not everyone can be so strict as you. Vasquez will be happy to take a step back.”

 

            “Give me a week to drink and sleep and gamble away my savings ‘fore you get me right back into work. It’s been one hell of a trek.”

 

            “No trouble on the road?”

 

            “A few dead,” Kara shrugged, removing her pack from her horse’s back. “Nothing Lena couldn’t sort out in a few moments. Otherwise, it’s been real quiet. I guess when you ain’t got a maniac rousing them, it’s not so bad.”

 

            “The bodies-” Lena started with a wince.

 

            Kelly’s mouth thinned, “we had to burn most of them. Disease started spreading pretty fast and graves couldn’t be dug quick enough. We gave them all markers though. Buried the ashes near the church and had them consecrated. God rest their souls.”

 

            Making a vague sound of contempt at the thought of a non-existent God, Lena smoothed Hecate’s nose. “I’ll settle the horses.”

 

            Leaving Kara and Alex to reunite with their friends and family, Lena made her way around to the back of the hotel and let herself into the stable. She didn’t think J’onn would have an issue with it after letting her stay for a few months, minding her own affairs, and she was brushing down the coat of Alex’s horse when a shadow blocked the doorway.

 

            “You’re back then.”

 

            She turned to find M’gann twisting a dish towel between her hands, a smile on her face as she raised her eyebrows slightly. “Yes, ma’am. I don’t think I really had a say in the matter; they showed up out of the blue and here I am.”

 

            “I’m familiar with the stubbornness of those two,” M’gann laughed. “Come and have a proper meal when you’re done here. I made pie.”

 

            The thought of M’gann’s food made Lena’s hollow stomach ache with hunger. She thanked her and quietly finished tending to the horses, all of their coats brushed free of dirt and dust and an abundance of hair, their manes and tails free from knots and enough oats and water to give them a good meal as they rested after their long trip. Lena hoped it would be the last long trip for a while, that Hecate could go out to pasture and enjoy her freedom before the next disaster sought her out.

 

            Drawing a bucket of cold water from the well, Lena washed her hands and face and wearily delayed the bath she desperately wished for before making her way through the kitchen of the hotel. It smelled of baking apples and roasting chicken, loaves of fresh bread on the counters and the warm cooking fire taking away the chill of outside. Slipping through to the saloon, Lena angled toward the bar and then froze at the sight of a prim and polished young woman sitting at a table, in deep conversation with Kelly and Alex.

 

            Lena felt a stab of anger and quickly unholstered her pistol as she changed the trajectory of her step. “You,” she barked. 

 

            She drew the attention of everyone in the saloon, her cheeks reddening as she knocked chairs aside in the long strides she took to cross the open space. J’onn continued to placidly pour a drink as he watched the bristling Witch Doctor bear down on the businesswoman who’d abandoned Midvale and swooped back in to reclaim her stake in the mine once the danger had passed. Lena wasn’t sure what had transpired while she was gone, what may have been put to bed and what deals shook on, but she’d made a threat and she intended to keep it.

 

            “I told you you were never to step foot back in this town again,” Lena seethed, pointing the gun at Andrea’s forehead as Russell jumped to his feet.

 

            “I don’t think that’s quite what you said,” Andrea replied in a clipped tone, an air of nonchalance about her, although her blue eyes flickered with sudden fear.

 

            “I told you I’d never let you see a single nugget out of that mine if you ran away. You have no business being here. Go.”

 

            Andrea smiled tightly, “I think you’ll find it’s exactly my business. I own the mine, and now it’s reopened - no thanks to you and your little stunt blowing it up. You should be thanking me for making this town profitable again, especially after you up and left before the clean-up. If you’re expecting payment for your help, I would think again.”

            

            “I want you gone.”

 

            “Oh, I’ll be off soon. Once I’m reassured that the mine is in good hands. I’ll be sending my own men to manage it so I can return to civilisation. I admit, the charm of this place is lost on me. I would have stayed in New York if I was in your shoes.”

            

            “I would have stayed far away from here if I was in your shoes.”

 

            Letting out a small laugh, Andrea raised her eyebrows. “While I own the mine, I’m free to come and go as I please. Unless your mama gave you enough money to buy me out, I don’t imagine your opinion holds any weight here.”

 

            Leaning in, Lena pressed the gun to Andrea’s forehead, and only Alex clearing her throat as she kicked her shoes up onto the table gave Lena pause from making a very serious threat to blow the woman’s pretty brains all over the saloon. It didn’t seem fair to Lena that she could have no claim to this town and swoop in to steal the spoils of the mine that Midvale had suffered so much over. Andrea hadn’t lifted a finger to reopen it, beyond signing her name to the deed after negotiating a deal with Kelly over the ownership of it.

 

            Jerking back and slowly holstering her gun, Lena cleared her throat and stared daggers at the heiress. She imagined a world where she’d never become a Witch Doctor, inheriting her father’s fortune and parading around in fine dresses as she undermined poor folk and became wealthier with little work. It wasn’t a life Lena ever wanted for herself.

 

            “Feet down,” J’onn murmured to Alex as he arrived behind Lena, gently touching her shoulder, stilling her and cooling some of her anger.

 

            He set down a round of drinks, nudging one towards Lena, but she spurned it as she turned on her heel and marched towards the batwing doors of the saloon. Bursting out into daylight, she heard Kara calling after her but thundered down the steps with her mouth a flat line. 

 

            Hecate was already stabled outside but she caught sight of a soldier leading her horse by the reins and made a bee-line for the young woman, whose eyes widened as Lena snapped her fingers at her, scowling. 

 

            “Here,” she said, reaching for the reins and nudging the woman aside. “I’ll be back shortly.”

 

            The soldier didn’t protest, her mouth open as she let Lena borrow her horse, and Lena left her in the dust as she rode out of town. The soldier had been taller than her, and her horse appropriately sized for the difference, but Lena was an accomplished rider and made do as she set off at a gallop down the beaten road out of town. 

 

            Already filthy, she was covered in wet mud as the horse thundered through puddles until they slowed to a trot and then a walk, the miles disappearing and Kara’s ranch soon in sight. It had been so long since she’d been inside that house that as she came to a stop in the yard, the chickens all gone, the pen for the horses empty and no winding thread of smoke from the chimney, she felt her heart ache. It had felt like home for a time and she was eager for it to return to that. 

 

            Dismounting, she let the horse wander freely as she walked towards the long, low ranch, bypassing the front porch and rounding the building. Tossing her hat down into the dirt, Lena sank down to a crouch and then onto her knees, peering beneath the thick beams raising the ranch up off the ground at this end. It only offered a scant two feet between the beams and the dirt but it was enough room to wriggle her way beneath, just as she’d done last time.

 

            Lena crawled beneath the raised portion of the ranch on her elbows, dragging herself forward until she reached the sack of stolen money. Grabbing it, she scuttled backwards, inhaling dust and catching her back and shoulders on the sturdy beams. She was filthy when she re-emerged, coughing and spitting out dirt on her knees before she put her hat back down and climbed to her feet, hauling the heavy sack with her.

 

            Whistling to the horse and murmuring softly, she climbed into the saddle and cradled the sack in her lap and set off at a steady pace. The day was wearing on and she was exhausted and irritated, her muscles aching at being back on horseback again, and her expression was taut and pointedly pissed off as she rode back into Midvale a while later, the soldier anxiously lurking about and looking relieved when Lena dismounted beside her and tossed her the reins, staggering slightly with the weight of the sack.

 

            Kara was sitting on the worn steps of the hotel and leapt to her feet, meeting Lena halfway across the road, a pinched look of concern on her face. “You alright?” she asked.

 

            Lena nodded and glanced sideways as Kara fell into step beside her. “Fine.”

 

            “You took off real fast. What you got there?”

 

            “I need you to pretend you don’t hear whatever you’re about to hear, okay? Don’t fret; it’ll just be parlour tricks. But don’t come in.”

 

            Stepping back into the saloon, Lena made a bee-line for Andrea, grabbing a fistful of her sleeve and dragging her to her feet. Andrea made a sound of protest and knocked over her chair, and when Russell leapt to his feet to help, the back of his knee was met by Lena’s boot and his leg buckled beneath him. Hauling the woman across the space to the private dining room they’d all shared dinner in upon arriving in town, when Andrea was grateful for Lena on account of an almost forgotten service rendered, and she let her go.

 

            Staggering backwards, Andrea spluttered as Lena locked the door and then turned on her. Her green eyes were cutting as they dismissively ran over the woman, her lip curling slightly with contempt. Raising the sack, Lena tossed it into the space between them and jerked her chin in a haughty manner.

 

            “Here. Payment for your mine.”

 

            “Excuse me?”

 

            “You asked if I had enough money to buy you out; that’s more than you bought it for. It’s a generous offer. Take it and pack your bags.”

 

            Letting out a confused laugh, Andrea cocked her head to the side. “What makes you think I’m willing to sell?”

 

            There was a knock on the door and Kara’s sheepish voice, muffled by the thick wood, but Lena blanked them dead as she pulled her gun free and pointed it at Andrea. “I told you before, I’m not in the business of making threats. Take the money.”

 

            She averted the barrel of the gun a few inches to the right of Andrea’s face and fired it. The loud bang filled the room and the bullet rocketed towards the faded wallpaper, taking a chip out of the wall and filling the air with the scent of gunpowder. Lena shrugged slightly and gave Andrea a sharp smile as the sound of shouts and thuds against the door followed the gunshot.

 

            “The next one will be a lot closer to home. And I won’t be rendering any services to you.”

 

            Andrea scoffed and Lena called on the aforementioned parlour tricks, the skin of her face tightening, giving her a hollowed, skeletal look, her bones painfully elongating and the room seeming to dim as she filled it with an ominous presence. She rolled a tooth between her thumb and forefinger and encouraged the small beads of blood building in her eyes and nose to spill forth in a frightening torrent before she reached out and then pulled her hand back. 

 

            Stumbling forward, her face a shocking shade of white, Andrea stared at her with wide blue eyes. Lena was almost unrecognisable, her teeth stained red as she grinned, rolling the tooth around in an idle manner, as if it was nothing, as if it wasn’t a threat. Her cheek dimpled slightly and she arched an eyebrow.

 

            “You’ve grown complacent, Miss Rojas. You’ve mistaken my aversion to violence as a surety that I won’t hurt you. You’re wrong. I’ve been more horrible than you can ever imagine. I’ve pulled people apart, limb from limb, burst their eyes in their heads, stopped their hearts, and let the flesh wither away on their bones. I’ll ask you nicely, just once more, to take the money and leave town. And then I won’t ask again.”

 

            Swallowing drily, her throat bobbing, Andrea stooped down and lifted the sack of stolen money. Even then, her stare was defiant, but Lena had spooked her too much for Andrea to protest. Holstering her gun, Lena gestured to the door and then rubbed the shallow, stinging cuts on her fingertips as Andrea made to step past her. 

 

            Reaching out, Lena grabbed her by the shoulder and arched an eyebrow. “The deed?”

 

            Quietly fuming, Andrea fished it out of a pocket and tossed the papers at Lena before scoffing and walking towards the door. She jerked it open and stepped outside while Lena lingered a moment, wiping at her mouth as blood ran over her lips.

 

            “What the-” Kara started before falling silent as Lena turned around, her face covered in bright, wet blood, although the skeletal tautness of it had returned back to its usual fullness.

 

            “Here,” Lena said, her eyes sliding past to Kelly, who was behind Alex in the doorway. “The deed to the mine.”

 

            “You can’t just take it from her,” Alex sighed.

 

            “I didn’t. I bought it,” Lena smiled. “With my giant sack of money she just walked out with. Overpaid, if we’re honest. So, I own it and I’m choosing to give it to the town. Free of charge, of course.”

 

            Mouths opened and closed but no one spoke for a moment. Eyes narrowing slightly, Alex made a vague sound of exasperation at the back of her throat and pinched the bridge of her nose as she spoke first.

 

            “So, you just happened to have a sack of money lying around?”

            

            “Yes.”

 

            “Right. It wouldn’t happen to be the money stolen from a train car by your brother, would it?”

 

            Rubbing the back of her neck, Lena hummed dubiously, mirth giving her eyes a dangerous gleam. “I don’t believe so, no.” 

 

            “Doc-”

 

            “Sheriff,” Lena lightly cut her off, walking forward and clapping Alex on the shoulder, “here’s the deed. Ask me no questions and I’ll tell you no lies. We’ll be better for it, believe me.”

 

            Scoffing, Alex hesitated and then took the deed from Lena, passing it back to Kelly and then giving her a stern look. Shaking her head, she let out a withering sigh and crossed her arms over her chest. “If you’re stayin’, I’ll have no trouble from you, you hear? I ain’t opposed to locking you up again, Doc.”

 

            “I must say I’m very surprised that you’re so accepting of me staying,” Lena said with smug amusement.

 

            “Don’t push your luck,” the Sheriff replied before stepping out of the dining room.

 

            Lena touched Kara’s arm and murmured her excuses to disappear out back and splash more cold water from the well over her face, trying to clean away the blood, leaving her cheeks tinged faintly pink before she stepped back inside. Her beer was still on the table and she took a drink and dug into the food brought out for her, feeling content to know that she wouldn’t have to go anywhere for a while.

 

            They stayed in town that night, at Eliza’s house, drinking late into the night in the kitchen as Krypto put his head in Lena’s lap and Alex refilled her moonshine, their pockets almost empty from a night of gambling. It felt good to be unburdened for the first time in a while, and when they finally went to bed, Lena slept soundly and rose late to the sound of rain.

 

            After breakfast, they went to fetch their horses from the stables at J’onn’s and led them out to the rutted road, sharing a relieved look of happiness. “Let’s go home,” Kara said, climbing into the saddle.

 

            It was a strange adjustment at first. Lena hadn’t lived on the ranch in any sort of capacity for a long time, and now she woke up every morning to the clucking of new chickens pecking at the grains embedded in the damp yard, and helped split the firewood - although she preferred to watch Kara do that - and swept the kitchen, cooked dinner and broke in the horses that had been sent out to pasture while Lex was approaching and been rounded back up by Kelly’s brother and the rest of his posse when they’d come back through, belated word of their impending doom drawing them home. 

 

            She woke up in Kara’s bed and fell asleep in Kara’s bed, ate her meals with her or with her friends and family, worked beside her all day and played cards and drank with her at night. That first week packed full of getting the ranch back into working order was filled with Kara, as much as it was filled with work, and Lena marvelled at how ordinarily comfortable it felt. Kara never explicitly asked her to stay, but between one week and the next, it stopped being her ranch and became theirs.
